Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE are looking to Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Africa is proving strategically vital for Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE
The European official smiled intently and asked a rather surprising question: "Have you been thinking about Djibouti?"
It was 2017 and there was a certain frisson of alarm going around the world about China and its ambitions for global power.
There was certainly alarm in Australia at a regional level: the South China Sea; China's massive 'Belt and Road' Investment spending initiative across the Pacific and the wider region.
And there was alarm across Europe too, where the Poles found themselves at the junction point for a Chinese-funded railway across Central Asia; where the Germans pointed out that Berlin is closer to Beijing than Sydney; and where a newly elected French president, Emmanuel Macron, was attempting to lift and expand French ambitions in foreign policy.
All reasons why all roads led to Djibouti. Or, more correctly, why all undersea cables led to the small kingdom on the north-east coast of the Horn of Africa.
Between 10 and 12 international cables land in Djibouti, making it a critical digital hub connecting Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
From about 2013 onwards, Chinese state-owned enterprises began making huge investments in local ports and infrastructure in the tiny Republic. By 2017 it had opened a significant military base there — following the French (the former colonial power) and then, post 9/11, the Americans.
It's not just the submarine cables that make Djibouti such a crucial location. It sits on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow stretch of water linking the Suez Canal, Red Sea and Indian Ocean — which daily threatens to come more into play as the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz continues.
The Iran-backed Houthis, who live on the other side of the strait in Yemen, announced on July 20 that they were imposing a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, and there is anxiety that they might try to impose a total blockade on Bab el-Mandeb.
Which is why the rapidly changing geopolitics of the region have to be seen in a wider context than just the conflict between the US and Israel and Iran.
A new maritime alliance
Another party that had spoken recently of building a military facility in Djibouti is Saudi Arabia. Given it has been getting around the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz by shipping oil to its western coastline on the Red Sea, it has a particular current interest in that shipping route staying open.
But rather than proceed with the military base, Saudi has now pivoted to establishing a 13-country maritime alliance to safeguard security in the Red Sea which includes Pakistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Comoros, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Somalia and Yemen.
Turkiye this week confirmed it was also joining the alliance — a move which follows the announcement of the collective security obligations agreed to earlier this month in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi, Pakistan and Turkiye.
While early analysis of the Mecca deal focused very much on what it meant for conflict with Iran, the collective actions of this group in keeping shipping moving in and out of the Red Sea will be the first real test of the arrangement.
But the testing of the new alliances in the Red Sea also shifts the focus of all these countries' interests — and those of others in the region — to Africa more broadly.
We don't hear much about Africa in Australia, unless its humanitarian crisis or a civil war.
But even in states which are seemingly failures, there has been the most extraordinary surge of investment and commitment by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkiye. It is no longer just a battleground for influence between China and Russia.
A new 'Scramble for Africa'
There is a new Scramble for Africa of sorts going on: not like the period of invasion and colonisation of its earlier namesake in the lead up to World War I but a tussle for footprints in infrastructure which is at least in part driven by estimates that Africa could be home to around 15 per cent of the world's rare earths.
What makes this particularly fascinating is that African nations are getting better at extracting outcomes from all this investment — for example, in the form of higher revenues, or commitments to manufacturing.
Global Policy Institute analyst Bob Savic notes that "nations like the Democratic Republic of the Congo which controls more than 70 per cent of global cobalt production, have instituted 'super-profit' taxes, while Zambia has repeatedly raised its mining levies".
"Zimbabwe has rapidly followed suit, banning exports of raw lithium — a mineral critical for electric vehicle (EV) batteries — in a bid to end the export of wealth in unprocessed form," he says.
"Across the continent more broadly, governments have increasingly embraced resource-nationalist measures."
Saudi Arabia has pledged over $41 billion in investments in industrial zones, development finance and export credits with African nations.
While it is heavily focused on the Red Sea and Horn of Africa, it has also been buying arable land for food production across East and West Africa as well as contracts for copper, cobalt and lithium.
Turkiye, meanwhile has also dramatically expanded its footprint across Africa, both through a massively expanded diplomatic footprint, new air routes, an eight fold increase in trade, (particularly driven by defence exports) and in infrastructure investments. It has also intervened in the past six years in conflicts in Libya; in confronting piracy off the coast of Somalia and to secure mining infrastructure in Niger.
But both these countries' investments, and interests, are dwarfed by the effort put into Africa by the United Arab Emirates.
Loading
UAE's massive African investment
The Financial Times reported last week that by since 2017, the UAE has announced "investments worth upwards of $US168bn [$237bn]" in Africa.
"The UAE's projection of power spans the continent, ranging from ports to green energy projects to industrial-scale farms," the FT wrote.
The massive state-owned logistical company DP World now operates or is developing ports, inland terminals and free zones in 13 African countries.
The FT says the UAE "has leased millions of hectares of agricultural land to bolster food security".
"It has acquired mining rights from DR Congo to Guinea to secure critical minerals for the energy transition and for its burgeoning defence sector. "
However, it notes "that engagement also comes at a price".
"The UAE is creating a complex system of commercial, industrial and military entanglements that sometimes reinforce but also undermine the sovereignty of fragile states — most notably in war-torn Sudan," the paper reported.
While Saudi Arabia is enmeshed in the conflict with the Houthis in its southern neighbour Yemen, the UAE's presence in the horrific war in Sudan is particularly troublesome.
The Emiratis categorically deny all claims of providing military, financial, or operational support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan — one of the two militia groups that have been fighting a civil war for control of Sudan.
But it is regularly accused of doing so, backed by analysis from intelligence agencies and human rights groups, and the RSF is also accused of committing documented war crimes on a vast scale.
The expansion of strategic ambitions by Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and the UAE into Africa, with the added factor of competition for rare earths, gives us another example of just how quickly global forces are shifting.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

====================================================================================================

What dozens of empty chairs revealed about Australia's racism inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
Empty chairs spoke loudest, months into racism inquiry testimony
A family who are alive only because a bomb that landed at their feet didn't explode.
An Olympian forced out of the sport that changed her life after being belittled and bullied.
A mother questioning whether sending her children to school is doing them more harm than good.
An elder who is too scared to gather with community in public after another attempt on their lives.
This is just some of the harrowing testimony given at the inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people.
Day after day, witnesses relived some of the darkest moments of their lives. Some spoke of violence. Others of fear, humiliation, and grief. Many did so publicly, knowing the personal cost, like former Olympic boxer Marissa Williamson-Pohlman.
"Institutions celebrate Blak excellence when it is convenient, but abandon us when it matters most," Williamson-Pohlman told the inquiry.
"I wonder where my energy would go … if not so much time was spent with me fighting the very system that was created to 'support' me and make my dreams come true."
Her story was one of many detailing personal and systemic harm through racism, but many of those invited to listen, explain, or respond never appeared.
The inquiry drew heavy hitters, including a former federal minister, lawyers, professors, land councils, and policy advocates, but in many places the absences were just as notable as those who attended.
Dozens of politicians, government officials, and national powerbrokers were asked to attend each hearing.
Most didn't show up.
Inquiries are not just for fact-finding
"It's disappointing. I think the public expectation would be if you are a big organisation, if you are a government service, that you front up to inquiries like this and you are accountable," Senator Jana Stewart told me in between sessions in Melbourne.
"I think the least they could do is show up."
As the senator put it, attendance matters because parliamentary inquiries are not merely fact-finding exercises. They are one of the few opportunities for people with little institutional power to speak directly to those who hold it.
The hearings make for hard listening, with First Nations people speaking plainly about the racism, violence, and abuse they suffer on a daily basis.
Now that the hearings have wrapped up, the weight of expectation is palpable, but the reality of repeated disappointments looms large, as Arrernte woman and chief executive of the peak body for Aboriginal and Islander childcare Catherine Liddle put it.
"I'm here because the story of racism is one of harm. It's a story of hate, it's a story of unfathomable damage — and it's a story that we can change," Liddle told the inquiry.
"Racism is pervasive and it always will be until we front up to reality."
Hanging over the inquiry is a thorny question: how can this process make change, when so many change makers didn't turn up?
A tale of two inquiries
Running in parallel to the national parliamentary inquiry has been the royal commission into antisemitism, stood up in the wake of the Bondi terror attack.
Like the royal commission, the First Nations racism inquiry came on the heels of an alleged terror attack.
A fragment bomb, filled with ball bearings and screws, was lobbed into a crowd of Indigenous people on January 26th.
It is not hard to imagine what would have happened had it exploded as intended, something Noongar and Yamatji woman Renae Isaacs-Guthridge has thought about often.
"We should be dead because it landed right in front of us," Isaacs-Guthridge told the hearing in Perth.
The trauma of a near death experience, was compounded by what she described as antipathy from leaders, police, and the media.
"In the days and weeks that followed, as we found out it was a confirmed terrorist attack on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and our allies … there was a distinct pattern of people who said absolutely nothing," Isaacs-Guthridge said.
"I believe because we were an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crowd, there is an underlying hate against us and so we're not taken as seriously."
Those sentiments have been echoed across the country as the inquiry travelled, with little acknowledgement outside the hearings themselves.
"We are First Peoples, where is the love and respect for us?" Aunty Muriel Bamblett asked in Melbourne.
Comparisons with the reach and scale of the antisemitism royal commission were unavoidable, despite warnings that measuring the pain of one community against another does little to address the root cause of racism.
"Why is antisemitism put on a pedestal compared to racial discrimination?" Biboolmirn Yorga woman Corina Abraham asked the inquiry in Perth.
"What about what First Nations people of our country go through? Why are we still down below?"
Failed referendum raises new problems
The silence that surrounds the Indigenous experience of racism and hatred from the broader community was noted by many, including inquiry chair Jana Stewart.
"We've certainly heard through lots of the evidence… the experiences of First Nations people aren't elevated or aren't talked about with the same level of importance as other parts of our community," Stewart told me.
"You can see that playing out probably in the experience of this inquiry as well."
But there are those who see the simultaneous inquiries as a built-in accountability system, like former federal minister Ken Wyatt.
"I suspect out of [the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion] will come a number of recommendations to do with changing attitudes and racist behaviour towards the Jewish community of Australia," he told me after he gave evidence in Perth.
"If we're prepared to do that, then we need to put just as much effort and energy into addressing racism that is faced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in this country. They are the First Peoples of the nation."
The existence of two separate inquiries into hatred directed at minority communities has prompted broader questions about the state of social cohesion in Australia, and what has led the nation to this point.
Some have pointed to the example set by politicians, with many years of culture wars and populist politics souring national discourse.
The referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament was described by many as "lifting the lid" on racism directed at First Nations people, as Apunipima Cape York Health Council Chief Executive Deborah Malthouse told the inquiry in Cairns.
"The outcome of the Voice to Parliament appears to have given mainstream Australians permission to be overtly racist," Malthouse said.
"Those who would otherwise stay hidden now have the courage to share their racist views openly and widely under the belief that their actions are unlikely to be challenged by wider society."
Loading
Great expectations
A Wemba Wemba and Mutthi Mutthi woman, senator Stewart is acutely aware of where the inquiry she is leading may go.
"I do not want to see another report gather dust on a shelf," Stewart told me during one of the hearings in Darwin.
"I think that it absolutely should be acted on with a sense of urgency that people have asked us to in this process."
Many previous inquiries, including a national report on racist violence, the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody, and the Bringing Them Home report, all laid out plans to make Australia a better, safer, more reconciled place for First Nations people.
But after three decades, most of the recommendations put forward have been ignored, or in some cases explicitly acted against.
Outcomes are also on the minds of those who gave evidence, like Minang-Goreng Noongar elder Dr Jim Morrison.
"This committees recommendations risk becoming another report that acknowledges harm without addressing it," Morrison said.
"We urge the committee to ensure its recommendations translate into funded, practical action, direct investment in community-controlled truth-telling and healing infrastructures, not another report that sits alongside the many that have come before it."
Last week, in one of the final sessions, Yorta Yorta elder Monica Morgan gave detailed evidence on her landmark case that proved she had been racially vilified — the first Indigenous person to win such a case in Victoria.
She then had a question for the committee.
"What is going to happen as a result of your inquiry? Will there be change?" Morgan asked.
"We hope so, absolutely," Stewart replied.
"We hope that recommendations and evidence given to this process and through this committee is honoured with action."
The survivors who gave evidence have now gone home, but their stories sit in the parliamentary records, proof that we cannot say we didn't know.
The question is whether those empty chairs will remain a symbol of indifference, or whether those who left them vacant will act on the inquiry's final report.

According to the source, the attack was launched in response to what it described as a Saudi military aircraft violating Yemen’s sovereignty by entering the northeastern airspace of Saada province.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities or Saudi Aramco on the Houthi claim.
The claim came more than a week after another attack targeting Najran. On Aug. 6, the Saudi-led Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen said 11 civilians, including seven Saudi nationals, were injured in an attack on the city.
Tensions in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden have intensified since early July after the Houthis expanded their attacks to include vessels linked to Saudi Arabia. In response, Riyadh has stepped up airstrikes on Houthi positions in Yemen’s western Hodeidah province, saying the sites were being used to threaten maritime navigation.
Saudi Arabia recently announced the formation of a multinational maritime defense coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The coalition includes the United States, Yemen, Kuwait, Oman, Jordan, Sudan, Morocco, the Maldives, Bangladesh and New Zealand.
Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognized government through the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy, while regional and Western countries accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.

Ukraine has been targeting Russia's energy sites with drones and missiles for months, hoping to hit a vital source of revenue for the Russian army.
Russia has shut down one major refinery at Orsk, around 1,300 kilometres from the front line, for six months after it was attacked this week.
"The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations," the government said in a social media post.
Oil companies are "taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions," according to the statement.
It said a government meeting had been held on the shortages and the Deputy Prime Minister responsible for energy, Alexander Novak, has ordered that fuel prices be monitored.
Companies and car drivers have suffered repeat shortages in recent months because of the conflict.
Nearly every Russian region has at some point had to limit fuel sales or impose other kinds of rationing, such as banning the filling of jerry cans.
The Krasnodar region on the Black Sea, known for its tourist beaches, has been one of the worst hit.
"The situation regarding petrol supplies at service stations has become complicated," regional governor Venyamin Kondratyev said.
Oil companies "have again started imposing restrictions on the amount of fuel supplied and reduced service station opening hours," he added.
"This is causing concern among the region's residents and visitors," the governor added, stating that he had asked the authorities to send more fuel.
The governor of the Orenburg region, where the Orsk refinery is located, said on Thursday it had been shut down and repairs would take months.
Rare admission
Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged for the first time in June that his country was facing a “certain deficit” of fuel.
Speaking at a meeting with officials that focused on the fuel situation, Putin admitted that the country was “going through a difficult period,” but insisted that Moscow would “honour all its social obligations.”
Shortly after, he told state TV that the country's arms industries will quickly ramp up production of air defence systems to fend off Ukrainian attacks.
Claiming the issues that arise are not critical, Putin also said that Russia will import more fuel and speed up repair works at oil facilities to end the “temporary deficit.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has referred to strikes on Russian energy sites deep inside Russia as “long-range sanctions.”

Pull up to the window, please, for a glimpse of an American icon: The drive-thru
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

Pull up to the window, please, for a glimpse of an American icon: The drive-thru
WASHINGTON (AP) — Full disclosure: this should really be two tales. How better to pay tribute to the natural and perhaps inevitable combination of two distinctly American icons: fast food and cars?
Those two massive sociological forces had already joined up, Voltron-style, early in the 20th century with the development of the drive-in restaurant – that classic scene evocative of “Happy Days” where customers sat in their cars while servers (ideally on skates) brought out food that was consumed on site from window trays.
But the real innovation dates to the late 1940s and is the brainchild of either (depending on which source you trust) an In-N-Out Burger in California in 1948 or Red’s Giant Hamburg in Springfield, Missouri in 1947. (In comparison, the first reported drive-thru in Europe didn’t open until 1985 in Dublin.)
By the mid 1960s, this had mushroomed into a robust American market, spawning imitators and innovators. Jack in the Box pioneered the drive-thru exclusive restaurant with no indoor seats and no parking — and a talking mechanical clown to take your order. In Western states, residents of a certain age will recall the Wienershnitzel chain with its distinctive A-frame structures specially built with a tunnel down the middle for cars.
The innovation sparked unexpected knock-on developments. Restaurant menus shifted heavily toward sandwiches, fries, chicken strips and other portables that could be consumed on the go. The cars themselves adjusted over the years to accommodate larger and larger drink holders. What sociological (and nutritional) impact this has all had on the actual consumers would be the subject of a much longer essay.
The innovation hasn’t stopped. Modern drive-thrus have evolved into tightly coordinated multi-lane affairs. At Chick-fil-As around the country, actual humans with electronic tablets now stand – breathing in exhaust fumes all day – to ensure a seamless ordering process with no mechanical speaker garbles.
The drive-thru, with its distinctly American creative spelling, has become woven into the fabric of the culture. It has been enshrined in the Smithsonian Museum of American History and has played a memorable role in recent and successful Presidential campaigns.
As one historian put it, somewhat pointedly: “The drive-in was less a pure novelty than an expression of great American passions that go hand in hand: speed, efficiency and, sometimes, laziness.”
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
18:53:02 UTC
03:53:02 KST

With US-Iran talks stalled, diplomatic efforts expand to unlikely European players
WASHINGTON (AP) — Faced with an increasingly bellicose Iran as talks to end the war have stalled, the Trump administration appears to be reaching out to a broader swath of countries that might be able to help pressure Tehran or ease its hardline position where traditional mediators have not succeeded so far.
While discussions between Iran and Oman, as well as between Iran and Pakistan, Turkey and Qatar, persist at an uneven and unpredictable pace, the U.S. administration quietly has expanded its outreach to include perhaps unlikely interlocutors in Europe.
Just this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in person in Washington with the foreign minister of Austria on Tuesday and held a call with the foreign minister of Greece on Wednesday.
Those interactions were not notable beyond the normal course of relations between the U.S. and two close European allies. The official State Department readouts of the discussions were bland and vague and did not mention Iran by name as a topic of conversation.
But it then emerged that both foreign ministers — almost immediately after their talks with Rubio — spoke Thursday with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The apparent new tack to break the negotiation logjam comes as the U.S. and Iran are both pushing for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial oil shipping corridor. President Donald Trump faces little wiggle room in his next steps as the economic fallout from the war and dwindling stockpiles of key weapons pose political problems for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm congressional elections.
A desperate push is on to break the diplomatic logjam between the US and Iran
The entry by Austria and Greece is likely less of a formal mediation attempt, analysts say, and more reflective of a desperate push to halt the conflict because of the impact it has on an increasing number of countries, beyond those in the Middle East.
“Everyone is just urging both sides to stop this reckless game of chicken,” said Ali Vaez, Iran project director at the International Crisis Group.
It also shows how much Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has forced countries, which otherwise were neutral bystanders to the larger conflict, to exercise any diplomatic sway they may have on their Iranian and American counterparts to kick-start a lasting resolution.
Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, warned that any efforts by Greece, Austria or any other non-mediating country could prove to be futile.
“While the calls to both sides may entail encouraging both Iran and the U.S. back to the negotiating table, such efforts fall short of mediation, which is a very complex endeavor and requires trust to be built by the mediator with both sides,” Yacoubian said.
She added that it’s not something that any country can “just jump into.”
Rubio discussed Iran with his Austrian and Greek counterparts
The State Department said Friday that it could not comment on the timing of calls by other countries’ foreign ministers and maintained that Rubio had made no requests of either to get in touch with Iran or pass messages to Araghchi.
One European diplomat, who was briefed on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive diplomatic conversations, said the timing of the calls was not an accident.
The State Department did allow, however, that Iran had been a topic of conversation in Rubio’s discussions, which occurred as Trump is facing serious political headwinds over a war for which he has offered shifting objectives.
No longer purely about making Iran incapable of producing a nuclear weapon, the immediate goal has become reopening the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil usually passes through and which was open before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.
“That’s goal number one: keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country,” Vice President JD Vance said in an interview Thursday on Fox News Channel. But he did not say anything about the strait being open and toll-free for transiting ships, as he had in the past.
The second goal, Vance said, is to ensure that Iran will never get a nuclear weapon.
The two European countries have key connections to the war’s fallout
Austria and Greece may not be obvious choices to assist on the Iran portfolio, but Vienna is home to the International Atomic Energy Agency, which will play a key role in any resolution to the Iran’s nuclear program, and hosted the final negotiations that resulted in the 2015 Iran nuclear deal. Greece is a major maritime nation in the Mediterranean and has significant shipping interests in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
In statements from the Austrian, Greek and Iranian foreign ministries, it was clear that Iran had been a top topic in all of the conversations this week.
The Greek foreign ministry said Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis had been briefed by Araghchi on “regional developments, and in particular on the ongoing talks regarding the Strait of Hormuz.” It said Gerapetritis “underlined the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security.”
The Austrian foreign ministry offered Austria’s services as a venue for further potential talks with Iran and said Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger had stressed to Araghchi “the urgency of restoring stability in the region through serious diplomatic efforts.”
“There can be no military solution,” it said. “A diplomatic solution remains possible. Our priority is to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.”
Iran’s foreign ministry, expectedly, took a different tack in explaining the calls.
It said Friday that in Araghchi’s calls with his European counterparts they discussed “mechanisms for the future management of the Strait of Hormuz,” which he said had been disrupted by the “unlawful aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”
In both calls, he accused the U.S. of violating the interim deal signed by both sides in June to end the immediate hostilities and begin broader talks to end the war.
___
Amiri reported from New York. Associated Press writers Derek Gatopolous in Athens and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland, contributed to this report.

During the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercises at the “Selija” training ground in Latvia, counter-drone systems, including interceptor drones, were tested.
A video showing the interception of a target drone was published by the Latvian Ministry of Defense.
Approximately 650 personnel from Latvia, NATO member states, and partner nations, including Ukraine, Australia, and Japan, participated in the exercises.
In addition, representatives of the technology industry from several European Union countries joined the maneuvers. Armed forces specialists tested their developments and projects under real-world conditions.
“Drone technology and countermeasures are evolving very rapidly. Just as important as the technology itself is the ability of different systems to work together effectively,” the ministry stated.
During the exercises, radars, sensors, cameras, electronic warfare systems, and other solutions designed to detect, track, and neutralize drones were tested.
In addition, the exercises tested a format unique to NATO that involves the private sector not only as an equipment supplier but also as a direct provider of necessary services and capabilities.
Under this concept, once a target is detected, military personnel can delegate the task of engaging it to industry representatives. To do so, companies will use their own equipment and unmanned systems, as well as deploy their own pilots and engineers.
In late July, Ukraine and Latvia signed a series of memoranda of understanding that expand cooperation in the development of unmanned systems.
The goal of this cooperation is to attract investment in UAV production, transfer Ukrainian technologies, and establish modern dual-use infrastructure in Latvia for testing these systems.
The memorandums formalized cooperation in this area between the Ministry of Defense, the Ministry of Economy, the Latvian Investment and Development Agency, Baltic Forces Ltd., Ukrainian partners, as well as Riga Technical University and the Latvian Association of Military Technologies, Drones, and Robotics.
And in late June, it was reported that Latvia, together with Ukraine, plans to establish a joint drone production facility in the border region of Latgale.

India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack
SRINAGAR: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned at an event in Islamabad on Friday that Pakistan would take any step to protect its water rights under the Indus Waters Treaty, saying “every single drop” of Pakistan’s water is a “red line” and “India must come to the right path” or it would “be given a direct response”. His comments drew a reaction from Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah who said the treaty has been kept in abeyance and should remain so.“Yes, our blood. We have been saying this only, that our blood has been sucked. Thankfully Shehbaz Sharif came to his senses. This (IWT) has sucked the blood out of us. These are our rivers. We have the first right on them,” Omar told reporters here. “For the sake of saying, Pakistanis say that they are great sympathisers of Kashmiris. But when it comes to water, their sympathy disappears. Where was his sympathy when our permission to use our rivers was taken away from us,” the CM said.“Out of the six rivers, three which belonged to Punjab were kept by India and our three rivers were handed over to Pakistan. From then till today we are suffering the consequences of this Indus Waters Treaty,” Omar said, adding that under the treaty J&K could neither extract drinking water from the Chenab nor use the Jhelum for irrigation or building a barrage at Tulbul. “Our blood has been sucked and now the IWT has been cancelled.
This should remain cancelled so that we can use this water properly,” Omar added.The IWT was signed between India and Pakistan in 1960. Under the treaty, India received full rights to use the waters of the three eastern rivers, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan received rights over the three western rivers, Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.
India placed the treaty in abeyance last year following the Pahalgam terror attack. In May last year, after the treaty was placed in abeyance, Omar called for restarting the Tulbul Navigation Project on Wular Lake in north Kashmir. The project is located on Wular Lake in the Sopore area of Baramulla district. Pakistan has opposed construction of a 439-foot-long, 40-foot-wide barrage, also known as the Wular barrage or Tulbul Navigation Project, with a navigation lock on the lake.The Union govt began work on the project in 1984 to regulate water levels and facilitate navigation. However, work was halted a year later after Pakistan objected. Pakistan raised the issue with the Indus Waters Commission in 1986 and work was stopped in 1987.The governing National Conference in J&K has opposed the IWT all along, calling it detrimental to the interests of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.

According to the Third Army Corps, Konovalets' urn was brought to the cathedral in an original Austin armored vehicle dating back to the Ukrainian Revolution, which was restored by servicemen of the corps' repair and restoration battalion.
A torch-lit honor guard of soldiers from the Third Army Corps and the Yevhen Konovalets Military School welcomed Konovalets outside the cathedral.
An artillery carriage was attached to the Austin armored vehicle, which, in Ukrainian and European military traditions, is a sign of the highest honor for a serviceman. It is an original 1917 artillery piece that was in service with the Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic, specifically with the Sich Riflemen Division commanded by Colonel Konovalets.
During the ceremony, servicemen paid tribute to Colonel Konovalets. Beams of light were projected into the sky.
On August 13, 2026, the ashes of Colonel Yevhen Konovalets were brought to Ukraine, where they were received with full state and military honors.
A monument from Konovalets' grave was also brought from Rotterdam to the Lviv region. It will be preserved at the colonel's museum-estate in Zashkiv.

Meltdowns and meager meals: How bad is the situation aboard US aircraft carrier attacking Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
18:44:23 UTC
03:44:23 KST

Meltdowns and meager meals: How bad is the situation aboard US aircraft carrier attacking Iran?
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been grappling with dismal conditions for months during the US-Israeli war on Iran, amid mounting reports of severe exhaustion, supply shortages, and mental-health problems among crew members. The problems have sparked an uproar among crew members’ families and prompted demands for answers from US lawmakers.
The vessel, a 5,000-person nuclear-powered Nimitz-class aircraft carrier capable of carrying up to 90 aircraft and conducting more than 100 combat sorties a day at peak capacity, left San Diego in late November. It has now been deployed for more than 260 days, including more than 200 consecutive days at sea – an extraordinary stretch by Navy standards.
On top of that, the flattop has spent much of that time in a combat environment, with Iran claiming to have targeted it on numerous occasions. Even as US officials insist the carrier remains operational, the hardships of a prolonged campaign appear to be taking their toll.
Here is what we know about the issues facing the aircraft carrier and its crew.
What are conditions like aboard the Abraham Lincoln?
The complaints from crew members and their families go well beyond the usual discomforts of a long deployment.
They include shortages of toothpaste, deodorant, and soap, problems with hot and potable water, broken toilets, unreliable laundry facilities, disruptions to food supplies, and mail delays so severe that some care packages reportedly disappeared into the system for months. Other reports describe mold, failing plumbing, and holes worn through parts of the flight deck from extensive use without adequate repairs.
Democratic Congressman Mike Levin claimed that the food situation is so bad that crew members’ meals “came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas.” The meager meals were first reported by USA Today as early as mid-April, although the Pentagon denied that there were food shortages at the time.
The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for more than 250 days, pushing its crew to the limit. Sailors report exhaustion, deteriorating living conditions, shortages of basic supplies and serious food problems: small portions, poor-quality meals and periods of depleted stocks. The… https://t.co/iWYaeKchzUpic.twitter.com/C4cheR4N2M
— Tom Antonov (@Tom_Antonov) August 13, 2026
According to Maritime Executive, the supply problems are partly due to logistics, as the main base of the 5th Fleet is located in Bahrain, deep inside the Persian Gulf, meaning many shipments must pass through the Strait of Hormuz and risk Iranian strikes.
Is the crew burning out?
There are strong indications that it is. One of the most striking episodes confirmed by CENTCOM occurred on August 3, when a sailor went overboard from the Abraham Lincoln and was recovered roughly an hour later.
🚨🇮🇷🇺🇸 Text messages from a sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln reveal no milk in three months and ROTTEN food arriving at sea...
He reportedly wrote that almost nothing fresh makes it out except meat, because only frozen goods survive the supply run, and called it the worst… pic.twitter.com/ylCgsHap26
Citing US officials, CNN reported that the Navy treated the incident as a mental-health episode, adding that the sailor was medically evaluated and later removed from the ship for further care.
Annabelle Loma, the serviceman’s wife, told Navy Times that her husband had become emotionally exhausted and confirmed that he had attempted to take his own life by jumping overboard. She added that he seemed “scared” and was afraid he would receive “a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out.”
At a meeting with Navy leaders, another spouse said her husband had sent a message saying he hoped he “doesn’t wake up tomorrow,” according to Stars and Stripes.
Other families have also sounded the alarm over the physical and mental exhaustion after months of long shifts, warning that such levels of fatigue could lead to deadly mistakes.
“The morale is not good,” one family member said, as cited by MS Now. “Apparently, the ship’s doctor or therapist said they need to hit port soon, or people are going to start, you know, losing their minds.”
The Navy, however, has pushed back against such concerns, telling CNN that “we have not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship.”
Could stress on the flattop lead to violence?
Citing an unnamed “informed military source,” Iranian news agency Tasnim reported earlier this month that seven US Navy personnel had been killed and several others wounded in a violent confrontation aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.
According to the report, an adviser to CENTCOM, commander Adm. Brad Cooper, boarded the carrier to address complaints about the prolonged deployment but was booed and pelted with water bottles before the confrontation escalated into a knife fight.
CENTCOM denied the allegation, saying that no crew members aboard the carrier had died during the Iran war.
How much pressure has Iran put on the Abraham Lincoln?
Multiple analyses have suggested that Iran, which is militarily inferior to the US, has been relying on attritional warfare to hold its ground and gain concessions from Washington. Kamal Kharrazi, head of Iran’s Strategic Council on Foreign Relations, said Iran was prepared for a “long war” and argued that the longer the conflict continued, the greater the economic pressure on other countries would become.
Maj. Gen. Mohammad Jafar Asadi, a former senior commander, described the conflict in July as an “attritional and never-ending war.”
As the conflict has dragged on, Tehran has claimed to have mounted numerous attacks on the Abraham Lincoln. On March 1, Iran announced it had fired four ballistic missiles at the carrier, with CENTCOM saying the missiles “didn’t even come close.” Later that month, Tehran claimed that missiles and drones had struck the vessel, rendering it inoperable and forcing it to withdraw – an allegation also rejected by Washington.
In early April, Iran said it had launched multiple waves of attack drones toward the Abraham Lincoln group in the northern Indian Ocean, forcing it to withdraw.
In July, it claimed to have struck logistics support centers serving US aircraft carriers in Oman, later adding that other targets included “one aircraft carrier refueling platform,” alongside fuel depots, naval stores, aircraft facilities, and other US military infrastructure. On Tuesday, the Iranian military claimed that the US had no warships left in the Persian Gulf region.
While it is unclear whether the Abraham Lincoln sustained any damage during the attacks, it was hardly operating in a benign environment, with CENTCOM reporting roughly 10,000 aircraft flights and the expenditure of about 1.5 million pounds of ordnance during the mission.
What beef do US lawmakers have with the Pentagon?
On Wednesday, a member of the US Senate’s Armed Services Committee, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, published an open letter to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, raising “serious concerns” about the situation aboard the ship and questioning whether it could sustain continued operations.
“The Lincoln is not an isolated case. Recent carrier deployments have repeatedly stretched beyond their originally anticipated durations, suggesting that extended deployments may be becoming a feature rather than an exception of the Navy’s force-generation model,” he added.
Fellow Senator Ruben Gallego has called for a bipartisan congressional oversight visit to the Abraham Lincoln, casting doubt on Pentagon assurances.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has gone further, blaming Hegseth personally and saying sailors are “paying the price” for Pentagon failures. “When Pete Hegseth was nominated, everyone knew he was completely incompetent... Pete Hegseth must be fired immediately,” he insisted.
What does the Pentagon say in response to the accusations?
Hegseth dismissed reports of poor living conditions and food shortages aboard the Abraham Lincoln as “completely misrepresented,” while acknowledging that some deployments could last longer and be tougher than others.
“We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain, has everything that we can provide them at every single moment,” he added.
Meanwhile, the AP reported that the USS George Washington is now moving toward the Middle East from Vietnam to replace the Abraham Lincoln. The redeployment is expected to weaken the US footprint in the Pacific amid tensions with China, however.
Bottom Line
While the Pentagon insists that the Abraham Lincoln “remains fully capable of meeting all mission tasking,” and there is no credible evidence that Iran managed to cripple the ship, its crew appears to have come dangerously close to the breaking point.
After more than eight months of deployment, the vessel appears to be struggling with logistics and supplies of basic amenities, amid growing concerns over its crew members’ mental health. While the Abraham Lincoln is expected to be relieved soon, its performance raises questions about Washington’s overall ability to sustain effective long-term operations against even a militarily inferior adversary.

What went wrong for the Suns this year and how 2027 can be much better
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
18:44:06 UTC
03:44:06 KST

analysis
Gold Coast Suns fell in the AFL this season but offered a glimpse to 2027
Sometimes an essay is needed to describe what has happened on the footy field. Sometimes a book will only start to scratch the surface.
But sometimes a single word will do it best. As the Gold Coast Suns filtered off a frigid Manuka Oval after beating GWS, one word seemed to sum up the mood in a nutshell: Finally.
For the first time since May 15, the Suns had entered the winner's circle. At the time of their last win, the Suns sat fourth on the ladder, with many believing they were poised for a real shot at a deep finals run.
But as the weeks drew shorter and the nights colder, their hopes faded.
By the start of July, the hopes of a top-four finish had effectively vanished. Two weeks later, their finals hopes were on life support. By the end of the month, even the wildcard spots were taken off the table.
Damien Hardwick summed up the year via the slightly misheard words of one of the big four of American thrash metal.
"There's a great line by Metallica that I'm going to butcher, where 'sometimes you can see the light at the end of the tunnel, but it's a freight train coming the other way'. That's how it's felt this year. That's the reality of it," he said.
Despite the season being lost, both Hardwick and his playing staff were overjoyed with the win.
"It's been … it's been a while. The boys were really hungry for a win today and I thought we brought the spirit and it was great to sing that song again," Suns star Matt Rowell told ABC Sport after the win over GWS.
For one week, everything worked as it should for the side many thought to be a premiership contender. The win wasn't just one in isolation, it also practically ended the season for their Expansion Cup rivals the Giants.
For both sides, the hope is that a small slice of pain in 2026 will set them up for success in 2027. But to do so, there has to be an understanding of what exactly went wrong.
Hardwick's hard year with Gold Coast
Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.
It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks, there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after mentoring by a few others.
Of all the jobs in elite football, that of the senior club coach may be the most coveted, and the most stressful. The coach operates as not only a leader to the players but also a figurehead for the club.
It's a job that many, if not most, of the league's assistant coaches and football staffers aspire to. But for roughly every 10 aspirants to the ranks there's only ever one opening. Those lucky enough to sit in the big chair often do so after a few others have mentored them.
Few coaches have been more highly credentialed in recent years than Hardwick. Beyond the three flags the Tigers won under his guidance, his impact across the league is clear.
While Hardwick served an apprenticeship under a more kick-mark style operator in Alistair Clarkson, his own method differed to that of former co-worker Chris Fagan. Instead, the influence of Hardwick is best seen through the defensive-first-yet-free-flowing styles exhibited by Collingwood and GWS under former Hardwick assistants Craig McRae and Adam Kingsley.
Hardwick's teams have an idiosyncratic stylistic footprint. Under his reign at Richmond, the Tigers overhauled teams with chaos, not control. The side often lost the marking battle but played surge football, running on adrenaline and enthusiasm. Instead of a side built on winning and scoring from clearances, their drive came from scoring on the intercept.
McRae and Kingsley, alongside West Coast's Andrew McQualter, have regularly influenced proceedings in September. The Hardwick school sits as a counterbalance to the way that sides such as Brisbane pick through defences by controlling the ball.
Despite being so influential to how football is played in 2026, Hardwick is quick to note that this may not have been his finest year.
"I feel I haven't had my best year as a coach with regard to bending a little bit of my system of how we want to play," he said. "So those realisations are very, very important. And these are the things that actually your greatest growth comes from."
In the wake of teams inspired by the control-heavy game styles influenced by Alistair Clarkson's Hawthorn sides, Tigerball was risky, dangerous and exciting.
All good coaches evolve over time. And all good "brands" are strategised against and countered. Football is not a solved game with a perfect way to play.
The developing Suns Hardwick inherited were quite different from the Tigers he left. Instead of building from a rock-solid counterattacking defensive unit, they led with the contested, stoppage game the premiership Tigers largely eschewed.
In 2025, Hardwick bent to accommodate both strands, leaning on rising stars Anderson, Rowell, Miller and Humphries to dominate in the middle and using Noble, Rioli and Jeffrey to provide drive on the counterattack.
There were clear parts of the game plan that held strong across both seasons. Gold Coast continued to lean on handball more than most and played into chaotic situations.
But the other part of the balance, that of the stoppage game, fell away.
Last year, the Suns finished +3.3 in clearance differential and third in the league for scoring differential from stoppages.
This year — with a group in flux with early season injuries to Matt Rowell and the incorporation of Christian Petracca — the Suns sit last for clearance differential and fourth-worst for stoppage scoring differential.
Notably, the win in Canberra came in one of the hardest, most contested games of the season. The game was cold, wet and physical and played largely at ground level. The sides combined for just 96 marks all day — about half of the average game this year.
"We love the wet weather footy, as you can tell, and I think it really suited us today," midfielder Bodhi Uwland told ABC Sport post-game.
"We like being a contested team, that surge mentality, like getting the ball forward. And I think we really showed that today and we're able to really adapt to the conditions."
The Suns played for territory first and results later in Canberra. Despite dominating hitouts and clearances, the Giants still scored more from stoppage. But the high defensive wall that the Suns were able to establish helped the Suns re-enter the winner's circle.
Reigning Brownlow Medallist Rowell led the way for the Suns with one of the finest games imaginable in tough conditions. Despite the number of accolades he has already accumulated in his short career, the game may have been one of his best yet.
"That's one of the best performances I've seen from Rowell, to be honest, like, especially from behind the ball. Seeing him u-turning out of stoppage, shrugging tackles and just getting it forward … and he did it so consistently throughout the game. It was an amazing performance." Uwland said.
It wasn't just his teammates who were effusive about his effort.
"Yeah, he's a difference maker. It's a pleasure to have a guy like that in our footy club who, you see, the way the game plays today." Hardwick added.
"You know, it's 40-odd possessions, 22 contested, I think 18 tackles and 12 clearances as well. It's just one of those games you go, 'Wow'.
"You know, they're video game numbers, but he revels in those conditions. You know, that's the way he plays the game and it's such a pleasure to watch those players that give absolutely everything."
Rowell's preseason Origin injury threw the Suns' midfield balance off at the start of the season and left the side looking for what was their best look through the middle as the season developed. The Suns are blessed with highly capable players at the contest, with more bodies than opportunities most weeks.
The game in Canberra was a hint of what it could look like when it worked for the Suns.
Despite reports in the media of a loss of connection in recent weeks, at least in wake of the win the connection between coach and group seemed to be growing and evolving through the adversity.
"We haven't had the year we've wanted, but I think he's been really impressed by the way we've kept our spirit as a group," Rowell said.
"Even though we can't make finals, we've still got a lot of pride as a group. I think that really showed today. Yeah, Dimma's (Hardwick's) connection with the group is growing each game."
Suns keen to rise in 2027
In the wake of the Canberra game, attention for both sides turned, at least a little, to next season. The balance between running out a season where a premiership is an impossible task and preparing for the next one is a tough balance to strike for all teams.
"Yeah (2027 starts now). We have spoken about that. You look at Sydney — a great example from last year. You know, they had a disappointing year, much like we have this year, and they sort of went to work on some things. Look where they are now." Hardwick said after the game.
"That was our challenge. We spoke to the players about it. Noah and his leaders have just been absolutely leading the charge in that space."
Given how few competitive games there are each year, not a single one needs to be wasted. A flag is always the goal for each of the league's 18 clubs, even if it's not this year's.
Having shown the quality to win a final last year, Gold Coast's prospects of recovery look reasonably bright. Roughly half of the teams in the 18-team era to win a final then dip to double-digit ladder placings returned to finals the following year.
Most of the rest took two years to get back, with Melbourne and Collingwood grabbing the 2021 and 2023 flags. Most encouragingly, only three times since 2012 has a finals-winning team immediately crashed down the ladder and failed to recover at all.
These gap years have almost become routine as footy becomes ever more even and competitive. Almost every year since 2020, at least one side has found itself dipping and another recovering from such a dip.
The one slight pause for both the Suns and Giants is the relatively low placement of all four of the Hardwick-styled teams in 2026. Of the four, only McRae's Pies will play finals, entering via the wildcard round. As always, the question will be whether that style of play is conducive to winning football in 2026 and beyond, or whether the next evolution is upon us already.
Still, the Gold Coast list might be the most talented in the league. If they can get the strategic balance right, and a little luck to fall their way, the sky is the limit for this Suns group.

Art offers young Gaza survivors solace and escape from war’s devastation

Art offers young Gaza survivors solace and escape from war’s devastation
Young survivors of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza find safe spaces to process trauma and rediscover joy.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Maryam sits in front of a blank sheet of paper, holding her pencil as she begins drawing the first lines. Her eyes focus on the details of the drawing while her hand moves calmly.
Amid a reality in which Israel’s genocidal war has imposed itself on the details of everyday life in Gaza, 16-year-old Maryam tries to create a different environment for herself, even if only for a few hours. The paper and pencil give her a chance to step away from the scene around her and return to something she loves and knows well.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Analysis: Israel’s government can’t disown West Bank settler violence
- list 2 of 3Kushner to visit Israel after Netanyahu rejects Gaza Board of Peace plan
- list 3 of 3Israeli PM Netanyahu calls UK ‘the Islamic Republic of Britain’
Maryam’s family’s home was bombed in January 2024, and she now lives in her grandmother’s house in Deir el-Balah. She has lost friends and people close to her, including her uncle, as a result of Israel’s attacks during the war – strikes that have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians since October 2023.
The art space she draws in – located at a cafe on the beach in Deir el-Balah – has become a refuge.
“The space helped me return to myself and rediscover my passion for drawing,” she says.
For Maryam, drawing means more than a hobby. It is a way of putting her feelings onto paper, especially those that are difficult to express in words.
“I feel a great sense of psychological relief, as if I can put my feelings on the paper instead of keeping them trapped inside me,” Maryam says. “Every drawing makes me feel that I have managed to describe a part of what I feel and convey it to people in my own way, even the things I sometimes cannot talk about.”
Providing a space for hope
Maryam has been drawing since she was a child, but began attending the art space in April, when it was set up.
She says that each completed drawing gives her a sense of achievement and opens a small space for hope amid heavy days.
“It made me wake up every day with a new passion, with drawing becoming part of my day. Every day, I finish a new drawing, it plants new hope inside me,” Maryam says. “If I hadn’t drawn, I would have given in to depression and the difficult circumstances I was going through. But I managed to get back on my feet and learn a new drawing, something new, every day.”
Helping children like Maryam is the reason 35-year-old Abdullah al-Ghafri set up the art space – and why he is working hard to keep it open, despite the expensive rental costs that have him continuously searching for investors.
“The idea was born out of necessity and the difficult reality,” al-Ghafri says. “With most educational and cultural centres in Gaza destroyed and bombed, we could not find a place to accommodate the talents of young people and children.”
“The main goal is to lift the participants out of the atmosphere of war and destruction,” al-Ghafri adds. “And to provide a space where they can release negative energy and replace it with positive energy and hope.”
Coping mechanism
Psychologist Asil Abu Shawish says art can give children and adolescents a way to express their feelings at times of great trauma.
“When a child draws, sings or plays an instrument, they are, in a way, releasing some of the pressure and emotions that have built up inside them,” she says.
Abu Shawish explains that having a safe space where children can engage in artistic activities can give them a sense of stability amid constantly changing circumstances.
“When a child enters a safe space and knows they have time for drawing or music, it helps them feel that they still have a part of their life that they can control. That feeling is very important psychologically.”
As the war continues – despite an official October “ceasefire” – children are exposed to high levels of fear, stress and loss. Abu Shawish, therefore, believes that artistic activities can give them an opportunity to deal with these emotions in a safer way.
“Art is not a treatment for all the psychological effects left by war, but it can be an important means of emotional release and coping, especially when the activity is appropriate for the child’s age and carried out under the supervision of people who are able to support them.”
She says the impact of these activities can be observed during the sessions themselves, through children’s interaction with one another and their ability to focus and engage in the activity.
“Sometimes we notice that a child who is quiet or withdrawn begins to interact with the group through drawing or music. The activity itself can become the starting point for a relationship, a conversation or a sense of safety.”
She believes some children find art to be an easier language than words.
“Not every child can say, ‘I’m afraid,’ ‘I’m sad,’ or ‘I lost someone.’ They may draw that feeling, choose a song that expresses it, or release their emotions through playing an instrument.”
Art can therefore become a means of coping with difficult circumstances, particularly when the activity continues over time and becomes part of a child’s life.
Musical therapy
In Nuseirat, at the Palestinian Student Care Association, Jabr Thabet coordinates activities with the Edward Said National Conservatory of Music, where children gather around their instruments and learn singing and music.
“We are trying to bring music to children wherever they are, even if the place changes and the centres are damaged,” Thabet, who is the projects and venue coordinator at the Conservatory’s Gaza branch, says. “We are not just teaching them music. We are trying to give them a space where they can experience a normal moment, feel joy and meet other children like them.”
The conservatory’s Gaza City location was damaged during the war, and so its teachers have continued their activities in displacement areas, including Nuseirat, Deir el-Balah and Gaza City itself.
During the sessions, Thabet watches the children’s interaction with music, from the moment they arrive until the training ends. “What stands out to me most is their enthusiasm. A child comes to the session waiting to learn something new and leaves wanting to come back again.”
“Music allows a child to bring out what is inside in a different way. A child may not be able to talk, but they can sing or play an instrument.”
Thabet adds, “For us, art is a form of resilience. When a child can sing, play and create something beautiful amid all this destruction, in a way, they are preserving a part of themselves and their life.”

21:42:03 EEST

Changed data on 10 people in the "Oberih" register — former head of the Kharkiv District Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center notified of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
The former acting head of a district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center in Kharkiv is suspected of unauthorized alteration of the data of 10 persons liable for military service in the "Oberih" register. A preventive measure in the form of detention with bail set at UAH 266,000 has been imposed on him.
The Prosecutor’s Office notified a former acting head of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers of suspicion of unauthorizedly changing information about 10 persons liable for military service in the Oberih register. This was reported by the Specialized Prosecutor’s Office in the Defense Sphere of the Eastern Region, according to UNN.
Details
Under the procedural guidance of the Specialized Prosecutor’s Office in the Defense Sphere of the Eastern Region, a former acting head of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Kharkiv was notified of suspicion under Parts 1 and 3 of Article 362 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine
According to the investigation, the official, possessing registrar powers in the Unified State Register of Conscripts, Persons Liable for Military Service and Reservists, used his own electronic key to enter false information into the Oberih information and communication system about the alleged mobilization of persons liable for military service and their assignment to military units.
In November–December 2025, he unlawfully changed data in the records of 10 persons liable for military service. At the same time, these individuals did not actually undergo the conscription procedure, did not report to military units, and were not enrolled in the personnel lists.
Despite this, the official entered information into the Register about their conscription and assignment for military service. As a result, the persons liable for military service unjustifiably acquired the status of having been called up for military service and were removed from active mobilization records.
The suspect’s actions were classified under Parts 1 and 3 of Article 362 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — unauthorized alteration of information processed in an automated system, committed by a person who has the right to access it, repeatedly.
At the prosecutor’s request, the court imposed pretrial detention on the suspect, with the alternative of posting bail in the amount of UAH 266,000.

Employees of the State Bureau of Investigation detained an officer of one of the district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers in Ivano-Frankivsk region who, while intoxicated, beat a serviceman.

‘We’ll Warm Ourselves With the Fire of Russian Oil Refineries’: Ukraine Hits Back at Russia

The strike package also included the Mich, Fire Point, Ramzay, Sichen, Trust, Khariok, Bober, Liutyi, and Dovbush aerial drones, as well as Sargan and Mamai unmanned surface vessels.

Russia rejected the temporary Black Sea ceasefire proposal on Friday.

'I live with the scars': Why the fight against HIV is not over
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
18:38:52 UTC
03:38:52 KST

Australia's fight against HIV is not over as new challenges disrupt progress
Not long after Stephen Borg was diagnosed with HIV in 2007, he was given a warning that has remained lodged in his heart ever since.
"I was told this is a diagnosis that perhaps someone cannot love you for," Mr Borg said.
"That really sat quite heavily with me.
"If someone was diagnosed with diabetes, you might get flowers or people coming to you with open arms. That's not often the case with an HIV diagnosis."
The human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, affects the immune system and can spread through body fluids.
Left untreated, it causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
As public attention has drifted toward other global health emergencies, those living with HIV, and the battle-hardened community around them, have fought tirelessly to achieve something considered internationally remarkable.
Forty-five years since the first globally diagnosed case of HIV/AIDs — and more than 40 million lives lost — Australia stands within reach of virtual elimination of HIV transmission.
But the fight is not over and the path toward that goal is not guaranteed.
The United Nations last month issued a dire warning that "the world is on course for a resurgence of the epidemic".
Experts now fear Australia's enviable position could be at risk.
"Australia is on the precipice of achieving something that to the generation before us was incomprehensible," said Dash Heath-Paynter, CEO of Health Equity Matters, the national federation for Australia's leading HIV organisations.
"It's almost like you can see the finishing line. But we can't get there with just a business-as-usual approach."
'I live with the scars'
There is a moment in the infamous 1987 Grim Reaper advertisement where the nightmarish hooded figure crashes a black bowling ball of death into a mother, sending a baby flying from her arms.
The government-funded HIV/AIDs campaign was considered so stigmatising it was later credited with contributing to greater violence against LGBTQIA+ people.
David Menadue was one of the first Australians diagnosed with HIV in 1984.
He watched on at the television ad with horror.
"It scared people into thinking, what am I looking at? Am I looking at a ghost or are these people like this?" Mr Menadue said.
"They became scared of people with HIV. It was very stigmatising."
Fearful of the fear that surrounded them, and with no treatments available, he and a small community of people living with HIV turned to one-another for support.
"We met in each of the group's homes from 1986 to 1993, which was a bad period," he said.
"There was very good reassurance [in having] other people you could talk to."
Those meetings were essential sources of connection and comfort, but they were also places where information was shared, emerging research discussed and advocacy initiated.
The subject of death was nonetheless inescapable.
"What we didn't expect was the level of mortality," he said.
"Of the 33 people we had in that group from 86 to 93, there's only four people left.
"That's a lot of friends to die and to have to attend funerals. Each time you think, am I going to be next?
"I live with the scars even today."
Amid the tragedy, communities like Mr Menadue's built what would become the foundation of Australia's response to HIV.
A new report from Health Equity Matters argues that "from the beginning, the Australian response was strongly community-driven" and the basis on which "a policy architecture [has] been built upon ever since".
"Community has been the most fundamental thing in my own survival," Mr Menadue said.
Change and challenge
While there remains no cure for HIV, the landscape for those with a positive diagnosis, those wanting to take preventative medication or those who simply want to get tested looks very different today.
Antiretroviral therapy has seen HIV turn from the death sentence it once was to something that, for many, can be managed as part of a long and healthy life.
The most recent data from the Kirby Institute found that of the estimated 30,000 people in Australia living with HIV, 97 per cent were receiving antiretrovirals.
Almost all of those recorded a suppressed and undetectable viral load, meaning they are at zero risk of onward transmission.
The local roll-out of pre-exposure prophylaxis – known as PrEP – has equally been heralded as a "game-changer".
The HIV prevention drug was first added to the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) in 2018.
Sustained community advocacy has seen that access recently expanded to include non-Medicare card holders – an acknowledgement that transmission among non-citizens is just as detrimental to the Australian cause.
"It was acknowledged that was a big gap in the response to HIV," said Chad Hughes, CEO of Thorne Harbour Health, an organisation once known as the Victorian Aids Council.
"You can't leave anybody behind in that situation."
Public health messaging also looks very different.
Gone are the ghoulish mass campaigns, replaced by targeted and often in-place messaging.
In Perth, the state's HIV advocacy group WAAC has run health promotion campaigns, pop-up testing and PrEP prescription services on-site at a popular male sex-on-premises venue.
There are now vending machines in every state and territory that distribute free HIV testing kits.
Positioned in discreet yet still easy-enough to find locations in university campuses and outreach settings, the vending machines have been predominantly accessed by people testing for HIV for the first time.
In Melbourne, a peer-to-peer sexual health clinic called PRONTO is staffed by people from typically non-medical backgrounds.
"What we don't want is someone to come in and behave like a clinician. We don't want [people] feeling like they're being clinically assessed," said Peter Locke, director of services for HIV clinical and community support programs at Thorne Harbour Health.
Following three months of training, employees administer free rapid finger-prick and blood tests for HIV and STIs.
The clinic's half-hour appointments – as distinct from typically shorter visits to a GP – also open the door to bigger conversations around sexual health.
"They may come from a religious background or a cultural background where they can't disclose [their sexual activity] to their family doctor," said Mr Locke.
"They may be married, they may be in a heterosexual relationship – they're having sex with men for a number of different reasons and they're just not going to disclose that [to a GP].
"A lot of GPs or nurses out there in the broader medical community aren't comfortable asking somebody. They'll make the assumption, 'oh, you're married, you couldn't possibly have HIV.' So they're not asking, are you having sex with men? Are you having sex with transgender people?"
Australia 'not on track' for target
Such initiatives have helped make Australia's aim of virtually eliminating HIV transmission a possibility.
The current national goal is to reach that milestone by 2030. A look to recent history suggests that may not be straightforward.
In 2014, the goal was to reach virtual elimination of transmission by 2020.
By 2020, the then Health Minister Greg Hunt updated the target to 2022.
It too was missed.
In 2023, an HIV taskforce was established with the new goal of a virtual end of transmission by 2030.
Despite the best efforts of many, and what those inside the sector call a "rare" level of multi-partisan support, new challenges are emerging that threaten to disrupt the progress.
"We're not on track," said Dr Skye McGregor, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute.
Anonymised data of HIV cases, which states and territories are required to provide to the Kirby Institute, show a consistent pattern.
The number of cases among Australian-born men who have sex with other men, sex workers and people who inject drugs is broadly tracking in the right direction.
It is in the roughly 30 per cent of cases involving people born overseas where more attention is needed.
"We know that the decrease [in cases] has been far higher among Australian-born people reporting male-to-male sexual contact – far closer to where we would want to be at this point," Dr McGregor said.
"But there's very different patterns in different populations.
"We're fortunate that we're at the point of needing to understand every population because we have done so well."
Chad Hughes, who has worked on HIV programs around the world for two decades, said the rise in cases among more recent arrivals to Australia can often be linked to countries with lower sexual health literacy.
"A large proportion of newly diagnosed people in Australia with HIV are newly arrived people who are young, whose English is probably a second or third language, who often come as students from Southeast Asia or South America to our universities," he said.
"They come from maybe conservative backgrounds where they live with their parents, they arrive in Australia and all of a sudden they are free to go and enjoy life and go to pubs and bars and saunas and have sex and do all the things that young adults want to do without their parents watching them.
"But they don't have the knowledge and skills to protect themselves, so they're not using condoms necessarily, they're not on PrEP."
There is now a concerted push among HIV advocacy groups to better target health messaging and support services to newly arrived communities.
Marc Mendoza came to Australia from the Philippines in 1991 as a seven-year-old and grew up, by his own characterisation, "Aussie, Aussie."
He was diagnosed with HIV in 2018.
After living through "really dark days," he now volunteers as part of a support group for other people from Asian backgrounds who have tested positive.
He said people in that community wrestle with a particular cultural stigma.
"If their families already know they're gay, it's like this other dark secret that they've now got to keep,"
Cuts and spikes
The challenge becomes far greater beyond Australia's border.
Cuts to global public health funding, like the Trump-ordered roll backs of USAID foreign aid programs, have seen access to HIV treatments and prevention rapidly diminish.
Late last month in Rio De Janeiro, delegates at the World AIDS Conference were presented with a bleak picture.
"Never has donor funding fallen so far, so fast, and those most vulnerable are already paying the price," International Aids Society President Beatriz Grinsztejn told the conference.
There were 1.2 million new HIV infections in 2025, according to a UNAIDS report released at the Rio conference, of which 280,000 were recorded in Australia's neighbourhood of Asia and the Pacific.
In global terms, Australia is responsible for the merest fraction of new HIV cases – just 757 in the most recent local reporting period of 2024.
Those who work in the sector nonetheless believe the country is at a "critical time" and caution against thinking the fight against HIV is "over."
"If you get [numbers] very low and then treat it as done, it will come back with a vengeance," Mr Heath Paynter said.
"We need to be innovative and we need continued political will and investment."
David Menadue remains proud of what the decades of community activism and advocacy have achieved.
Now in his seventies, there might be a fragility to his movement, but there's a strength that refuses to leave his body.
"I think some people think because I look unwell, I must be. But my actual physical health underneath is all right," he said.
"I've got an inner strength, a resilience that all those years with HIV has probably given me.
"I'm still here."
