US intelligence has assessed that Russia could seek to test NATO’s resolve as early as this fall through a limited attack on an alliance member.
Possible scenarios range from cyberattacks and sabotage to operations involving unidentified armed groups or a limited incursion into a NATO country on the alliance’s eastern flank.
But Moldova could offer Moscow a different route to destabilizing Europe.
Why Moldova matters
Western intelligence officials told the NYT that conquering Ukraine remains Putin’s top priority, while establishing control over Moldova is reportedly second.
Moscow’s strategic goal, according to the officials, goes beyond political influence in Chisinau. Putin is still believed to want to seize southern Ukraine and create a land corridor connecting Russia to Moldova.
That would put Moldova – a small country of about 2.4 million people wedged between Ukraine and NATO and EU territory – in an extremely vulnerable position.
Poland Uncovers Russian Plot to Kill US-Ukrainian Citizen in Warsaw
Moldova also has the Russian-backed separatist region of Transnistria on its territory, where Russian troops have been stationed for decades. That gives Moscow an existing military foothold just across the border from Ukraine and within striking distance of Moldova’s capital, Chisinau.
Control over Moldova could therefore give Russia another platform for pressure on Ukraine while placing the EU and NATO’s eastern flank under additional strain.
Moscow already has pressure points
Russia does not need an open invasion to destabilize Moldova.
In March, a Russian strike on a Ukrainian hydroelectric plant triggered an oil spill that polluted the Dniester River and disrupted water supplies in Moldova, including the country’s third-largest city.
Russian drones later struck a high-voltage line in western Ukraine that supplies Moldova with a large share of its electricity, exposing how closely the country’s infrastructure is tied to the war next door.
The pressure is also political. Moldova has been moving decisively toward the EU, while Moscow has repeatedly sought to exploit political divisions, disinformation and economic vulnerabilities to weaken that shift.
“Hybrid attacks every day”
German Chief of Defense Gen. Carsten Breuer has warned that Russia is already conducting hybrid operations across NATO, particularly on the eastern flank.
Poland and the Baltic states are now increasing security around dams, power plants, gas facilities and other critical infrastructure amid fears Russia could stage a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones.
A Baltic intelligence official told Reuters that such an operation could be designed less to cause physical damage than to create political chaos inside NATO – forcing Washington and European capitals to debate whether Russia was responsible and whether the alliance should respond.

Europe significantly increased its military support for Ukraine, but US weapons still play a key role in continued aid to Kyiv, a study revealed.
In its Ukraine Support Tracker report released Thursday, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy said Europe significantly increased its aid allocations to Ukraine in May and June 2026.
The increase was mainly driven by the newly introduced Ukraine Support Loan, through which European institutions allocated nearly €11 billion ($12.7 billion) over the two months, the institute said.
Beyond the Ukraine Support Loan, European donors also accounted for the majority of newly allocated aid.
However, the research suggested that financial and humanitarian aid remained well below last year's level, while Europe still relies heavily on US weapons for its military aid to Kyiv.
From January to June 2026, European donors procured military aid worth at least €3 billion ($3.4 billion) from US defense companies, the institute said.
That corresponded to around 30% of Europe’s military aid provided through defense industry procurement, according to the report.
"Europe continues to depend on access to US weapons systems to sustain its military support for Ukraine," said Federico Mellace, lead analyst of the Ukraine Support Tracker.
Mellace added that the US remains a key supplier of systems such as Patriot, for which Europe currently has only limited alternatives.

UK Charity Commission acts over Great Israeli Real Estate event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:37:38 UTC
21:37:38 KST

Breadcrumb
UK Charity Commission takes action after complaints over Great Israeli Real Estate event
The UK Charity Commission confirmed on Thursday that it formally engaged with the trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue after a barrage of complaints was received regarding the Great Israeli Real Estate event that took place in London on 14 June.
The event promoted the sale of properties in illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories, triggering protests at the time.
The Charity Commission said it exercised its statutory powers under section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011 to issue regulatory advice and guidance concerning the charity's decision to host the event.
It added that the trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue must now take account of and act upon the guidance moving forward.
The development comes after the Commission said its statutory regulatory powers reflect its assessment that the issues raised by the complaints, such as that from the International Centre of Justice of Palestinians (ICJP), warranted formal regulatory engagement.
The complaint from the ICJP argued that the synagogue had allowed its charitable resources and premises to host a commercial event, where attendees were persuaded to buy properties in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The group also said that the event had gone ahead despite the trustees receiving detailed legal warnings before it took place, raising concerns over trustee governance, the discharge of trustees' legal duties, due diligence, the use of charitable assets, and reputational risk.
Another key concern about the event was the obligation of trustees to act exclusively in the best interests of their charity, while maintaining public trust and confidence.
The ICJP argued that by allowing the event to proceed, the trustees failed to consider the legal warnings and obligations, despite being made aware of the issues.
A statement from the ICJP, however, said that the Commission’s response was not sufficient, noting the serious nature of the matter.
The group said that they had submitted thorough evidence which showed the event raised serious concerns under both international law and UK laws.
“Where a charity permits its premises and resources to be used in connection with conduct that raises such serious legal concerns, the Charity Commission should take robust regulatory action to uphold charity law and protect public trust and confidence in the charitable sector,” a statement from the ICJP said.
The organisation called for a more adequate response and called for the Charity Commission to show that it is ready to use all of its powers in cases where charities risk being connected to serious breaches of law.
“Failing to do so risks undermining public confidence in charity regulation and sending the wrong message to trustees about the standards expected of them under charity law,” the ICJP said.

Russia builds another tanker to circumvent sanctions via northern seas
Konstantin Posiet, Russia's second newly built ice-class tanker for transporting liquefied natural gas, has left Bolshoy Kamen Bay in Primorsky Krai and set course for the Northern Sea Route.
Source: Reuters
Details: For Russia, this tanker represents another step in circumventing Western sanctions.
The vessel was built at the Zvezda shipyard, one of Russia's most advanced shipbuilding facilities, to serve the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 plant, which is under US sanctions.
According to LSEG data, the Konstantin Posiet is due to arrive at its destination on 30 August. The destination of the gas carrier has not been disclosed.
The Zvezda shipyard specialises in building large Arc7 ice-class tankers, capable of breaking through ice up to two metres thick.
The shipyard was due to build 15 tankers for Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project, but sanctions have delayed the programme.
The first domestically built ice-class LNG tanker from the Zvezda shipyard, the Alexey Kosygin, entered service in December last year.
With this new vessel, the company now has three ice-class tankers in total, allowing gas to be transported via a significantly shorter route.
Background: Russia relied on a single icebreaker to continue exporting liquefied natural gas from a US-sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project throughout the winter.

Zelensky Struggles to Find Ukraine’s Next Envoy to Trump

2026-08-14
12:35:04 UTC
21:35:04 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is struggling to find a senior enough candidate to represent Kyiv in Washington as relations with the Trump administration enter a critical stage, Politico reported Friday, Aug. 14.
The vacancy follows the dismissal of Ukraine’s previous envoy to the United States, Olga Stefanishyna, and has complicated Zelensky’s broader government reshuffle. According to two former senior Ukrainian officials and four lawmakers cited by Politico, several potential candidates have been reluctant to take on the demanding position.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ambassador will face the difficult task of dealing with US President Donald Trump’s unpredictable approach to military support for Ukraine, possible peace negotiations and Washington’s decisions on air defense and other critical military assistance.
Zelensky’s first choice rejected the post
The need to appoint a new ambassador reportedly influenced Zelensky’s plans for the government reshuffle.
According to a former Ukrainian senior official and a Republican foreign policy expert, Zelensky had hoped to offer the Washington post to Yulia Svyrydenko, who was then leaving the position of prime minister.
Zelensky later confirmed that he had offered Svyrydenko the ambassadorship.
“It is no secret that I counted on and offered Yulia Svyrydenko the post of ambassador to the United States,” he said at a press conference in late July.
Putin Has an Unexpected Ally in Ukraine’s War
The president said he wanted someone with the highest possible qualifications, ideally “a person at the level of a deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister.”
Svyrydenko declined, however, disrupting Zelensky’s plans.
Other potential candidates have reportedly also been hesitant to take the position.
Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, a Ukrainian opposition lawmaker and former deputy prime minister, said candidates with enough political influence and experience may be concerned that they would not have the conditions needed to work effectively in Washington.
“Certainly that would be the case without having the ear of the president or his trust,” she said.
A former Ukrainian diplomat, speaking anonymously, said it would be an oversimplification to say that nobody wants the job.
“There are people who want the job, but there’s no one who really measures up to it,” the diplomat said. “Zelensky is having a hard time filling the position.”
A difficult moment for Kyiv
The ambassadorial vacancy comes as Ukraine faces increasingly important decisions in its relationship with Washington.
The Trump administration has repeatedly changed its position on military assistance and the future of the war. Kyiv is also trying to persuade Washington to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot air defense missiles under license.
Trump initially indicated that Ukraine would receive permission to produce the interceptors, but later backed away from the idea.
The issue has become particularly urgent as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian attacks and faces a growing shortage of air defense missiles.
Zelensky has said deliveries of air defense missiles from Ukraine’s allies have fallen by two-thirds compared with 2025.
At the same time, Washington may seek to revive stalled peace negotiations with Russia. That would make the role of Ukraine’s ambassador particularly important, as Kyiv would need a senior representative capable of communicating directly with the White House and Congress.
The envoy would also have to lobby US lawmakers on weapons, air defense, intelligence sharing and other forms of support.
Government reshuffle adds to political pressure
The difficulty of filling the Washington post is part of a broader political challenge for Zelensky following his government reshuffle.
According to a Socis Center for Social Research survey cited by Politico, more than 55% of Ukrainians believe the country is moving in the wrong direction.
The president’s decision to dismiss Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in July sparked positionsprotests and political criticism, while several in the government remain unresolved.
Opposition lawmaker Mykola Knyazhitskiy questioned why the reshuffle was necessary in the first place.
“No one has explained to Ukrainians why exactly the government had to be changed,” he said.
He also questioned Svyrydenko’s dismissal, noting that she had received a standing ovation from lawmakers during her farewell address.
The uncertainty surrounding the government reshuffle has raised broader questions about whether Zelensky is willing to look beyond his closest circle when selecting senior officials.
Washington post could remain vacant
The ambassadorial position could remain unfilled for some time.
Opposition lawmaker Yaroslav Yurchyshyn said it was possible Zelensky would not appoint a new envoy before the US midterm elections.
“It will be hard to judge who would fit the political landscape best until those elections have been held,” he said.
For Kyiv, however, leaving the position vacant carries significant risks.
Washington remains central to Ukraine’s ability to sustain its defense against Russia, while decisions on Patriot missiles, other weapons, intelligence cooperation and a possible new peace initiative could come in the months ahead.
The next ambassador will therefore need not only diplomatic experience but also direct access to Zelensky and enough political weight to navigate an administration where US policy toward Ukraine can change rapidly.

Helsinki gained its 700,000th resident early on Friday, the city has announced.
The city is celebrating the milestone today based on the latest population data and city information service calculations.
The City will honour the new resident with a €700 grant. The baby was born at the Women's Hospital at three minutes past midnight on Friday 14 August to the Lehtola family.
The newborn weighed in at 4.084kg and measured 54.5cm, the family's first child.
Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (NCP) visited the Women's Hospital on Friday morning to congratulate the family.
"I warmly congratulate the 700,000th Helsinki resident and the entire family at this important, happy and unique moment," Sazonov said in a city announcement.
'Record-breaking' growth
A city press release noted that the capital has experienced "record-breaking population growth" over the past few years.
"Helsinki's growth into a city of 700,000 residents is a testament to our city's appeal, its opportunities and its vibrant urban life," Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov (NCP) commented. "The most important thing is that every Helsinki resident can feel that they are part of our city and live a good and meaningful life in Helsinki on their own terms."
The previous population milestone, 600,000, was reached in August 2012, according to calculations by the city's Urban Research and Statistics Unit.
People moving to the capital from abroad, as well as from elsewhere in Finland, account for approximately 80 percent of the city's annual population increase, according to the city's figures.
"The number of Helsinki residents born abroad has more than tripled this century. The share of Helsinki residents who were born abroad is 19 percent, while the share of foreign nationals is 13 percent," the press release noted.
The largest incoming population group is people of working age, whose numbers are expected to continue to grow strongly in the coming years.
Based on the city's population projections, Helsinki could hit one million residents by the 2060s.
The city will mark reaching the 700,000 milestone with an ad campaign, launching next week, which "tells the stories of Helsinki residents, the city's diversity and the life stages behind the population growth", the statement said.
The multi-channel campaign will be rolled out in eight languages, reflecting the fact that Helsinki's residents speak over 150 languages.

Ukraine's National Bank expects slight rise in forex demand following Aug easing

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
15:32:37 EEST
21:32:37 KST

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) expects the August package of foreign exchange liberalization measures to generate only moderate additional demand for foreign currency, which will be insignificant compared with the size of the foreign exchange market, the regulator said in response to a request from Interfax-Ukraine.
The National Bank explained that most of the transactions covered by the package do not involve the purchase of foreign currency. These primarily concern transactions with foreign currency accounts, including cash withdrawals and payments for goods, works and services, including housing rentals abroad.
An assessment of the impact of each individual measure shows that the liberalization will not have a decisive effect on the foreign exchange market and will not create risks to its stability.
Regarding the change effective September 1 in the procedure banks use to calculate their foreign exchange position, the NBU expects minimal additional demand for foreign currency.
"This is because the inclusion by banks of that portion of provisions formed against active operations that is currently not included in the calculation will take place very gradually, in accordance with the schedule approved by the National Bank," the regulator said.
As reported, on August 11 the National Bank introduced a new package of foreign exchange liberalization measures for individuals and legal entities and the financial sector. In particular, the regulator raised the monthly limit on individuals’ purchases of foreign currency in non-cash form from UAH 50,000 to UAH 200,000, increased limits on cash foreign currency withdrawals and payments abroad, and expanded a number of opportunities for businesses.
Starting September 1, banks will also be able to gradually include in their calculation of the foreign exchange position a portion of provisions formed against active operations that is currently not included in the calculation.

What is China’s response?
Guo Jiakun: Huangyan Dao has always been China’s territory. It is within China’s sovereign rights to establish and administer the Huangyan Dao national nature reserve. The U.S. is in no position to point fingers, and the “South China Sea arbitral award,” which is illegal, null and void, provides no solid ground for the U.S. to speak for the Philippines. This meeting will be the largest as to the number of participants and events. It will strive to achieve more outcomes across various fields and mechanisms under the APEC framework, laying the groundwork for the leaders’ meeting in November.

It is expected to have the participation of more than 2,300 representatives from member economies of APEC, the APEC Secretariat, the APEC Business Advisory Council and the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council.
The host city Dalian serves as a window to learn about China’s opening up in Northeast China. It boasts a robust industrial foundation, sound business environment, geographical advantages, beautiful scenery and liveable environment. We welcome friends from the media to actively report on the third Senior Officials’ Meeting and related meetings, and continue following and supporting the APEC “China Year.”

China urges the Japanese side to abide by the postwar international order enshrined in the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and other international legal instruments.

Guo Jiakun: Foreign nationals in China should abide by Chinese laws and regulations. China’s immigration authorities perform their duty in accordance with the law and protect the lawful rights and interests of the personnel concerned. The actions do not target any specific country.
It’s learned that it was exactly this defense secretary who personally led the armed forces to seize and detain Chinese nationals lawfully working in the Philippines. This person’s consistent attacks and smears against China harm not only the bilateral relations. It is the interests of the Philippines and all its people that will bear the brunt.

Arms manufacturers call on MoD to ensure continuity of defense procurement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

Arms manufacturers call on MoD to ensure continuity of defense procurement
The “Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers,” an industry association of Ukrainian manufacturers, addressed the Ministry of Defense with a corresponding appeal, the text of which is available to Ukrinform.
The arms manufacturers note that as of mid-August, one of the key problems for the Ukrainian defense industry remains the insufficient level of contracting. According to market participants’ estimates, up to 25% of existing production capacity is currently under contract. Manufacturers of various types of weapons and military equipment are left without a sufficient volume of orders.
For the industry, a prolonged period without sufficient domestic orders poses the risk of losing engineers and production teams, scaling back production lines, reducing working capital, and limiting opportunities to invest in improving and scaling up Ukrainian developments.
“In recent years, the Ukrainian defense industry has significantly expanded its capabilities in response to government requests and the needs of the military. It is important to prevent the loss of these capabilities due to interruptions in contracting,” the association emphasizes.
At the same time, disruptions in contracting are not just a problem for companies. Due to the long production cycle for weapons, delays in signing contracts in August pose a risk to supply volumes in the fall and winter.
Funding remains another challenge. Assistance from international partners is critically important for Ukraine; however, certain financial instruments have their own conditions and limitations and cannot fully replace domestic resources for procuring the full range of equipment required by the Defense Forces.
In this regard, the Ukrainian Arms Manufacturers Council calls on the Ministry of Defense to:
- ensure the continuity of contracting with Ukrainian manufacturers, regardless of personnel, structural, or procedural changes in the defense procurement system;
- prevent any gaps between current and future orders, taking into account the length of the production cycle and the need for advance procurement of components;
- ensure sufficient and predictable financial resources for the procurement of weapons and military equipment needed by the Defense Forces, particularly those items that cannot be fully funded through available partnership programs.
The industry association also calls for providing manufacturers with a clear order outlook that will allow them to plan production, retain their teams, procure components, and continue developing Ukrainian technologies.
It is also proposed to maintain an ongoing dialogue with the industry regarding the current level of contracting, production capabilities, and risks to future deliveries.
“What matters to the market is the result: the military must receive the necessary weapons and military equipment without interruption and on time, and Ukrainian manufacturers must receive a sufficient volume of orders to meet these needs today and maintain their production capacity for tomorrow,” the association emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Defense Procurement Agency has denied reports of a “halt in contracting.”

‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan PM Takaichi condemns Putin’s visit to disputed Kuril Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:28:54 UTC
21:28:54 KST

Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has criticized Russian President Vladimir Putin's first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, saying they were "inherently Japanese territory."
In a post on X, Takaichi said Thursday that Tokyo had "repeatedly requested the Russian side to ensure that the president does not visit the Northern Territories." The Northern Territories refers to the Kuril Islands.
She added that Putin's visit was "absolutely unacceptable."
The Kuril Islands sit between the southern tip of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula and the northeastern corner of Japan's Hokkaido. The sparsely populated and volcanic archipelago separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Pacific Ocean. The four southernmost islands of the chain were annexed by the Soviet Union when it launched an invasion of Japanese territory toward the end of World War II.
During his trip, Putin visited the island of Iturup, where Russia operates a strategically important military base. Russia's president toured a fish processing complex, a hospital and a school, before holding a meeting with Valery Limarenko, the regional governor of Sakhalin.
The visit was also criticized by Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, who posted on Facebook that "Japan strongly protests this visit."
Japan renounced "all right, title and claim to the Kuril Islands" in the 1951 Treaty of San Francisco but did not recognize Soviet sovereignty over the territory.
The dispute over the islands has prevented Tokyo and Moscow from signing a peace treaty since the end of the war, although a 1956 joint declaration ended the state of war between the two nations.
Japan's defense white paper
Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said that Putin's visit was likely part of the Kremlin's response to Japan's latest defense white paper and aims to undermine Takaichi's efforts to improve Japan's defense capabilities.
Japan published its defense white paper earlier in the month, prompting outcry from Putin, as well as Russia's ally, North Korea. Russia's president criticized the white paper for identifying Moscow as one of Tokyo's critical threats.
"Russia is continuing active military activities in the Northern Territories, which are inherent territories of Japan, under illegal occupation," the white paper said.

Can a massive Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:27:00 UTC
21:27:00 KST

Can a giant Madonna help slow secularization in Poland?
August 14, 2026
With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Now there is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary towering above all this.
Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue.
The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is more than 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform.
The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base.
'Pile of concrete' or 'fantastic achievement?'
The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar.
Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months.
Opinion about the project is divided.
"It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete."
"This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout woman visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci.
Madonna statue financed by Poland's Warren Buffett
The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals.
Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school.
He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles.
Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street.
His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie.
A 'gesture of gratitude'
Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media.
The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million.
The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude."
According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses.
This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site.
Artist feared seeing the finished statue
"I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July.
"I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us."
Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife.
Polish region hopes for economic boost
Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce.
Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth.
"The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media.
Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records.
Not the first statue of its kind in Poland
Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures.
Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale.
The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers.
Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound.
Rising secularization
Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable.
Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline.
For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity.
In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia.
After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship.
During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police.
Pope John Paul II, himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime.
Catholicism in modern-day Poland
Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe.
According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period.
In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people.
Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend.
This article was originally published in German.

How to grow long hair: hairstylist names the main care rules
Ukraine

How to grow long hair: hairstylist names the main care rules
Kyiv • UNN
Hair grows about 1 cm per month, but breakage can hinder length retention. The expert recommends proper care, nutrition, and timely trimming of the ends.
Growing long hair is not always hindered by slow growth; instead, the length often fails to increase for other reasons. Hairdresser and colorist Oleksandra Sorokina told UNN journalist in more detail about which habits and care rules help preserve hair length.
According to the expert, hair grows by approximately one centimeter per month on average. However, it is important to work not only on growth but also on preserving the length that has already been grown.
The most common problem is not slow growth itself but hair breakage. On average, hair grows 1 cm per month, but damaged ends can break off, making it visually seem as though the length is not increasing
In particular, daily habits and at-home care affect the condition of the hair. In addition, Oleksandra Sorokina emphasizes that nutrition plays a separate role, since the body needs nutrients to maintain healthy hair.
First of all, it is properly selected at-home care. This means avoiding high temperatures, combing carefully, and avoiding constantly tight hairstyles. A complete diet is essential. Hair needs vitamin D, protein, iron, zinc, and other elements
Regarding regular haircuts, the hairdresser emphasizes that a haircut itself will not make hair grow faster. At the same time, timely removal of split ends helps preserve the length itself and can make the hair look thicker.
A haircut itself does not speed up hair growth because the hair shaft grows from the root. And timely trimming of split ends can visually increase density and preserve the length that has already been grown
The specialist also advises consulting an appropriate professional in order to have a basic set of hair products individually selected for daily care, which will make your particular hair shiny and healthy.
The essential at-home care products that everyone should have are shampoo, conditioner, a mask, and heat protection. At-home care should also be properly selected specifically for your scalp and hair type, and it is important to use it regularly
One of the common mistakes when trying to grow long hair, Oleksandra Sorokina says, is trying to focus solely on accelerating hair growth, while people may not pay enough attention to the condition of the length and ends.
The same common mistake is trying to accelerate hair growth specifically while ignoring the length and failing to care for it. To see hair growth, first of all, we need to properly select at-home care, preferably with a specialist. Balance your diet, address all vitamin deficiencies, and regularly assess the condition of your hair and trim the ends in a timely manner
In addition, the expert warns that one should not expect a significant increase in length over several months. According to Oleksandra Sorokina, during this time hair may grow by only a few centimeters.
It is also necessary to have realistic expectations, because over several months hair may grow by two, or at most 4 cm - under favorable circumstances. It is also better to focus specifically on preserving the hair ends and their quality

Europe must protect external borders amid migration crisis, says Meloni
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:25:31 UTC
21:25:31 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Friday that the migration crisis in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta demonstrates the need for Europe to protect its external borders.
"The vast majority of European nations share the position Italy has expressed in recent days: that Europe's priority is to protect its external borders from uncontrolled immigration, exclude any risk of security and terrorism and defend the freedom of movement that is the foundation of the Schengen system," she told Italian financial newspaper Milano Finanza.
She said the "serious migration crisis" in Ceuta and the possibility of another influx on Saturday required Italy to remain "extremely vigilant" and take all necessary measures.
Italy recently introduced temporary air and sea border controls with Spain following the arrival of more than 70,000 migrants in Ceuta in late July.
Madrid has criticized the Italian measure, noting that Ceuta is outside the Schengen area, meaning migrants arriving there cannot freely travel onward to other European countries. It also accused Rome of using the issue for domestic political purposes.
Spain, in turn, imposed similar border controls on travelers from Italy.
Rising energy costs
Meloni also addressed rising energy costs, saying her government would allocate €14 billion ($16.1 billion) in additional resources over the next two years to ease the financial burden on households and businesses.
She reaffirmed her government's commitment to nuclear energy, describing it as "the real solution" for improving Italy's energy security and achieving substantially lower costs over the medium and long term.
"The Italian economy is holding up well, and the data for the first two quarters of 2026 are encouraging," she added.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects the Italian economy to grow 0.5% in both 2026 and 2027, according to its July World Economic Outlook.
Meloni also said Italy's budget deficit had declined from 8.1% of gross domestic product when her government took office to 3.1%, while spending on health care, welfare and public-sector contracts had increased.

‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:23:04 UTC
21:23:04 KST

It ended, perhaps fittingly, on a rather baffling note. After 34 days of campaigning to regain the parliamentary seat of Clacton on England’s south coast, Nigel Farage, the leader of the Reform UK party, declined to turn up to the town’s leisure centre to hear himself declared the winner and MP. It was quite the thing. The last high-profile winning candidate to fail to enjoy his moment of victory was Bobby Sands in 1981. The IRA man had his reasons: he was on hunger strike in a prison in Northern Ireland, and went on to die 26 days later.
Instead Farage attended a gathering of his supporters at an airfield on the outskirts of Clacton billed by his party as “Farage Fest”. He told fans he would be damned if he was going to stand on a stage “having won a resounding victory” and “be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”.
But he also said Essex police had advised him of an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”. A Reform UK spokesperson went further: “Essex police advised Nigel not to attend the count tonight due to a credible threat against him.”
Not true, suggested the police. No such advice had been given. One of the shoutiest members of Farage’s anti-immigration party, Lee Anderson, had a slightly refreshed explanation by 8.10am when interviewed by the BBC. His leader had not wanted to disrespect those who had flocked to Farage Fest. He was, actually, if you will just listen just for a moment, a man of principle. “It was a great occasion that it is only right that he spends that time with his members, with his activists, with his supporters,” Anderson fumed.
All this left one intergalactic explorer, with his arms raised and a bin on his no doubt sweaty head, to take the starring role at Clacton leisure centre. The candidate who went by the name of Count Binface made a declaration on social media: “I came first in the Clacton byelection! Of the candidates who bothered to turn up for the results.”
Count Binface, for those who have not been following this latest fever dream of a moment in British politics, is the parody figure who declared himself the unity candidate when Farage triggered the byelection by resigning the seat back in July.
Farage had explained his resignation at the time as a challenge to the establishment that would show them that the people did not want him scrutinised and investigated by the parliamentary authorities over an undeclared £5m gift from a crypto billionaire or any of the other financial scandals orbiting Reform UK.
The other major political parties called his bluff. It was a stunt, they said, and none of them stood, leaving Count Binface, a familiar and striking figure at elections, whose real name is Jon Harvey, to harvest the anti-Farage vote. And he could reasonably be said to have done rather well, given that he won just 95 votes at the recent byelection in Makerfield, in Greater Manchester, where Andy Burnham, now the prime minister, won his parliamentary seat.
Binface, who describes himself as an “independent space warrior” from the planet Sigma IX, won 26.93% of the ballot with 9,455 votes, leaving him second to Farage who secured 22,239 votes (63.34%). There was a healthy 44% turnout.
Perhaps – and it is only a theory going round the leisure centre in Clacton – Farage was actually not at the count because he did not fancy the inevitable photograph of him next to his ludicrous competition?
“That means I’ve got – against Nigel Farage – 10,000% more votes than I got against Andy Burnham,” Binface later said of his electoral tally. “What does that tell you? Well it tells you that Nigel, who said that he didn’t want to be humiliated, maybe has been. As for me, I’m over the moon – I’m over your moon, I’m over my moons – and what comes next, well we shall see. But you know what, we know this for a fact: over one in four people in this constituency would rather have Count Binface as their MP than the leader of Reform UK.”
That was the Binface take on an election estimated to have cost the public purse £250,000. Others were available. For the fired-up Anderson, who scolded the BBC presenter Justin Webb for being “very rude” for interrupting him on Friday morning, there was one clear reading of that night’s events.
“[Nigel Farage is] celebrating a stunning victory in Clacton and the people have decided: they’ve stuck two fingers up to people like the BBC, the establishment, the blob, the whole of Westminster,” Anderson said. “There has been a constant witch-hunt by people in the media.
“There’s been a witch-hunt against Nigel Farage and he said: ‘You know what? Enough’s enough. Meet me at the ballot box.’ And when it comes to a crunch, when he does throw the gauntlet down to the other political parties, what happens? They run away like the cowards they are. He challenges them at the ballot box and he wins.”
Naturally enough, that wasn’t how the other main parties saw it. “All Farage can brag about this morning is beating a bloke with a bin on his head,” said a Conservative party spokesperson. “What he should do is answer the serious outstanding questions about why he hid his £5m from the public.”
Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the governing Labour party, said: “There’s no hiding place now and Nigel Farage needs to answer to the public as to exactly what’s going on.”
As election workers sorted through the voting ballots at the leisure centre in the early hours of Friday morning, one moment caught by photographers also tells a story.
Across the 90cm long ballot paper containing all the names of the parody and independent candidates for the seat of Clacton (it was the longest ballot paper in UK electoral history), a disgruntled voter had made their mark: “What a disgraceful waste of money.”
Three hours after Farage’s victory was declared, the suspended parliamentary standards investigation into the Reform UK leader over accusations he failed to declare gifts and donations had resumed.

21:23:01 KST

Vote counting suspended then restarted under heightened security in Zambia election
LUSAKA, Zambia (AP) — Vote counting in Zambia’s presidential election was suspended Friday and then restarted hours later under heightened security after the electoral commission said there had been attacks against some polling station officials and some ballot papers had been stolen.
While the counting was suspended, riot police and army vehicles deployed to parts of the capital, Lusaka, including the main vote tallying center, though there were no immediate reports of any major unrest.
It was an unusual development for the southern African country of 22 million people, which has held largely peaceful elections since it returned to multiparty democracy in 1991.
“The violence is targeted at poll staff and in some instances has resulted in the theft of marked ballot papers in ballot boxes,” the Electoral Commission of Zambia said in a statement announcing vote counting had been halted.
It did not say who was responsible for the violence or the alleged theft of ballot papers.
Electoral commission head Mwangala Zaloumis later announced counting would start again and said the violence affected a small number of polling stations in Lusaka.
“Following a review of the security situation and consultations with the relevant law enforcement agencies, I’m pleased to inform you and to inform the nation that the security threat to the electoral process has been contained,” she said at a press briefing.
The main opposition candidate said his alliance of parties had “received deeply troubling reports from several parts of the country” and called into question the credibility of the vote.
Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema, who ran for a second five-year term, called for Zambians to “remain peaceful, patient and patriotic as we await the official outcome from those entrusted with managing the vote” in a statement on X.
Thursday’s election was seen as a test of Hichilema’s economic recovery plan after the copper-rich nation was plunged into a debt crisis in 2020. Hichilema was elected in 2021 and oversaw the restructuring of Zambia’s sovereign debt while reining in inflation and stabilizing the currency.
But critics say that economic stability has not trickled down to many people in Zambia, where poverty is widespread. The most prominent issues for the election were the high cost of living and electricity shortages.
Hichilema, 64, was one of 14 candidates in the presidential election, but his biggest challenge was thought to come from Brian Mundubile, a 55-year-old law graduate who emerged this year as the leader of an opposition alliance.
Zambians also voted for members of Parliament and local government councilors. About 8 million people were registered to vote at more than 13,500 polling stations.
On Friday, Mundubile said the suspension of the vote counting could lead to “an opportunity for interference with or manipulation of the results.”
“Put the records before the nation and allow every number to be reconciled. The people of Zambia voted. Their decision must be respected,” he said.
Mundubile said he had received information that members of the military had taken control of vote counting stations in at least one town and boxes containing ballots had been taken away from stations in other places, though he did not provide any evidence for those claims in a statement he made on video.
Zambia gained independence from Britain in 1964 and was a one-party state from 1973 to 1991. It has held largely peaceful votes and transfers of power between parties and political alliances since then.
However, there was some criticism of Hichilema ahead of this election by the opposition and independent rights groups, which said his government was squeezing dissent. Mundubile’s alliance accused the government of being behind a law enforcement agency raid on its offices days before the election and claimed the action was designed to hurt the alliance’s campaign.
Hichilema himself was once imprisoned on charges of treason when he was an opposition leader in 2017 during a bitter rivalry with then-President Edgar Lungu. He was held for four months after his motorcade did not give way to Lungu’s on a road and claimed he was tortured during his imprisonment.
Hichilema was released after international condemnation of the arrest and beat Lungu in an election in 2021.
Mundubile served in Lungu’s government and rose to lead the opposition alliance challenging Hichilema after Lungu died last year.

How to help after Colombia’s devastating earthquake

How to help after Colombia’s devastating earthquake
Just weeks after twin earthquakes devastated Venezuela, neighboring Colombia suffered its own deadly temblor Monday, leaving responders, volunteers and loved ones desperately searching for missing people and tending to those displaced or injured.
The 7.4 magnitude earthquake affected a large swath of western Colombia, from urban centers like Cali and Pereira to remote and rugged areas in the department of Chocó. As of Friday morning, authorities had confirmed more than 280 dead, thousands injured and over 12,000 dwellings destroyed. Responders have managed to rescue about 350 people, but hundreds remain missing.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has promised a robust governmental response. But with so much need spread across a large area, aid groups will also play important roles helping those needing shelter, supplies and economic assistance.
“Institutional capacity does not remove the humanitarian need,” said Catalina Vargas, Colombia country director for the humanitarian group CARE. “The most severely affected area, Chocó, is also one of the most isolated and underserved parts of the country, so access remains the binding constraint regardless of the strength of national institutions.”
For those who can help, giving cash is often ideal to give groups flexibility and agility, said Abe Diaz, head of disaster relief for Amazon, which is providing requested supplies to partners.
“Unrequested product donations overwhelm communities and force responders to divert resources from life-saving work just to sort and store unwanted supplies,” Diaz said.
Here are some organizations collecting donations for Colombia earthquake recovery, including U.S. groups responding on the ground and some local organizations accepting outside funds.
U.S.-based groups already on the ground
All Hands and Hearts has provided search and rescue tools like jackhammers and pickaxes to the Pereira fire department as well as blankets and rehydration supplies for those affected. Link to donate.
CARE has a longtime presence in Colombia. Its immediate support will focus on food assistance through cash and vouchers, emergency supply care packages, and protection and emotional support for affected families. Link to donate.
Direct Relief is funding medical responders on the ground and preparing to deliver requested medications and healthcare supplies. Link to donate.
GEM is joining with local partners to provide essential kits with food, water, and hygiene necessities. Link to donate.
Operation Blessing is focusing its initial response on providing food and water, as well as solar lanterns, to displaced people. Link to donate.
Save the Children has worked in Colombia for over 40 years and has begun psychosocial support activities and set up multiple child-friendly spaces in affected areas. Link to donate.
World Central Kitchen is providing food and water for displaced people, first responders and volunteers, including in more remote mountain communities. Link to donate.
Marc Anthony leads Sunday benefit concert for Colombia and Venezuela
Latin music stars Marc Anthony, Luis Fonsi, Chayanne, Feid, Jay Wheeler and many more will perform at an international benefit concert for Venezuela and Colombia on Aug. 16 at 6 p.m. EDT at Miami’s Kaseya Center. It will be carried live on Univision, ViX, WAPA and TelevisaUnivision radio stations, iHeartLatino and Venevision Play in Venezuela.
Viewers can donate by scanning onscreen QR codes, texting UNIDOS to 707070 or visiting univision.org during the broadcast. Proceeds will go to All Hands and Hearts, CARE, GEM, TECHO and World Central Kitchen.
Colombia-based groups accepting outside donations
Abaco Colombia, an association of 26 food banks across Colombia, is distributing food to affected families across the impacted regions. They accept online donations, though the payment processor requires a passport number.
Cruz Roja Colombiana teams are doing search and rescue, offering medical attention and psychosocial support, and filling other needs. They accept online donations, though the payment processor requires a passport number.
Fundación Solidaridad por Colombia supports youth initiatives, nutrition and health, and community building. It’s helping deliver relief supplies and food to displaced people in Pereira and other locations. They accept PayPal.
Fundación Semillas de Oportunidades supports youth through art and sport from its base in Quibdó, Chocó. They are supporting families of young people across Chocó. They accept PayPal.
Manos Visibles, a network of organizations dedicated to racial and territorial equity, is collaborating with a local trade school with a goal to restore at least 100 homes in the city of Buenaventura. They accept online donations, though the payment processor requires a passport number.
Presentes Corporation, a 43-year-old organization in Colombia focused on community resilience, is partnering with the Miami-based nonprofit Give to Colombia to facilitate donations from the U.S. Their Colombia Se Levanta fund accepts online donations.
Refugio Huellas de Amor in Pereira is supporting rescue animals already in their care as well as other impacted animals. Huellitas Callejeras Barranquilla is sending vets and medical supplies to affected areas. Both accept PayPal.

Myanmar faces rise in diarrhea as monsoon flooding continue to worsen in many parts of the country
BANGKOK (AP) — Myanmar’s largest city has registered a concerning rise in acute diarrhea cases, state media said Friday, adding to the hardships of a country grappling with severe flooding and civil war.
The state-run Myanma Alinn newspaper said 182 patients from Yangon were admitted to the city’s general hospital with diarrhea the past four days, including 93 who tested positive for diarrhea-causing pathogens.
The report did not specify the pathogens detected or whether the cases were confirmed as cholera.
The Myanmar news outlet Eleven Media, citing Aye Mya Thae Phyu, a lawmaker from Yangon’s Latha township, reported on Wednesday that the patients who tested positive had cholera.
The military’s information team told journalists Thursday that a 92-year-old patient died from the disease.
Aung Lin Aye, deputy medical superintendent at Yangon General Hospital, was quoted in Friday’s newspaper as saying that the number of diarrhea cases had increased significantly over the previous days and the hospital was providing treatment with a focus on preventing deaths.
Nanda Win, head of the Yangon Regional Department of Public Health, said cases were particularly concentrated in downtown Yangon’s Chinatown area, where street food vendors, restaurants and bars are clustered, according to the report.
He pointed to takeout food and contaminated water used by street vendors as possible sources of the illness, while noting that the number of cases had begun to decline.
Another state-run newspaper, Global New Light of Myanmar, said authorities asked street food vendors selling high-risk items to close for about three days to curb the spread.
Three bars and restaurants in Chinatown confirmed the three-day closure to The Associated Press.
Acute diarrhea is a recurring challenge for Yangon during the monsoon season. In 2024, more than 2,200 people were hospitalized with acute watery diarrhea in Yangon, with 15 deaths reported, according to World Health Organization data.
The latest development comes as flooding continues to affect communities elsewhere in the country, adding to the pressures on a population already struggling with years of conflict after the army seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

Copper wire thefts hit 650 electric vehicle charging stations in France this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:20:50 UTC
21:20:50 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Copper cable thefts have affected 650 electric vehicle charging stations across France since the beginning of the year, causing an estimated €13 million (about $15 million) in losses, an industry representative said Friday.
Matthieu Dischamps, secretary-general of Charge France and managing director of charging operator Powerdot, told French broadcaster BFMTV that the thefts were also disrupting travel for the country’s 3 million electric vehicle users and discouraging other motorists from switching to electric cars.
Public fast-charging stations are particularly vulnerable because their cables are attached to the units and remain easily accessible, Dischamps said.
Thieves receive only around €20 to €30 for the copper in each stolen cable, while replacing one costs operators approximately €1,500, he added.
Charging companies have introduced reinforced cable protection, video surveillance and GPS tracking devices in response. Some cables are also being filled with pressurized methylene blue, which leaves an invisible, indelible trace on offenders to help police identify them.
Authorities in the most affected departments have begun incorporating charging stations into police and gendarmerie patrol routes. Operators’ telephone numbers are also receiving priority status so authorities can respond more quickly when companies detect cables being cut.
Dischamps warned that around 10% of France’s charging network had been affected and that continued thefts could lead to higher charging prices or even bankruptcies among some operators.
Copper theft has also disrupted telecommunications infrastructure.
Jean-Philippe Brun, mayor of Porte-de-Seine in the northwestern Eure department, said the entire municipality lost internet and telephone services late Wednesday after thieves cut cables in eight underground access points spread across approximately 2 kilometers (1.2 miles).
The thieves apparently cut both copper and fiber-optic lines because they could not distinguish between them, he said.
Brun said the perpetrators appeared to be highly organized, as removing and transporting cables over such a distance would probably require a truck.
The gendarmerie has opened an investigation.
Fiber-optic services were subsequently restored, but residents still relying on copper telephone connections, particularly older people who may need to contact emergency services, were most severely affected.

Two killed on A59 as tractors head to farmers’ protest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:20:36 UTC
21:20:36 KST

Jetten tells farmers to get off motorways after two die in crash
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Prime minister Rob Jetten has said it is “unacceptable” that tractors were driving on the A59 motorway on Friday, after two people were killed and six injured in a crash. The collision happened at the back of a queue that had built up as the tractors drove to a protest in Den Bosch.
“It is unacceptable and incomprehensible to demonstrate on the motorway because it leads to very dangerous situations,” Jetten said during a press conference.
Jetten also said the decision not to stop the tractors earlier was not a good signal and would have to be reviewed. News agency ANP reported that 50 tractors were driving on the A2 towards Utrecht as he spoke. “Don’t do it, get off the motorway,” Jetten said.
Police said four cars were involved and that they were still investigating what caused the collision, but no tractors were involved.
The victims have not been identified. The tractors had been in the right-hand lane and other traffic could pass on the left, but a traffic jam still built up.
Disputed agreements
 Tractors are not permitted on Dutch motorways. Earlier this week the public prosecution department (OM) and the police said they would not stop farmers who drove onto them, citing the right to demonstrate.
A spokesperson for the OM in Oost-Brabant told broadcaster NOS that this had not been agreed. The authorities help demonstrations go ahead, the spokesperson said, but once a tractor is on the motorway it is up to the local mayor, police and prosecutors to decide when and how to step in.
“A tractor on the motorway is never allowed, and is a criminal offence” the spokesperson said. The OM did not answer questions from NOS about what had been agreed instead, or why nobody intervened.
Provincial council members held a minute’s silence for the two dead. Mark van den Oever of Farmers Defence Force called on farmers at the provincial offices not to travel home by motorway.
What the protest is about
 Noord-Brabant’s provincial executive intends to revoke the nature permits of five poultry farms close to protected nature areas, after environmental groups won a court case in April 2025.
The court found the protected areas were overloaded with nitrogen, and that the farms were a significant cause. But it stopped short of ordering the permits withdrawn, giving the province, the farmers and the environmental groups a year to come up with a plan that would cut nitrogen levels for good.
The farmers sent in their plans in November 2025 but in July were told their permits would be revoked, although that decision is not yet final. The provincial executive has admitted it never gave them a proper response to those plans, Omroep Brabant reported.
Members of the provincial council, which oversees the executive, broke off their summer break on Friday for a debate on the plan demanded by seven opposition parties, led by farmers’ party BBB. Saskia Boelema, the executive member responsible, told them the province should have sat down with the farmers earlier and apologised for the way the process had been handled.

Russia’s state statisticians report the growth Putin demanded—economists doubt it will hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:20:15 UTC
21:20:15 KST

Russia's economy grew 1.3% in the second quarter of 2026, the state news agency TASS reported on 12 August, citing preliminary estimates from the state statistics agency Rosstat — a figure that, if accurate, would end a slump that had opened the year with the country's first quarterly contraction since 2023.
And it comes from a state agency months after Putin dressed down his economic team in April and demanded "concrete measures" to restore growth — the print then beat the government's own economists in exactly the direction he wanted.
The quarter may have brought a real if shallow rebound, or the state's statisticians may have produced the figure the president wanted. Either way it matters, because Russia's economy is what pays for its war, and its strength sets the ceiling on how long the Kremlin can keep fighting.
Barely growing all year
Even taken straight, the rebound is thinner than it looks. The first quarter had closed 0.2% down, and across the whole first half of the year output rose just 0.6%, half of last year's pace and close to seven times slower than the wartime boom of 2023 and 2024. The quarterly figure jumped. The underlying trend barely moved.
The weakness had been building for over a year. War spending drove the 2023–24 boom and overheated the economy; to curb the resulting inflation, the central bank raised its key rate to 21%, choking lending and investment. It has cut rates since, to 14% in July, but money is still tight and inflation is rising again as Ukrainian strikes push up fuel prices.
Growth the war paid for
As The Moscow Times set out, reviewing the data and the economists reading it, most of the quarter's growth rested on one-off factors: more working days than a year earlier, a temporary oil-revenue spike during the Iran war, and a budget that lifted spending 16%, a third of it on the army and weapons. The split underneath is the tell.
Military plants kept raising output; civilian industry kept shrinking, down 3.2% from a year earlier by the Center for Macroeconomic Analysis and Short-Term Forecasting (CMASF), a Russian forecasting institute, according to its estimate.
Rosstat also billed the quarter as its strongest in six, and said it had beaten the forecasts of both the economy ministry, which had projected 0.9%, and the central bank, which saw 0.8%.
Few expect it to last
Russia will "remain in a state of stagnation" for the foreseeable future, said Liam Peach of Capital Economics, citing high interest rates and the fuel crisis.
Ukraine's long-range drones are adding to the strain. Their strikes have cut Russian oil refining to its lowest level in more than two decades, draining fuel supply and pushing prices up at home, and forcing Moscow, an oil giant, to import gasoline from as far as Morocco.

The remains of Yevhen Konovalets were brought to a UGCC cathedral in Kyiv
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
15:17:39 EEST
21:17:39 KST

The remains of Yevhen Konovalets were brought to a UGCC cathedral in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
The remains of Yevhen Konovalets, the founder of the OUN, were returned to Ukraine after being exhumed in Rotterdam. They will be temporarily reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery and, in the future, transferred to the Pantheon of Heroes.
The remains of Yevhen Konovalets, the founder and first head of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, have been returned to Ukraine 88 years after his death. This was reported by UNN.
Details
As reported by Deputy Head of the Office of the President Iryna Vereshchuk, they were received with state and military honors.
The farewell ceremony for the prominent Ukrainian will take place at the Patriarchal Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ of the UGCC in Kyiv, after which the remains will be temporarily reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery. At the same time, it will not become the final eternal resting place for one of the leaders of the Ukrainian liberation movement. In the future, Konovalets’s remains are planned to be transferred to the Pantheon of National Heroes. This will take place immediately after its creation.
Before the farewell ceremony, the colonel’s remains underwent a comprehensive examination using modern methods. According to Vereshchuk, specialists, historians, and anthropologists were involved in the work. Even computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging were used.
Exhumation in Rotterdam
The exhumation of Yevhen Konovalets’s remains was carried out on August 11 at the “Crooswijk” Cemetery in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
A memorial service was held at the burial site, led by Bishop Ihor Rantsi of the Paris Eparchy of St. Volodymyr the Great of the UGCC, in a joint service with Ukrainian priests in the Netherlands.
The ceremony was also attended by Oleksandr Alfiorov, head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory.
It was decided to preserve the gravestone, cross, and other elements of Konovalets’s grave in the Netherlands. They were transported to the colonel’s native village of Zashkiv in Lviv region, where his museum-estate is located.
The return of Konovalets’s remains was organized with the participation of the Office of the President, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory. Before this, the Ukrainian side obtained the necessary permits from the Rotterdam authorities for the exhumation and transportation of the remains.
Who was Yevhen Konovalets
Yevhen Konovalets was a colonel in the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, commander of the Sich Riflemen, one of the founders of the Ukrainian Military Organization, and founder of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists.
After the OUN was established in 1929, Konovalets became its first head and led the organization until his death.
On May 23, 1938, Konovalets was killed in Rotterdam as a result of a special operation by the Soviet secret services, carried out on the personal orders of Joseph Stalin. An NKVD agent, Pavlo Sudoplatov, a native of Melitopol, gave him an explosive device disguised as a gift—a box of chocolates. Konovalets died at the scene of the explosion.
On May 28, 1938, he was buried at the “Crooswijk” Cemetery. After the funeral, Konovalets’s comrades announced their intention to transfer his remains to Ukrainian soil in the future, after the restoration of an independent state.
The colonel’s body was returned to his homeland 88 years after his death.
Context
The return of Yevhen Konovalets’s remains is part of the process of reburial in Ukraine of prominent figures of the Ukrainian liberation movement who died or were killed abroad.
In May 2026, the remains of another OUN leader and colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Andrii Melnyk, and his wife, Sofiia Fedak-Melnyk, were returned to Ukraine. On May 24, they were reburied at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
In the future, the Ukrainian side is also considering the possibility of returning the remains of Yevhen Konovalets’s wife, Olha, and their son, Yurii, who are buried in Rome.
Reminder
Earlier, we reported that the Government ordered the reburial of the remains of Colonel of the Army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic and first head of the OUN Yevhen Konovalets at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.

NATO jets shoot down drone over Latvia
August 14, 2026
NATO fighter jets have shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the alliance and Latvian authorities said Friday.
Two Italian Eurofighters were scrambled and one destroyed the unmanned aircraft, while two Turkish F-16s were also deployed under NATO command.
What happened over Latvia?
Latvia's military initially issued an air alert and urged people in affected areas to remain indoors and seek shelter.
Authorities said the foreign drone entered Latvian airspace over the Balvi region as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity.
It was not immediately clear where the drone originated, and NATO said an investigation was underway.
Latvian authorities did not identify the drone as Ukrainian.
However, the reference to Russian electronic warfare raised the possibility that a Ukrainian drone targeting Russia had been forced off course by interference.
Ukrainian forces had attacked targets in northwestern Russia overnight, according to Latvian media.
Has this happened before?
Latvia and other NATO countries along the alliance's eastern flank have faced repeated incursions by drones since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A stray drone was also shot down over Latvia in early June, while other Ukrainian drones heading toward northwestern Russia have previously entered Latvian airspace and crashed.
Romanian and Spanish fighter jets were also deployed on Thursday after drones entered Romanian airspace near Ukraine.
Why are Italian jets defending Latvian airspace?
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not operate their own fighter aircraft, so NATO allies rotate responsibility for policing their skies.
The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday's interception are based at Siauliai air base in Lithuania.
