Tehran brings back cleric behind 2009 protest crackdown to head its Basij militia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:52:20 UTC
19:52:20 KST

Hossein Taeb commanded the Basij during the mass demonstrations of June 2009 and led the IRGC's intelligence service for 13 years, overseeing operations against journalists, dual nationals and dissidents. His return signals that Tehran fears it might need to manage unrest in the near future.
Hossein Taeb, the cleric who commanded the Basij during the 2009 crackdown on the Green Movement and led the Revolutionary Guards' intelligence service for 13 years, has been reappointed as head of the IRGC's militia.
The decision to bring back one of the Islamic Republic's most senior internal security figures to a frontline position in the early months of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei's rule is part of a recent reshuffle among the Islamic Republic's political, military and security elites.
The appointment signals that the Tehran regime's new leadership is preparing for possible unrest at home, amid the ongoing war with the US and mounting economic pressure from sanctions.
Who is Hossein Taeb?
Taeb joined the IRGC as a teenager and later served in the Ministry of Intelligence before returning to the Guards.
He became Basij commander in July 2008, less than a year before Iran's disputed presidential election triggered the mass demonstrations of June 2009 known as the Green Movement.
The Basij played a central role in the crackdown that followed. The US sanctioned Taeb in 2010 over his command responsibility for the violence, with the EU following suit in 2011.
In late 2009, he was appointed the first head of the newly created IRGC Intelligence Organisation.
He held that position for roughly 13 years, during which the body became one of the country's most powerful security institutions, at times competing with and frequently overshadowing the civilian Ministry of Intelligence.
Under his tenure, the organisation expanded into cases involving political opponents, journalists, environmental activists and dual nationals.
The most prominent operation associated with his time as IRGC intelligence chief was the capture and extradition of Ruhollah Zam, an Iranian dissident living in France who ran the popular Telegram channel Amad News.
The IRGC brought Zam to Iran in 2019. He was executed in 2020.
Taeb was replaced in June 2022 by Mohammad Kazemi and moved to an advisory role under the IRGC commander.
His removal followed a period of significant intelligence failures, including operations attributed to Israel that exposed serious weaknesses in Iran's counter-intelligence.
These included alleged penetrations of sensitive sites and the killing of nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh in November 2020 outside Tehran.
Iranian authorities never publicly confirmed those failures as the reason for his departure.
Taeb was not expelled from the security establishment, but was instead moved directly into another senior position.
Taeb and Mojtaba Khamenei are reported to have longstanding ties dating back to the Iran-Iraq War, during which both were associated with the Habib battalion of the IRGC's 27th Mohammad Rasulollah Division.
Networks formed at the time later became significant pathways to institutional advancement within Iran's security structure for the most loyal cadre.
His return to the Basij under Mojtaba Khamenei's leadership, rather than his retirement after the 2022 setback, suggests those ties remain close.
Why the Basij matters
The Basij maintains a presence in neighbourhoods, places of worship, universities and government offices and has been used to monitor citizens and communities, mobilise regime support and suppress protests.
The order appointing Taeb emphasised expanding the Basij's "popular intelligence network," improving training and integrating new technologies — language that points to Tehran's renewed interest in its domestic surveillance.
Placing a veteran intelligence official in charge of the Basij could allow the force to shift from a body deployed reactively after protests erupt to one embedded in a broader system that detects and contains dissent before it spreads.
The choice of Taeb — who has moved from one top position to another within the security apparatus over four decades without being permanently removed from the establishment's core — also indicates that the IRGC, an elite paramilitary corps that answers directly to the ayatollah, remains crucial to decision-making in Tehran.
Former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad publicly accused him in 2018 of fabricating cases against political opponents, in a rare public dispute over power between the presidency and the IRGC intelligence apparatus.
During Hassan Rouhani's presidency, the IRGC intelligence service under Taeb openly challenged the civilian Ministry of Intelligence in several high-profile cases, in another shift in security and political power toward institutions directly linked to the ayatollah.

Admissions-2026: 175,000 applicants admitted to the first year
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Education and Science announced the completion of the first stage of the admissions campaign. A total of 175,013 people have been admitted to bachelor's programs and medical master's programs, of whom 69,748 will study at public expense.
Higher education institutions in Ukraine have completed the first stage of admissions to bachelor's and medical master's programs — 175,013 applicants have been enrolled in the first year, the Ministry of Education and Science reported, UNN writes.
The first stage of the admissions campaign is over — 175,013 applicants have been enrolled in the first year
As of August 14, as stated, the enrollment orders include:
-  165,585 applicants — to bachelor's programs; 
-  9,428 — to medical, pharmaceutical, and veterinary master's programs; 
-  69,748 — state-funded; 
-  105,265 — contract-funded. 
In total, during the first wave, applicants received 212,837 recommendations for enrollment in state-funded places and places financed by individuals and/or legal entities. The enrollment requirements were fulfilled for 180,022 applications.
Among the applicants admitted under Quota 2, 6,141 students have been enrolled.
Which priorities did applicants fulfill the requirements under
Most applicants had the opportunity to study under one of their most preferred applications — 85.3% of confirmed applications correspond to the three highest priorities.
Among applicants admitted to state-funded places, the share of the three highest priorities is even greater: of the 70,867 confirmed applications for state-funded places, 66,166, or 93.4%, correspond to the first three priorities. More than 73% of applicants admitted to state-funded places fulfilled the requirements under their first-priority application.
The admissions campaign continues
Applicants who did not receive recommendations or did not confirm them may continue to participate in the competitive selection, but only for vacant contract-funded places. The enrollment of applicants from this group will continue until August 30.
In addition, starting September 1, higher education institutions may hold additional admissions to contract-funded places within the time frames specified in their Admission Rules.
Therefore, if an applicant did not use the entire application limit (this year, up to 10 applications could be submitted, including up to 5 for state-funded places), they may use the remaining slots if the educational institution conducts a corresponding additional admission process.

Russia to abolish border zones with occupied Ukrainian territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:50:40 UTC
19:50:40 KST

Moscow will begin removing border zones between Russia and occupied areas of Ukraine, according to internal FSB documents obtained by independent Russian media outlet Agentstvo and published on Aug. 13.
Border zones in Rostov and Voronezh oblasts along Russia's boundary with occupied parts of Luhansk and Donetsk oblasts will be eliminated due to the "completion of the annexation" of the so-called Luhansk People's Republic and Donetsk People's Republic, the documents state.
The border zones between occupied Crimea and the occupied parts of Kherson Oblast will also be eliminated for the same stated reason. In Crimea, Russia will retain a border regime "within the Black Sea islands belonging to the Russian Federation," according to the documents.
Russia illegally annexed Crimea in 2014 and declared the annexation of the partially occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts in 2022, treating sovereign Ukrainian territory as part of Russia.
It is not clear whether the elimination of the border zones will mean the removal of checkpoints connecting territory Russia claims to have annexed, or whether this will be merely an administrative change.
Since Russia first occupied Ukrainian territory in 2014, Russian-occupied areas have gained a reputation for gangsterism and lawlessness.
Russian authorities kept border controls in place in an attempt to stop smuggling of guns, drugs, and other illicit cargo back into Russian territory.
The border move is the latest in a long line by the Kremlin to Russify Ukrainian territory. 
Russian President Vladimir Putin in March signed a decree that indefinitely extends the ease of obtaining Russian citizenship in the occupied territories, a move that experts say is a sign that Russia is consolidating its occupation by pursuing mass passportization.
The March 4 decree removed the deadline for residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to obtain Russian citizenship through a simplified process established by a 2022 Russian law, effectively making the policy permanent.
"The goal of the new decree is to passportize as many people as possible, pressuring them," Nataliia Yurlova, lawyer for the NGO Donbas SOS, told the Kyiv Independent.
"In general, Russia has been issuing passports to Ukrainians in occupation for quite a long time, and each time new requirements are imposed on our citizens."
Also in March, Human Rights Watch (HRW) called on Russia to end what it described as "illegal property seizures" in occupied Ukraine, along with pressure on residents to obtain Russian citizenship, nationality-based discrimination, and restrictions on Ukrainians' travel to Russian-occupied territories.
Putin signed a law in December 2025 enabling the seizure of Ukrainian-owned housing in occupied territories by allowing occupation authorities to declare it "ownerless."
According to the HRW report, displaced Ukrainians face major obstacles to reclaiming their property, including the need for a Russian passport and the dangers of traveling through Russia, as it is nearly impossible to return to the occupied territories from Ukrainian-controlled areas.

Russia exploits Poland-Ukraine dispute to step up disinformation campaign, officials and experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:50:22 UTC
19:50:22 KST

Russia exploits Poland-Ukraine dispute to step up disinformation campaign, officials and experts say
WARSAW, Aug 14 - Russia has significantly stepped up its online disinformation campaign in Poland, using a dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv over World War Two massacres to inflame tensions between Ukraine and its key ally, Polish officials and researchers say.
The messaging, mostly posted on social media accounts in Polish, also focuses on fomenting anger in Poland against refugees, as opinion polls show support for the far-right growing ahead of closely contested parliamentary elections in 2027.
The long-running World War Two dispute centres on the Volhynia massacres, in which Poland says Ukrainians killed around 100,000 Poles between 1943 and 1945. Thousands of Ukrainians died in reprisal killings.
The dispute intensified after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy named an army unit after insurgents who perpetrated the massacres, prompting hard-right President Karol Nawrocki to strip his Ukrainian counterpart of a top Polish honour in June.
Polish deputy digital minister Pawel Olszewski told Reuters the dispute saw Russian disinformation "explode" across social and official Russian media platforms, including Telegram, in posts later repeated by Polish outlets.
An analysis by the state-backed Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM) found online anti-Ukrainian content in Polish on X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube increased by more than 250% following Zelenskiy's naming of the army unit.
Much of the increase across those platforms and others appeared to be artificially generated through bot activity designed to create the impression of rapidly growing anti-Ukrainian sentiment, said PISM's Filip Bryjka.
The messaging focused largely on amplifying the controversy rather than disseminating false information, in what analysts said may be a new Russian disinformation tactic.
Moscow denies spreading disinformation and says Western leaders are intentionally exaggerating the threat from Russia for their own political ends.
"The Russian Federation does not interfere in the relations between other states," the Russian embassy in Warsaw said in an emailed statement, adding that accusations about Russia spreading disinformation to undermine support for Ukraine are baseless.
POLICY TOWARDS UKRAINIANS COULD INFLUENCE ELECTION
Because the underlying facts are often real, analysts say such campaigns are harder to identify and counter than conventional disinformation through fake news.
"The event is real, but the interpretation is imposed by an external actor," said Wojciech Pokora, analyst at Info Ops Poland Foundation, an independent research project.
Though Poland remains a staunch ally of Ukraine in its war against Russia, opinion polls show deteriorating support for Ukraine. An IBRiS poll published early last month found that 33.6% of respondents said their attitude towards Ukrainians had worsened following the dispute linked to World War Two.
A separate IBRiS survey published last month found support for continued military assistance to Ukraine had fallen to 52% from 78% in 2022.
Experts say negative sentiment towards Ukraine cannot be explained solely by foreign influence and also reflects weariness with an estimated 1.8 to 1.9 million Ukrainian migrants, disputes over grain imports and the legacy of the World War Two killings.
The flood of disinformation about the dispute has "fallen on fertile ground", the digital ministry's Olszewski said.
Ukrainians living in Poland have faced mounting hostility in recent months, prompting Prime Minister Donald Tusk to call for an end to xenophobic attacks.
Pollsters say policy towards Ukrainians could be a key election theme as polling suggests Tusk's pro-European government may struggle to retain power next year. REUTERS

Israeli strikes on Hamas officials seeks to 'destabilise' Gaza ceasefire
The sound of Israeli warplanes has returned to parts of Gaza after days of relative quiet, reviving fears that the ceasefire may be little more than a pause before another escalation.
On Thursday, Israeli strikes killed two Palestinians, including Gaza's police chief, Jamal Abu Kmeil, and a man identified by Palestinian sources as a Hamas member.
Israel claimed the men were Hamas operatives involved in planning attacks and maintained that its forces were operating within the terms of the ceasefire.
Hamas, however, described the strikes as violations of the agreement and accused Israel of seeking to destabilise Gaza.
For Palestinians, the distinction offers little reassurance.
"The word ceasefire means very little when we still hear strikes and people are being killed," Mohammed Ayoub, a Gaza resident, told The New Arab. "We thought the quiet meant that perhaps the war was finally ending. Now we are afraid that the strikes will start increasing again."
The attacks come as negotiations over the next stage of the ceasefire remain centred on Hamas's disarmament, an Israeli withdrawal and future security arrangements in Gaza.
Israel continues killing Hamas officials
Abu Kmeil, 43, was travelling in his vehicle in the Sheikh Ajleen area of southwestern Gaza City when an Israeli aircraft struck it, according to Gaza's Interior Ministry and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
Several people were wounded and taken to Al-Shifa Hospital.
Abu Kmeil had remained at his post throughout the war, according to Gaza's Interior Ministry, and had spoken publicly about efforts by police and local community leaders to maintain order.
The Israeli army claimed the strike was carried out under Shin Bet direction and described Abu Kmeil as a "Hamas operative who infiltrated Israeli territory during the 7 October 2023 massacre."
It accused him of advancing plans for attacks against Israeli troops and civilians during the war and in recent months, saying it acted "to eliminate the threat."
The army provided no further details about the alleged plans or Abu Kmeil's role in the 7 October attack.
Hamas called the killing a "treacherous and brutal crime", saying Israel was seeking to create "chaos and lawlessness" in Gaza.
It identified Abu Kmeil as the director of the civil police in Gaza Governorate and called on mediators to intervene over what it described as Israel's "daily violations".
The killing has also raised concerns among Palestinians about the future of basic security in the Strip, where much of the civilian infrastructure has been devastated.
"Even if Abu Kmeil worked for the Hamas-run government, that does not mean he was a Hamas member," Jalal Abu Hasira, a Gaza resident, told TNA. "And if Israel kills all the policemen in Gaza, what do you think the situation will be like?"
"People need someone to keep the streets safe. We are already living without functioning hospitals, schools and many basic services. When those responsible for security are also targeted, it makes everyone feel more vulnerable," he said.
Fears of wider war
Hours earlier, another Israeli strike hit an electric motorcycle near a Palestinian Red Crescent building in the Al-Amal neighbourhood west of Khan Younis, killing Huzaifa Kawareh and critically wounding another person.
Israel confirmed the attack and claimed, with no evidence, Kawareh as a "company commander in Hamas' military wing in the Khan Younis area", accusing him of planning attacks against Israeli troops.
It said the strike was intended "to eliminate the threat to the troops" and that forces under the Southern Command were operating "in accordance with the agreement".
The army did not provide details about the alleged attacks or explain why it considered the threat immediate.
Palestinian security sources said the strike was the third Israeli attack since Wednesday to hit an area beyond the Israeli-proclaimed "Yellow Line", the demarcation separating areas where Israeli forces remain deployed from other parts of Gaza.
On Wednesday evening, an Israeli strike targeting a motorcycle in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza also killed a Palestinian and wounded others.
Palestinian sources have accused Israeli forces of pushing the "Yellow Line" westwards, bringing more territory under de facto Israeli control, while demolition operations have continued in several areas.
"We do not know where the 'Yellow Line' is anymore or whether it will move again tomorrow," Saied Hamada, a Gaza resident, told TNA. "Every time people begin returning to an area or trying to rebuild their lives, something happens, and they are reminded that the war is still around them."
"People are exhausted. They do not want to hear about another war. Whatever Israel and Hamas disagree about, they need to find a way to stop the killing," he said.
The latest attacks have sharpened fears that the ceasefire could gradually erode without formally collapsing.
Truce terms
Israel maintains that the agreement does not prevent it from striking Hamas members it considers to be posing a security threat. Hamas says such attacks violate the ceasefire.
Yedioth Ahronoth, citing an Israeli security source, reported that Israel had told the US it would continue targeting Hamas operatives involved in the 7 October attack as well as "any emerging threats, whether immediate or subsequent".
The source claimed Washington accepts the Israeli position and that coordination with the American headquarters in Kiryat Gat had been strengthened.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem rejected Israeli accusations that the movement had resumed military operations or violated the ceasefire, describing them as "propaganda" intended to justify what he called Israel's continuing violations.
Qassem reiterated Hamas's "full commitment" to the ceasefire agreement and its roadmap, and called on mediators to compel Israel to respect the terms already agreed.
The dispute comes as negotiations over the second phase focus on Hamas's weapons and the future of Israeli forces in Gaza.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's 3 August meeting in Tel Aviv with Nickolay Mladenov, a representative of the so-called "Board of Peace," focused on implementing the second phase, including Hamas's disarmament and an Israeli withdrawal.
Gaza-based political analyst Akram Attallah told TNA that Israel's continued targeting of Hamas members reflected its desire to maintain military pressure on the movement while negotiations continue.
"Israel views the targeting of Hamas figures as a way to prevent the group from rebuilding its military capabilities and to reinforce its demand for the movement's disarmament," Attallah said.
He said the strikes also showed that Israel does not view the ceasefire as preventing military action against people it considers security threats.
But Attallah warned that continued attacks could undermine the truce and make the transition to the next phase more difficult.
The unresolved questions of Hamas's disarmament, an Israeli withdrawal and future security arrangements leave the ceasefire vulnerable to further escalation, he noted.
Gaza's Health Ministry says 1,260 Palestinians have been killed and 4,154 wounded since the ceasefire took effect on 10 October 2025.
The ministry puts the overall death toll since October 2023 at more than 73,389, with 174,266 wounded.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Friday pledged to restore the honor and dignity of women who were forced into sexual slavery by Japan during World War II.

Lee said preserving the painful history was necessary to prevent such atrocities from recurring and pledged to establish a foundation for women’s human rights and peace, with South Korea playing a leading role in promoting those values across Asia.

Trump imposes drone tariffs of up to 100% with a lower rate for the EU and UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:45:07 UTC
19:45:07 KST

US President Donald Trump has imposed tariffs of up to 100% on imported drones and their components, with EU manufacturers facing a preferential rate of 15% and British firms 10%, in a measure meant to rebuild American production of a technology central to modern warfare.
Imported drones will be taxed at rates reaching 100% under an order the US president approved on Thursday.
European producers escaped the harshest tariff bracket. Equipment from the bloc will be charged 15% and British-made models will face a 10% rate. Washington's argument is that the US can no longer afford to depend on foreign factories for a weapon that has reshaped the battlefield and is central to modern warfare.
US President Donald Trump used Section 232 to impose the tariff rate, the national security provision already applied to steel, aluminium, copper, cars and pharmaceuticals.
The 100% rate covers drones weighing more than 25 kilograms at take-off or carrying thermal imaging, plus their docking stations and certain critical components. Smaller, less capable models and other parts face a 25% tariff.
Alongside the EU, the 15% band covers Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Taiwan, with the UK being the only one with the lowest 10% tariff. However, the caveat matters more than the rate.
To qualify for the lower band, all of a drone's hardware, software and technology must substantially originate in those countries or the US. That is a demanding test for European manufacturers, whose motors, batteries, cameras and flight controllers are still often bought from Chinese suppliers that dominate global production.
A drone failing it does not merely lose the discount, it falls back into the 25% or 100% category, depending on size and capability.
The tariffs will take effect 21 days after the signing of the order, or 180 days for less sensitive components, and the US Secretary of Commerce has been told to design a programme rewarding companies that move production onshore.
Who in Europe is exposed
The continent's drone industry is among the fastest-growing corners of European technology, and the US its most coveted export market.
France's Parrot is the most directly exposed listed manufacturer as its ANAFI range is certified under American defence procurement rules and is the default non-Chinese option for Western police and security forces.
Germany's Quantum Systems, valued above €1 billion, sells its reconnaissance aircraft to American customers, while Portugal's Tekever, worth over €1.1 billion, has been expanding into the US.
For some, geography limits the damage.
Quantum Systems already operates production facilities in the US, and several peers have been building American capacity to satisfy procurement rules favouring domestic suppliers. For them, the tariff is an argument for accelerating plans already under way.
Part of Trump's wider military overhaul
The tariff proclamation is one of several defence measures moving at once.
On the same day, US President Donald Trump signed a memorandum ordering a fifth naval shipyard be built, the first in more than 80 years, to expand submarine and aircraft carrier repair capacity, alongside a new component repair centre and a reorganisation of the Naval Sea Systems Command.
The same order instructs the navy to abandon electromagnetic catapults on its newest carriers and return to steam.
Behind it also lies a supply problem.
US media reported that US President Donald Trump confronted US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth at Camp David in late July over depleted munitions stocks, after separate reporting suggested the Iran conflict had consumed much of the American inventory.
Those accounts have not been independently verified and the White House denies the exchange took place, with the US president insisting publicly that there is no shortage and calling the coverage false.
The proposed US defence budget for next year is around $1.5 trillion (€1.3bn).

Ukraine will provide foreign museums with samples of destroyed Russian equipment
Kyiv • UNN
The government has allowed captured military equipment to be transferred free of charge to museums in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Denmark, and the Netherlands. This will help document the consequences of Russian aggression and advance cultural diplomacy.
At the initiative of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine, the government has allowed destroyed enemy equipment to be transferred free of charge to foreign museums. This was reported by the Ministry of Defence, UNN writes.
Details
This concerns captured military equipment seized or received during the repulsion and deterrence of the armed aggression of the russian federation. It will be transferred free of charge for use as museum objects or for the organization of exhibitions.
The transfer of destroyed examples of captured equipment to foreign museums will contribute to the international documentation of the consequences of Russian aggression against Ukraine.
In particular, museums in Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Denmark and the Netherlands will receive T-72 captured tanks for organizing exhibitions. The enemy equipment has lost its combat capabilities, contains no explosive elements and can be displayed to visitors abroad.
Such exhibitions abroad will help convey objective information about the course of Ukraine’s struggle for independence and demonstrate to the international community real evidence of the war
In addition, the project’s implementation will contribute to the development of cultural diplomacy and the strengthening of cooperation with foreign museum institutions.
The Ministry of Defence, together with other government agencies, is increasing efforts to inform the public about the armed aggression of the russian federation, as well as work to preserve international support for Ukraine and consolidate the efforts of partner states to restore Ukraine’s territorial integrity and achieve a comprehensive, just and lasting peace

Israel plans shift in West Bank security structure amid settler violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:43:14 UTC
19:43:14 KST

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Aug. 14 ordered the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to draw up a plan to transfer responsibility for enforcing civilian law among Israeli settler in the occupied West Bank to the Israeli police.
Under the proposed arrangement, the police will establish a specialized unit responsible for law enforcement involving Israeli settlers in the West Bank and would be provided with the necessary powers and funding.
The transfer would not grant the police independent access to Areas A and B of the West Bank, where officers currently require IDF support to operate.
Katz said the move would enable the military to concentrate on its primary security responsibilities, including combating “Palestinian terrorism” and protecting Israel’s borders and communities
“The IDF’s role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on defending the borders and the communities against threats, and not to chase after youths on the hills,” he said.
The directive follows recent clashes near the Palestinian village of Qusra, where Israeli settlers established unauthorized outposts on Palestinian land.
For five nights, Israeli settlers surrounded three Palestinian homes on the outskirts of a town in the occupied West Bank, preventing the families from leaving safely as their food and water supplies dwindled.
The standoff in the northern West Bank town of Qusra is the latest in a wave of settler violence convulsing the territory, which Israel seized in the 1967 Mideast war and which would make up the main part of a future Palestinian state.
On Aug. 13, U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee referred to the settlers as “terrorists,” a word American officials usually reserve for Palestinian militants. It was an unusually sharp rebuke from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has given unprecedented supportto Israeli settlement over the years.

Mobilisation Rumours: Kremlin Under Pressure?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:43:11 UTC
19:43:11 KST

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has stalled on the ground – and the war is taking an ever bigger toll on the Russian economy. Meanwhile, Kyiv claims to have recaptured 745 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory since the start of the year. Against this backdrop, talk of a new mobilisation is growing louder in Moscow – although this is unlikely to happen before the Duma elections in mid-September. What would the impact be?
Risky move
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A large-scale mobilisation would be Putin’s second big mistake after the invasion of Ukraine, Handelsblatt (Germany) comments:
“The already negative mood in Russia could turn into open outrage. Putin’s approval ratings are likely to drop – just as they did after the first mobilisation in September 2022. Back then, there were public protests, and tens of thousands of Russians fled abroad. The stagnating economy would be deprived of even more workers. On top of that, it’s doubtful whether the plan would succeed. Ukraine has neutralised the Russians’ numerical superiority with its drones. If Putin now sends twice as many soldiers to charge against the Ukrainian drone wall, twice as many will die.”
Acid test for Russians and regime
Journalist and soldier Pavlo Kazarin (Ukraine) comments on Slawa.tv:
“Mobilisation in itself will not lead to political protest or political action in Russia. However, it may place additional strain on the administrative system, as it would mean finding recruits, conscripting them, issuing them with uniforms, transporting them to their posts, arming them, training them and finding commanders for them. It will also place additional burdens on society, which opinion polls tell us is weary in this fifth year of the war and must now watch as Ukrainian drones bring the war back to Russian territory.”
Putin Has an Unexpected Ally in Ukraine’s War
Not the right moment
Political scientist Abbas Gallyamov offers the Kremlin advice on mobilisation in a Facebook post (Russia):
“As with any other unpopular measure, mobilisation – whether covert or overt – must be carried out from a position of strength, not from a position of weakness. The Kremlin should not link mobilisation to elections – which, strictly speaking, don’t even exist as an event – but to some sort of breakthrough on the front line. People should be called up when they see the prospect of a swift victory. Then everything will go more smoothly. ... But as long as the government has nothing to show for its efforts, it’s better not to place an unnecessary burden on the population.”
Triumphant mood has evaporated
A year ago tomorrow, Putin met with Trump in Alaska. In Ukrainska Pravda, former diplomat Lana Serkal describes how the political climate in Russia has changed since then (Ukraine) :
“Within a year, the ‘spirit of Anchorage’ has lost its imperialist undertones. Instead, the all too familiar stench of resentment has returned. ... Russian newspapers are full of headlines claiming that ‘the West dreams of Russia’s collapse’. ... Together with the accusations levelled at Ukraine regarding a ‘sharp escalation’, this can be interpreted as an attempt to prepare public opinion in Russia – both for a possible mobilisation and for the search for scapegoats to blame for the fact that the war has now arrived on Russia’s doorstep.”
North Koreans buying time for Putin
At this point the Kremlin is still trying to avoid a mobilisation, Rzeczpospolita (Poland) notes:
“Putin is once again in dire need of Kim’s support, not least to avoid a further mobilisation. According to Ukrainian sources, Pyongyang has sent more troops to Russia – this time between 30,000 and 50,000 – along with a ballistic missile unit comprising nine launchers and 100 to 120 missiles. On 30 July, Kyiv reported that the first two North Korean missiles had struck Ukrainian cities. If this is true, the Kremlin will have a brief respite from deploying its own missiles, allowing it to build up reserves and prepare for truly large-scale missile strikes.”
Undermine the system
Contact with members of the Russian elite must be re-established, Corriere della Sera (Italy) advises:
“Cracks are now becoming perceptible in Moscow. ... German Gref, CEO of Russia’s largest bank, has even gone so far as to say in public that all Russians should want peace and that the country’s economy cannot carry on like this. For Europeans, the time has come to seek out covert contacts with those elites close to Putin who are compromised but potentially disloyal. ... Merely imposing sanctions on all of Putin’s men may satisfy our sense of justice, but it leaves the oligarchs confined to their own country and forces them to rally around the Kremlin. ... Instead, we must pull the rug out from under Putin’s feet and undermine loyalties within his system.”

Tallinna FC Flora out of UEFA Conference League after home loss
Tallinna FC Flora's UEFA Conference League campaign ended in the third qualifying round after a 4–0 second-leg loss at home against Andorran side Inter Club d'Escaldes.
As last season's Meistriliiga champions, Flora started their European campaign in the qualifiers for the top-flight Champions League no less, but lost their first round of the qualifiers for that tournament to Georgian side FC Iberia 1999.
This resulted in them being bounced down to the Conference League, the third tier, but they won their next qualifier over two legs by seeing off Welsh team The New Saints F.C.
Against Inter, reigning Andorran league champions, the Tallinn team lost the first leg 2–0 away last week, making for a 6–0 loss on aggregate after Thursday's result.
"Towards the end of the game, we took more risks and had few players left in defense. They were able to break forward and finished their chances quite well," Flora striker Rauno Alliku said post-match. "It's very difficult to get anywhere in Europe if we aren't scoring goals. We got some chances in the previous game and in this game, but unfortunately we didn't put them to bed," Alliku went on.
"It's very difficult to give our European campaign a grade," Alliku added. "Obviously, we're very disappointed. We came into the game with different expectations, so this result is disappointing."
Spanish midfielder Pablo Molina gave Inter the lead in the 17th minute of the return leg. In the second half, Faysal Chouaib struck twice, then Borja Arellano added the fourth.
Inter will face either Kosovan champions Drita or San Marino champions Tre Fiori in the final play-off round.
The result means no Estonian club is left in the UEFA Conference League, the third tier of European club football, for this season: Paide exited the same tournament at the same stage after losing 6–1 on aggregate to top Austrian side Rapid Vienna, while Levadia had gone out in the previous round after a first-leg away win against IFK Göteborg was overridden by a 4–3 aggregate loss a week later.

Russia rejects Türkiye's proposal for Black Sea ceasefire
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has said Russia sees no point in returning to the 2022-2023 Black Sea Grain Initiative or suspending hostilities in the Black Sea.
Source: Zakharova in a comment to the press; Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in an interview
Quote from Zakharova: "If we're talking about the 2022-2023-style unilateral scheme, better known as the Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Moscow suspended hostilities in the Black Sea – or, more precisely, response measures to protect Russian port infrastructure and energy facilities – then returning to that option makes no sense. The condition for implementing the agreement was equivalent reciprocal steps from the other side, and those simply never happened."
Details: Zakharova gave this response when asked whether the Russian side received a proposal from Türkiye to introduce a moratorium on military action in the Black Sea and whether it was prepared to consider the option.
According to Zakharova, Türkiye's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan recently told the press that Turkish proposals for a moratorium on military action in the Black Sea have been passed to both the Russian and Ukrainian sides. However, she said, Russia has not received any formalised Turkish appeal through official channels.
During his interview, Lavrov also accused Türkiye and the US of failing to react to Ukrainian attacks in the Black Sea.
Quote from Lavrov: "But we weren't the ones who started this. When a drone belonging to Ukraine's armed forces strikes a Turkish dry cargo ship, a tanker or a civilian vessel, when these same drones repeatedly attack infrastructure belonging to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium in the Caspian Sea, hitting vessels directly linked to American companies Chevron and ExxonMobil, in response neither Türkiye nor the United States say that the actions of Ukrainian terrorists are unacceptable."
More details: Lavrov claimed that Türkiye and US Vice President JD Vance have privately signalled to Ukraine that the Caspian Pipeline Consortium should not be targeted.
Background:
- Last week, Türkiye called on Russia and Ukraine to take steps to ensure the safety of shipping in the Black Sea after a drone attack near the Russian port of Novorossiysk damaged a Turkish-owned vessel and left three crew members seriously injured.
- On 9 August, Fidan said that Türkiye has called on Ukraine and Russia to impose a moratorium on strikes against merchant vessels in the Black Sea. Commenting on the prospects for ending the war, Fidan acknowledged that neither side is inclined to make concessions while they still have the ability to continue military operations. In his view, once both sides have become exhausted, they will conclude that they need to sit down at the negotiating table and reach a peace agreement.
- On 12 August, The Financial Times reported that Ukraine has halted its intensive campaign of drone strikes against oil tankers using the major Black Sea port of Novorossiysk after a request made by Vance at the end of last month.
- Washington was concerned that Ukraine could further destabilise oil markets and harm US companies by striking tankers carrying oil transported by pipeline from Kazakhstan to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) terminal at the Russian port of Novorossiysk.
- Since then, Ukraine has not struck tankers near the CPC terminal and has agreed not to strike CPC infrastructure facilities or non-Russian vessels, provided that the vessels are not subject to Ukrainian sanctions and are not carrying Russian oil or other Russian cargo.
- On the night of 28-29 May, Russian forces conducted a deliberate strike on a Turkish-operated dry cargo ship travelling from a port in Odesa Oblast to Türkiye on the night of 28-29 May. The attack caused a fire and left crew members injured.

Italy recovers Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse works stolen from museum

Italy recovers Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse works stolen from museum
ROME, Aug 14 - Italian police have recovered three paintings by French masters Paul Cezanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were stolen from a museum near the northern city of Parma in March, officials said on Friday.
Carabinieri officers from Italy's cultural heritage protection unit found the works of art in an apartment in Parma, AGI news agency reported, adding that nine Moldovan nationals had been placed under investigation over the theft.
The paintings were taken from the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum in Mamiano di Traversetolo, near Parma, during the night of March 22 to 23. Art experts said their estimated value exceeded €9 million ($10.4 million).
The recovered works are Cezanne's "Tasse et Plat de Cerises" ("Cup and Plate of Cherries"), Renoir's "Les Poissons" ("The Fish") and Matisse's "Odalisque sur la Terrasse" ("Odalisque on the Terrace").
Police on Friday released a video of the theft, showing two masked burglars entering via a window, grabbing the three paintings off the wall and then immediately exiting the building, in an operation that took less than three minutes.
The Fondazione Magnani Rocca houses a private collection assembled by the late music critic Luigi Magnani, including works by Titian, Francisco Goya, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo, Claude Monet, Peter Paul Rubens and Giorgio Morandi. REUTERS

Russia allegedly sent a hitman after a US-Ukrainian citizen in Warsaw. Poland caught the suspect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14

19:40:08 KST

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said authorities had detained a Russian citizen recruited by Moscow to kill a man in Warsaw. The target holds US and Ukrainian passports, the Associated Press (AP) reported on 13 August. Tusk said Polish security services stopped the alleged attack “at the last minute.”
Since 2022, AP has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson, and disruption across Europe that officials have linked to Russia. European governments say the campaign aims to intimidate Ukraine’s supporters and disrupt military aid, while Ukrainian authorities report similar recruitment tactics inside Ukraine.
The suspect was detained on 7 August and remanded for three months, Warsaw police said. Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister overseeing Poland’s intelligence services, said the operation involved US services.
PM Tusk called it the first Russian-ordered attempt of its kind against a US citizen in another NATO country. He said the target was “inconvenient to the Putin regime,” without explaining why.
In their bulletin, Reuters reported that Russia’s Warsaw embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow denies conducting a sabotage campaign in Europe.
Russia has already gone after a German arms CEO and critics of the Kremlin
European authorities had already reported plots against arms-industry figures supplying Ukraine. CNN reported in 2024 that US and German services foiled a plot against Rheinmetall chief Armin Papperger.
Former Bellingcat investigator Christo Grozev said an intelligence insider told him he was on Russia’s kill list. He also warned Putin critic Garry Kasparov that a Russian agent trained in assassination had infiltrated exile groups to approach him.
Russia has also been accused of targeting Kremlin opponents abroad. In June, Kremlin critic Robert Kuzovkov was shot dead in Poland. Tusk said the killing resembled a political assassination, but Warsaw has not attributed it to Russia.
Russia uses disposable agents, not career spies
The alleged recruitment in Warsaw resembles tactics reported elsewhere in Europe. German investigators identified a former Ukrainian bricklayer and an untrained Romanian woman as the suspected operatives surveilling Stefan Thumann, head of Bavarian drone maker Donaustahl. German intelligence later classified the case as a suspected planned assassination.
Ukrainian authorities have reported similar recruitment at home. The SBU said an FSB-directed foreign pair killed Colonel Ivan Voronych in Kyiv in July 2025. Both suspects later died in a shootout with law enforcement.
Ukrainian police say Russian recruitment can escalate from surveillance and simple deliveries to arson, terrorism, and murder. Since the start of 2026, police and the SBU have registered 31 terrorist attacks and prevented another 14.

Exiled Putin Critic Says Push for Peace Put Him in Danger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:39:36 UTC
19:39:36 KST

Veteran Russian politician Boris Nadezhdin never planned to flee to France.
“I stayed in Russia for as long as I could,” the anti-war politician told AFP from a hotel in the suburbs of Paris.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I tried, until the very last moment, not to cross any red lines, but apparently the red lines have shifted.”
Nadezhdin, 63, is an unlikely rebel. Critics long described him as a token member of Russia’s liberal opposition.
He knows Vladimir Putin personally, and the two repeatedly had tea together when Putin came to power a quarter of a century ago. He worked with Sergei Kiriyenko, now Putin’s powerful first deputy chief of staff, and for many years took part in political propaganda shows on Russian television.
But after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, even the faintest semblance of pluralism has disappeared. Criticism of the war was outlawed, and top Kremlin critics ended up in exile, prison or dead.
Nadezhdin hoped he might be safe as long as he played by the rules. But his calls for peace and tame criticism of the “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, proved too much.
Nadezhdin, known for his affable demeanour, attempted to run for president in 2024. But he was barred after he became a magnet for anti-war sentiment, with images of long lines of his supporters published around the world.
In July he learned that any further attempt to challenge the Kremlin could land him in jail. He tried to stand in tightly controlled parliamentary polls in September, but was declared a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Russian Oil Refinery Shuts Down for Months After Ukrainian Drone Strike
“If in 2024 I could get away with criticising Putin and the war, now I can’t anymore,” he told AFP.
He packed his bags and left through Kazakhstan on July 22 after being summoned for questioning by investigators. He feared that authorities were preparing to launch a criminal case against him. With a history of heart disease, he figured he might not get out of jail alive.
Soon after Nadezhdin fled, Russia’s only anti-war party, Yabloko, was barred from contesting the polls too.
- ‘They want peace’ -
Demand for change is “enormous”, he said, pointing to his conversations with Russians before his campaign was cut short.
“I met with hundreds, perhaps even thousands, of young people. They say they want peace, and they all say they want a return to normal life,” he said.
“I think that’s why they didn’t let me and Yabloko run,” he added. “Putin thinks that everyone supports him and that the Russian army is about to win.”
Former president Dmitry Medvedev this week called anti-war youths “morons” with “brain problems”.
Russians are increasingly feeling the consequences of the fighting, as Kyiv seeks to bring the war back to Russia and cripple its economy with strikes on oil refineries and logistics infrastructure.
“Every day Ukrainian drones fly overhead and people die,” Nadezhdin said. “Children die. There are problems with gasoline. The internet isn’t working. Prices are rising.”
“Go to the cemetery of any Russian city. You can see right away just how many men have been killed.”
Assessing opposition to the war is challenging due to censorship.
According to a July survey by the Levada Center polling organisation, which is on Moscow’s list of foreign agents, 62 percent of people back peace talks with Ukraine, while 28 percent are in favour of continuing the fighting.
Nadezhdin, who worked in the government in the 1990s and was also a lawmaker in parliament, said Russian elites are frustrated but too afraid to act.
“They all toe the line, and they keep telling me: ‘Boris, you get it, don’t you? One step in the wrong direction, and we’re finished.’”
- ‘Cost of victories’ -
While 73-year-old Putin’s popularity has taken a hit, observers say his grip on power remains firm.
Nadezhdin said further escalation could further hurt Putin’s popularity.
“Over five years of war, Russian voters have come to understand very well the true cost of these supposedly great victories.”
He said he had no regrets about cooperating with the authorities in the past.
“I would have made a good European politician,” he said with a smile. “A politician in Europe is someone who knows how to seek compromises, find common ground, understand the public mood, and adapt to it.”
Nadezhdin said diplomats from several countries had offered help, but he chose to come to France.
The father of four still does not know where he will live or how he will earn a living. His elderly parents and children remain in Russia and he dreads uprooting his family.
“I don’t have a clear idea of my plans for the next few weeks or months,” said Nadezhdin, a physicist by training.
“But I’ll do my best to make it through until the day I can return to Russia.”

Zahra Al-Najjar takes Iraq's visual history to the runway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Designer Zahra Al-Najjar brings the Iraq of vintage magazines, beauty queens and family memories to the runway
Every fashion designer has somewhere they return to for inspiration, whether it is an era, a place, a person or a particular image. For Iraqi-Canadian designer Zahra Al-Najjar, it has always been magazines.
From a young age, Zahra would leaf through her mother’s Arabic magazines, studying the clothes, beauty looks and photography across the pages. They offered glimpses of a side of the MENA region, particularly Iraq, that felt familiar through her family but distant from her own life.
Now 27, she collects vintage magazines from across the region, particularly from Egypt and Lebanon, sourcing old issues on eBay, some dating back to the 1950s.
For her, they are more than fashion references; they are records of how people dressed, lived and saw themselves.
"I've always gravitated towards magazines," Zahra tells The New Arab. "They were how I discovered visual references, both from the Arab world and from fashion, through my mum's Arabic magazines."
Her interest in these publications eventually led her to the Iraqi Print Archive, which holds Iraqi magazines, books and other printed material documenting the country’s cultural life, particularly before 2003.
Much of the archive is available online, with publications also translated into English.
She turned to the archive while developing her Central Saint Martins graduate collection, asking to see publications from the 1960s through to the 1990s and early 2000s, with a particular focus on Iraqi women and their contribution to society.
The archive sent her a wide selection, which she narrowed down to stories about Iraqi women working in factories, contributing to the workforce and the arts, as well as other glimpses of Iraqi life before the 2003 US-led invasion.
One publication focused on vinyl and the music industry, with some of its images later appearing as prints across her collection.
For Zahra, the focus on women was personal.
Born in Montreal and raised in Milton Keynes, she has only visited Iraq once and grew up hearing about the country from her parents and grandparents. She also grew up around women who were engineers and doctors, while her grandmother raised seven children in Iraq and ran a large factory.
"Everything I know about Iraq comes from my parents and grandparents, and the stories they have told me about growing up there. They're also very proud of it and have always spoken about it with so much love," she says.
This was part of what drew Zahra towards stories that showed Iraq before 2003, rather than the country as it is often represented through the 2003 invasion and the wars that followed.
“We're often known for the invasion, but a lot of people don't know about the heritage and everything we achieved as a society before then," she adds.
She saw how much these images could mean when she showed her mother the publications she had selected. Her mother had not seen them in more than 30 years.
"She actually started crying," Zahra recalls. "She said she had reached a point where she almost believed it had never happened because it had been so long ago."
Zahra says her mother's reaction captures what sits at the heart of the collection: these are not simply old magazine pages being repurposed as fashion prints, but fragments of a visual history that her generation can look back on and her parents' generation can recognise, giving the images another life while bringing a part of Iraq that once felt distant much closer to home.
A collection rooted in memory
Reflecting on her participation in the Central Saint Martins graduate runway, Zahra says it was a really special experience.
Of the around 140 final-year students who presented their work, only 40 were selected for the press show, making her inclusion an important opportunity to represent an identity she says is still underrepresented at Central Saint Martins and in the wider fashion industry.
“There aren't many Arab students at Central Saint Martins either," she says. "There might be one or two in each year, and we all kind of know each other. So it was really meaningful to have that platform and bring this part of my identity into the space."
That sense of identity also influenced the collection, which brought together prints from the Iraqi Print Archive with references to her family and the clothes she grew up around.
Two of the six looks feature archival imagery, printed using sublimation so that the small text and photographs from the original magazines remained clear. She also worked with wool, cotton, silk chiffon and vintage fabrics, using layering throughout the collection.
The idea of layering came directly from photographs of Zahra’s family after they moved to Canada in the early 1990s.
Used to a much warmer climate, they would wear draped dresses underneath large coats, mixing lighter fabrics with heavier ones. Zahra brought that same combination into the collection, pairing chiffon and silk with wool.
That contrast between lighter and heavier fabrics can be seen in one of her three favourite looks, a pair of black-and-white trench coats. One is layered over the other, with both featuring text, imagery and faces from the Iraqi Print Archive, including an iconic photograph of a former Miss Iraq.
"I wanted it to feel like physical media right in front of you, where you can see the identities and the faces, and feel like you've been transported into that world," she explains.
Another favourite is the calligraphy dress, created with London-based artist Nayab Ahmed. Nayab travelled to Egypt during the collaboration to train with traditional calligraphy artists, before returning with the materials they used.
The pair then created a print that looks like Arabic calligraphy but says nothing.
For Zahra, the decision to create calligraphy without a specific meaning reflects her own relationship with Arabic. She speaks the language but is less confident reading and writing it, so she wanted to explore calligraphy through its appearance rather than its meaning.
"I wanted to stay true to myself, and I wanted it to reflect what Arabic calligraphy is to me," she says. "It's beautiful, but maybe because of my reading and writing, I'm not able to appreciate it as much. Just appreciate it visually."
The calligraphy print was then transferred onto silk chiffon, which was crystal-pleated and paired with two jackets finished with a fraying technique Zahra developed during her final year.
Her third favourite look takes a different approach, featuring a leather jacket covered in small vintage frames.
Each frame features an Arab female singer, including Fairuz and Umm Kulthum, alongside other singers who influenced Zahra as she grew up.
These references extend beyond the clothes and into the collection’s accessories. Zahra sourced vintage headpieces from sellers in Europe and the US, some of which were decorated with feathers that looked like hair from a distance.
She also built small mobile phones into headbands underneath the headwear, inspired by her mother and aunties putting their phones into their hijabs in the early 2000s.
"I thought that was quite a funny pop culture reference," she says.
The early 2000s references also carried through into the beauty looks.
Zahra looked to the vintage magazines she collected, particularly Egyptian publications, for the models’ thin eyebrows, dark lips and heavy eye makeup.
While the look may recall the late 1990s and early 2000s, Zahra found the same beauty style much further back in Egyptian magazines from the 1950s, particularly Al-Kawākib Magazine, where she found narrow eyebrows, dark red and almost-black lips and heavily lined eyes.
To complete the look, Zahra gave the models a serious expression that reflected the same early-2000s references, asking them not to look angry but "as if they're on the phone, focused and on their way somewhere."
What comes next
Upon reflection, Zahra says the references in her collection reflect a wider interest in archival fashion among young diaspora designers today, as a generation looks back at the places their parents came from and finds its own ways of engaging with that history.
"I think that it's growing because we are growing," she says. "We're kind of expressing our childhood, and we're expressing what we've been through here in the West."
For Zahra, that connection to heritage also gives her work a political edge, even when she does not set out to make political fashion.
“I wouldn’t necessarily say my work is political, but because of my background, it becomes political,” she says.
That is also where the archive plays a larger role in her work. The images allow Zahra to present a side of Iraq that she feels is often missing from the way the country is represented.
"We're trying to change the narrative and communicate a different perspective that isn’t often seen," she says. "That's why it's so important."
With her graduate collection now complete, Zahra is turning her attention to what comes next.
She has been accepted into a master's programme at Central Saint Martins and is awaiting news on her scholarship applications, while also considering returning to the fashion industry for a few years.
She has already gained experience at Viktor & Rolf in Amsterdam, working in the couture department, and at Louis Vuitton as an assistant designer for women's leather goods.
The two placements exposed her to very different sides of the industry.
At Viktor & Rolf, she learnt couture techniques and worked on showpieces, while Louis Vuitton gave her insight into the commercial side of design, from researching trends to developing products for a wider market.
Both experiences, she says, helped build her confidence when she returned to Central Saint Martins for her final year.
Ultimately, Zahra hopes to build a fashion house of her own, with "my own atelier and my own team."
For now, her work is already attracting attention, with a museum expressing interest in acquiring several looks from her graduate collection. Zahra cannot reveal more yet, but says she will share the details when she can.
Zainab Mehdi is a British Iraqi journalist and the Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS

EDF: Russian mobilization would put pressure on Ukraine and change wider security situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

EDF: Russian mobilization would put pressure on Ukraine and change wider security situation
If Russia announces a mobilization following September State Duma elections, it would increase pressure on Ukraine and also change the security situation in this region, said Col. Janno Märk, chief of staff of the EDF Division.
International media have recently reported extensively on the possibility of mobilization in the Russian Federation, which, according to speculation, could take place after the country's State Duma elections in mid-September.
"If Russia decides in favor of mobilization, pressure on Ukrainian forces will certainly increase in the fall, particularly during a period when weather conditions also reduce the effectiveness of drones," Märk said.
He added that mobilization would also change the situation among units stationed in border areas, affecting security in this region as well.
According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a strong position on the battlefield would allow Ukraine to enter negotiations from a fairly strong position.
"Ukraine wants to do everything possible to end the war with Russia before winter arrives, although based on current assessments, that is very unlikely," Märk said.
Over the past week, Russia continued carrying out long-range strikes against Ukraine's logistics, agricultural, industrial, energy and transportation infrastructure. The strikes hit targets in at least 12 Ukrainian regions.
As a result of these attacks, shipping remains suspended at ports in Odesa region, while Ukrainian Railways has been forced to reorganize its operations and transit services.
The share of jet-powered drones used in Russian attacks has also increased in an effort to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles, including those used against ballistic missiles. Russia is using munitions produced both domestically and in North Korea.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, Russia is producing these missiles at a faster rate than planned and is prioritizing the production of weapons that have a better chance of penetrating Ukrainian air defenses, Märk explained.
Ukraine has also continued its own long-range strikes, targeting six oil refineries over the past week, as well as a petrochemical plant in Russia. Märk particularly highlighted a Ukrainian attack on the naval base in Novorossiysk.
"The attack involved a combination of different weapons and, according to preliminary information, succeeded in damaging two frigates and one Buyan-M-class small missile ship," the colonel said.
The extent of the damage to the vessels still needs to be determined, but the attack itself continues Ukraine's campaign that forced Russia's Black Sea Fleet to leave Crimea.
Maj. Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and also known by his call sign Magyar, said Ukrainian forces have succeeded in expanding the engagement zone along the front line, which is also slowing the advance of Russian units.
"Ukraine has been intensifying this type of medium-range deep battle since the end of last year and its effectiveness increased significantly in the first half of this year. Targets immediately behind the front line, within a zone roughly 100 kilometers deep, include concentrations of enemy personnel, supplies, fuel, ammunition and various types of military equipment before they can reach the battlefield," Märk said, explaining that this has also allowed Ukraine to offset its shortages of conventional systems and personnel.

Sofia among Europe’s most affordable capitals and cites for weekend getaway

PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Sofia ranks sixth among the most affordable cities in Europe for a short break, with the cost for two people remaining significantly below the European average. The Bulgarian capital is the only destination outside Poland in the top six, according to a new study comparing accommodation, food, and transportation costs in 100 European cities, BGNES reports.
The study was conducted by virtual card provider Getsby, using data from the travel website Budget Your Trip.
The analysis compares typical daily expenses for accommodation, food, and local transportation for two travelers on a mid-range budget. Airfare was excluded because ticket prices vary considerably.
Sofia ranks sixth, behind six Polish cities, while the Bulgarian capital comes ahead of Zagreb, Malmö, Budapest, and Warsaw. The average daily cost for a traveler in Sofia is approximately €77.25.
Wrocław ranks first, with an average daily cost of around €41 per person.

Bucharest declares energy crisis, seeks EU extension for coal-fired power plant
Romania has asked the European Commission and the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) to conduct a new regional assessment to support the country amid the worsening energy situation. The request comes against the backdrop of the shutdown of Unit 2 of the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant due to the continuing low water levels of the Danube.
State Secretary for Energy Cristian Bușoi said Bucharest wants to know how much electricity neighboring countries could provide if Romania’s domestic generation were restricted. Under Romania’s commitments to the EU, Unit 5 of the Turceni Power Plant is due to be shut down by August 31, Digi24.ro reports.
PHOTO Reuters
Law grants amnesty to PKK militants who give up their weapons
The Turkish parliament has passed legislation aimed at the reintegration into society of Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) militants as part of a peace process that began two years ago, Anadolu Agency reports.
The law provides for the return to civilian life of PKK members who surrender their weapons, but does not establish a blanket amnesty after more than 40 years of armed conflict. Those wishing to benefit from the law will have six months to do so.
The legislation does not address broader Kurdish demands for expanded political and cultural rights or changes to Turkey’s counterterrorism laws. The PKK-linked ANF news agency described the law as a “beginning,” but said it contains “serious shortcomings and gaps.”
The PKK is designated as a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and the European Union.
PHOTO Reuters
After three snap elections, Kosovo still has no functioning regular parliament
Kosovo risks losing millions of euros in EU funding allocated under the Western Balkans Growth Plan because of the political crisis and institutional deadlock, Radio Free Europe reports.
Two months after the June 7 snap parliamentary elections, Kosovo’s 11th parliament in Pristina remains caught in a procedural crisis. The Self-Determination Movement has 53 of the 120 seats, while the Democratic Party of Kosovo holds 22, the Democratic League of Kosovo 18, and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo 7. Representatives of ethnic minorities hold 10 seats.
Before proceeding with the election of a parliamentary speaker and the country’s president, Self-Determination is demanding the signing of a governing agreement. The opposition has rejected the demand and has boycotted parliamentary sessions, with verbal and physical confrontations breaking out in the chamber.
PHOTO BGNES
Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić threatens to alter the flow of the Ibar River
“Because of the harassment of Serbs in Kosovo, we are considering changing the course of the Ibar River in Serbia,” Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić said.
He added that engineers and specialists had already been brought in to examine the possibility of restricting the flow of water to Kosovo, BTA reports. Kosovo’s acting president, Vjosa Osmani, described the idea as “absurd” and “chauvinistic.”
The Ibar feeds the Gazivoda Reservoir, and seven municipalities receive water from the river. In addition to irrigation, its waters are used to cool the Obilić power plant, which produces most of Kosovo’s electricity.
The European Commission, the United States, and Albania have criticized the threat. Brussels said that such actions would not contribute to the normalization of relations between Belgrade and Pristina.
PHOTO greekherald.com
Greeks abroad urged to register as voters
Greeks living abroad can now register to vote in the next parliamentary elections through a new online portal, The Greek Herald reports.
Under recently adopted legislation, voters abroad will be able to cast their ballots by mail or in person at designated polling stations outside Greece. Previous registrations for the 2023 elections are no longer valid, while registrations for the 2024 European Parliament elections remain valid only for voting within the EU.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has urged Greeks living abroad to exercise their right to vote in the upcoming elections, expected in spring 2027, BGNES reports.

State prosecutors in the northwestern city of Pskov have asked a judge to sentence veteran opposition politician Lev Shlosberg to 12 years and one month in prison for “discrediting” and spreading “fake news” about the Russian military, the liberal Yabloko party said Friday.
The requested sentence combines maximum penalties under wartime censorship laws with a previous November 2025 conviction in which Shlosberg was sentenced to 420 hours of community service for violating Russia's “foreign agent” law, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported.
Shlosberg, a senior member of Yabloko, pleaded not guilty, instead accusing prosecutors of “discrediting” Russian law.
The military “fakes” charge stems from a Feb. 25, 2022, Telegram post in which Shlosberg reshared content from the now-defunct Ekho Moskvy radio station. The post featured a British tabloid cover depicting President Vladimir Putin alongside a bloodied woman.
Shlosberg argued in court that he made the post before Russia passed its wartime censorship laws.
The separate “discrediting” charge, meanwhile, is linked to a January 2025 public debate in which Shlosberg was accused of calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Shlosberg denied publishing a video of the debate on social media and noted that the specific statements cited by prosecutors were actually made by his debate opponent.
The legal proceedings have been marked by procedural irregularities, according to independent news outlets. Novaya Gazeta reported that the Pskov City Court judge refused to question Shlosberg directly, reading transcripts from earlier sessions instead.
In addition, after Shlosberg’s three defense attorneys missed hearings due to illness and scheduling conflicts, the judge appointed a state lawyer and rejected motions to decline the representation.
The sentencing request comes days after Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko’s federal candidate list from upcoming State Duma elections. An appeal of that ruling is scheduled for Monday.
A date for Shlosberg’s verdict has not yet been announced.

Ukraine has begun forcibly filling a reservoir due to the shallowing of the Danube
Kyiv • UNN
On August 10, the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in Odesa Oblast began due to a critical drop in the water level of the Danube. This is necessary to stabilize the water level, reduce environmental risks, and meet the needs of the population and the agricultural sector.
Due to the critical drop in the water level of the Danube, the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in Odesa region has begun, the Ministry of Economy reported on Friday, UNN writes.
On August 10, the State Agency of Ukraine for the Development of Melioration, Fisheries and Food Programs began the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in the Izmail district of Odesa region. To this end, the main pumping station of the Suvorivka Irrigation System of the Izmail Water Management Department was launched
The need for such measures arose due to the critical decline in the water level in the reservoir and the Danube River. "The situation created risks for the water ecosystem of the Danube region, the water supply of the population, and the needs of the agricultural sector," the statement said.
Katlabukh, as noted, is a critically important water body for the Danube region. Its forced filling was called "a necessary step to stabilize the water level, reduce environmental risks, and meet the needs of the population and the agricultural sector."
As stated, to ensure the stable filling of the reservoir in the long term, the first stage will involve reconstructing the power supply system of the main pumping station of the Suvorivka Irrigation System. The project is expected to be launched this year, with the energy-independent pumping station scheduled to begin operating in April 2027.
In summer, virtually all of Europe faced unprecedented low water levels on the Danube. In some areas, the water level fell to record lows.
"While chairing the International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River, Ukraine initiated the preparation of a joint overview of the low-water situation in the Danube Basin countries. We seek to show that climate change recognizes no state borders, and therefore the response to these challenges must also be developed jointly," said Iryna Ovcharenko, Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment of Ukraine.

Oxy fire in Brussels: cause remains unknown a month after tragedy

A month after the fatal fire at the Oxy building in central Brussels, the cause of the disaster remains unknown. Construction on the former Muntcentrum remains at a standstill.
Around 250 workers were on the building site at the time of the fire. Hours after the evacuation, the bodies of six workers were recovered from a lift shaft. They included five Belgians and one Romanian.
A further two people were taken to the military hospital in Neder-over-Heembeek with severe burns and were in a critical condition for some time. Brussels mayor Philippe Close described the disaster as “a tragedy that affects us all deeply”.
The Labour Inspectorate has launched a criminal investigation into persons unknown. This includes examining whether health and safety legislation was complied with. An inspection by forensic experts immediately after the fire revealed that one of the lift cables had been damaged.
“It is a very large building; there are many pieces of the puzzle to put together,” said auditor Brecht Speybroeck at the time.
A month later, the exact circumstances of the fire remain unclear, the Labour Inspectorate confirmed in a statement to VRT NWS. Although most of the findings have been established, the investigation is still under way. The construction site remains cordoned off in the meantime and the Labour Inspectorate is unable to say when work can resume.
Four of those who died in the fire – one of the worst workplace accidents in recent history – worked for contractor On Time Metalworks from Alken in Limburg. Relatives of all six victims visited the scene last month.
