Amid the Ceuta crisis, how do EU citizens view refugees?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:05:41 UTC
19:05:41 KST

Migration is a hot topic in the EU: the issue of refugees in particular has become even more pressing following the surge of migrants into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, but how do citizens feel across the bloc?
Migration is a hot-button issue, especially when displacements peak, such as the recent episode in the Spanish territory of Ceuta, which saw around 80,000 people cross the border from Morocco in just 48 hours at the end of July.
Despite the global number of refugees falling by 3% in 2025 compared to the end of 2024, according to the UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, the issue remains firmly on people's minds: Google searches on the topic have increased by 150% in the past five years.
While overall public support for offering refuge remains strong, there are still widespread doubts about whether the people claiming to be refugees are in actual need of protection, according to Ipsos Global Attitudes Towards Refugees 2026.
In general, among EU countries, support for refugees is strongest in Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain, with almost eight in 10 people agreeing that people should be able to seek refuge to escape from war or persecution.
In contrast, those in Hungary and Poland tend to show the least support among EU countries, at 54% each.
Opinions on how countries should deal with refugees vary significantly. For instance, more than half of the Hungarian, Belgian, and German respondents claim that their country should close the borders to refugees entirely and not accept any refugees at this time.
Some countries' positions have shifted over time, however: support for accepting refugees in France has climbed to 68%, up from 43% in 2019.
Do Europeans see most refugees as genuine?
Around 54% of German respondents believe many people claiming to be refugees are not genuine, as they say that these individuals appear to have adequate financial resources already, such as being able to pay smugglers or owning smartphones.
Meanwhile, 46% of Dutch respondents state that genuine refugees would seek asylum in the first safe country they reach, rather than travelling further to other countries.
In addition, more than six in 10 respondents in Germany and Ireland believe that most refugees just want to come to their countries for economic reasons or to take advantage of the country's welfare services, while respondents in Sweden and Italy tend to agree the least with that idea.
Who do EU citizens think should assist refugees?
Three in 10 German respondents believe the governments of other wealthier nations should contribute more to assist refugees globally.
Meanwhile, the rest of the countries say that international organisations, such as the United Nations and the World Bank, should be the ones contributing more to assist refugees globally.
While not as prevalent, some respondents also support the idea that foundations and non-governmental organisations that fund charitable causes should do more to support refugee funding.

New Zealand withdraws support for beleaguered FIFA chief Gianni Infantino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:05:38 UTC
19:05:38 KST

The Oceania Football Confederation issued its own statement on Friday, welcoming FIFA's decision to ditch the FFE investment proposal and signalling its support for Infantino.
New Zealand has announced that it has withdrawn its support for beleaguered FIFA President Gianni Infantino, in a break from Oceania's governing body.
In a statement on Friday, New Zealand Football (NZF) said: "After careful consideration, NZF has formed the view that decisions and actions within FIFA have contributed to a breakdown in trust and increased division within international football, and that an independent review is required to restore confidence and trust."
"NZF believes this point in time represents an opportunity for all FIFA member associations to advocate for stronger governance, accountability and transparency which are fundamental in maintaining confidence of the administration of the global game," it added.
NZF also called for an independent review into the circumstances surrounding FIFA's highly controversial - and now-scrapped - private investment plan, which would have seen third-party investors invited to take stakes in a commercial subsidiary dubbed the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE).
The NZF's move puts it at odds with the Oceania Football Confederation, which issued its own statement on Friday welcoming the decision to ditch the FFE proposal and signalling its support for Infantino.
"OFC recognises the progress achieved over the last decade in advancing football development in Oceania under FIFA’s leadership and encourages FIFA to use the review as an opportunity to identify and implement any changes that may be necessary," it said.
A deepening chasm has opened up in world football over the president's position, with regional confederations and individual nations split over whether he should continue. Infantino is due to run for re-election in 2027.
European governing body UEFA, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) have all called for a change in leadership, while South America's CONMEBOL and the Confederation of African Football (CAF) have backed Infantino, who was first elected as president in 2016.
New Zealand has now joined a growing list of nations to have announced their individual stances on the issue.
Wales, Finland, Serbia, and Sweden were among the first to announce that they would no longer back the FIFA president for another term. They were followed by England, Jordan, Albania, the Republic of Ireland, and Norway - the latter of which went a step further and called for Infantino to resign.
Others such as Paraguay, World Cup runners-up Argentina, and tournament cohosts Mexico have gotten behind the FIFA boss, however, with Qatar, Egypt, Morocco, Mauritania, Lebanon, and Sudan also expressing their "full support" for Infantino in a joint statement on Thursday.
"We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together," the statement from the six Arab football associations reads.
Infantino also received backing from his friend Donald Trump earlier this week.
In a post on Truth Social, the US president said the football world governing body "would be making a terrible mistake" if it decided to part ways with Infantino.
"He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented," Trump wrote, adding: "If he is gone, it will never be as successful or profitable again."

A yearslong truce in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed authorities appeared to collapse last month, with the rebels carrying out deadly attacks on government-held areas.
The rebels have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi ports, striking ships in the Red Sea and claiming strikes on oil infrastructure.

Two security personnel were among the six killed, the official said.
Houthi media, meanwhile, quoted a rebel military source as saying the group had attacked a Saudi Aramco site in Najran, in southwest Saudi Arabia, "by means of a drone, and the operation achieved its objective."

Trump orders new aircraft carriers to revert to steam catapults
President Trump has directed future aircraft carriers to scrap their advanced systems for launching warplanes and return to using older but "proven" catapult technologies, which could dramatically drive up military costs.
Mr. Trump made the announcement Thursday as part of a national security presidential memorandum to "fix critical long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding and ship repair programs and restore capacity and competition to the maritime industrial base."
Recent conflicts, including the Iran war, have highlighted problems with aging Navy vessels and lengthy procurement periods.
The president bemoaned "an atrophied shipbuilding industrial base" which he said made building and repairing warships slower and more costly.
His order directs the Pentagon to draft a plan to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Weapons Elevators with steam and hydraulic systems for forthcoming aircraft carriers. The first ship affected will be the USS Doris Miller, the fourth Gerald R. Ford-class carrier which has a projected delivery date of 2034.
Sen. Mark Kelly, a former astronaut and retired U.S. Navy combat pilot, mocked Mr. Trump's order as unnecessary meddling in military operations.
"I've launched off the front of aircraft carriers hundreds of times, have a Master's degree in aeronautical engineering, and am a test pilot and even I wouldn't suggest to the Navy how to engineer specific systems on its ships," Kelly posted on X.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine jumped in July as Russia hit cities, UN says
- Civilian deaths in Ukraine rose by nearly 30% in July, reaching the highest level since May 2022, with missile and drone strikes hitting cities far from the frontline.
- Long-range weapons, especially ballistic missiles and Russian glide bombs, caused most civilian casualties, while short-range drones near the front line also killed and wounded many.
- Kyiv was the hardest-hit city, with child casualties at their highest since April 2022, and overall civilian deaths likely underreported due to limited information in Russian-occupied areas.
AI generated
KYIV - Civilian casualties from the war in Ukraine rose by nearly a third month-on-month in July, to the highest level since May 2022, as Russia struck towns and cities far from the battlefield with missiles and drones, the UN said on Aug 14.
The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said in a report that it had confirmed at least 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured in July, a 30 per cent rise from June and a 70 per cent jump from the same month in 2025.
Long-range weapons, such as missiles and drones, remained the leading cause of civilian deaths in July, accounting for 38 per cent of the total.
“Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the front line in urban centres,” the UN report said.
Ballistic missile attacks
In recent months, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine with ballistic missiles, which due to their speed and steep trajectory are much harder to intercept than drones or cruise missiles.
Ukraine has a chronic lack of US-made Patriot interceptors needed to defend against these attacks. President Volodymyr Zelensky urgently appealed to Washington this week for more supplies.
Russian glide bombs – an air-launched guided munition – became the second-largest cause of death. Civilian casualties from aerial bombardments increased by 143 per cent month on month in July to 105 killed and 753 wounded.
The UN also noted a rise in the number of deaths from short-range drones near the front line, which killed 111 people and wounded 710 in July, the highest monthly level since the war began in February 2022.
Residents in cities close to the battlefield – such as Kherson and Zaporizhzhia – have coined the term “safari” to refer to Russian drones “hunting down” civilians and vehicles in the streets.
Overall, Kyiv was the hardest-hit city, with a total of 54 civilians killed in July, followed by Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, the UN said.
“The number of child casualties (17 killed; 166 injured) was the highest since April 2022,” the report stated.
The figures also included 25 civilians killed and 50 wounded in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia, the UN said. Due to increasingly limited publicly available information – the actual figure was probably significantly higher, it noted.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
More than 16,000 civilians have been killed in nearly 4½ years of fighting, according to the United Nations – the overwhelming majority of them Ukrainian.
Ukraine is also increasingly attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, some of which have caused civilian casualties, the Russian authorities say.
On Aug 10, the authorities said that a Ukrainian drone strike in the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk killed at least 13 people.
The Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent group that tracks the war, estimated that a total of 634 civilians were killed in July on both sides of the front line. Reuters was not able to verify that figure independently. REUTERS

Trump to tout drop in US crime rates with an eye on midterms
WASHINGTON, Aug 14 - U.S. President Donald Trump is set to showcase falling violent crime rates on Friday as evidence that his law-and-order agenda is working, seeking to shift attention away from economic concerns that have dented his approval ratings ahead of November's midterm elections.
Trump will visit the Nassau County Police Academy in New York to unveil 2025 data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation that a White House official says will show the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime on record.
FBI Director Kash Patel and newly sworn-in Attorney General Todd Blanche are expected to join the president at the event with police.
The appearance comes as Republicans look for issues that resonate with swing voters amid concerns about inflation and the economic fallout from the war with Iran, while casting Democrats as out of step on public safety.
"President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
According to excerpts from the FBI report shared by the White House before its publication, murder and non-negligent manslaughter decreased an estimated 18.1% in 2025 while robberies fell an estimated 18.5%.
Some violent crimes, including homicides, surged at the end of the first Trump administration during the COVID pandemic to the highest levels in decades. But the data shows that the subsequent fall predates Trump's return to office, with homicide rates plummeting in 2023 and 2024 to pre-pandemic lows.
The decline has occurred in cities big and small, in places with officials touting both aggressive policing and progressive police reform and with both a high density and low density of police officers, suggesting no single policy explains the nationwide trend.
Trump has long complained of a "crime epidemic," particularly in Democratic-run cities, and used that message to justify aggressive federal intervention, including last year's deployment of federal agents and National Guard troops to Washington.
Trump's touting of the crime decline comes as he has also sought in recent months to make socialism and communism a defining theme in the midterms. He has recently intensified attacks on self-described democratic socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other progressive candidates.
Democrats say Republicans are overstating the role of federal policy in a crime decline that began before Trump returned to office, and progressives have largely backed away from supporting the "defund the police" movement that emerged after George Floyd's murder in 2020.
They now say policing should be reformed while arguing that immigration officers, who have killed two U.S. citizens, have made communities less safe. REUTERS

Breadcrumb
Time for a new 'civilian constitution'? Turkey's ruling AKP says so
Efkan Ala, deputy chairman of Turkey's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), told The New Arab that the party, which marks 25 years since its founding on 14 August, is preparing for the next elections, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as its candidate.
To mark the 25th anniversary of the Justice and Development Party, The New Arab interviewed the second-in-command of Turkey's ruling party, discussing the party's trajectory, the challenges it has faced, its future and its position on the most important events that have taken place and are taking place.
Efkan Ala stressed that the Justice and Development Party had worked to resolve the country's problems through democracy, including electing the president by the people, for which constitutional amendments were introduced and the issue was resolved.
In the next phase, the party has set the goal of making Turkey one of the world's 10 most developed and advanced countries.
He revealed that preparations are still underway to amend the constitution, while explaining that Turkey's "terrorism-free" process is continuing and that the issue of non-Turkish elements will be resolved through diplomacy with neighbouring countries, particularly Syria and Iraq.
He explained that Turkey supports the two-state solution in Palestine, warning that the policies of Benjamin Netanyahu's government leave it without a future.
The following is an edited version of that interview:
The Justice and Development Party marks 25 years since its founding. What challenges did it face, and how did it overcome them?
The Justice and Development Party was founded 25 years ago, when the atmosphere in Turkey at the time was affected by the events of 28 February 1997. The Turkish National Security Council held a meeting that led to decisions resulting in the removal of former Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, leader of the Welfare Party, and the end of his coalition government.
The economy was facing major difficulties, a severe economic crisis and political instability, and the party was founded amid all these challenges.
There is no doubt that the events of 28 February 1997, dealt a severe blow to freedom of belief. The atmosphere was suffocating, and freedoms were restricted, particularly freedom of belief.
Amid these circumstances, the Justice and Development Party was founded. The party founder, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said on 14 August, 2001: "From now on, everything will not be as it was in Turkey."
Since then, as a party in power for 24 years, we have achieved a great deal across various fields and brought about real revolutions. We did all this for our people.
The Justice and Development Party put every problem it faced on the political arena before the people and resolved it through the ballot box.
We are a movement that has held 19 elections and referendums during our 24 years in power.
For example, presidential elections had always been a problem in Turkey before the Justice and Development Party. There were always difficulties that led to political crises.
We also witnessed the 360 crisis during our period in power, referring to the 2007 presidential election in Parliament, when problems emerged, but we resolved them.
We did not stop there. We amended the constitution and put the change before our people and said: Since presidential elections have always been a problem, let us give them to their rightful owner.
Who is their rightful owner? The people.
We said: Let the people elect the president directly.
Have the goals for the second quarter-century of the party's life or its vision been determined?
In the second century of the Turkish Republic, we set our main goal as becoming one of the 10 most developed and advanced countries in the world.
To achieve this, we shared the vision of the Turkish Century with our people, and from now on we will begin the second wave of reforms that are necessary.
With the first wave of reforms that we implemented over 25 years, we in fact demonstrated achievements and hard work spanning an entire century in Turkey.
With the reforms we will undertake in the future, we are laying the foundations and core principles for Turkey in the coming century.
Therefore, as our president said, a more just world is possible, and we believe that the world is bigger than five because the world needs these policies.
During our 25 years in power, while confronting many problems, we also succeeded in unifying Turkey and giving it all the opportunities available.
We implemented highly important infrastructure projects.
In foreign policy, Turkey previously adopted a more passive approach, but during our period in power and under the effective leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Turkey became a regional power and a global actor.
Nevertheless, without ever overlooking the principles I mentioned at the beginning, we opposed all forms of injustice and declared this to the world through our foreign policy.
We have always been a country that denounces the genocide in Gaza and crimes against humanity elsewhere in the world, even from the platform of the United Nations.
If there is anything positive that needs to be built, we have worked hard to take the initiative in doing so.
That is why we pursue an active foreign policy that is just, fair and virtuous.
We continue our path by supporting this foreign policy through developing our defence industry, as well as other economic, social and political fields, and providing the necessary opportunities and means.
When talking about the future, there are upcoming presidential and general elections. In this context, what preparations is the Justice and Development Party making?
We have a distinctive approach, and this is a political method that our president taught us.
Elections are held, and the people choose us to come to power, but the very next day we begin working as if no election had taken place, as if there were another election the following day.
We begin preparing for the next election from the day after the election, which concerns the entire people.
We turn to them, go into the field, meet our people, and have representatives in every neighbourhood, village, city and province.
We hold monthly programmes to meet our people, explain our vision and listen to their demands.
We discuss their demands in our relevant institutions.
In our party and government committees, we conduct research and public opinion polls, and we do this every month.
We assess matters. The people's priority is our priority, the people's wishes are our wishes, and the will of our people is our will.
Everything our people oppose, we oppose, and everything our people support, we support.
What are the current public opinion trends regarding the party? What do the polls show?
Public opinion is very positive.
In the public opinion polls we are currently conducting, our president is clearly in the lead.
This is because our people are closely following what is happening in the world and our region.
Here, our president's initiatives, which are just, humanitarian and accepted by people's consciences, have broad public support, and our people continue to maintain their strong support for our president.
When problems emerge elsewhere, such as the Russian-Ukrainian war, our president demonstrates a high level of leadership experience and is able to take the most effective initiatives to save the world from problems arising from the grain crisis.
Within the party itself, there is cohesion, and the country is witnessing cohesion and progress.
Of course, there are problems, but there is a government that resolves problems through democracy.
There is a president who does not surrender his will or the will of the nation in the face of any threat.
Therefore, the situation of the opposition in Turkey is also difficult, as it suffers from serious internal problems.
Accordingly, what will lead the Justice and Development Party to achieve its goals is its ability to renew itself internally and maintain its unity, a leader who has demonstrated his position and will, and a people who trust him.
We are continuing on our path and hope that the research will show this clearly.
Do you have any statistics? Can you give some figures?
Well, first and foremost, we are 10 points ahead even of our closest competitors, so I can say that today, of course, we will continue with the People's Alliance.
Looking at it this way, our president can easily exceed 50% in the presidential elections.
Likewise, when looking at the Justice and Development Party within the alliance, the percentage is much higher, because our people see that the other parties are incapable of solving their internal problems.
A party that cannot solve its internal problems cannot in any way solve Turkey's problems.
It cannot connect Turkey's opportunities with the people.
Therefore, the Justice and Development Party and our president enjoy very strong popular support.
Justice and Development Party spokesman Omer Celik previously announced that the party's presidential candidate in the next elections is Erdogan. But how will the constitutional obstacles be overcome?
When our parliament decides to hold elections, this is clear and explicit in the constitution.
There are no obstacles.
The matter depends on a decision by parliament, and when parliament decides, Erdogan is the candidate of the alliance and the Justice and Development Party, and, God willing, the people will support him.
No one can oppose what the people want.
Therefore, through a decision by our parliament and the nomination of our president, he will have the opportunity to serve Turkey in the best possible way during the next term.
After the 2023 elections, there was a focus on a new constitution, but this issue is no longer on the agenda as it was previously. Is a new constitution or constitutional amendments on the agenda?
Turkey has witnessed constitutional debates since the constitution was adopted in 1982.
Because it is a constitution dating back to the coup era, many amendments have been introduced since then.
However, every amendment requires further amendments.
We have therefore also made many changes.
But the constitution should be viewed as a whole, in terms of its spirit, its drafting methodology and its understanding of the principle of consensus.
We have a committee formed by our president dealing with the constitution, and I am a member of it.
We have completed our work and are currently conducting several assessments.
We will then conduct studies to assess them with the relevant parties.
We will meet civil society organisations and non-governmental organisations to assess them.
Our desire to unite Turkey through a new constitution has remained alive from the beginning, and we still believe in it.
We believe that the time has come for Turkey to adopt a civilian constitution.
For this reason, we have completed our work from our perspective.
We have concluded, but discussions and assessments with other parties and non-governmental organisations will certainly reveal the issues on which we agree and those on which we disagree.
The aim is to draft a constitution through consensus and with the participation of all segments of society, and, if possible, with the participation of all political parties, which would ensure political consensus.
If this is achieved, the constitution will have a longer lifespan.
Then, with the support of the people, Turkey will have achieved the constitutional amendments it aspires to.
Therefore, we want a more robust constitution that guarantees rights and freedoms, including freedom of work, thought and belief; a constitution that builds an effective state, strengthens predictability, prioritises transparency and enables the participation of all segments of society.
Most importantly, the constitution must be drafted through civilian consensus, and the importance of following the same civilian procedures in this process is clear.
Therefore, our programme for drafting a new constitution is continuing.
Will the constitution be amended before the elections, or will it remain unchanged until after them?
Of course, we will continue this process, but because it concerns many parties, parliamentarians and civil society organisations, we want to complete it as soon as possible.
Nevertheless, the timing, timeframe and duration will be determined based on consensus and negotiations.
What is the timetable for the next stage of Turkey's terrorism-free process, and what mechanism will you follow?
Turkey has been fighting terrorism since the 1980s.
Terrorism is a major problem for all humanity. We want to completely eliminate terrorism in our region.
We say a terrorism-free Turkey and a terrorism-free region.
In other words, there should be no terrorism in the Middle East or anywhere else, because its costs are enormous, it has a huge capacity to cause harm, and there is no hope of victory.
Therefore, Turkey has brought the situation to this stage.
With broad participation and support from all sides, we submitted the bill to parliament and established specific mechanisms in it to eliminate the terrorist organisation and hand over weapons.
We are assigning tasks to state institutions under the law, and we will work with society to manage the dialogue transparently.
We have established these mechanisms, selected them and defined them in the law, and we will complete them soon, freeing Turkey from these constraints and implementing policies that will enable Turkey to move forward confidently towards its long-term goals.
We are working hard to do everything we can through an active foreign policy to end the suffering in our region, in Syria, Iraq and the Middle East, and to establish terrorism-free areas in those regions.
Are you concerned about external interference or the possibility of international actors intervening and sabotaging this process?
The possibility of provocation always exists, and this is what happens in the Middle East.
Even coincidences are orchestrated.
Therefore, we have to act with great caution while being aware of this.
That is why we pursue a firm foreign policy to resolve these issues peacefully and decisively and implement these policies by taking measures to thwart the plans and schemes of these powers.
Within the legal framework, details have been set out regarding the fate of Turkish citizens belonging to banned organisations. Is any work underway regarding non-Turkish nationals?
Some of our foreign policy issues can be resolved within the Turkish legal system, while others are resolved through international negotiations.
Turkey has sufficient experience in these matters, has an active foreign policy, maintains good relations with its neighbours, and pursues a high-quality and effective foreign policy.
I believe these issues will be resolved through cooperation with the Syrian and Iraqi governments, as well as regional and central governments, in a way that benefits the countries and peoples of the region.
I am certain of this as long as we maintain our active position.
The Israeli government recently issued statements against Turkey, and Erdogan was also targeted. What is Israel's aim with these provocations?
Israel issues these statements, but it receives a strong response from Turkey.
Since its establishment, it has pursued a policy based first on destabilising areas outside its borders, then occupying those areas and then attempting to annex them.
This is happening before the eyes and ears of the entire world.
It has committed a crime against humanity in Gaza, a horrific genocide.
Once again, our president was the one who strongly protested against this, and we have always stood on the side of justice and stood with Gaza.
Our policy is completely clear regarding the two-state solution.
We know that without recognising a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, it is impossible to build lasting peace in the region with Israel.
We have always supported this solution and will continue to support it.
The policy pursued by Netanyahu's government today has no future and benefits no one.
While they bury the people of Gaza, they are also burying their own future.
It has never been known for a state to prosper through an unjust foreign policy, an unjust system or repression.
Therefore, we believe that the two-state solution is the only solution, the just solution in the region and the region, and we are working hard to achieve it.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

€9m treasure trove found by construction workers: ‘I thought they were €1 coins’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:03:58 UTC
19:03:58 KST

“At first I thought they were €1 coins,” says Kobe, the 18-year-old student who found a gold hoard while working on a building site in Dendermonde. The haul is thought to be worth around €9 million. It’s not yet clear who is entitled to keep the money.
What began as a normal working day turned out to be something completely different for Kobe and his colleagues. They were set to demolish a building on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde on Tuesday when they discovered a trove of gold coins and ingots bricked into a wall in the cellar.
“Our first reaction was actually disbelief, amazement. We certainly hadn’t expected to find gold,” Kobe said. “We stumbled across it while carrying out groundworks to lay a pipe for the sewerage system.”
Then we saw a gold nugget lying there. That’s when we realised it was something bigger
When they removed a section of the foundations, they saw something unexpected. “At first, I thought they were €1 coins. But then we also saw a gold nugget lying there. That’s when we realised it was something bigger.”
Site manager Mario couldn’t believe his eyes. “They shouted: ‘We’ve found gold!’ I went to have a look and picked up the gold,” he says. “We kept digging up more coins and bars. Only then did it really sink in what we’d found. It was a strange feeling.”
Mario rang his manager, who told him to notify the building owner and the police. Did the workers consider keeping the gold for themselves? “There are so many coins and bars; it would be almost impossible,” he says. “Besides, that would be theft.”
“That’s what I thought too,” says Kobe. “Of course, we did briefly consider keeping it. But it’s simply too much money. If it were a few thousand euros, it might be feasible. But €9 million – you simply can’t keep that hidden.”
After 33 years in the construction industry, this is the first time I’ve experienced anything like this
He hopes there might be a finder’s fee for him and his colleagues. Any fee, and the question of who the money belongs to, are still to be determined. The gold is with the police at a secure location and the East Flanders public prosecutor is conducting an investigation to determine how it ended up at the site. “For all we know, this discovery is the result of some kind of fraudulent activity and the gold has been hidden there,” a spokesperson for the building owner said.
“After 33 years in the construction industry, this is the first time I’ve experienced anything like this,” says site manager Mario. “I don’t think it will ever happen again.”

'First time we did something like this': Former women Naxalites share their Raipur ramp-walk experience
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 14, 2026, 15:33 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Surrendered women naxals walk on the ramp during a participation in a Tribal fashion show programme.
NEW DELHI: For nine women from Chhattisgarh's Naxal-affected Bastar region, the stage in Raipur offered a strikingly different kind of experience. Once part of an armed insurgency, they recently walked the ramp in handloom outfits at a National Handloom Day event, as part of efforts to help surrendered Naxalites rebuild their lives.The women, all from Sukma, took part in a Swadeshi fashion show organised as part of rehabilitation efforts for former Naxalites.Sukma SP Mayank Gurjar said the event also gave them an opportunity to promote Swadeshi products.For some of the women, the experience was unlike anything they had done before. One former Naxalite, who had worked with the Pamed Area Committee, said she surrendered in 2026 and travelled to Raipur for six days of training before taking part in the programme."I used to work in the Pamed Area Committee. I surrendered in 2026. We went to Raipur recently. There, we were trained by people who had come from Bombay...prominent ministers also came. The training was of six days...it was the first time we did something like that...we enjoyed it," the former Naxalite told news agency ANI.Another participant, Poonam Devi, said her journey with the Naxalite movement had begun in November 2007.
She surrendered on July 12, 2025, bringing that chapter of her life to an end."I surrendered on July 12, 2025. I liked the program...we were trained for it...I joined the Naxals in November 2007 and left in 2025," she said.According to Gurjar, the women's participation reflects the opportunities being offered under the rehabilitation policies of the Central and Chhattisgarh governments to those who surrender and choose to return to mainstream society."As you all know, through the rehabilitation policy of the Government of India and the Chhattisgarh Government, various benefits and advantages are being provided to surrendered Naxalites. In that context, on National Handloom Day, nine surrendered women who had surrendered in Sukma participated in a Swadeshi fashion show," he said.The nine women had held different positions within the Naxalite organisation. Some were associated with the Pamed Area Committee, while others had served as gunners for senior Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One had worked as a school teacher within the organisation, according to the SP."Among the nine surrendered women, some were working in the Pamed Area Committee. Some worked as gunners for major Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One of the surrendered women Naxalites was working as a teacher in a school," Gurjar said.Their past also included handling weapons. Gurjar said one of the women had carried an INSAS rifle and that the participants had surrendered around six months earlier.Now, instead of carrying weapons, the women are being encouraged to explore skills and opportunities that can help them build a different future.
Gurjar said their participation in the fashion show showed a change in their outlook and suggested that their confidence in the rehabilitation process was growing."They are now actively promoting Swadeshi products and refining their artistic skills," he said.For women who once lived amid the forests and violence of the Naxal movement, walking a ramp in handloom clothing may appear like a small moment. But within the larger rehabilitation effort, it represents something much more significant, a visible step away from an armed past and towards an ordinary life.

Where to go in Kyiv on the weekend of August 15–16
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
13:02:02 EEST
19:02:02 KST

Where to go in Kyiv on the weekend of August 15–16
Kyiv • UNN
A number of cultural events will take place in Kyiv on August 15–16: a workshop for children, a play, chamber music concerts, and a Rammstein tribute. You can also attend a full-dome film about space and an Italian music concert.
This weekend, Kyiv will host numerous cultural and entertainment events for adults and children. UNN will tell you where you can go on August 15 and 16.
A workshop for children on drawing pets
When: August 15 at 11:30.
Where: Kyiv Cultural Cluster "Krakow", 12 Rusanivska Embankment.
How much: UAH 400.
About the event:
In Kyiv, children will take part in an Art Island creative workshop dedicated to drawing pets. Participants aged 5 to 10 will work with soft chalk pastel and create their own picture depicting a cat or a dog.
The class will be led by artist, painter, and teacher Viktor Veres, who will help the children complete all stages of the work. The organizers will provide all the necessary materials on site. After the workshop, each child will be able to take their work home.
Performance "Andriivskyi Descent. Lantern. Pierrot"
When: August 15 at 14:00.
Where: "Koleso" Theater, 8 Andriivskyi Descent.
How much: UAH 270.
About the event:
The "Koleso" Theater will present a joint production with the M. Kulish Kherson Theater, "Andriivskyi Descent. Lantern. Pierrot," based on a play by Serhii Pavliuk. It is the story of an actress who left the stage and went to another country for the man she loved. The lead role is performed by Honored Artist of Ukraine Oleksandra Tarnovska.
"Music of August": Bach, Vivaldi, Dvořák, Rolla
When: August 15 at 15:00.
Where: St. Catherine's Church, 22 Lutheran Street.
How much: UAH 350–450.
About the event:
An evening of chamber music featuring the National Chamber Ensemble "Kyiv Soloists" will take place in the historic St. Catherine's Church. The program includes works by Vivaldi, Bach, Rolla, and Dvořák. Antonii Kedrovskyi will conduct, and the soloist will be violist Yaroslav Venher.
Voyager: Journey into Infinity + Earth from the ISS
When: August 15 at 17:00.
Where: Kyiv Planetarium, 57/3 Velyka Vasylkivska Street.
How much: UAH 300–500.
About the event:
The Kyiv Planetarium will screen a fulldome film about the Voyager space mission. Viewers will travel to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune and learn more about the two spacecraft launched in 1977. The film also tells the story of their exploration of interstellar space and the Golden Record containing messages for extraterrestrial civilizations.
RAMMSTEIN TRIBUTE
When: August 15 at 18:00.
Where: "Solomianska Brewery," 2B Solomianska Square.
How much: UAH 250–350.
About the event:
A Rammstein tribute concert will take place at the "Solomianska Brewery." The band Rammstahl will perform well-known songs by the German band, including "Du Hast," "Sonne," "Ich Will," "Deutschland," "Engel," and "America."
D.I.S.C.O. dance project
When: August 5 at 19:00.
Where: Docker Pub, 25 Bohatyrska Street.
How much: UAH 250–300.
About the event:
The D.I.S.C.O. project is an event for those who want to spend the evening with music and dancing. Guests can look forward to a dynamic program in the atmosphere of a club night.
Organ and Vocals Under the Stars: Bella Italia
When: August 15 at 19:30.
Where: Kyiv Planetarium, 57/3 Velyka Vasylkivska Street.
How much: UAH 800–1,200.
About the event:
The Kyiv Planetarium will host the fulldome concert "Organ and Vocals Under the Stars: Bella Italia." The program features Italian music, from works by Vivaldi to Neapolitan songs, accompanied by video projections on the dome of the Star Hall. People's Artist of Ukraine Valeriia Balakhovska will perform on the organ, while the vocal part will be performed by Honored Artist of Ukraine, tenor Serhii Androshchuk. The program will include works by Vivaldi, Rossini, Petrali, Bixio, Capua, and Puccini.

Marcos says Philippines will not attack China if it invades Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:01:53 UTC
19:01:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Philippines will not allow offensive operations from its territory if China invades Taiwan, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said Friday.
He was responding to questions during a luncheon with the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines, the Manila Bulletin reported. He was asked whether he would allow the US military to launch offensive operations from bases in the Philippines.
The country would not be a belligerent nation in the region, but would only promote peace and stability, Marcos said. He added that allowing an attack from the Philippines against anyone contradicted its policy of defending regional peace and stability.
Marcos described decisions by the US and other countries as their own internal matters and part of their foreign policy, the Manila Bulletin reported. The Philippines is only interested in defending its own sovereign rights and territorial independence, he said.
The president also said that cooperation with Taiwan would continue as the two are close neighbors, per Liberty Times. The “one China policy” will remain an important principle governing relations with China and with Taiwan, he said.
As to talks with Japan about maritime borders east of Taiwan, Marcos described them as a bilateral process, but they would welcome hearing the views of other interested parties. He said there was no timetable for the talks, but he hoped Japan and the Philippines could reach an agreement before the end of the year, per Liberty Times.

Two more workplace deaths in Italy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:00:26 CEST
19:00:26 KST

Friday saw two more workplace deaths
in Italy as a long spate of fatal accidents at work which has
spurred government action continued.
                                    
                                       
				In the first, a 31-year-old mechanic died in a workshop in
Cinquefrondi, in the province of Reggio Calabria, near the
entrance to the highway connecting the Gioia Tauro plain with
the Locride area.
                                    
                                       
				According to initial reports, the young man was working under a
car that had been raised and supported with jacks when, for
reasons currently under investigation, the jacks failed, causing
the vehicle to fall.
                                    
                                       
				The man was crushed to death
The second accident took place at Diano d'Alba, in the Cuneo
area.
                                    
                                       
				The victim, a 22-year-old woman, died when a tractor overturned.
                                    
                                       
				The young woman was working on a local farm.
                                    
                                       
				On Thursday a worker at the San Vito Lo Capo sewage treatment
plant in Sicily died from fumes coming from the plant.
                                    
                                       
				118 paramedics responded, and during the rescue effort, a rescue
worker who was performing CPR also died.
                                    
                                       
				Workplace deaths are in fact a major problem in Italy and
Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has said boosting health and
safety is a major priority.
                                    
                                       
				In November the cabinet launched a digital badge for contractors
and sub-contractors on construction sites, aimed at improving
safety.
                                    
                                       
				Trade unions say an average of three workers a day die in
workplace accidents in Italy.

El Niño may peak at the worst time for the Amazon – and it should worry us all
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

As a supercharged climate scorches Europe with wildfire and deluges Asia with floods, the Amazon is bracing for a drought that strikes fear into the hearts of forest defenders and food producers alike. But it should worry even more of us.
Scientists are predicting that the peak of El Niño will occur at the worst possible time for the world’s biggest tropical rainforest: the end of the dry season between October and December, when rivers are at their lowest and undergrowth is most likely to be tinder dry. This will be a period of extreme vulnerability for the forest, which plays a globally important role in stabilising the climate and irrigating crops.
The planet’s life-support system is already reeling from a double whammy. Human-driven climate disruption, caused by burning fossil fuels and trees, is relentlessly heating the world and amplifying extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and storms. On top of this long-term trend is the latest El Niño, a naturally occurring phenomenon of high Pacific Ocean temperatures that leads to warming – and drought and fire – for much of the rest of the world.
Scientists say this El Niño is on course to be the strongest in 150 years by a “mind-blowing margin.” Even in its incipient phase, it is wreaking havoc havoc across the planet.
Western Europe has endured the hottest June and July in history, with exceptionally low rainfall, sparking extreme wildfires in France, Greece and other Mediterranean countries and water shortages in the Seine, Rhine and Danube basins. Three-quarters of England is in drought and baked by what is forecast to be the hottest UK summer on record.
In Asia, South Korea and Japan are sweltering in a record heatwave, while China has been battered by Typhoon Dolphin, which has turned Shanghai’s streets into rivers, torn roofs from houses and forced the evacuation of more than 1 million people. Floods have killed more than 100 people in India’s Assam state, with more rain forecast.
Swathes of the world are burning. In Canada, “out of control” wildfires have forced tens of thousands to flee British Colombia and darkened the skies of distant New York. Huge fires are also raging on Java Island in Indonesia and Utah in the US, which has also been scorched by a record July heatwave.
In Africa, the UN is predicting a severe hit to food production. In the Middle East, local temperature records are being broken almost every day, with the United Arab Emirates registering 51.2C in Al Dhafra.
Meanwhile, sea surface temperatures are trending far outside previous parameters, threatening coral reefs and other marine life. Because the oceans are the world’s main heat absorber, their temperatures are a prelude to what follows on land.
But among the greatest concerns about what comes next is the Amazon, which is essential for maintaining biodiversity and ensuring rainfall for food-producing regions across South America.
A few decades ago, the idea of drought in the rainforest would have seemed outlandish. The Amazon is the world’s biggest river and its principal tributaries – the Xingu, Negro, Tapajós, Madeira, Purus, Juruá and Japurá –are among the planet’s main sources of freshwater. The forest around them has always been famed for humidity, with giant trees that sucked up moisture and pumped it into the atmosphere, generating “flying rivers” that cooled and watered an entire continent. The trillions of trees and plants in the Amazon also draw down huge quantities of carbon dioxide with benefits to the entire planet. Any weakening of this function adds to the risks of instability, food insecurity and extreme weather.
Now, the Brazilian meteorological agency has released a forecast that the unusually strong El Niño will delay the onset of the Amazonian rainy season, raise temperatures, deplete rivers and intensify fire risks.
As in many other parts of the planet, this creates an emergency within an emergency: the onset of a natural but extremely powerful “Godzilla” El Niño that could last well into the new year, on top of human-driven warming.
Scientists and Indigenous residents say the Amazon is struggling to recover from the devastation caused during the last El Niño in 2023-24, which left some of the world’s greatest rivers at record-low levels, sparked unprecedented fire outbreaks and caused mass deaths of dolphins and fish.
With a third of the Amazon now degraded by farming, mining and human-caused climate disruption, the trees and undergrowth are more flammable and vulnerable to “megafires,” raising concerns that many parts may tip beyond the point of no return.
The government is trying to address this with satellite monitoring, enforcement operations and greater investment in firefighting capacity. This produced positive results last year, when the burned areas of the Amazon fell to their lowest level since records began in 1985.
But one year is not long enough for the forest to recover, and it now faces a far greater threat.
Three previous El Ninõs (1997-98, 2015-16 and 2023-24) proved disastrous for the Amazon. Prof Jos Barlow, an Amazon specialist at the Lancaster Environment Centre, said the prospect of a still stronger phenomenon was deeply worrying: “It is hard to imagine the outcome of even more severe droughts and heat.”
The Amazon fire season has already started but the peak is still a couple of months away.
Indigenous communities are setting up their own firefighting units to cope with outbreaks in deeper parts of the forest. Dr Erika Berenguer, a forest expert at Oxford University and author of a book on how to deal with rainforest fires, said: “It’s crazy. The humid forest should not be burning.”
A major part of the problem, Berenguer said, was multiple El Niños hitting in a relatively short space of time: “It’s similar to if you are already sick and then you get an infection. That infection is going to have much greater impacts on your body because your immune system is already compromised fighting the sickness.”
The brutal conditions are likely to drag on – and possibly intensify – in 2027 because there is a lag of about three months between the peak of El Niño warming in the Pacific Ocean and temperature rises elsewhere in the world.
Carlos Nobre, a professor at the University of São Paulo and one of Brazil’s leading climate scientists, said: “The Amazon has to be very prepared from now through the beginning of 2027, at least up to March, because this El Niño is very likely to induce a severe drought.”
Farmers are bracing for a turbulent year. “Fellow ranchers, GET READY FOR EL NIÑO,” reads a post on a popular WhatsApp group for beef producers in the Amazonian state of Pará. “El Niño will impact Brazilian cattle farming by causing heat stress in animals, reducing pasture quality, and leading to ‘water scarcity’. This drives up supplementation costs and can reduce weight gain and milk production.”
Other agricultural businesses post apocalyptic images of parched soil or flooded cities (the south of Brazil is forecast to get much more rain). “The 2026 Super El Niño has evolved from a mere weather phenomenon into a symbol for a new era of global instability,” warns one post.
The industry magazine Agroforte reports that Brazil’s soya bean harvests have fallen during previous strong El Niño years, but omits any mention of the human causes for the more hostile climate: deforestation – usually by farmers – and the burning of fossil fuels.
Indigenous groups, in contrast, tend to preserve the forest and help to maintain a stable climate – but they, too, face the triple threats of a global heating, forest clearance and El Niño.
The government has warned that traditional lands will face increased fire risks, and has stockpiled food in case of shortages. During the previous El Niño, some forest communities in the Xingu and Tapajós basins were left isolated, thirsty and worried about hunger when rivers – the main transportation route – ran dry and vegetable gardens shrivelled up. Anything worse next year and Brazil could face the apocalyptic scenario of drought refugees in a rainforest.
That this is even a possibility should alarm the world. A severely weakened Amazon will further disrupt the climate and agricultural production at a time when farmers across many parts of the world are already saying that changes are too quick for them to adapt. Global food prices are at a three-year high as falling harvests combine with the fuel inflation caused by the US-Israeli attack on Iran. The UN is predicting that 49 million more people are likely to face acute hunger because of El Niño.
Much more needs to be done to protect biomes such as the Amazon, on which the world depends. Investing more in firefighters is a necessary short-term step, but it only deals with the consequences rather than the local and global causes. Unless deforestation is halted and fossils fuels are phased out, the atmosphere will continue to warm and amplify extreme weather. Even this year’s Godzilla El Niño will seem like a pussycat compared with what is coming.

Luigi Mangione hearing fuels speculation of a guilty plea in federal case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:00:25 UTC
19:00:25 KST

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday in a federal case in relation to the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson in 2024.
Mangione confessed that he shot and killed Thompson outside a New York City hotel on 4 December 2024. In his federal case, he faced stalking charges, after other charges, including murder, were dropped.
“I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said towards the end of a hastily scheduled, 45-minute hearing. He added: “I knew what I was doing was illegal” but did not say that what he did was wrong or that he had any regrets.
The judge, Margaret Garnett, scheduled his sentencing for 18 December. Mangione’s federal trial had been due to begin next year but will not now happen, while state charges against him were still in the balance on Friday afternoon.
In the separate state case, Manhattan prosecutors have charged Mangione with murder and weapons counts and that trial is scheduled for 8 September. He had previously pleaded not guilty in both cases.
Within minutes of the guilty plea to stalking charges in the federal case and his admissions in court on Friday morning, Mangione’s defense lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said she had filed a motion to dismiss the state murder case against him. Federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald told the court the government would seek life imprisonment for the killer.
Maryland-born Mangione, 28, came into court on Friday morning in beige jail scrubs with his ankles shackled, a change from recent appearances where he was in a jacket and shirt. He had been brought to the Manhattan courthouse from custody in Brooklyn. Relatives of Thompson were in court in a rare occurrence, sitting in the front row, and some of the family members began crying as Mangione told the judge what he had done.
Among the relatives in court was Brian Thompson’s widow, Paulette Thompson, who was breathing heavily and grasping a loved one’s arm as Mangione described shooting her husband on a busy city sidewalk. Other family members held each other’s hands.
Mangione told the court that “after years of enduring severe back pain, a broken back, [and] navigating the obstacles of the health system”, he learned that UnitedHealthcare would be holding its annual investor conference in December 2024.
The location was not public but he traveled to New York City and emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an institutional investor, to get more information, getting a response within an hour.
He also researched who would be attending. Mangione then said he printed a gun with a 3-D printer and affixed it with a silencer. “I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he said. “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”
There were gasps in court as the prosecution described how Brian Thompson was probably aware of what had happened to him as he turned to face his killer between the first and second bullets hitting him, as Mangione stood in the street with his gun raised.
The judge said earlier that Mangione was in a fit state to plead. He was asked a series of questions.
Mangione’s case has drawn extensive global attention as Thompson’s death spurred intense discussion about the US’s heavily criticized for-profit healthcare system. The attention has also been fueled by Mangione’s rise to virtual folk-hero status among some of his supporters, although there were almost none of the most vocal fans, dubbed “Mangionistas” outside the courthouse on Friday, as there had been for previous hearings.
Mangione’s decision to plead guilty in the federal trial came after days of intense speculation that his case would resolve before a trial. Mere hours after a final pre-trial conference in his state case, federal prosecutors and his defense had submitted a joint letter requesting a proceeding.
New York double jeopardy law could now preclude the state case from going ahead.
Under New York state law, “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”. A state appeals court decision points out, however, that these statements precede the word “unless”, with a list of exceptions.
Mangione was arrested at an Altoona, Pennsylvania, McDonald’s on 9 December 2024 after a dramatic manhunt to find Thompson’s killer. Mangione in April 2025 pleaded not guilty to federal charges that he stalked and murdered Thompson.
Not long after Mangione’s arrest, Pam Bondi, then the US attorney general, announced that she would instruct prosecutors to seek the death penalty. She said that Thompson’s killing was a “premeditated, cold-blooded assassination that shocked America”.
Bondi also said that her position was aligned with “Trump’s agenda to stop violent crime and Make America Safe Again”.
But Judge Garnett on 30 January threw out two of the four counts in Mangione’s federal indictment including the death penalty-eligible charge of murder through use of a firearm, meaning this punishment was off the table. Garnett said that US supreme court precedents made the murder charge “incompatible” with the two stalking charges.
“This case will proceed to trial on counts one and two, which charge the defendant with causing Brian Thompson’s death under two federal stalking laws,” Garnett said in her order. “The potential maximum punishment for each of those offenses is life in prison without parole.
Defense attorney Friedman Agnifilo said that Mangione took full responsibility for Thompson’s death. She added, about his experience with the insurance giant UnitedHealthcare that: “Like the thousands of people who have reached out since this tragedy to share their own experiences, he believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.”
Brian Thompson’s family issued a statement saying that the “guilty plea marks an important step toward justice for Brian and for our family. While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable.”
The prosecutor, McDonald, said that there could be no celebrity in assassination and any person encouraging or excusing actions like Mangione’s was “fundamentally wrong”.
“Violence is not a legitimate instrument to promote any political or social message,” he said.

Typsa Arquitectura weaves library in Luanda around existing trees

Census 2027: Centre notifies 40 questions; caste enumeration to take place 1st time since Independence
NEW DELHI: The Congress on Friday questioned the Centre's approach to caste enumeration in the upcoming Census, saying the decision not to provide a pre-prepared list of castes for respondents to choose from raised “serious doubts on intent”. The party also alleged that political parties had not been consulted on the questionnaire.Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said it was widely expected that the caste question would include a state-wise list, similar to the caste surveys conducted in Bihar and Telangana, with respondents required to tick the appropriate option.“This has, unfortunately, not happened, raising serious doubts on intent,” Ramesh said in a post on X.
Kharge's suggestions 'ignored'
Ramesh also shared Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's May 5, 2025 letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the caste census, saying Kharge's “very first and fundamental suggestion” had been ignored.
Kharge had urged the government to draw on the Telangana caste survey model while finalising the Census questionnaire and had also called for consultations with all political parties.
He had argued that caste data should not be collected merely for counting communities but should help achieve wider socio-economic objectives.
Centre notifies 40 questions
The Centre on Friday notified 40 questions to be asked during the population enumeration phase of Census 2027, including questions on caste and the place of Covid vaccination, news agency ANI reports.A government notification said respondents would be asked whether they belonged to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe and, separately, about their caste. Sources said the questionnaire is unlikely to carry a pre-prepared list of castes, with responses instead being recorded as provided by respondents.This will be the first time caste details are being collected as part of the decennial Census.

Gene-editing therapies not yet ready for human trials, Stanford expert says
Human testing could take up to five years to ramp up, but AI approaches will yield results in time, Karoly Nikolich says
Gene-editing therapies for the nervous system may need at least another round of studies before they are safe enough to enter human trials, according to one of the world’s most influential figures in the commercialisation of brain science.
“The techniques are reasonably well established for animal experiments, but they really haven’t been as mature for human studies,” said Karoly Nikolich, an adjunct professor at Stanford University School of Medicine, in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. He added that it could be up to five years for human studies to get going.
The treatment for her rare genetic brain disorder – which caused delayed development in speech and motor skills – involved injecting viral particles into her spine to “rewrite the mutated gene in her neurons”, according to the report, co-published by the journal Science and the Retraction Watch blog. She died in March last year, days after the treatment triggered a severe immune reaction.
“This was too adventurous,” Nikolich said, adding that the case showed that scientists still “don’t know precisely how changing a gene will affect the whole body”.
In a separate case, a boy died in Shanghai in August last year after receiving a high dose of HuidaGene Therapeutics’ CRISPR gene-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a first-in-human trial.

A 73-year-old Chinese female entrepreneur has recently become the 22nd passenger of the domestically developed spacecraft CYZ1.
On August 8, Huang Xiaochi was officially designated as passenger No 022 for CYZ1, a project by the commercial space start-up InterstellOr.
Huang is scheduled to embark on a suborbital mission aboard the spaceship in 2028, reaching the Kármán line, the widely recognised boundary of Earth’s atmosphere where outer space begins, allowing her to view Earth from that vantage point.
Other passengers announced for the inaugural CYZ1 flight include Li Licheng, an 85-year-old academician at the Chinese Academy of Engineering, Qiu Heng, CMO of the robotics start-up AgiBot, and actor Johnny Huang Jingyu.
Reports indicate that presale tickets for the spacecraft are priced at three million yuan (US$440,000) each.

====================================================================================================

Is There a ‘Religious Revival’ Happening Among Gen Z?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

A couple months after Anthony Gross moved to New York, he came up with an idea for a new TikTok series: He decided to visit and rank different Catholic churches in the city.
“As someone who just moved there from out of state, Midwest, I don’t know anything about New York,” the 23-year-old recalls thinking. “I don’t really have that many friends. I don’t have community. And I definitely don’t know where to go to mass. I would just look it up on ChatGPT. Like I would want to go at night, I’d say, ‘What’s a 5 p.m. mass near me?’”
Some of those videos garnered tens of thousands of likes on TikTok. And, at some of the services he went to, he noticed a lot of other Gen Zers; one Sunday, Gross attended mass at St. Joseph’s Church in Greenwich Village at the recommendation of another content creator, and he recalls that he was “blown away.”
“The place was packed,” he says. “You had to show up 10 minutes early. You could barely get a seat. Everybody was under the age of 30.”
Gross says this is part of a broader religious revival among young people in the U.S.—a sentiment echoed by many people in the Christian community.
Pastors and priests from across the country have said that they’ve observed more young people attending their services: Bishop John Dolan of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Phoenix, for instance, says his diocese saw hundreds of people baptized over Easter weekend, most of them Gen Z. Young Christian influencers have also gone viral online. Media outlets have published articles about church being the new Gen Z “hot spot.”
Throngs of young people are turning out for religious conferences and gatherings around the U.S. as well. During the first weekend of August, nearly 2,000 people convened for a three-day Catholic youth conference in Houston, where attendees hailed a resurgence of faith among young people in interviews with the local press. A similar Catholic youth conference will be held in New Orleans for students in grades seven through twelve next month. And in November, thousands of teens will flock to Long Beach, California for the National Catholic Youth Conference—what’s considered to be the largest gathering of Catholic youth in the country. The Passion Conference, a broader non-denominational Christian event designed for 18- to 25-year-olds, is then set to take place—and for the first time ever, the conference will be held in two stadiums, one in Texas in December and another in Georgia in February, which organizers said will “mak[e] room for more students than ever before.”
But researchers and political scientists have cast doubt on whether those anecdotes are reflective of a widespread trend. In a report released in December, the Pew Research Center said that its polls, as well as other reputable surveys, “show no clear evidence” of a “nationwide religious resurgence” among young people. (The center’s report breaks some of its findings down by “Christianity,” “no religion,” and “other religion.” Many other religion-related surveys don’t break their findings down by different religious traditions; political scientists say that the majority of Americans are Christian, so it can be difficult to draw nationwide trends on other faiths based on the data.)
In fact, the data shows that young adults are still less religious than their older counterparts. According to data released by the Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) in April, more than 75% of Americans ages 65 and older identify as Christian, compared to 54% of Americans between the ages of 18 and 29.
If you look at survey findings, says Ryan Burge, a former pastor who is now a professor of practice at the John C. Danforth Center on Religion and Politics at Washington University in St. Louis, there’s no indication of a religious revival among young people. The data does show that religiosity, which refers to the depth of a person’s religious beliefs, has been holding steady since about 2020 after years of decline—but, Burge says, “that’s not a resurgence.”
“I do think that young people are just more open to the idea of religion because they don’t have all this religion background that prior generations did,” he acknowledges. “But at the end of the day, it’s butts in seats. That’s what religion is.”
Burge says the dissonance between the narrative of a religious revival and what the nationwide data is showing could be because “outlier stories are the ones that stick in our minds.”
Another possible explanation he posits for the split between the data and the anecdotes is that the media tends to draw attention to stories that show a reversal of trends. Other experts put forward the same theory.
“One reason we might be seeing the dissonance is that the news media often likes to run stories that run counter to the typical conventional wisdom,” says Melissa Deckman, the chief executive officer of the PRRI. “So I think there might be some legitimate cases where we see an uptick in individual churches where more young people are coming to join or attending services regularly … but I would caution against looking at anecdotes as being the same things as general trends.”
Some experts say that certain pieces of data do suggest that there might be a revival—for instance, Gallup polling released in April found an increase in the number of young men who said that religion is “very important” in their lives. But other metrics, such as regular weekly church attendance, analyzed by other pollsters don’t show this same uptick.
“I would not say that the evidence [of a revival] has been convincing, but there are hints in the data,” says David Campbell, a professor of political science at the University of Notre Dame. “It’s entirely possible that the anecdotal reports are a leading indicator—so one possibility is three years from now, we’ll be having this conversation and say yeah, it turns out there really was a religious revival; it just takes a while to show up in the data.”
“And yet another [possibility] is there really isn’t a religious revival at all,” he continues. “There have always been examples of particular congregations that are able to draw in young people; it’s just nobody had stitched them together into a common narrative until now.”
Deckman also says that the idea of a religious revival “fits into the larger narrative of younger people struggling to find meaning and connection in life,” particularly in this era of the rise of social media and AI, when people are searching for more human connection—which, for some people, religious institutions can provide them with.
Last year, the Roman Catholic Diocese of Phoenix began working on an initiative that involved holding listening sessions with young people about their thoughts and feelings on various topics, including faith and family life. What the diocese found, Dolan says, is that young people are wanting—and finding, through the church—“a sense of belonging, a sense of healing from family instability and personal trauma and mental health struggles, [and] a sense of formation.” Young people also said they are searching for “a sense of safety,” Dolan says, adding that the church is “kind of a refuge of reverence and stability; it’s a place where they can step out of this hectic world.”
Rachel Janfaza, a youth political analyst and founder of the research and strategy firm The Up and Up, says that she has also been hearing from many young people that religion is important to them—which “makes sense,” she adds, given the times they’re living in.
“When we look at Gen Z, which has grown up amid constant chaos and really a loneliness epidemic, it makes sense why this cohort would be moving into religion as an organized form of not only community and a sense of belonging, but it also gives them purpose and a way to find meaning in a world that has felt very chaotic,” Janfaza says.
Gross, who recently moved to Fort Lauderdale, says it seems to him that, in New York, “definitely the numbers are up.” His TikToks of St. Joseph’s in Greenwich Village show packed pews. Sometimes, he says, people have to stand in the back.
And he attributes that to young people craving community, particularly in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic.
“I mean, some people may call us the crisis generation; there’s been a lot of stuff that we’ve gone through that has made us feel anxious, uncertain, lost, not loved, lack of community,” Gross says.
“And in times like that,” he says, people may feel like, “‘I can’t play this game of life alone, and I need somebody else that I can put my trust in, and someone else that I can believe in, and someone else that I know at the end of the day loves me and is going to lead me down a path for a greater good.’”
