Unprotected minors and alleged illegal returns: NGOs warn of Ceuta humanitarian crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:50:45 UTC
18:50:45 KST

Thousands of minors remain unprotected in overwhelmed Ceuta as Spain weighs moving them to the mainland or sending them back to Morocco. Five organisations tell Euronews about the limits of humanitarian aid and warn of possible human rights violations.
Thousands of illlegal migrants who arrived Ceuta late-July are still in the autonomous Spanish enclave while reception facilities struggle to cope with an emergency that has overwhelmed their capacity.
Many migrants are sleeping in the open on the streets, with residents handing out food and NGO and associations cooking non-stop for almost two weeks.
The situation is one of "complete vulnerability", Halima Ahmed, spokesperson and social educator for Ceuta-based NGO Luna Blanca, tells 'Euronews'.
There are people who eat only once a day and rely on humanitarian organisations or even on neighbours cooking food in their own homes. On its first day of response, Luna Blanca distributed 3,500 food containers and since then has continued cooking every day with the help of volunteers and donations.
Within the crisis,one particularly vulnerable group is being mentioned: children.
Among those still outside the reception system are boys and girls who have yet to enter the child protection scheme. Some of them, according to organisations working in Ceuta, remain in hiding because they are afraid to go to the centres set up by the authorities.
Knowing how many there are is part of the problem.
Around 1,500 unaccompanied minors have already been identified and are within the protection system, but Save the Children estimates that more than 4,000 are still unidentified in Ceuta.
Some are hiding or remain beyond the reach of child protection services, while reception facilities are overwhelmed.
Their situation has sparked worry and another crisis, this time a political one: the question of what to do with them hangs over the Spanish government.
While Ceuta insists it does not have the capacity to take them in on its own, the transfer of minors to the Spanish mainland is dividing Spain's autonomous communities, and the possible return of some to Morocco raises questions about the safeguards that must accompany any repatriation.
At the same time, NGOs trying to meet the most immediate needs are also facing accusations of going beyond humanitarian assistance and supposedly helping migrants leave Ceuta irregularly for the mainland. 'Euronews' has spoken to five organisations to map out a crisis where humanitarian emergency, child protection, the debate over sharing responsibility and the limits of aid all intersect.
Children at risk of violence, trafficking and exploitation
Precariousness hits particularly hard for those who crossed the border alone. "Every night a boy or a girl spends on the street exposes them to serious dangers, from a risk of violence, trafficking or exploitation to psychosocial or even health risks", warns Catalina Perazzo, Director of Advocacy and Territorial Development at Save the Children.
The organisation says that, through other groups working on the ground, it has received accounts of violence and sexual assault, although it notes that it has not dealt with these cases directly.
The problem does not affect only those who remain on the streets. Facilities opened for those already inside the protection system are also stretched to the limit. "With the resources the autonomous city has, with the reception centres and the means they have, it is impossible for them to uphold the rights of children and adolescents", says Perazzo.
Unicef shares that assessment. The agency says many minors are still on the streets and that protection centres are "totally saturated". Its immediate priority is to know how many there are, who they are and where they are. "Right now not all children in Ceuta are protected, they are not safe; they are in a situation of neglect," José María Vera, executive director of Unicef Spain, tells 'Euronews'.
The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) also warns that minors who have not yet been identified cannot fully access the protection system or care tailored to their needs, including psychological support or legal advice. "They are in situations of abandonment", says Verónica Laorden, national head of CEAR's Advocacy, Research and Studies Service.
Organisations agree that the urgent priority is to locate, identify and protect all minors. But with reception resources at breaking point, another question immediately arises: if Ceuta cannot cope on its own, who should?
The controversial question of relocation: mainland or Morocco?
While some autonomous communities have expressed reluctance to take in unaccompanied minors, the organisations consulted by 'Euronews' argue, with varying nuances, that Ceuta cannot handle the situation alone.
For Amnesty International, the debate cannot be reduced to which regions are willing – or not – to receive minors. "The state must ensure the best interests of the child, and that best interest of the child takes precedence over other statuses, such as migration status," says Amnesty International researcher Dani Canales.
Save the Children likewise believes it is necessary to speed up the transfer of minors to the mainland, where they can be taken in while the best solution for each child is assessed individually. The organisation calls for shared responsibility between Spain's regions and reminds that managing migration flows also requires a joint response at European level.
But transfer to the mainland does not have to be permanent. Also on the table is family reunification in Morocco. Unicef, Save the Children, CEAR and Amnesty all agree that any decision must be taken on a case-by-case basis, according to the best interests of the child.
Before any return, organisations insist on checking whether the child needs international protection, listening to their wishes, locating their family and determining whether this really is a safe environment. "There can be no mass returns", says Laorden.
Save the Children also points out that the two options are not mutually exclusive: a child can be temporarily moved to another region while the authorities assess whether later family reunification in Morocco is the right solution.
When help arrives before the authorities
While institutions decide how to reorganise reception, much of the immediate response has fallen to organisations and local residents. But NGOs warn they cannot permanently replace the state.
"Humanitarian assistance cannot rest solely on organisations", says Laorden. For CEAR, once the initial days of emergency are over, it is up to the state to guarantee care and rights for those left without support.
This is where one of the paradoxes of the crisis appears: some organisations say they have staff and resources to act, but do not always have the legal powers to intervene on their own.
Save the Children says it has offered its services both to the autonomous city and to the central government, but child protection is a public responsibility and the organisation needs authorisation for certain interventions. "Our only frustration is that we need to be given permission to do it", explains Perazzo.
The battle against disinformation
Meanwhile, accusations have circulated on social media, claiming that certain humanitarian organisations are helping migrants leave Ceuta irregularly for the mainland. These include unverified messages and images linked to people carrying Red Cross bags on a ferry.
'Euronews' explicitly asked the organisations interviewed whether they knew of cases in which NGOs had irregularly facilitated such transfers. None of the sources consulted provided any cases that would support that accusation.
The Red Cross declined an interview with 'Euronews', but denied the allegations in comments to 'RTVE Verifica' .
Amnesty International says it has also tracked other episodes of disinformation linked to the crisis, including images of disturbances presented as recent and as having taken place in Ceuta which, according to the organisation, did not match either the location or the time claimed.
For Canales, disinformation ends up pushing aside debate about an emergency in which people still need assistance and protection.
"It diverts the discussion elsewhere and does so on the basis of false information in order, in some way, to instrumentalise certain messages", he says.
Amnesty sees signs of possible rights violations
In the meantime, Amnesty International continues to gather information about the conduct of the Spanish authorities during the crisis and has raised its concerns with the Interior Minister and the government's delegate in Ceuta. Among them is the possibility that returns may have taken place without the necessary safeguards.
Canales stresses that the investigation remains open and avoids presenting the possible violations reported to them as established facts. However, he says the evidence gathered so far suggests, "at this preliminary stage", that there may have been human rights violations and "summary and unlawful returns".
The issue has taken on particular importance after Spain and Morocco agreed to step up coordination in order to repatriate "as soon as possible" people who entered Ceuta irregularly. The agreement was confirmed both by Spain's Interior Ministry and by official Moroccan sources.
The criticism is not directed solely at Spain. Moroccan civil society organisations have also condemned the political use of migration by Rabat and demanded accountability for the situation driving thousands of young people to try to leave the country.
For Amnesty, what has happened in Ceuta cannot be viewed in isolation. The organisation places the crisis within a broader problem of European migration policy which, in its view, has prioritised "closing borders" over establishing "safe and legal routes for migration" and for seeking asylum.
According to Amnesty, the lack of legal alternatives is pushing some people towards increasingly dangerous routes. The organisation insists that any return, regardless of how people arrived, must respect the safeguards required under international law and allow possible vulnerabilities or needs for international protection to be identified.
CEAR also stresses that the urgency of the situation cannot justify diluting legal safeguards. "We cannot play games with human rights", says Verónica Laorden.
A city torn between solidarity and exhaustion
Almost two weeks on, Luna Blanca also describes Ceuta as a city on its knees. Ahmed talks of overwhelmed neighbourhoods, dirt and a growing sense of insecurity among some residents, but rejects the idea that this frustration should be used to criminalise all those who have arrived.
"This is not about criminalising people. They are not numbers, they are people", she says.
As the debate continues over how many minors should be moved, where they should be housed and who should take responsibility for their protection, the organisations interviewed agree that there is still one unresolved question for all of them: knowing who they are, where they are and ensuring they are safe.

American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:48:11 UTC
18:48:11 KST

An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said.
Serving in Mission International said Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family.
Donald Trump, who claimed to have helped secure Rideout’s release, later said he was “back in United States Custody” on Friday.
The 50-year-old missionary pilot was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Other details about his rescue remain unknown.
The US president’s administration had made the release of Rideout a priority in its latest strategy on African Sahel states, after years of fighting extremism found limited success. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident.
“I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!”
Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. A “continually deteriorating security situation” across the country was cited by the military junta that took power in 2023 when deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum.
The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. One former US base has since been occupied by Russian soldiers.
Trump described the broader region of west Africa as “the epicenter of Islamist terrorism” in his social media post on Friday, claiming there had been “more deadly attacks in the past year” there than anywhere else on Earth.
Washington has since shifted its focus to coastal west African states including Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, sharing intelligence with local security personnel to prevent extremist threats from spilling southwards from the arid Sahel.
However, the insurgency continues to escalate in the region. In Niger, data from Acled, the armed conflict data aggregator, shows that civilian fatalities rose by nearly 50% in the year after Bazoum was ousted.
Cities and urban centres in the Sahel region have also been increasingly targeted by armed non-state actors as the crisis reaches new dimensions.
The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”.
In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport, a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the Alliance of Sahel States, the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.
In April, Mali’s defence minister, Gen Sadio Camara, was killed in his home on the outskirts of the capital Bamako during coordinated assaults staged by insurgents including the west African affiliate of al-Qaida.
Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

Trump Imposes Tariffs of Up to 100% on Drone and Component Imports

18:48:08 KST

On August 13, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing tariffs on imports of drones and their components.
This announcement was made on the White House website.
Tariffs of up to 100% will be imposed on drones that are of particular importance to U.S. national security.
This category includes drones with a maximum takeoff weight of more than 25 kg, as well as those equipped with thermal imagers.
A 25% duty is imposed on drones with a maximum takeoff weight of up to 25 kilograms.
A 15% rate applies to drones from the European Union, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan, while a 10% rate applies to imports from the United Kingdom. This is possible provided that a significant portion of the hardware, software, and technology originates from these countries and the United States.
Most tariffs will take effect 21 days after the order is signed. For drone components that are not classified as particularly sensitive, the tariffs will take effect 180 days later.
Officials in Washington noted that drones are a key technology in modern armed conflicts and are of critical importance to current and future U.S. military operations.
Drone production in the United States needs to expand rapidly to ensure the country’s national and economic security.
Last month the U.S. military received the first 2 000 F10 FPV drones from the Ukrainian company F-Drones.
The supply was made following the results of the first phase, Gauntlet I, of the Drone Dominance Program, in which the F10 drone was selected by the Pentagon.
This is the first Ukrainian drone to receive official approval for export to the United States. The F-Drones participated in the program alongside its American partner, UDD Tech Corp.

Rai.

burning inside me.

Ukraine tests jet-powered interceptor capable of exceeding 600 km/h
Ukraine's first jet-powered interceptor drones designed to counter jet-powered Shahed drones are undergoing combat testing.
Source: former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov after visiting a facility producing the drones
Details: "The team was among the first in Ukraine to develop a jet-powered interceptor drone which, thanks to its jet engine, can reach speeds of more than 600 km/h. The system is now undergoing combat testing," Fedorov said.
According to Fedorov, the results of the interceptor's testing and its first confirmed shoot-downs are now awaited.
He also noted that several Ukrainian manufacturers have solutions designed to counter jet-powered drones.
"We are now seeing a trend: the Russians are gradually replacing regular Shahed drones with jet-powered ones. This represents a change in the strategy of aerial warfare. Our response must be swift so that we can continue to beat Russia in every technological cycle," he said.
Fedorov said that last year, the Defence Ministry began a coordinated effort to develop interceptor drones by opening up the market, conducting combat tests and increasing procurement. He noted that Ukraine now has one of the world's most advanced short-range air defence systems, and that its experience is being studied by other armed forces.
"The task now is to put in ten times more effort to counter the threat of jet-powered drones as quickly as possible," Fedorov stressed.
He reiterated that over the past year, the Defence Ministry team has supported manufacturers developing solutions to counter jet-powered drones through grants provided via Brave1, Ukraine's defence technology cluster, as well as by assessing their systems and assisting with testing.
Background: It was reported that Ukraine's Defence Ministry had officially approved the TAF Kolibri-i10 interceptor, developed by TAF Industries, for use by Ukraine's defence forces. The drone can reach speeds of more than 200 km/h, has a range of up to 25 km, can remain airborne for more than 20 minutes and operate at altitudes of up to 3,000 m.

The Soft Skills Summit 2026 Will Bring Together Over 70 Experts in People and Team Development in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:41:47 EEST
18:41:47 KST

The international Soft Skills Summit 2026, dedicated to the development of people, teams, and organizations in the context of the spread of artificial intelligence, will take place September 12–14 in a hybrid format and will bring together over 70 Ukrainian and international experts.
According to the event organizers, the first day of the summit will take place in person in Kyiv with an online livestream, while the remaining two days will be held online. More than 5,000 participants are expected to attend.
The summit will also feature the inaugural Soft Skills Summit Awards 2026—a professional award for corporate programs in the areas of leadership development, talent development, team development, corporate culture, and soft skills.
According to the organizers, the Soft Skills Summit program is structured around three levels of development: the individual, the team, and the organization.
On September 12, the program will focus on individual development. On this day in Kyiv, there will be presentations on the main stage, panel discussions, hands-on Soft Skills Hubs, a Mindfulness Zone, an EXPO, Guided Speed Networking, and the awards ceremony for the winners of the Soft Skills Summit Awards 2026.
On September 13, the online program will focus on team development, communication, psychological safety, and modern approaches to leadership.
On September 14, participants will discuss corporate culture, talent and change management, organizational effectiveness, and corporate transformation driven by artificial intelligence.
“Today, a company’s competitive advantage is determined not only by technology. It is determined by people—their ability to think, interact, learn, and lead others through change. That is why we created the Soft Skills Summit—a platform that brings together global expertise and Ukrainian experience to help people, teams, and organizations prepare for the future,” said Ihor Lukianenko and Nataliia Novhorodska, co-founders of UpPro School and the Soft Skills Summit.
The organizers note that the development of soft skills is becoming increasingly important amid the spread of artificial intelligence technologies and changing labor market demands.
According to a World Economic Forum forecast, approximately 39% of the professional skills required for work will change by 2030. Among the competencies expected to grow in importance the fastest are analytical thinking, resilience, adaptability, creativity, leadership, and social influence.
For Ukraine, the relevance of this issue is also linked to labor shortages, the integration of veterans and internally displaced persons into the labor market, the potential return of Ukrainians from abroad, the need to develop management teams, and the implementation of AI tools in business processes.
Among the announced speakers for the Soft Skills Summit 2026 are Andriy Fedoriv, founder of Fedoriv Group; Richard E. Boyatzis (U.S.), communications expert and TED speaker Julian Treasure (UK), SoftServe’s Senior Vice President of HR Renta Delporte, Advanter Group Chairman Andriy Dligach, PwC Ukraine Academy Leader Iryna Blinova, business consultant Frank Pucelik (U.S.), Shola Kaye (UK), an expert in communications and People-First culture, and Chen Lizra (Canada), a somatic transformational coach and TED speaker.
The full program and information on participation are available on the Soft Skills Summit 2026 website.
The summit is aimed at business owners, CEOs, team leaders, HR and L&D professionals, business trainers, coaches, psychologists, consultants, and other specialists working in the field of people and organizational development.
As part of the Soft Skills Summit Awards 2026, the best programs will be recognized in five categories: leadership development, talent development, team and corporate culture development, mental health support, and innovation in soft skills training and development.
Projects will be evaluated using a unified methodology developed by the UpPro School Analytical Center in collaboration with the non-governmental organization “Independent Association of Psychology and Coaching” and an independent panel of experts. The organizers state that the main criteria will be the program’s professional value, the quality of its implementation, and its actual impact, regardless of the company’s size.
Detailed information about the award and the terms of participation is available on the Soft Skills Summit Awards 2026 page.
The summit is organized by UpPro School—an international educational center for training and professional development of psychologists, HR and L&D specialists, managers, and other professionals working in the field of people, team, and organizational development. According to the organizers, UpPro School is an accredited CPD provider in the United Kingdom; over 150,000 participants have taken part in the center’s educational events, and more than 8,000 students have completed professional training.
For readers of “Interfax-Ukraine,” the promo code INTERFAX is available, offering a 10% discount on tickets to the Soft Skills Summit 2026. The promo code is valid through September 11, 2026.
For partnership inquiries, contact Svitlana Chaurova at [email protected].
Interfax-Ukraine is the event’s official media partner.

'No substitute': Kuwait's future tied to Hormuz strait fate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:41:24 UTC
18:41:24 KST

Breadcrumb
'No substitute': Kuwait's future tied to uncertain fate of Strait of Hormuz
Kuwait's once prosperous oil sector has stood largely paralysed for months, with petroleum exports plummeting as fighting raged across the Gulf—triggering the country's largest crisis in decades.
Half a year into the war, Kuwait remains a hostage to its uncompromising need to access the Strait of Hormuz—where the war between the US and Iran has choked off the once plentiful energy exports that moved across its waters.
Oil has long been the bedrock for the tiny Gulf state's economy—where more than 90 percent of government revenue and nearly all export earnings rely on reliable crude sales. The country is also home to roughly six percent of total oil reserves globally.
Unlike Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait has no pipelines bypassing the strait—forcing its crude exports to sail through the contested waterway to the international market.
"Without a doubt, this is the toughest and biggest crisis that we have faced in the oil sector in Kuwait since the 1990 invasion by Iraq," said Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) chief executive Shaikh Nawaf Saud Al-Sabah.
Then, as Saddam Hussein's forces retreated from a US-led onslaught to liberate Kuwait, the Iraqi army torched hundreds of wells, destroyed massive storage tanks and targeted refineries—causing catastrophic damage to much of the country's oil sector.
'Crisis'
Kuwait has been spared the same levels of destruction during this war but has not emerged unscathed.
Just days into the war, the state-owned KPC declared force majeure—a legal maneuver that protects an enterprise when they cannot meet their contractual obligations due to unforeseeable events, like wars and natural disasters.
The notice was lifted in June.
The country has also weathered repeated waves of Iranian strikes targeting water desalination plants and energy installations, including petroleum infrastructure along with salvos aimed at US military bases.
"This crisis has presented us with a new challenge," Al-Sabah told AFP during an exclusive interview from a temporary office space he relocated to after KPC's headquarters was hit by a drone strike in April.
Before the US-Israeli war on Iran, Kuwait was producing slightly more than 2.6 million barrels of oil per day, with an ambitious plan to reach 4 million barrels daily by 2040.
"Once the strait is open, it reverts to free movement, then we can easily go back to our pre-war production levels and even higher," said Al-Sabah.
But when asked how much Kuwait was now able to deliver on a given day, the executive refused to provide a figure.
"It's something that—during this crisis—we prefer to keep to ourselves," he told AFP.
According to preliminary official data, Kuwait's economy contracted 4.6 percent year-on-year during the first quarter of 2026, with its oil-sector GDP collapsing by 12.5 percent.
The true toll is likely more damning, with available economic data only accounting for the first month of the conflict.
'In our blood'
Kuwaitis have largely remained resilient in the face of the war, despite Iranian attacks and talk of a Tehran-backed military buildup at the nearby Iraq-Iran border.
At night, lights at most of the country's major energy installations, including power stations and water plants, have been switched off.
Scaffolding has also been constructed around many of Kuwait's storage tanks -- where vast quantities of crude are held—hoping to protect the structures from any future strikes.
"We have recovered from worse. We are Kuwait. Resistance is in our blood," Noura, 45, told AFP at the historic Al-Mubarakiya market.
But in private conversations, Kuwaitis are much more frank, with some criticising American forces or lambasting US President Donald Trump's willingness to continue the war.
Al-Sabah insists the company is working tirelessly to execute contingency plans and said storage tanks outside of the region have helped buffer the strait crisis.
But even with such plans, experts said the strait's fate remains crucial to Kuwait's future.
"Kuwait's dependence on Hormuz has become a strategic vulnerability," said Amena Bakr, head of Middle East insights at Kpler.
According to Bakr, estimates predict that Kuwait's oil production could likely be restored to pre-war levels in two to three months.
"The country does have financial resources to withstand a serious temporary shock," said Bakr.
"But the longer the war drags on, the more the economy is exposed to the risks of not having a safe export route for this oil."
But Al-Sabah warned there was "no substitute" for unfettered access to the strait.
"If you do not have free flow of hydrocarbons through the Strait of Hormuz and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, you will end up with another energy crisis very quickly," he said.

Eurozone economy grows 0.4% in 2nd quarter, matching expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:37:56 UTC
18:37:56 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
The eurozone economy expanded by 0.4% in the second quarter of 2026, matching market expectations, according to a flash estimate released by Eurostat on Friday.
The quarterly growth marked an acceleration from the first quarter, when gross domestic product (GDP) remained unchanged.
The EU economy grew by 0.5% quarter-on-quarter in the April-June period, following growth of 0.1% in the previous quarter.
On an annual basis, GDP increased by 1% in the euro area and 1.2% in the EU during the second quarter, compared with respective growth rates of 0.5% and 0.8% in the first quarter.
Among EU members for which data were available, Ireland recorded the strongest quarterly growth at 3.9%, followed by Slovenia at 1.8%, Lithuania at 1.7% and Sweden at 1.4%.
Spain’s economy expanded by 0.7%, while Germany, France and Italy each posted growth of 0.2%.
GDP remained unchanged in Belgium, Austria and Romania.
On an annual basis, Slovenia recorded the highest growth rate at 4.8%, followed by Lithuania at 3.8%, Poland at 3.7% and the Greek Cypriot Administration at 3.3%.
Romania and Ireland were the only countries to report annual contractions, of 2% and 5.6%, respectively.
Employment in both the euro area and the EU increased by 0.1% in the second quarter compared with the previous three-month period.
Compared with the same quarter last year, employment rose by 0.5% in both regions.
For comparison, the US economy grew by 0.4% quarter-on-quarter and 2.1% year-on-year in the second quarter.

Iran claims 'trillion-dollar' pollution damage as Gulf oil spills spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:36:48 UTC
18:36:48 KST

Oil residues from a struck bulk carrier reached Iran's Qeshm Island and its protected mangrove forests, while a sanctioned Russian shadow fleet tanker grounded off Oman has leaked a slick that has grown to more than 2,000 square kilometres, fouling 40 kilometres of Omani coastline.
An oil spill has reached Iran's Qeshm Island and a separate, far larger spill from a stricken Russian shadow fleet tanker is fouling Oman's southern coastline, as the war in the Gulf produces its first significant environmental fallout.
Dark oily residues appeared along the shores of Qeshm Island earlier this week, spreading from Soza beach to the Shib Deraz area and the Hara mangrove forests near the village of Naqasheh.
Iran's environmental officials said cleanup operations had largely cleared the slick by Wednesday evening, although monitoring continues.
Iran's Foreign Ministry said preliminary evidence pointed to a foreign bulk carrier as the source and called for compensation from those responsible.
"Restoring the marine ecosystem of the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman, and preventing further pollution, must be part of any future management arrangements for the Strait of Hormuz," Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said.
"All parties that benefit from commercial shipping in this waterway have a legal and moral responsibility to address the environmental damage," he added.
Baghaei said the incident was "only one example" of decades of pollution, claiming it caused "trillion-dollar damage to Iran’s coastal areas."
"Who is responsible for compensating for these losses and damages: the countries that consume the region’s cheap exported energy, shipping insurance companies, or the aggressor parties and their partners," Baghaei asked.
TankerTrackers, a maritime monitoring service, said satellite imagery showed the slick most likely originated from the Minoan Pioneer — a Liberia-flagged, Greek-managed bulk carrier struck by a projectile on 3 August approximately 20 nautical miles northeast of Khasab in Oman's Musandam Governorate.
The attack triggered a fire, caused a complete engine room blackout and left one crew member missing. Multiple maritime security firms attribute the attack to Iranian forces, citing historical patterns in the area. Iran has neither confirmed nor denied involvement.
"The spillage then drifted across the strait over to Iran," TankerTrackers said on X, describing it as "a self-inflicted wound by Iran."
International compensation rules complicate Iran's position: the International Oil Pollution Compensation Funds explicitly exclude liability for damage caused by an act of war or hostilities.
Qeshm is the largest island in the Persian Gulf, with an area of around 1,500 square kilometres. The Hara mangrove forests cover an estimated 20,000 hectares and serve as breeding and feeding grounds for fish, migratory birds and marine mammals.
The island's southern coasts are nesting grounds for the hawksbill sea turtle, listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Oman: Russian shadow fleet tanker sending oil ashore
Another environmental crisis is unfolding 500 kilometres to the south-east, where the Caroline Bezengi — a Suezmax tanker carrying approximately 1 million barrels of Russian crude — has been leaking since running aground on the Hallaniyat Islands off Oman's Dhofar coast in June.
The vessel left Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in April and was hit by an explosion on 8 June while off the coast of Yemen. The crew was taken off without injury. The tanker subsequently grounded on rocks off Jazirat Al Qibliyyah.
No party has claimed responsibility for the explosion. The EU and UK have sanctioned the Caroline Bezengi for transporting Russian crude. Its registered owner and operator are both based in China.
The spill has grown fast. From covering 45 square kilometres on 26 July, the oil spread to around 150 square kilometres by 2 August, 390 square kilometres by Oman's own assessment on Monday, and more than 2,000 square kilometres according to satellite imagery analysis done by Reuters on Wednesday.
Oil reached beaches at Ras Madrakah on the Omani mainland, fouling up to 40 kilometres of coastline. The IMO confirmed the oil had reached shore on Wednesday.
The Hallaniyat Islands, designated a nature reserve by Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tarik last year, support Arabian Sea humpback whales, Socotra cormorants, endangered sea turtles and coral reefs.
The monsoon season brings unpredictable sea and weather conditions to the region from June to September.
Russia's shadow fleet consists of several hundred ageing tankers, allowing Moscow to continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions imposed after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.

Iran rejects US claims of sending arms to Yemen by flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:36:05 UTC
18:36:05 KST

In a letter addressed to UN chief António Guterres and the president of the UN Security Council, Gholamhossein Darzi strongly rejected the allegations raised by the US representative and some other Security Council members during a meeting on Yemen on Thursday. Darzi said the claims are “without any supporting evidence,” particularly the US assertion that Iranian commercial flights to Sana’a are being used to transport military forces or equipment in violation of UN Security Council Resolution 2216.“
The allegations are completely baseless and unsupported by any credible evidence,” Darzi said, slamming Washington for attempting to mislead the Security Council. He described the allegations as a “hypocritical” effort by the United States to divert attention from its own actions in Yemen and across the region and to evade responsibility for its destabilizing conduct.
It is particularly “regrettable” for a UN member state to level such accusations while itself having repeatedly resorted to “unlawful uses of force and acts of aggression with serious consequences for regional and international peace and security”, the envoy said.
Addressing Iranian flights to Sana’a, Darzi said they had a purely humanitarian character. “The recent flights from Iran to Sana’a have been humanitarian in nature,” he said, stressing that the prolonged closure and severe restrictions imposed on Sana’a International Airport, along with the blockade, have inflicted devastating humanitarian consequences on the Yemeni population.
Darzi said portraying humanitarian assistance intended to alleviate these consequences as a destabilizing activity is “factually false as well as morally and legally indefensible.” The Iranian envoy also challenged Washington’s claim to be a defender of peace and stability in Yemen, saying the United States could not credibly assume such a role while seeking to avoid responsibility for the destruction inflicted on the Yemeni people.“
Yemenis have endured for nearly a decade the consequences of a devastating war,” Darzi said, pointing to the prolonged blockade and restrictions on vital civilian infrastructure that had been made possible with US political and military support.
Darzi also criticized the United States for directly undermining the political process in Yemen. “Washington’s military actions against Yemen in March 2025 violated the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and were contrary to the UN Charter and Security Council resolutions,” he said.
According to the Iranian diplomat, those actions also created further obstacles to the UN-facilitated political process aimed at resolving the conflict.He further criticized Washington’s efforts to secure political support for Security Council Resolution 2722, adopted in 2024, followed by a selective and abusive interpretation of the resolution to justify military action against Yemen and its civilian infrastructure.
Such actions, Darzi said, have again violated Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, escalated regional tensions and weakened prospects for a political settlement. “It is therefore highly significant that the same regime whose actions have repeatedly undermined peace, violated Yemen’s sovereignty and resorted to unlawful force in flagrant violation of the UN Charter and international law is now seeking to accuse Iran of destabilizing Yemen,” he said.
Darzi described the US allegations as an attempt to “distort the facts” and shift responsibility away from those responsible for aggression and destabilization. “
Iran will continue to support a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process that is Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned, under the auspices of the United Nations, as the only viable and sustainable way to resolve the conflict,” he said.
He also stressed that lasting peace in Yemen could not be achieved through military escalation, pressure or coercion, or by excluding relevant Yemeni parties from the political process. Darzi called on the international community to engage “meaningfully, impartially and practically” with all relevant Yemeni parties while addressing the country’s humanitarian crisis and working to lift the blockade to create conditions for a sustainable political solution.
He also urged the Security Council to reject attempts by some members to use the body as an instrument for political objectives and instead “focus on the suffering of the Yemeni people and support a genuinely Yemeni-owned and Yemeni-led peace process.” The exchange comes amid a renewed escalation in Yemen following Saudi airstrikes on Sana’a International Airport last month, which were aimed at halting humanitarian flights carrying patients and stranded civilians.
In response, Yemeni forces carried out missile and drone strikes targeting Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport. The Yemeni armed forces also announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, saying the measure was aimed at ending a 12-year Saudi-led siege of Yemen. The Yemeni forces have since announced operations targeting Saudi-linked vessels in the Red Sea, Saudi-backed mercenaries, as well as Saudi oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia, along with its allies, launched a war on Yemen in March 2015 and imposed a blockade on the country. The offensive received military, political and logistical support from the United States and several Western countries. The war has killed tens of thousands of Yemenis and triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, while Riyadh has failed to achieve its stated objective of restoring a government aligned with its interests in Sana’a.

Russia’s defense ministry threatens to “freeze” Ukraine this winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:35:55 UTC
18:35:55 KST

Russia's defense ministry posted photographs of attack drones in flight on its Telegram channel, captioned "like snow on your head," and told Ukrainians that "in winter, you'll get a freeze." The ministry attached the threat to its own earlier claim of strikes on Ukrainian port infrastructure and vessels.
The post puts in writing what Russia has done to Ukrainian civilians through every winter of the full-scale war: strike the power and heating grid to leave homes cold and dark. What is new is not the tactic but the candor — a ministry that usually insists it hits only military targets openly advertising the coming assault on the systems that keep civilians warm. And the taunt lands as Ukraine heads into the season more exposed than at any point in the war: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN this week that the country holds about 1% of the Patriot interceptors it needs to get through winter.
The winter campaign Russia is advertising
Since late 2022, Russia has systematically struck Ukraine's electricity, gas, and heating infrastructure, causing rolling blackouts and cutting heat and water during freezing weather. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly called the campaign "energy terrorism," and grid operators say the strikes have shifted toward knocking out entire energy districts rather than staging single mass barrages. This summer Russia widened the target set again: on 13 August a Russian drone set port infrastructure alight in Odesa Oblast and damaged a civilian vessel at a Mykolaiv port, the national rail operator and regional officials reported — the same kind of strike the ministry's post was boasting about.
Ukraine enters winter short of the weapon that stops ballistic missiles
The threat is heavier because Ukraine cannot reliably stop the missiles that would carry it out. Zelenskyy told CNN that selling Kyiv 5% of current US Patriot stocks would carry it through winter and 10% would let it "destroy all the Russians' ballistic missiles" — but that he holds 1%. On 5 August, Russia fired 28 ballistic and anti-ship missiles at Kyiv and Ukraine intercepted none, killing 17 people. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to the UN.
Europe is scrambling to add generation before the cold sets in. Finland said on 13 August it would fund a €28.5 million ($33.2 million) power plant project for Ukraine, one of several efforts to keep the lights on when the strikes resume. Ukrainian officials have warned that the coming winter could be more difficult than any before it.

First Swiss F-35 fighter jets on production line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:35:33 UTC
18:35:33 KST

First Swiss F-35 fighter jets on production line
The first fuselage section and wing of a fleet of F-35 fighter jets has been assembled in Italy, according to Swiss defence procurement body Armasuisse.
The factory in in Cameri, Piedmont, is the only F-35 final assembly line in Europe and forms part of the international production network involving over 2,100 supplier companies worldwide.
+ Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
Once production at Cameri is complete, the fuselage section with the wings already fitted will be transported to the United States, where it will be assembled with the other aircraft components at Lockheed Martin’s facility in Fort Worth, Texas.
The first eight F-35s destined for Switzerland will be deployed, from mid-2027, at the US Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas for the training of Swiss pilots and ground crew.
Subsequently, these fighter aircraft will be gradually transferred to Switzerland to enter service at the military airfields in Payerne, Meiringen and Emmen.
Deployment will begin at Payerne in mid-2028, followed by Meiringen from 2030 and finally Emmen from 2032. Switzerland is expected to purchase a total of 30 jets of this type, rather than the 36 originally planned.

Wildfire forces evacuation of more than 2,000 people in western Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:35:29 UTC
18:35:29 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
More than 2,000 people were evacuated from a town in western Germany on Friday as a rapidly spreading forest fire approached residential areas, according to local media.
The evacuation of Gey, part of the municipality of Hurtgenwald in North Rhine-Westphalia’s Duren district, was completed after the blaze came within about 200 meters (656 feet) of the town, public broadcaster WDR reported.
Around 300 hectares (741 acres) of forest were believed to be burning, while approximately 200 emergency personnel were deployed. An additional 150 firefighters were requested as authorities described the situation as highly dangerous.
The Fire Department declared a “Red Flag Day,” citing shifting winds and low humidity that were fueling the flames and complicating containment efforts.
Firefighting operations were largely being conducted from the air because of unexploded World War II munitions buried in the area. Several explosions were reported on Thursday.
Larger firefighting helicopters capable of carrying 2,000 liters (528 gallons) of water were also requested.
Local farmers joined the response using tractors and water tanks, while fields surrounding the affected area were being plowed to prevent the fire from spreading.
Hurtgenwald Mayor Stephan Cranen said three fires had broken out in the area, two of which had been brought under control.
Authorities also relocated an emergency shelter after ash began falling in the nearby district of Strass.

A total of 2.6 million passengers used Brussels Airport in July, the highest monthly figure since 2019 and a 2.8% increase on last July.
Brussels Airport sees passenger numbers reach highest level since 2019
The start of the summer holidays led to a sharp rise in the number of flights at Zaventem. The busiest day was 20 July, with more than 92,000 passengers processed. The month’s most popular destinations were Spain, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Morocco, Germany, Portugal, France, the US and Switzerland.
“Brussels Airport recorded strong passenger traffic in July despite the ongoing impact of the situation in the Middle East, with flights to Tel Aviv remaining suspended,” the airport said in a press release.

Freight volumes at the airport were down, however: the total volume of freight fell by just over 3% in July to nearly 67,000 tonnes.

====================================================================================================

Explainer: What message does Putin's visit to Southern Kuril Islands send?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
17:33:53 CST
18:33:53 KST

MOSCOW, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday made his first visit to the Southern Kuril Islands, known as the Northern Territories in Japan, and made tough comments on Russia-Japan relations.
What did Putin do during the visit? What considerations lie behind his trip? How has Japan responded, and what does the visit mean for the future of Russia-Japan ties?
WHAT HAPPENED
Putin is on a tour of Russia's Siberia and Far East regions. On Wednesday, Putin boarded the Varyag, the Pacific Fleet's flagship missile cruiser, in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the administrative center of the Sakhalin region, where he attended the final stage of the Pacific Fleet drills and met with senior fleet commanders.
On Thursday, Putin landed on Iturup, the largest island of the Southern Kuril Islands. He visited a fish processing plant, a local school and a hospital. Kremlin-released footage shows Putin also speaking with residents and commenting on "fine weather."
During a meeting with Sakhalin Governor Valery Limarenko, Putin reviewed the region's economic development, including the impact of fluctuations in the ruble exchange rate on the local economy
According to TASS, the visit marks Putin's first trip to the islands. Other Russian presidents and prime ministers have visited the archipelago several times. Dmitry Medvedev made four visits -- once as president and three times as prime minister -- while incumbent Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin has also visited the islands.
MESSAGE TO JAPAN
The territorial dispute over the Southern Kuril Islands remains one of the biggest sticking points in Russia-Japan relations.
The long-running dispute has prevented Moscow and Tokyo from signing a post-World War II peace treaty. Japan's sanctions against Moscow over the Ukraine crisis have brought bilateral negotiations over the islands to a halt.
While attending drills in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, Putin recalled that Russia once maintained constructive engagement with Japanese leaders, including former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, before Tokyo changed its policy toward Moscow.
Under Abe's administration, the two sides set aside territorial frictions to advance trade and economic cooperation, and Abe attended multiple sessions of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
In its newly published Defense White Paper, Japan has classified Russia as a major threat for the first time, although "we do not pose a threat to Japan. We have absolutely no claims against it," said Putin.
Japan continues to press territorial claims over the Southern Kuril Islands, he said, noting that the current status of the Kuril Islands "is enshrined in international documents as a reality that arose following the outcome of World War II."
"But even here, Russia was prepared to seek a solution with the goal of concluding a peace treaty with Japan," he said.
Analysts say Putin's visit and remarks strike a balance between firm messaging toward Japan and a degree of tactical openness. Moscow appears keen to keep dialogue channels open, while seeking Japanese concessions on sanctions and a possible resumption of economic cooperation.
JAPAN'S REACTION
In a press conference on Thursday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi "strongly protested" Putin's visit to the disputed island, which she said is "absolutely unacceptable."
Putin's visit "is incompatible with the Government of Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories," said Takaichi.
"This visit has further hardened public sentiment toward Russia in Japan and made it more difficult to restore Japan-Russia relations over the medium to long term," she added.
On the same day, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned the Russian ambassador to Tokyo to lodge a formal protest over Putin's visit.
The Japanese government plans to consider countermeasures against Putin's visit, Japan's public broadcaster NHK reported early Friday, adding that one possible measure is strengthening existing sanctions that Tokyo has already imposed on Moscow.
NO EASY RESET IN SIGHT
Russia-Japan ties have undergone steep deterioration since 2022. Japan imposed sweeping sanctions against Russia over the Ukraine crisis, with direct air links severed, and bilateral trade and investment contracted sharply.
Moscow has protested over Japan's provision of economic assistance and geospatial intelligence to Kiev, its support for using frozen Russian sovereign assets held by Western states to aid Ukraine, and cooperation with Ukraine in drones.
In 2022, it suspended peace treaty talks with Japan "because it is impossible to discuss this fundamental document on bilateral relations with a state that holds an explicitly unfriendly position and seeks to harm the interests of our country."
It also suspended visa-free travel for former Japanese residents of the Southern Kuril Islands to the places of their former residency.
Since taking office, the Takaichi administration's push for greater remilitarisation has raised Russia's security concerns.
In late July, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko argued that the belligerent stance of the Japanese authorities negatively affects stability in the Asia-Pacific region and directly undermines the security interests of neighboring countries.
Regarding Russia-Japan relations, the diplomat said that only if Japan takes concrete steps to abandon its anti-Russian stance can the two countries resume dialogue and cooperation.
Analysts say the prospects for a breakthrough in Russia-Japan relations remain slim. Neither side appears to have much room for compromise on the territorial dispute, while Japan's alignment with the West over the Ukraine crisis makes a significant easing of sanctions against Russia unlikely. ■

====================================================================================================

Parashat Shoftim: Wholehearted – and well
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:33:48 UTC
18:33:48 KST

Among many people, a tamim – a “simple” or “naive” person – is considered someone who is easily deceived, who believes everything he hears, and does not exercise sound judgment. Yet in the language of the Torah, the word has an entirely different meaning. Tamim expresses wholeness and completeness.
The sacrifice offered in the Temple had to be tamim – whole and without blemish. Jacob, our forefather, the chosen of the Patriarchs, is also described as an ish tam – a “wholehearted man,” an expression denoting a person who is complete, upright, and free of moral defect. In Judaism, then, being tamim is not a shortcoming, but a great virtue.
This idea is expressed in one of the central verses of this week’s Torah portion, a verse that conveys a profound principle of Jewish faith.
The Torah describes practices that were widespread in the ancient world: turning to sorcerers, magicians, diviners, and those who claim to communicate with the dead, in the belief that they could reveal the future or control hidden forces. Many people were drawn to these phenomena because they appeared to possess power and influence. Yet the Torah unequivocally rejects them. It teaches that human beings do not possess an independent power to change reality through mysterious forces, and that such practices are not a genuine source of knowledge or control.
Our Sages extended this prohibition to superstitions that developed over the generations. Often, even educated and intelligent people adopt baseless practices: a “lucky” shirt, a sequence of actions believed to bring success, and the like. It is interesting to see that even those who do not believe in the Creator at all may cling to such beliefs. As one thinker put it: “There is no person who does not believe in something.” The question is whether one chooses to believe in a truth that is stable and grounded, or in beliefs that have no real foundation.
Indeed, after the Torah lists all these forms of sorcery and divination, it concludes with a short, clear, and unequivocal statement: “You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 18:13).
Rashi: We should accept our fates 'wholeheartedly'
Rashi explains this as a fundamental principle of faith:
“Walk with Him wholeheartedly and look forward to Him, and do not investigate the future. Rather, whatever happens to you, accept wholeheartedly, and then you will be with Him and share in His portion.”
At first glance, one might think that the wholeheartedness of which the Torah speaks is the same kind of naivety that the world tends to disparage – as the common saying goes, “A fool believes everything.” It might seem as though the Torah is asking a person not to question, not to investigate, but simply to accept everything. For this reason, throughout the generations, there have been those who have portrayed believers as ignorant and unintelligent people who blindly do whatever they are told without thinking.
But this is not the meaning at all. The wholeheartedness of which the Torah speaks is inner wholeness and confidence in one’s path. A complete person is not swept away by every new idea and is not impressed by every passing belief. Once a person has established for himself that there is a Creator of the world, that He guides reality, gave us the Torah, and watches over every detail, he has no need to seek other sources of security or success. He finds stability in a steadfast path that does not change with the spirit of the times.
One of the foundations that distinguishes Jewish faith is its emphasis on learning, inquiry, and understanding. Throughout the generations, an enormous body of literature has developed seeking to explain the foundations of faith, the reasons behind the commandments, and their meaning – from the simple interpretation of Scripture to the worlds of Jewish philosophy, Kabbalah, and esoteric thought. A person needs only to ask questions and delve deeper, and ultimately, he will find an answer to everything.
Superstitions, by contrast, generally rest on habit, fear, or popular tradition, without any clear foundation. A person who needs amulets, lucky signs, or various rituals in order to feel secure is, in fact, revealing a lack of inner security. The truly whole person finds his security in his faith in the Creator of the world, and as a result, his heart is more at peace.
Rabbi Levi Yitzchak: One's wholeheartedness brings them closer to God
This idea is also expressed by the great Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev:
“The principle is that the way of the Creator, blessed be He, is to do good, and especially toward Israel, His close and beloved people, who are called children of God. Surely, a father fulfills his child’s needs and desires before the child even has to ask. And a person who has such faith in the Creator will certainly have his needs fulfilled. This is the meaning hinted at in the words, ‘You shall be wholehearted with the Lord’: when you attain a state of wholeness, when you have faith in the Creator, blessed be He, that He will certainly fulfill your needs, then you will know that you are indeed ‘with the Lord your God’ – that surely, the Lord is with you” (Kedushat Levi, Shoftim).
His words illuminate a profound principle: the greater a person’s wholeheartedness, the closer his relationship with God becomes. A person who believes with a full heart merits, in Rabbi Levi Yitzchak’s words, that God accompanies him and bestows His goodness upon him.
It thus becomes clear that being a “wholehearted Jew” is a title of honor. It describes a person who has found a stable and clear path and is not shaken by every passing idea or changing spiritual trend. Precisely this wholeheartedness – in its deeper sense of wholeness – creates a close bond with the Creator and gives a person stability throughout his life. From a broader perspective, it often becomes clear that the person who does not chase after every novelty, but remains faithful to the path he has carefully chosen for himself, is the one who ultimately goes farther than all those who pride themselves on being sophisticated.
Yet we should not forget the words of Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz:
“Wholeheartedness is greater than wisdom, but great wisdom is required of a Jew before he reaches the level of ‘You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God.’”
The writer is the rabbi of the Western Wall and Holy Sites.

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's current account balance recorded a surplus of 10.8 billion ringgit (about 2.64 billion U.S. dollars) in the second quarter of 2026, supported by a stronger goods surplus that offset a deterioration in the services account, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said on Friday.

The current account surplus was supported by strong demand for electrical and electronics products, petroleum products, and machinery, equipment and parts.
Goods imports rose 21.7 percent quarter-on-quarter to 318.6 billion ringgit.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) recorded a net inflow of 7.4 billion ringgit, down from 22.8 billion ringgit in the first quarter. The services sector, particularly information and communication, attracted the largest share of FDI, followed by manufacturing.
Direct investment abroad moderated to a net outflow of 7 billion ringgit from 8.1 billion ringgit previously. Singapore, Angola and the Netherlands were the main investment destinations. ■

Diia.Signature Not Working: What to Do and How to Quickly Restore Access
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
12:30:08 EEST
18:30:08 KST

Diia.Signature Not Working: What to Do and How to Quickly Restore Access
Kyiv • UNN
Diia.Signature may not work due to a failure in photo verification, a change of smartphone, or problems on the service's side. To restore access it is worth updating the app, restarting the device, or creating the signature again.
"Diia.Sign" has become one of the main tools for Ukrainians' electronic interaction with the state and businesses. It can be used to sign electronic documents, verify one's identity, and authorize oneself in information systems that support the relevant integration.
However, anyone may encounter a situation in which "Diia.Sign" does not activate, the photo verification fails, signing cannot be completed, or the required service does not respond to the request at all. The reason does not necessarily lie within "Diia" itself. The problem may arise on the smartphone, during identity verification, or in the information system where the user is trying to obtain a service.
How to resolve such a situation and use the service is explained by UNN.
What is "Diia.Sign" and how does it actually work
"Diia.Sign" is a remote qualified electronic signature. It is an electronic equivalent of a handwritten signature and makes it possible to identify the signatory and confirm the authenticity and validity of an electronic document.
To create such a signature, a person needs to log in to the "Diia" app, go to the relevant section in the menu, create a signature, pass photo verification, and set a five-digit code. This can be done free of charge. "Diia.Sign" remains valid for one year, or until the person deactivates it.
Individuals who want to obtain such a signature must have an ID card (which replaces the Ukrainian citizen's passport booklet) or a biometric international passport in the mobile administrative services app "Diia". During verification, the system compares the image taken by the user with the photograph in the document. The resulting facial image is needed directly for verification. After verification, the system deletes the photo .
The personal key of "Diia.Sign" has a special architecture. One part of it is stored on the user's smartphone, while the other is held in a special secure device of the qualified electronic trust service provider "Diia." Therefore, merely knowing the PIN code is not enough if an intruder decides to use the signature. Before signing, the user must pass photo verification and enter their code.
This feature also explains why "Diia.Sign" is linked to a specific device. If a user switches to another smartphone, they need to log in to "Diia" on the new device and create a new "Diia.Sign." The system deletes the previous one. Likewise, the signature is not retained after logging out of the account or deleting the app.
Why "Diia.Sign" may not work
There may be several reasons, and not every error means a large-scale failure of "Diia."
The most common problem point is photo identity verification. It is mandatory both when creating the signature and when using it. The system compares the user's face with the photograph in their electronic document. If the verification is not completed successfully, it will not be possible to sign the document.
The problem may also arise after changing smartphones. Since part of the key is stored directly on the device, an already created "Diia.Sign" cannot be transferred to a new phone. It will have to be created again. We should separately emphasize that after February 2026, in order to create an e-signature in the mobile administrative services app, one should purchase a smartphone with NFC scanner technology. It is needed to read biometric documents.
It is also worth checking whether the user has logged out of their account or reinstalled "Diia." In both cases, the previous "Diia.Sign" is deleted, so it must be created again after logging in once more.
Another group of reasons is related not to the signature itself but to a specific electronic service. "Diia.Sign" is integrated into the information systems of government bodies, enterprises, and other organizations. Therefore, a situation in which it is impossible to log in or sign a document on a specific portal does not in itself prove that the e-signature has stopped working. The failure may also occur in the service that receives it.
Finally, temporary technical problems with the "Diia" app itself or government information resources may occur. In such a situation, the user cannot always resolve the problem independently, and repeatedly reinstalling the app is unlikely to make the government server care about their deadline.
What to do if photo verification fails
First of all, make sure that your smartphone camera is working properly and has access to the app. During face verification, follow the instructions that appear directly on the "Diia" screen.
It is important to distinguish between the service's official requirements and general technical recommendations. For example, online sources often advise users to обязательно remove their glasses, hold the smartphone strictly at eye level, or perform a specific sequence of head movements. The official instruction of the "Diia" Qualified Electronic Trust Service Provider does not contain a universal set of such requirements. Therefore, you should primarily follow the prompts displayed by the app during the specific verification. At the same time, in practice, you should ensure that your face is well lit, make sure the front camera lens is clean, and ensure that your face is clearly visible.
If verification repeatedly ends in an error, it is advisable to close and restart the app and check your internet connection. It would also be worth updating the app itself in the official Play Market store. Restarting the smartphone may also help resolve a local software malfunction.
However, the widespread information online that "Diia.Signature" usually stops working because of a VPN should be treated with caution. The official instructions on the administrative services portal describing the creation and use of the signature do not establish a general ban on using a VPN. Therefore, disabling the VPN may be a way to test the network connection, but it would be incorrect to call it a confirmed typical cause of the malfunction.
How to create a Diia.Signature again
If the problem is specifically related to a previously created signature, the user can deactivate it. This can be done directly through the app on their smartphone. To do so, open the "Diia" menu, go to the "Diia.Signature" section, and select deactivation. After that, the signature can be created again by repeating photo verification and setting a new five-digit code.
How to determine exactly where the failure occurred if "Diia.Signature" does not work
If "Diia.Signature" does not work when using a particular government or commercial portal, it is useful to check whether other app functions work and whether the same problem occurs in another service that supports an e-signature.
At the same time, checking ordinary authorization on the "Diia" portal is not an accurate test of whether the service is functioning properly. Authorization, receiving an electronic service, interaction with a government register, and applying a qualified electronic signature may use different components of the digital infrastructure. Therefore, it is entirely possible for one function to work while another does not.
If the problem is widespread, information about technical maintenance or malfunctions may appear on the official resources of "Diia" and the Ministry of Digital Transformation. In the event of a failure involving a specific register, it is also worth checking announcements from the body that administers it.
What can replace "Diia.Signature"
If a document needs to be signed urgently, it is not necessary to wait for "Diia.Signature" to be restored. Other qualified providers of electronic trust services operate in Ukraine and can issue a qualified electronic signature. The list can be found on the website of the Central Certification Authority.
You can also use a qualified electronic signature issued by the Qualified Electronic Trust Service Provider of the State Tax Service. To obtain electronic trust services for the first time or after the certificates expire, a person must prepare the necessary documents and contact the relevant registration point. For holders of valid State Tax Service certificates, the service provides a number of remote operations, including the reissuance of certificates.
Qualified electronic signatures are also provided by banks and private qualified providers. However, it is worth bearing in mind that in this case, the terms, key format, method of obtaining it, and supported services depend on the specific financial institution.
A document can also be signed using a valid key, in particular via the Diia QES web service. It supports personal keys and certificates from all qualified providers of electronic trust services. According to the service, the user's file is processed directly in the browser during signing and is not transmitted to the provider's side.
Can BankID replace Diia.Signature?
The NBU's BankID is often mistakenly included among the alternatives to a QES. In fact, these technologies perform different functions.
The NBU's BankID is an electronic remote identification system. It allows the bank where the user has already completed identification to transmit the necessary personal data to the institution where the person is receiving an online service. That is why BankID can be used to log in to many government, financial, and commercial services.
However, a user's BankID is not the person's QES and therefore cannot automatically replace "Diia.Signature" where legislation or a specific electronic service requires the application of a qualified electronic signature. The confusion usually arises because, when information is transferred via BankID, the bank itself applies its QES or qualified electronic seal to the data. However, this protects and verifies the data transmitted by the bank; it does not create the client's personal QES.
Where to turn if Diia.Signature still does not work
If the standard steps have not helped, the problem keeps recurring, or the app constantly displays the same error, it is worth contacting the official Diia support service. This can be done via the official support Telegram channel. The request should include the smartphone model, the operating system and app versions, a description of the exact stage at which the problem occurs, and the precise text of the error message. If technically possible, a screenshot should also be attached.
At the same time, do not provide third parties with the PIN code for "Diia.Signature," passwords, bank card details, or any other information that is not required to diagnose the technical problem.
What users of the service should remember
If "Diia.Signature" suddenly stops working, this does not mean that the user has lost the ability to sign electronic documents. First, it is worth determining exactly where the problem occurs: during photo verification, in the app itself, when interacting with a specific website, or when applying the signature.
If the problem is local, restarting the app, checking the internet connection, updating Diia, or creating the signature again may help. If the failure occurred on the side of an external system or state registry, reinstalling the app will not fix the situation.
For urgent documents, it remains possible to use another valid QES from a qualified provider, if the specific service supports it. BankID should be regarded specifically as a means of remote identification, rather than a universal replacement for an electronic signature.
The main rule in the event of a technical problem is not to deactivate the signature or reinstall the app unnecessarily. It is better to first check whether "Diia.Signature" is actually malfunctioning, rather than the website or electronic service in which the user is trying to use it.
Let us remind you
Earlier, we wrote that the "Army+" app launched multiple-signature support for reports. This innovation significantly speeds up the document approval process, reducing the administrative burden on military personnel.

This Art Project Slows Down Citi Bikes to Make NYC’s Rent Crisis Feel Real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Justin Blinder lost his job two weeks before the Covid-19 pandemic hit in 2020. To pay his rent, he turned to delivery services, riding his bicycle across New York City to deliver food. As he went, he noticed the disparities in where the food items went. Which order of Nomé sushi went where and how much people tipped.
“The city started to feel much more economically and psychologically disparate,” Blinder tells WIRED. “It really changed so much on a block-by-block level. These inequalities and demographic differences were happening in such close proximity.”
That experience has morphed into an art-project gadget called Ground Truth that Blinder hopes will raise awareness about the housing affordability crisis in New York City and beyond by making a Citi Bike—one of the ever-present ebike rental options across the city—harder to ride through places where it’s harder to live.
Blinder, a Brooklyn artist and contractor at Meta, received a $10,000 grant for the project from a Brooklyn arts organization called Idle Hands.
Ground Truth is a box that will trigger the brakes on the Lyft-owned bicycle, adding more resistance to the pedals when riding through rent-burdened neighborhoods, where people living in those areas spend more than 30 percent of their income on rent. Ride past an economically well-off block, and the bike is easier to pedal. Going past a block where rent takes the bulk of the households’ incomes can slow the bike down to a crawl.
There are two versions, one that can work on a regular bicycle and one built specifically for Citi Bikes.
The box mounts on the bike’s fork and is then attached to the front brake line. A battery-powered GPS component tracks the bike’s location. As it moves, the location is cross-referenced with household economic data from the US Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, stored on the device. When the bike passes a block the dataset says has a higher percentage of rent insecurity, the microcontroller triggers a small motor that applies the brake to add resistance, and the bike gets physically harder to pedal.
Blinder is also the creator of the Covid-inspired Pandemic Pulse, an app that used real time Covid statistics to change the brightness of your device’s screen. The screen would darken whenever data showed infections growing, and then black out briefly whenever a death was recorded. As with Ground Truth, Blinder says the goal of these projects is to help people understand large datasets in a more tactile way.
“It’s really trying to make the way we traditionally visualize a lot of big data more tangible and embodied,” he says. “Create something a bit more confrontational and try to force people to consider how they traditionally look at data.”
Blinder says the device is not a working product or something other people will be able to use. (Likely for legal reasons, as you can’t just change how a rideshare electric bicycle drives.) But he has ridden about 35 miles or so, filming the experience as Ground Truth changes its resistance in different communities.
He hopes the project will also call attention to the rising cost of renting a Citi Bike. The service has raised its prices for the past five years in a row.
“The price has just become so astronomical that it felt like this really nice connective tissue in the affordability crisis, connecting all of those different elements,” Blinder says. “It’s really thinking about how affordability changes throughout the city on a block-by-block basis and how this system could allow people to experience that.”
