ZHITKOVICHI DISTRICT, 14 August (BelTA) –I expect this year’s harvest to surpass the record set in 2025, Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko said during a working trip to Zhitkovichi District on 14 August, BelTA has learned.
 
 
The head of state heard a report from the Gomel Oblast governor on the progress of harvesting campaign in the country’s southern region. According to the report, 95% of the areas sown with grains, legumes, and rapeseed have been harvested in the region. More than 980,000 tonnes of cereal crops alone have been collected, and the region is set to hit the one-million-tonne milestone as early as on 15 August, which is a strong indicator for the area. The expected gross grain harvest stands at 1.051 million tonnes, up 20,000 tonnes from the 2025 level. With the corn harvest projected to reach 450,000 tonnes, the region aims to hit an aggregate grain yield of 1.5 million tonnes. 
 
 
 
                    
                    
                                        
                                    
                                                        
                
                
            The head of state heard a report from the Gomel Oblast governor on the progress of harvesting campaign in the country’s southern region. According to the report, 95% of the areas sown with grains, legumes, and rapeseed have been harvested in the region. More than 980,000 tonnes of cereal crops alone have been collected, and the region is set to hit the one-million-tonne milestone as early as on 15 August, which is a strong indicator for the area. The expected gross grain harvest stands at 1.051 million tonnes, up 20,000 tonnes from the 2025 level. With the corn harvest projected to reach 450,000 tonnes, the region aims to hit an aggregate grain yield of 1.5 million tonnes.
Work continues to clear fields of straw and prepare the land for winter crop planting. The president issued a strict warning regarding winter rapeseed cultivation, emphasizing that farming protocols must be followed to the letter, with the proper application of fertilizers, pesticides, and growth regulators. This is the only way to protect crops under any weather conditions and secure a solid harvest in the future.
The governor also reported an increase in agricultural production for January-July of 2026 by more than 18% compared to the same period in 2025.
The president recalled that he had set last year’s record 2025 harvest as the benchmark for the country’s farmers.
“Last year was a record one. I have set it as a benchmark, after all. If we see growth nationwide compared to last year, that is already good, a positive dynamic. Therefore, it is crucial that we build upon last year’s results. It was a very high, record-breaking year,” Aleksandr Lukashenko emphasized

Why not learn from him? He is a goldmine of knowledge. Just come and copy it,” the head of state said.

This 16th-century Renaissance palace in Spain was just converted into a five-star hotel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:00:35 UTC
18:00:35 KST

A 16th-century Spanish Renaissance palace has been transformed into a luxury stay, blending historic grandeur, thermal wellness experiences and even a menu for four-legged guests.
Fancy checking into a five-star hotel with all the grandeur of a Spanish Renaissance palace?
Castilla Termal, a luxury hotelier, has unveiled the sixth hotel in its portfolio – a restored Renaissance palace in the medieval village of Peñaranda de Duero.
Palacio de Avellaneda, an 80-key stay, took three years to restore, with rooms and suites now blending contemporary comforts with the palace’s 16th-century original architecture. A night’s stay in September starts at €314.60.
Built by the Zúñiga and Avellaneda family in the 16th century, the palace-turned-five-star hotel was declared a monument in 1923 before passing state hands in 1940.
The junior suite room includes a separate sitting area as well as views of the Plaza de los Duques de Miranda, while the larger suite also features frontal views of the Plaza.
When it comes to dining, guests will soon have two in-house concepts to choose from. Los Zúñiga Restaurant sits beneath the arches of the palace’s Renaissance cloister and serves local and seasonal produce. Its lunch and dinner service includes shareable dishes, such as a board of local cheeses with quince paste and dried fruit, fish, meat and salad dishes, as well as sweet treats.
The second restaurant, the Condes de Miranda Gastrobar, will open at a later date.
Beyond being a historic retreat, the stay is also a destination for rest and relaxation. The palace’s waters have been declared oligometallic mineral-medicinal and thermal water by the Regional Government of Castile and León’s authorities.
That therapeutic water is a core component of its wellness experiences, which include body scrubs, an array of massages and facials. There are also plans for a thermal pool and contrast circuit soon to come.
Four-legged guests are welcome, too. One dog is permitted per room with pre-reservation and the hotel will take care of its bedding and has space for dog walking. There is even a dedicated pet menu, with duck, chicken and lamb dishes on offer.

‘What’s happened to us? Where did we get lost?’ Zimbabwe reckons with the reality of violence against women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

The three white coffins were draped in white lace and topped with small sprays of flowers. The mourners who filled a Bulawayo church last week to pay their respects to Zandile Tshuma and her daughters, Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, had not engaged in the usual tradition of first viewing the dead at their home: the bodies of this family had travelled all the way from England to reach their final resting place at Luveve cemetery on the edge of Zimbabwe’s second city, in Matabeleland.
While the deaths attracted few news reports in the UK, in Zimbabwe and South Africa, the tragic case has reignited concern over the region’s high rates of femicide. Many commentators on TV and social media expressed shock that a well-educated woman with a successful career abroad seemed as vulnerable to familial violence as a poorer woman in a southern African township.
Tshuma’s elderly parents were at the gravesides. The father, in a blue suit and clutching a wooden cane, and her mother, in the black-and-white uniform of her church’s elders, sat in silence. Never Mpofu, 44, a neighbour, was taught at primary school by Tshuma’s mother. He says he was saddened by the violent way the family had been killed.
Tshuma, a 42-year-old financial data analyst, Natalie, an avid computer science student and budding sportswoman, and Nala, described as a bubbly little girl, were all found dead at their home in Britain on 6 July.
Bedfordshire police have said that “work is now underway” to have a British-Zimbabwean man returned to the UK from South Africa in connection with the murders. “Zandile never really said if there were problems,” Mpofu says. “Whenever she came home, she was happy to see her family, but now we can see the monsters are out here.”
At the funeral service, Theophilus Khumalo, an uncle, says the family is deeply hurt by the killings and he hopes they will find justice.
“We will allow the law to take its course. We will not be drawn into anger or bitterness; we will not allow this tragedy to define us. Instead, we choose to honour their memory with grace, unity and unwavering faith in God’s justice,” he adds.
Each day, an estimated 137 women and girls around the world are killed by someone they know. Femicide – defined by the United Nations as an “intentional killing with a gender-related motivation” – is driven by discrimination and inequality.
Zimbabwe does not keep specific data on femicides, but according to government statistics, nearly 40% of Zimbabwean women aged 15 to 49 have experienced physical violence and an estimated 12% to 25% of them have been sexually assaulted.
Musasa, a local organisation set up to help survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), reported more than 30,000 GBV incidents in 2024, while the Zimbabwean police recorded nearly 19,000 cases. Much of the abuse happens inside the home. During Covid lockdowns, GBV rose by 60%.
Judith Ncube, minister of state for provincial affairs, says she is deeply concerned as southern Matabeleland, which borders Bulawayo, has the highest rates of intimate partner violence in the country.
“In the region of Matabeleland, it’s as if we take the silver medal. What has gone wrong, what’s happened to us, where did we get lost? In marriage, not everything is smooth, but it shouldn’t lead to death and a home of fear,” she says.
Ncube has called for an urgent debate about domestic violence and suggests launching home-care programmes for community elders to contact families to discuss problems.
“Something has gone wrong in our social fabric: we no longer have aunts and uncles who are go-betweens in marriages,” she says. “We need to capacitate caregivers to be professional and sit down with our young people and talk. We have pastors that can help, too.”
Samkeliso Tshuma, founder of the Zimbabwean advocacy group The Girls Table, says there is a critical need to educate people about domestic violence.
“It’s heartbreaking,” she says. “We need to use social media to raise awareness of what intimate partner violence does to a community, to a society and the families that we are building.
“We need people to renew their minds, because as long we have people who still think that there is a reason for a man to abuse a woman, then we have a long way to go,” she says.
Bulawayo’s courts are only too familiar with femicide cases. In July, a 43-year-old church elder was charged with murdering his wife with an axe then attacking the couple’s children with a metal rod in the city’s suburb of Nkulumane.
A study in Zimbabwe carried out by the Swedish International Development Agency (SIDA) and the United Nations put the direct and indirect costs of gender-based violence at up to $2bn, taking into account the cost of injury, trauma and death, multiplied by the loss of productivity and of young girls dropping out of school due to violence.
Miranda Tabifor, the representative in Zimbabwe of the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), calls on the government to invest more in addressing domestic violence because of the far-reaching costs to the state.
The cost to the government to “address issues of psychosocial support [and] the social scars that continue to haunt the survivors of gender-based violence” Tabifor puts at more than $1bn, but she warns that the government will continue to lose up to 3.8% of its $57bn GDP if the violence continues to be unaddressed.
“We should all unite,” she says. “Every woman, every girl in Zimbabwe has to live a life free from violence, not just because it is their right but because it is the right thing to do.”

Colombia vows to keep searching for hundreds missing after quake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:00:21 UTC
18:00:21 KST

Colombia’s disaster relief chief vowed Friday to keep searching for hundreds of people still missing after a massive earthquake, as rescuers combed through rubble in a desperate effort to find survivors despite the end of the critical 72-hour rescue window.
The 7.4-magnitude earthquake, the strongest to hit Colombia this century, devastated the western cities of Cali and Pereira, destroying nearly 13,000 homes across the coffee-growing region and along the coast.
The quake struck Monday, killing 281 people and injuring nearly 4,000, President Abelardo de la Espriella told reporters. Another 379 people remained missing.
Rescuers faced diminishing hopes of finding survivors, as most people trapped beneath earthquake rubble who are rescued alive are typically found within the first 72 hours. Still, emergency teams continued digging through collapsed buildings and debris in search of those unaccounted for.
David Tamayo, head of Colombia’s disaster relief agency, acknowledged that the “likelihood of finding survivors is going to diminish.”
“But our commitment is to never stop searching ... The order is to not rest until we find all the missing persons,” he said in a video posted by his agency late Thursday.
In Cali, many families who lost their homes sought refuge in makeshift camps set up in streets and parks.
Maria del Carmen Rodriguez, 72, lost the apartment she had saved for her entire life.
Cradling a cup of coffee, she gazed at her destroyed home from the football field where she had bedded down with her 76-year-old husband.
“We wonder what aid we’re entitled to, whether they’re going to relocate us somewhere else, because this is going to last a long time,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
De la Espriella declared the disaster an “economic emergency” and announced three days of national mourning.
“We will do what is necessary,” the newly appointed leader said, vowing to “emerge again as a country and as a society.”
Javier Alzate, a 79-year-old psychologist, was trying to remove tiles and chunks of debris that were blocking access to his damaged home in Pereira.
“It’s very distressing. Very sad. You work 40 or 50 years to buy a little house, struggling all that time to get it. I finally got it, and a few days later it’s gone,” Alzate said. “I lost my home and my car.”
The impoverished Choco region on the Pacific coast also suffered immensely, with some of its remote communities yet to be surveyed.
In the neighboring Valle del Cauca region, Gov. Dilian Francisca Toro said officials were conducting a census of damaged and destroyed homes to determine which buildings could still be occupied.
“We have to begin working because people simply cannot bear staying out on the streets any longer,” she said.
“People are telling us: ‘If you give us the materials, we’ll do the work ourselves,’” Toro said, describing plans for community-led reconstruction efforts.
Many Colombians have mobilized to help, bringing water, food and supplies to affected neighborhoods, while long lines have formed outside blood donation centers.
“Quake victims are not alone, that is a message we want to convey,” Laura Mendoza, a 47-year-old volunteer organizing donations in the capital, Bogota, told AFP.
“We are here giving what we can so that they at least have the most basic things,” she said.
A musician in Cali took to offering hugs to anyone who needed emotional support.
“We are going through a collective trauma, and I think the best way I could help was by giving away the energy I have and the vitality I have left,” Andres Solomon, 46, told AFP.
Colombia was preparing to receive international urban search-and-rescue teams from the United States, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, disaster authorities said.
Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said Thursday that Colombia had refused entry to Mexican rescuers over claims that they lacked the proper certification.
De la Espriella’s administration is facing criticism over allegations that it blocked rescue teams from countries with leftist governments, but it has denied the accusation.

Russia unlikely to withdraw Black Sea Fleet from Novorossiysk after strikes – Ukrainian Navy spokesman
He made the statement in a television interview, Ukrinform reports.

In his opinion, the Russians are more likely to simply lose their ships in another attack than make another "goodwill gesture" by withdrawing them.

He stressed that the enemy had drawn conclusions from the attack and would try to reinforce its vulnerabilities.
"However, as you can see, a massive attack still produces results, no matter how you defend yourself. This tool works both ways," he added, explaining that Russia has begun carrying out mass attacks on civilian vessels in Ukrainian waters, and that it is difficult to counter such attacks when they reach a certain scale.
Pletenchuk said three surface warships and two submarines remain in Novorossiysk.
"But, of course, the damaged vessels were the key ones. And, by the way, this isn't the first time they have come under attack. We destroyed them several times before, but, as you can see, they continued to operate them despite that," he said.
As reported, Ukrainian forces struck four Russian warships in Novorossiysk, Krasnodar region, overnight on August 12.
According to preliminary information, four warships sustained varying degrees of damage: two Project 11356 frigates, the Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen; the Project 21631 Buyan-M small missile ship; and the Project 22160 Vasily Bykov patrol ship.

Reds on the blacklist: Locarno revives Hollywood’s radical authors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Reds on the blacklist: Locarno revives Hollywood’s radical authors
The Locarno Film Festival’s major retrospective explores the work of left-wing filmmakers targeted during the McCarthy era, revealing a body of cinema whose critiques of nationalism, careerism and conformity resonate strongly today.
There are many ironies about staging an ambitious retrospective section at a large contemporary film festival. Novelty is the base currency of the movie industry, and a celebration of films made by dead people nearly a century ago provides scarce opportunity for the distribution of business cards.
The Locarno Film Festival retrospective section, housed primarily in the historic Gran Rex theatre, must therefore provide a kind of micro-environment within the festival, talking back to the main slate and making a case for an alternative mode of relating to the cinema.
This year’s retrospective topic, “Red and Black: Hollywood Left and the Blacklist”, speaks to the tumultuous present in a few ways. Members of the “Hollywood Left” were censored by the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) throughout the 1950s, accused of having ties to Communism.
Though censorship of left sentiment in popular media has long been a facet of American life – whether tied to criticism of Israel, trans advocacy, or critical race theory – this trend has been exaggerated since the start of the second term of President Donald Trump, who even branded the milquetoast TV host Jimmy Kimmel a dangerous revolutionary.
Challenging the Blacklist history
Ehsan Khoshbakht, who has curated the Locarno retrospective section since 2024, and additionally co-directs the Il Cinema Ritrovato festival of film history in Bologna each year, intends to challenge the history of the Blacklist as it has typically been told.
“I’m very critical of the American approach to the question of the Blacklist,” Khoshbakht told Swissinfo, “because they tend to disregard one central fact: that these people were, in many cases, devoted Communists. Some were even Stalinists, and they made very analytical films dissecting their society.”
Take, for example, Abraham Polonsky’s Force of Evil from 1948. John Garfield (who, like Polonsky, was blacklisted for refusing to cooperate with HUAC in 1951) stars as Joe Morse, a crooked lawyer working to monopolise and legitimise the “numbers racket”, a popular and unauthorised lottery system before such contests were legal in the United States. Morse’s relatively innocent brother is himself a small-time crook in this racket, and his even more innocent secretary, Doris, is seduced without too much trouble into this bright, guilty world.
Bearing out Khoshbakht’s sentiments, in his vivisection of American society, Polonsky finds rot at every level. His anti-nationalist sentiment is clear from the jump: Morse’s cadre’s big scam relies on rigging the numbers to come up “1776” on July 4, the number bet by every patriotic rube in America.
Careerism in America
A common thread in many of the retrospective films is a suspicion of the twin American virtues of ambition and careerism. Edgar G. Ulmer’s Ruthless (1948), with a script featuring contributions from the blacklisted writers Alvah Bessie and Gordon Kahn, tells the cautionary tale of Horace Vendig (Zachary Scott), a rags-to-riches philanthropist who steps over friends, wives and lovers to make it to the top.
The film plays something like Citizen Kane (1942) in a slightly harder emotional register, with Orson Welles’ psychological complexity replaced with something a little closer to pure hatred. “You’re the only friend I have,” Vendig tells his childhood friend Vic (Louis Hayward), after he has betrayed everyone else. “And I hate your insides,” Vic responds, as if the writers were speaking directly to their informants.
These filmmakers and writers – Bessie, Kahn, Polonsky, and so many more – were stolen from audiences at the peak of their powers, along with their vision of a popular American cinema that could dissent from national consensus. Khoshbakht carries something of this anger with him.
“It’s such a waste,” Khoshbakht tells Swissinfo. “It’s really painful, to this day, when you think of how this flow of talent, ideas, imagination, commitment, was stopped in its tracks. We are still catching up.”
In the Blacklist era, the filmmakers of the Hollywood Left were forced to make a choice between their careers or their principles. Those who named names for HUAC continued, in many cases, onto long and successful careers in America, while those who refused had their livelihoods ruined, and are only now being properly celebrated. The films of the Hollywood Left, made before and after the Blacklist, turned their scorn to this prevailing culture of every man for himself.
The Intimate Stranger (1956), made by blacklisted director Joseph Losey, sets its sights on a film industry where ruthlessness is the order of the day. Exiled from Hollywood, like Losey, film editor Reggie Wilson (Richard Basehart) moves to England, where he weds a major film producer’s daughter and assumes a head post at the company. His motives are only further called into question when a woman from his past claims that he dropped her in order to get ahead in the industry with his new wife.
When asked if he hoped the retrospective might impart something of this anti-careerist bent to the rest of the festival, Khoshbakht demurs. “I can’t know how the retrospective corresponds with the contemporary film programming,” Khoshbakht says. “That’s a question for the audience.”
The fruits of careerism are on display everywhere in modern society – children, some observers noteExternal link, can no longer identify ambition as a “fatal flaw” in Shakespeare (Macbeth). It’s tempting to hope that these films of the Hollywood Left are able to raise their voices to chastise the ruthless ambition that has continued apace in the film industry since the days of the Blacklist. But it’s not a problem a film, even a retrospective, can solve, and so Khoshbakht defines a more modest aim.
“I just find it gratifying when someone who is in Locarno to watch new films gets tired of too many digital images, randomly enters a retrospective film and is blown away by it,” he said.
Dylan Adamson is a film critic and curator based in Toronto, Canada. His writing can be found at the Globe and Mail, The Toronto Star, Filmmaker Magazine, Senses of Cinema, among other outlets. His curated programs have played at TIFF Cinematheque, Anthology Film Archives, and the San Francisco Cinematheque.

The Real Reason Data Center Gas Power Plants Are So Dirty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Amazon has acquired a massive off-grid power plant being built in Texas for one of its data centers that could be one of the biggest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in the US.
But size isn’t the only reason its climate toll will be so high. The plant will rely on a much less efficient set of gas turbines than regular power plants use; these kinds of turbines are also increasingly being put to use at other data center projects around the US. That could have big implications for the environmental impact of artificial intelligence—and the future of the US grid.
Amazon’s Texas power plant is permitted to emit up to 33 million tons of greenhouse gases a year. The project will rely solely on simple cycle turbines, which mix fuel and air in a combustion chamber to create energy, letting off a significant amount of waste heat in the process. Combined cycle units, which are generally used at on-grid power plants, add an additional steam turbine component to capture the waste heat and turn it into more energy. That means they release fewer emissions for the same amount of energy.
Permitted emissions on natural gas plants are usually much higher than their actual emissions. But even if Amazon’s facility emits half of what’s on the permit each year, it would still create more greenhouse gas pollution than 78 average-sized natural gas plants, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.
The Texas plant provides “on-site generation that won't raise electricity costs for Texas families,” Amazon spokesperson Margaret Callahan writes in an email to WIRED, adding that the site would also have solar and battery storage and that the company is still committed to reaching net-zero emissions by 2040.
Using simple-cycle turbines is becoming an increasingly common practice for data center power developers looking for flexible power that’s quick to install. At least three power plants being developed in Ohio by oil and gas company Williams for Meta will also rely on simple cycle units, according to permit applications. In Abilene, Texas, Crusoe is building a power plant on its Stargate campus to power a Microsoft data center with 39 simple-cycle turbines. The permit application for Google’s Goodnight data center at another Texas site being developed by Crusoe describes relying on 20 simple-cycle turbines. And both xAI’s Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers in Memphis are being powered by dozens of simple cycle turbines. All of them are permitted to release millions of tons of greenhouse gases. (Both Williams and Crusoe tell WIRED in an email that their gas plants comply with local and national regulations and are outfitted with emissions control technology.)
Britt Burt, a senior vice president at Industrial Info Resources, an energy market intelligence firm, says that he didn’t expect data center developers to lean so heavily on simple cycle turbines for power.
“It’s not the most efficient way to use a gas turbine,” he says.
For companies racing to get data centers online, though, it’s a lot quicker—and cheaper—to install a handful of simple-cycle turbines than wait for the additional equipment needed for combined-cycle units, especially given a yearslong backlog for turbine orders and associated parts.
“Right now, because of the way the supply chain is for turbines, they’re having to go with what they can get their hands on,” says Burt.
Then there’s the energy needs of data centers, especially those training AI models. Thanks to their fewer moving parts, simple cycle turbines can start up and shut down more rapidly than combined cycle units. That suits AI training, which requires big spikes of energy on demand. (In fact, those spikes are so big that many data center operators have reported turbines breaking thanks to the extreme stress of turning on and off.)
“If you have a highly fluctuating load, it's better to have 30 things that can individually turn on and off than to have one giant thing that doesn't like to be turned on and off,” says Stephen Lynch, a professor of mechanical engineering at Penn State and director of the school’s Center for Gas Turbine Research, Education, and Outreach.
Simple cycle turbines also generally don’t require water, which itself is an increasingly hot-button issue for communities near data centers. Burt estimates that a 250-megawatt combined-cycle plant could use about 75,000 gallons per hour. The permit application for the new Amazon plant specifically lists simple cycle technology’s lack of water use as an “environmental benefit.”
The federal government and a growing number of state governors across the political spectrum are encouraging data center power providers to bring or build their own energy to avoid raising consumer electric bills.
Some companies have promised to integrate their power plants with the grid eventually. Callahan, the Amazon spokesperson, said that the Texas plant is “designed to transition to grid-connected service as interconnection timelines allow.” Williams told WIRED earlier this month that it may consider the Ohio plants for interconnection in the future.
There are power plants designed with simple-cycle turbines, known as peaker plants, which are used to rapidly provide power to the grid when demand is high. But for now, the rapid construction of new islanded power plants with inefficient turbines—many of which are designed to last for decades—threatens to create a parallel fossil fuel grid that generates millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions.
If the AI bubble bursts or tech companies’ energy needs dip, though, it’s possible that the massive, inefficient gas plants could no longer have a purpose.
“We call that a stranded asset,” Burt says, chuckling.
Update: 8/14/2026, 3:05 PM EDT: WIRED updated the article to correct the name spelling of the Amazon spokesperson.

BANGKOK, August 14. /TASS/. The US and Israel are attempting, through barbaric methods, to deprive Iran of its inalienable right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy, Iranian Ambassador to Thailand Nassereddin Heidari told a TASS correspondent.
"The bitterness of this story is that, two nuclear powers - one of which has a history of using the atomic bomb for mass slaughter, and the other, despite possessing nuclear arsenals, is not a party to any disarmament treaty including the NPT (the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons - TASS) - are attempting illegal and barbaric methods to deprive a nation of its inalienable right to the peaceful use of nuclear energy," the diplomat said.

There is no evidence in the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) documents indicating any diversion in Iran's nuclear activities. More than 15 reports by the Agency to the Board of Governors regarding the non-diversion of Iran's peaceful nuclear program confirm this fact. Based on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons Treaty (NPT), to which Iran is a party, all countries have the inalienable right to [the] peaceful use of nuclear energy, including nuclear enrichment for peaceful purposes. To deprive a nation of these rights is against the NPT, the documents of the NPT Review Conferences, and the sovereign rights of a nation," Heidari emphasized.

Hong Kong raises growth forecast after best half-yearly showing in nearly 5 years
Hong Kong revises full-year economic growth forecast for 2026 to a range of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent
Hong Kong has raised its full-year economic growth forecast for 2026 to a range of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent following a 4.3 per cent expansion in the second quarter, supported by buoyant external trade and resilient domestic demand.
Releasing its half-yearly economic report on Friday, the government revised its 2026 growth forecast from the previous range of 2.5 to 3.5 per cent, citing a stronger-than-expected performance in the first half of the year and taking into account the near-term outlook.
It said the economy should experience “solid growth” in the second half, with global demand for artificial intelligence-related electronic products expected to support merchandise trade, while rising visitor arrivals would benefit the exports of services.
The Tourism Board said Hong Kong received 26.71 million visitors in the first half of 2026, a 13 per cent increase from a year earlier.
Arrivals in June rose by 7 per cent year on year to 3.72 million, with mainland Chinese visitors accounting for 2.88 million.
The second-quarter figure, unchanged from the advance estimate released last month, was slower than the 5.9 per cent growth recorded in the first three months.

No casualties were reported in the blast, which occurred near the town of Colleferro, about 45 km southeast of Rome, on Thursday.

Global markets welcomed moderate US inflation data released this week, while strong corporate earnings also fueled risk appetite, but continued uncertainty over efforts to reach peace in the Middle East limited optimism.
The US Producer Price Index (PPI) remained unchanged month-on-month but rose 4.7% on an annual basis in July, below estimates, while energy prices continued to decline.
The ongoing decline in the energy component of US consumer inflation also strengthened expectations that forward-looking price pressures could ease.
Expectations for Fed rate hikes were pushed back to December as the New York Stock Exchange closed at record highs and the US Dollar Index eased below the 100 threshold.
The Fed is increasingly expected to keep its policy rate unchanged next month, while the probability of a rate hike stands at 54% in October and 92% in December.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack reiterated that rate hikes are needed to bring down persistently high inflation.
Meanwhile, continued uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the US-Iran conflict in the Middle East remained on investors’ radar.
The US 10-year Treasury yield fell five basis points to 4.66%, while the US Dollar Index was trading sideways at 99.8. Gold was down 0.6% at $4,324 per ounce on Friday despite waning rate hike expectations, amid delays in reaching peace in the Middle East, profit-taking and a shift toward riskier assets led by the technology sector.
October-delivery Brent crude was trading flat at $87.10 a barrel at the same time.
Investors also turned their attention to corporate financial results during the ongoing earnings season.
US technology company Cisco reported results above estimates, but its shares fell 8.4%, while the recovery in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks on the US market continued.
The S&P 500 gained 0.65% and reached a new record, the Nasdaq rose 0.81%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.13% on Thursday. US indexes opened Friday on a mixed course.
In Europe, risk appetite was dampened by high oil prices.
European statistical office Eurostat is set to release second-quarter growth estimates for the EU and the eurozone on Friday.
The eurozone’s gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow 0.4% on a quarterly basis and 1% year-on-year.
The eurozone’s industrial production remained flat on a monthly basis but increased 0.1% year-on-year.
The UK economy grew 0.4% in the second quarter from the previous quarter, while industrial production fell 0.5% in June, a larger-than-expected decline.
Coal’s share of EU electricity generation fell to 9.2% last year, its lowest level on record.
The UK’s FTSE 100 fell 0.56%, France’s CAC 40 declined 0.28%, and Germany’s DAX 40 was down 0.12%, while Italy’s FTSE MIB 30 remained flat on Thursday. European indexes opened Friday mixed.
Asian equity markets also traded mixed amid uncertainty over peace efforts in the Middle East, high energy prices and corporate developments.
China’s Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) raised prices amid strong AI demand, pushing its shares up 1.9%.
Near Friday’s close, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 0.3% and South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.5%, while China’s Shanghai Composite fell 0.5% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng declined 1.1%.

‘Like Snow on Your Head’: Russia Threatens Ukraine With Winter ‘Freeze’ as Kyiv Pushes for Ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:59:01 UTC
17:59:01 KST

Russia has threatened Ukrainians with a new “freeze” this winter, appearing to signal that Moscow could intensify its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population – just one day after Kyiv offered Russia a mutual ‘freeze’ on attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.
On Friday, Russia’s defense ministry posted a photo of attack drones with the caption “Like snow on your head.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It followed with a message directed at Ukrainians: “Winter will bring you a ‘freeze.’”
The post appeared to be a threat to step up Russia’s drone campaign as temperatures drop, potentially targeting the energy infrastructure that keeps millions of Ukrainians warm through the winter.
Just one day earlier, on Thursday, Ukraine offered Russia a mutual halt to attacks on civilian ships and port infrastructure in the Black Sea. Kyiv transmitted the proposal through an unnamed third country.
The Russian defense ministry declined the proposal on Friday, saying that “the Russian Armed Forces continue to strike Ukraine’s port infrastructure and vessels at sea being used in support of the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Kyiv’s truce offer came amid a Black Sea escalation
Ukraine’s proposal was made as Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping have severely disrupted the country’s vital export routes.
Ukraine’s grain exports fell 76% year-on-year in the first part of August, according to Reuters, as intensified attacks disrupted maritime trade.
Ukraine Proposes Mutual Halt to Black Sea Attacks
Around 90% of Ukraine’s agricultural exports normally move through the Black Sea, making the security of its ports and shipping lanes critical to both the Ukrainian economy and global food supplies.
On Tuesday, Ukraine launched a major coordinated strike on Novorossiysk, Russia’s key Black Sea naval and grain-export hub.
The attack forced three major grain terminals to suspend operations and hit Russian naval infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the operation involved 15 domestically produced missile, aerial-drone, and naval-drone systems.
Novorossiysk has become a principal sanctuary for Russia’s Black Sea Fleet after repeated Ukrainian attacks forced Moscow to relocate many of its vessels from occupied Crimea.
Russia’s winter threat
The Kremlin has previously used winter attacks on Ukraine’s energy system as a weapon, targeting power plants, substations, and other critical infrastructure in an effort to leave civilians without electricity, heating and water.
Andriy Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said Russia’s message could ultimately rebound on its own population.
“Russians already know who will be responsible for them having no electricity or heating this winter,” Kovalenko said, referring to the Russian defense ministry’s threat.
He added that Russia’s statement was effectively aimed at Russians as well as Ukrainians.
“Everything is thanks to the Russian Defense Ministry. The mirror always works. What you sow, so shall you reap,” Kovalenko said.

The report by the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), a body appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, documents a year-long investigation into alleged “war crimes and crimes against humanity” committed by Myanmar’s military and its linked militias, as well as by armed opposition groups.

They find a sword, we find a shield: Ukrainian soldier on why drones will never replace infantry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:58:38 UTC
17:58:38 KST

Serafim Hordiienko enlisted at 19 in 2022, fought as a mortarman near the front line, then moved into drone warfare as it grew central to Russia's war on Ukraine. In an interview with RBC-Ukraine, he pushed back on the idea that unmanned systems are phasing out infantry, arguing the two perform separate functions neither can absorb.
The debate is live inside Ukraine's own military. Ukraine's Third Army Corps has said it plans to replace roughly 30% of its infantry with ground robotic systems by the end of 2026, and other officers have called full infantry replacement an eventual goal. Hordiienko's account, shaped by his own shift from rifle-and-mortar combat to drone operations, argues against that trajectory ever completing — infantry holds ground; drones strike and surveil; neither substitutes for the other.
"Different functions of war"
Hordiienko compared infantry and drones to two halves of a single system rather than competing tools. Infantry cannot operate without supporting fire and reconnaissance, he said, and drones — while efficient at surveillance and strikes — cannot hold territory the way ground troops can. If war is still fought over front lines and captured ground, he argued, only infantry can perform that function; drones deliver cost-effective damage but do not occupy space.
He traced Ukraine's drone advantage not to hardware alone but to the system around it — production, battlefield communication, and rapid adaptation to frontline needs. Ukrainian manufacturers he named, including Skyeton, Ukrspetssystems, DeviRO, and Firepoint, built reconnaissance and strike capabilities under resource shortages that Russia's more centralized, state-linked defense industry did not face in the same way, he said.
The end of romanticized war
Hordiienko dates a turning point in how Ukrainian soldiers relate to the war to the 2023 Zaporizhzhia counteroffensive. Before it, he said, volunteers who joined in 2022 operated in an emotionally charged, maximalist mode — young men competing to reach combat before the war, as they assumed, ended quickly. After the counteroffensive stalled, he said, that gave way to a more systematic, mechanized phase he calls "a war of military machines."
He illustrated the shift with a sword-and-shield framework: each side develops a new method of attack, the other adapts a defense, and the balance resets every few months. The side that adapts and scales fastest gains the advantage, he said — a dynamic he sees as running through the drone war specifically.
Hordiienko enlisted through an unusual path. He and three other volunteers, all under 21 and already carrying combat experience from the war's opening months, could not sign standard military contracts because of their age. They were enlisted only after Ukraine's then-commander-in-chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, issued a personal order on their behalf.
What newer recruits are owed
Speaking about troops mobilized later in the war — arriving without the volunteer surge's initial urgency — Hordiienko said commanders now owe recruits honesty rather than appeals to abstract duty. He described his approach as a direct exchange: a commander sets out the conditions of service, and the soldier meets specific obligations in return, with consequences if either side breaks that arrangement. Motivation, in his account, rests less on invoking "fighting for Ukraine" and more on concrete terms of service, fair treatment, and — where the national cause doesn't land for a given recruit — the practical case that military service builds expertise, particularly in drone and other technical specialties, that carries into civilian life.

Presidential hopeful Tiit Land: 'I am no pawn in any political game'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

Presidential hopeful Tiit Land: 'I am no pawn in any political game'
Potential presidential candidate Tiit Land says he does not see himself as a pawn of Isamaa and the Center Party.
Speaking to "Aktuaalne kaamera", Land, rector of Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) may find himself up against Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, if he gets formally nominated.
Madise is backed by nearly all coalition Reform Party and Eesti 200 MPs as well as by opposition Social Democratic Party (SDE) members at the Riigikogu, while Land has met with the opposition Center and Isamaa parties.
Why do you want to be president?
I feel I have enough experience for the role, since I have served as rector of two universities and have extensive leadership experience, as well as international experience. I personally believe that my strength lies in communicating with people, listening to them and talking to them.
Your rival as a candidate is Ülle Madise. In terms of personal qualities and knowledge, what makes you a better choice than her?
I believe my strengths lie in my many years of work in the world of education and research, as well as my international experience. If we look at the issues we face today – how we can move Estonia forward, what will drive our economic growth, what our family policy should look like – I believe Estonia needs a stronger economy and more innovation. That is a strength of mine. As I also mentioned, I am neutral, and I believe a strength of mine is my ability to talk to all the different groups in society and to comprehend their problems.
What do you think about the fact that Madise currently has at least three parties who have got behind her?
It shows that Ülle Madise now has the signatures needed, and will be nominated as a candidate.
But don't you think you are simply a pawn on a political forces' chessboard, or that there is something else happening behind the scenes?
No, I haven't thought about it in that way. I'm not someone who believes in conspiracy theories, and I believe I have enough common sense to recognize if this had been the case.
You have been an advocate of the green transition both within academia and more widely. Did the Center Party and Isamaa also quiz you about Estonia's energy policies?
Yes, they did, and we had a frank discussion about it. I support the green transition, but the question is how we define it. I would say that the green transition has perhaps become too ideological here – the direction and the goals are the right ones, but the question is how we achieve them. What matters most to me is that the green transition results in the creation of new clean and climate-friendly technologies, as I noted earlier when talking about technology and innovation.
You also talked about Estonia's population. What are your solutions on changing Estonia's family policy?
I don't have a ready-made solution that would immediately put Estonia's population on a growth path through an increase in the natural population rate. There simply isn't one. The issues are very wide-ranging. I already mentioned the economy – young people are certainly either not starting families or have been putting off doing so due to their financial situation.
There are certainly issues in education too. Having served as a university rector, I know that there is currently a massive gender imbalance in Estonian higher education. Nearly two-thirds of university graduates are women, which is great – they are highly educated – but the corollary is we have fewer young men. This is a social issue: Are young people forming relationships and finding one another while studying at university, or are highly educated young women not starting families, then moving abroad instead?
The registration process for candidates opens a week today, August 21, and closes the following Monday, August 24. The three rounds of Riigikogu voting are set for September 2-3.
As of Thursday, 62 MPs had given their signature to Madise's candidacy, far in excess of the 21 signatures needed to run, and only six short of the total number of votes needed to elect a president at the Riigikogu. Center and Isamaa together have 15 Riigikogu seats, so more MPs are needed to sign off on his candidacy, including those from the 20 currently independent members.

Assumption Day: Greece prepares to celebrate the summer "Easter" this weekend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:56:20 UTC
17:56:20 KST

The 15th of August is one of the most important religious festivals in the Orthodox church and a day when traditions revive and endure across Greece.
From the alleyways of Tinos, the villages of Kefalonia to Siatista and to the mountains of Epirus, Greece is set to put on its festive finery this weekend of Saturday, 15 August.
The Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary is not only one of the most important religious celebrations in Orthodox Christianity. It is also a major summer gathering of people, places and traditions, where faith meets celebration and old customs come alive again.
For many Greeks, the Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary is an opportunity to return to their place of origin, to meet up with family and to take part in village festivals whose roots go back many decades.
In Tinos, faith becomes a personal vow
On the island of Tinos, the heart of the celebrations, thousands of pilgrims every year arrive to venerate the Virgin Mary and fulfil their personal vows.
The sight of worshippers making their way on their knees along the road to the Church of Panagia Evangelistria is one of the most emblematic images of the festivites in Greece. For some it is an act of gratitude, for others an expression of hope or a prayer for a personal miracle.
The snakes of Kefalonia
One of the most unusual customs of the festival is found in Kefalonia. In the villages of Markopoulo and Arginia, small snakes appear in the churches during the days of the feast. Although the phenomenon has sparked much discussion, for local residents their presence is part of a tradition that has been preserved over time. The so-called "little snakes of the Virgin Mary" are seen as a good omen and are associated with blessing and good fortune for the year ahead.
In Astypalaia, the feast is not confined to religious ceremonies. In Pera Gialos, the "Koukania" turn the day into a major folk festival, with games and competitions that spark laughter and bring together locals and visitors.
Contests such as feeding yoghurt while blindfolded lend a lighter tone to the celebration and are a reminder that 15 August in Greece is at once a day of faith and of joy.
A celebration that keeps tradition alive
In Siatista, the celebrations unfold against a different backdrop. The famous horsemen revive a custom that has become a defining feature of local tradition.
Pilgrims on horseback, riding decorated horses, make their way to the monastery of Mikrokastro.
The procession is an impressive spectacle, but the feast does not end there. On their return to Siatista, streets and squares fill with music, brass instruments, songs and dancing, as the religious element gradually gives way to a big traditional party.
In Palaiopyrgos in the Ioannina area, the "Ntolia" offer a different example of the way tradition serves as a means of social cohesion.
At the centre is the shared table and a symbolic role, that of the "archontas", the master of the feast. Through a specific ritual of exchanging glasses with the fellow diners, the signal is effectively given for the start of the celebration. The custom is also linked to restoring relationships and the effort to leave old disagreements behind.
The Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin Mary is perhaps one of the most emblematic moments of the Greek summer, precisely because it effectively combines a religious feeling with social life.
After the church service, squares fill up with tables, music and people. Residents meet up with visitors, younger generations discover customs handed down from the past and older people once again take on the role of custodians of a tradition that is determined not to disappear.

MINSK, 14 August (BelTA) - Belarusians are increasingly keeping their savings in the national currency, BelTA learned from the press service of the National Bank of Belarus.
 
In July, the level of dollarization in the economy continued to decline. The share of the ruble component in broad money rose to 68.6%, up from 63.3% a year earlier.
 
The ruble segment of the money supply is growing at a faster pace. The average ruble money supply increased by 29.5%, while the average broad money supply rose by 19.5%.
 
Household savings in the national currency continue to grow steadily. The average volume of fixed-term ruble deposits increased by 28% year-on-year, including a 40.3% rise in deposits held by individuals.
 
Overall, the National Bank noted that Belarusians’ savings activity remained high in July. As of 1 August, fixed-term ruble deposits by individuals reached Br18.4 billion, up by Br512.9 million, or 2.9%, over the month. Over the first seven months of the year, these deposits grew by Br3.2 billion, or 21.2% (compared with a Br2.2 billion increase, or 20.3%, in the same period of 2025).
 
 The share of fixed-term ruble deposits in total fixed-term deposits held by individuals stood at 72.8% as of 1 August 2026, up from 63% a year earlier.

Ukraine Needs At Least One Year to Repair High-Capacity Power Plants - US Intel

17:55:32 KST

Ukraine Needs At Least One Year to Repair High-Capacity Power Plants - US Intel

====================================================================================================

Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast | Jack Watling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:54:50 UTC
17:54:50 KST

“Invincible.” That was how Vladimir Putin described Russia’s latest generation of ballistic missiles in 2018. In 2022 he would unleash this arsenal to strike across Ukraine, hitting command centres, critical infrastructure and airfields. Then, in 2023, Ukraine received Patriot air defence systems from its international partners. The US-supplied missile interceptor would prove to be an effective shield against Russian strikes.
But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out and Kyiv has suffered the consequences. Intercepts have gone from more than 70% to none, so that night after night Russia strikes Ukraine’s infrastructure with impunity. This tragedy was long foretold, and there are no quick fixes.
While the military narrative of the war has largely been of cheap mass-produced Ukrainian weapons overwhelming exquisite Russian military hardware, most of the serious damage from Russia’s long-range strikes has come from cruise and ballistic missiles, and Ukraine’s campaign has suffered for want of them. Countering ballistic missiles is not a simple or cheap activity.
To intercept a tactical ballistic missile, such as Russia’s Iskander, a defensive system needs to be remarkably sophisticated. Its target will be descending from the high atmosphere at more than five times the speed of sound. The incoming missile will also be manoeuvring through the air, rather than following a predictable ballistic trajectory. The defensive system needs to be able to track the precise location of this incoming missile and communicate this to the intercepting missile, allowing the latter to adjust course while climbing against gravity. Building the radars, data links and interceptors for such a task involves a huge amount of research and development, and across Nato most states have been happy for Washington to invest over decades to make the Patriot up to the job.
The US and licensed manufacturers in Germany and Japan are able to produce about 840 Patriot interceptors a year. About 240 of these are older, larger PAC-2 interceptors, which climb until they are close to the target and then explode – meaning they must carry the weight of a warhead to the target – and 600 are PAC-3s, which are smaller and fly directly into the target. The latter approach is more effective but requires even more precise navigation. The former can be used against other target types.
Russia produces about 750 Iskander missiles a year and is looking to increase production. In addition, Russia uses air-launched Kinzhal ballistic missiles and repurposed air-defence missiles to conduct strikes, along with its arsenal of cruise missiles and drones. To have a high probability of success, it is generally recommended to fire two to three interceptors against each ballistic missile. When you also factor in that the launchers themselves can only protect a relatively small area, and Ukraine is a vast country, then it becomes clear that Kyiv would ideally have three to four times the annual global production capacity of Patriot missiles to protect itself. Countries supporting Ukraine have therefore had to give their own stockpiles to Kyiv.
Even before the US decision to attack Iran, western allies were nervous about depleting their own stocks by giving Patriot missiles to Ukraine, knowing that it would take a long time for them to be resupplied. The US attack on Iran – prompting Tehran to fire ballistic missiles across the Middle East – has created an acute global shortage. Where Russia usually fires fewer than 10 ballistic missiles in a single attack, Iran has launched upwards of 170 a day during the current and last year’s war. A portion of Iran’s missiles were also advanced. In one instance, it took 17 Patriot interceptors to defeat a missile. And Iran has many more missiles in storage.
The point is that Ukraine is not going to receive enough Patriots between now and the winter to save its critical national infrastructure, irrespective of whether some countries make the political gesture of releasing a few more from their stockpiles. At this point, Kyiv must plan for a winter with severely disrupted power, and disperse and fortify life-support systems such as water, sanitation, power and heating.
Kyiv is trying to convince the US to activate Starlink satellite navigation modules over Russian territory to enable its drones to hunt for the Russian missile launchers. But, as the US recently found in Iran, pulling off this kind of mission over a large area is extremely difficult. Another line of effort in Kyiv is to attack the production of Russia’s ballistic missiles. These factories are well defended. To succeed, Ukraine’s partners will need to expand the funding and industrial capacity behind Ukraine’s nascent cruise-missile industry, or reopen questions of providing weapons systems such as Germany’s Taurus (which Berlin didn’t provide to Ukraine for fear of military escalation).
But the real lesson here is that Nato members have abjectly failed in defence planning. The numbers in this equation have been known since before 2022 and yet the investments to expand Patriot production (or mature alternative systems such as the Franco-Italian SAMP-T) have not been made. Such a level of complacency is devastating for Ukraine today, but it also risks Europe being bereft of defences in the future. It remains remarkable that Europe – watching the consequences unfold on its very borders – has remained so idle.
- 
  Jack Watling is senior research fellow for applied military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute

BP returns to Venezuela with Gulf partners as post-Maduro energy opening speeds up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:54:18 UTC
17:54:18 KST

Venezuela has awarded BP a licence to develop the offshore Loran gas field alongside state-backed partners from the UAE and Qatar, marking the British company's return to a country whose energy sector has been reopening to foreign investors since US forces captured Nicolás Maduro.
BP is going back into Venezuela.
The agreement signed in Caracas on Thursday gives the company operatorship of Loran phase two, an offshore gas project holding more than four trillion cubic feet of proven gas resources, with Abu Dhabi's XRG, Qatar's UCC Oil and Gas Holding taking equal stakes beside it.
It is the clearest signal yet that the opening of Venezuela's energy industry to foreign capital, underway since Maduro's removal, is gathering pace.
All three companies will hold equal working interests, with BP as operator, and the licence remains subject to regulatory approvals.
PDVSA Gas, the state producer's gas arm, transferred part of its interest to XRG, the international investment vehicle of Abu Dhabi's ADNOC. For both XRG and UCC, a unit of the Qatari conglomerate of the same name, this marks a first entry into Venezuela.
The field itself is shared as Loran forms the Venezuelan portion of the Loran-Manatee accumulation, which straddles the maritime boundary with Trinidad and Tobago and holds roughly 10 trillion cubic feet of recoverable gas in total.
Shell won the licence for the first phase in June and is separately developing Manatee on the Trinidadian side, where first gas is expected next year.
BP says both Venezuelan phases will now be developed in parallel and signed a further memorandum of understanding covering exploration at the Carúpano East Block.
The agreements were concluded during a visit to Caracas by CEO Meg O'Neill and David Campbell, BP's senior vice president for Latin America and the Caribbean.
A sector reopened under US pressure
The licences are the product of a bargain struck with Washington.
After Maduro was seized by US forces in January, interim president Delcy Rodríguez rewrote the country's energy law at the Trump administration's urging, opening the world's largest proven oil reserves to foreign firms.
In return, the US relaxed sanctions that had frozen most Western investment, including the licences it revoked from BP, Shell and Chevron in 2025.
Eni, Repsol and Shell have all signed since.
The awards process stalled after the earthquakes of 24 June, which killed more than 6,300 people, and resumed only on Thursday, when the three Loran permits were issued and the agreements signed.
"I have a special interest in gas to promote national development," Rodríguez said at the ceremony, which was broadcast on state television.
BP is not a newcomer as it held a licence for the Cocuina field from 2024, before Washington withdrew its permission to use it.

Serbian national Ljubisa Karović was nearly sucked head-first through the broken window but was saved as other passengers, including his wife, held onto him.
Debris from a broken engine fan smashed a window on a Ryanair plane shortly after it took off from Greece last month, according to a preliminary report into the incident, which saw a passenger partially sucked out of the opening.
The flight had been on its way from Thessaloniki to Memmingen, Germany when the aircraft "experienced a No. 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out," the report from the US's National Transportation Safety Board said.
"Engine fragments breached the fuselage and the cabin depressurized," it continued. "The crew elected to return to SKG where they made an uneventful landing."
Two pilots, four flight attendants, and 149 passengers were on board the aircraft when the incident occurred. The NTSB said one passenger sustained serious injuries.
In a statement at the time, Ryanair said the flight returned to Thessaloniki when a "passenger window dislodged inflight."
The airline said the aircraft "landed normally" and that passengers made their way to the terminal before a replacement service was organised.
Serbian national Ljubisa Karović was nearly sucked head-first through the broken window but was saved as other passengers held onto him.
Speaking to Serbian outlet Nova at the time, his wife, Svetlana Grković, said: "The pressure pulled Ljubiša out; luckily he was strapped in, but half his body was sticking out of the plane."
"I reacted immediately and grabbed his legs. I thought, 'If we're going to die, we're going to die together'. It was awful," she added.
According to the NTSB, it was delegated the investigation "in full" by Greek authorities the week after the incident.
The investigation has so far determined that the fan blades had undergone ultrasonic inspections as recently as May, "with no findings."
It also found that flight crews had reported four suspected bird strikes to the same engine in the 12 months leading up to the Thessaloniki incident.
While no damage was recorded in subsequent maintenance checks, it noted that "bird remains were reportedly found in two of the cases."
The investigation remains ongoing.

The bodies of two Belgian hikers missing since 1992 are thought to have been found after melting ice on a glacier in the Swiss Alps exposed their remains, according to the Missing Persons Unit.
Last month, local police informed the unit that the bodies had been found on the Trift Glacier near Saas-Grund. Authorities have yet to definitively confirm that the bodies are those of the two men from the Kempen, but identification documents were also found and DNA analysis is under way to confirm their identity.
“The bodies were found because the glacier’s ice has retreated, exposing part of the area,” says Gerry Van Loock of the Missing Persons Unit. “This made the area more accessible, and the remains were uncovered.”
The grieving process can begin and they can move on with their lives, however difficult that loss may be
This is not the first time a melting glacier has revealed secrets. Last year, in Tyrol and Pakistan, human remains were recovered after several decades because the glaciers are shrinking.
“When our international colleagues find human remains, they ask us to check our open files to see if there are any descriptions of individuals that might match details from the remains found, such as documents, clothing or similar items,” says Van Loock. The fact that such documents remain well-preserved after 34 years depends on the circumstances, he says.
“We have numerous examples where documentation turns up years after the time of disappearance. For example, in a vehicle recovered from the water during a search operation, where we find vehicle documents in the glove compartment that are in fairly good condition. These allow us to identify a vehicle and, consequently, to establish a person’s identity.”
For Van Loock, one thing is paramount: that the families of the hikers receive an answer after 34 years. “That way, the grieving process can begin and they can move on with their lives, however difficult that loss may be, of course. A bad answer is still better than no answer at all.”
Last month, the remains were found of a 72-year-old hiker from Antwerp province who disappeared in September 2024 while trekking in Albania. His remains and belongings were found on a mountainside in North Macedonia near the Albanian border.

Money in the account is not yet a guarantee: how to obtain a tourist visa to Britain
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
11:51:08 EEST
17:51:08 KST

Money in the account is not yet a guarantee: how to obtain a tourist visa to Britain
Kyiv • UNN
The UK immigration service assesses not only the availability of funds, but also their source and whether they are consistent with the financial circumstances of the trip. The absence of formal employment is not an automatic reason for refusal, but it is important to provide documentary proof of income.
Applying for a tourist visa to the United Kingdom in 2026 is increasingly moving to a digital format, in particular through the use of eVisa. At the same time, the requirements for applicants themselves have not become simpler: when reviewing an application, the UK immigration authorities assess not only whether funds are available, but also their origin, the regularity of income, and whether the financial situation corresponds to the planned trip. Valeriia Nahorna, a visa lawyer at LLC "Law Company "LOGIC", told UNN about this.
According to her, one of the key mistakes applicants make is trying to demonstrate only a certain balance in a bank account without explaining the origin of the funds.
The British side pays very close attention to the origin of funds. It is important for the officer to see not simply a certain amount in the account before the documents are submitted, but to understand where this money came from. That is, we look at regular incoming payments, account turnover, sources of income, and how much this entire financial picture corresponds to the information provided by the applicant in the form
eVisa: digitalisation does not mean simplified requirements
In 2026, the United Kingdom continues to transfer its immigration system to a digital format. eVisa is an electronic record in the UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) system that confirms a person's immigration status and is linked to their UKVI Account.
For applicants, this means a gradual move away from physical documents as the primary means of confirming status. At the same time, the transition to eVisa does not automatically mean that the procedure for obtaining a tourist visa has been simplified.
When applying for a Standard Visitor visa, applicants must still convincingly confirm the purpose of their trip, their financial capability, and their intention to stay temporarily in the United Kingdom.
Is formal employment required?
The absence of conventional formal employment in itself does not mean an automatic refusal of a tourist visa. A person may be self-employed, engage in business activities, receive income from providing services, or have several sources of income.
At the same time, in such a case it is important to explain with documents what the person does and where they receive their money from.
The absence of conventional formal employment in itself does not mean that a person cannot apply for a British tourist visa. But in that case, it is especially important to properly explain to the officer what the applicant does, where they receive their funds from, and how their income is generated. If a person actually has a regular income, but this is not reflected in the documents at all, the officer cannot simply guess what their real financial situation is
Thus, what matters is not so much the employee's formal status as a clear financial history that can be confirmed by documents.
Is having enough money for the trip alone sufficient?
Another common mistake is to calculate the required amount solely based on the cost of tickets, accommodation, and other expenses during the trip.
According to the lawyer, the British side assesses the financial situation more broadly: the applicant's income, savings, regular expenses, and financial obligations are taken into account.
We always recommend assessing finances more broadly than simply the cost of tickets and a hotel. After the trip, the person must return home and continue to support their life. If the documents show that, for the sake of a one-week tourist trip, the applicant is spending practically all of their available funds, a logical question arises as to how much such a trip corresponds to their actual financial situation
In other words, a large amount in an account in itself does not guarantee a positive decision. It is important that the travel expenses appear realistic in comparison with the person's financial means.
Why is topping up an account before applying risky?
Particular attention should be paid to large or unusual incoming payments made immediately before the documents are submitted.
The mere fact of receiving a substantial amount is not automatically a problem. It could be, for example, the sale of property, a contractual payment, dividends, a transfer between the person's own accounts, or the repayment of a debt.
However, the source of such an incoming payment must be clear and, where necessary, supported by documents.
If a person has had low account turnover for an extended period, and immediately before applying for a visa an amount suddenly appears in their account that is several times higher than their usual income, this may raise additional questions.
The application form and bank statement must tell the same story
Another important point is that the information in the application form must correspond to the financial documents.
If an applicant states one level of income, while the movement of funds in their accounts shows an entirely different picture, the visa officer may have questions.
One of the biggest mistakes is preparing each document separately. The application form is completed one way, the bank statement is simply attached, and information about employment is provided separately — and no one checks whether it all forms one logical picture. With a UK visa, it is important to look at the case through the officer’s eyes: is it clear to them who this person is, what they do, where they get their money from, why they are travelling to the United Kingdom specifically now, and why this trip is financially realistic for them
According to her, all the documents must form a consistent and clear story about the applicant.
Can you travel at a sponsor’s expense?
A tourist trip may be funded by another person — for example, a husband or wife, parents, or another sponsor.
However, in that case it is also necessary to explain exactly who is funding the trip, what relationship exists between the applicant and the sponsor, what the sponsor’s financial capacity is, and precisely which expenses they are covering.
Sponsorship does not eliminate the need to explain the applicant’s overall circumstances.
What is most important for a tourist visa
Thus, in 2026, the digitalization of the UK immigration system primarily simplifies the technical side of the process, but does not abolish the requirements for tourists.
For a positive assessment of a visa case, it is important not simply to show a certain amount in the account. The applicant must demonstrate a clear source of income, logical movement of funds, expenses that correspond to their financial means, and consistency across all the information in the application form and documents.
