Putin Has an Unexpected Ally in Ukraine’s War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:51:00 UTC
17:51:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has an unexpected ally in the war against Ukraine: a hotter and drier Europe.
Extreme heat and drought are putting pressure on the backup systems Ukraine has relied on to keep its economy and infrastructure functioning as Russia attacks its ports, power plants, railways and bridges, Newsweek reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine has repeatedly adapted by finding alternatives. When Russian attacks made Black Sea shipping dangerous, grain exports shifted to rail, roads and the Danube. When Russian strikes damaged power generation, Ukraine increased electricity imports from Europe. When rainfall declined, farmers turned to irrigation.
But those alternatives are now facing pressure of their own.
Russia targets Ukraine’s alternative routes
Russia has intensified attacks on the infrastructure around Odesa and Ukraine’s alternative export routes.
In July, Ukraine recorded 35 attacks on vessels in ports, 22 attacks on ships at sea and 67 strikes on port facilities, according to figures cited by Newsweek.
Russia has also targeted infrastructure connecting Ukraine with alternative trade routes. On Aug. 9, Russian forces struck the Mayaki bridge, which links Odesa toward Moldova and Romania. The Institute for the Study of War assessed that the bridge was likely targeted to disrupt the land corridor used for maritime exports.
At the same time, drought has weakened the Danube, another crucial route for Ukrainian exports.
Ust-Luga Ablaze Again as 54 Ukrainian Drones Hit Russia’s Key Baltic Oil Port
An analysis by World Weather Attribution found that highly evaporative conditions in eastern Europe between January and June 2026 had become about 40 times more likely because of human-caused climate change.
Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky told Reuters that slightly more than 30 million tons of grain and oilseeds could fail to reach international markets if the disruption continues.
Rail and Danube routes together can handle only about a third of the capacity of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, according to Vysotsky.
Ukraine’s power system faces another test
The same problem is emerging in the energy sector.
Russia sharply intensified its campaign against Ukraine’s power infrastructure in 2024. By early June, Ukraine had lost roughly 9 gigawatts of generating capacity.
During a heatwave the following month, Kyiv reached 94 degrees Fahrenheit (34.4 degrees Celsius), while grid operator Ukrenergo introduced emergency power cuts in seven regions after an equipment failure worsened the electricity deficit.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on the European power grid to compensate for domestic shortages. Electricity imports were 41% higher in February than in January, according to Newsweek.
But Europe’s energy infrastructure is also vulnerable to extreme weather.
By July, Ukraine had again become a net electricity exporter, with Hungary its largest customer. At the same time, Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant was forced to reduce output to about 10% of capacity as low Danube water levels affected its cooling system.
Romania faced similar problems at its Cernavoda nuclear plant. Authorities had to remove a rock obstruction, dredge the riverbed and use four rock-filled barges to redirect cooling water.
On Aug. 11, the plant’s operator warned that Romania could be forced to shut down its last operating reactor despite the emergency measures.
The examples show that some of the infrastructure Ukraine depends on for resilience is itself increasingly exposed to extreme weather.
Heat and war are driving more fires
Ukraine’s experience with wildfires also illustrates how climate conditions can amplify the effects of war.
Satellite data from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre showed that about 965,000 hectares burned in Ukraine in 2024 – more than twice the area burned across the entire European Union that year.
Most major fires occurred during hot, dry weather and were concentrated near the front line.
A peer-reviewed study published in Fire Ecology found that rising temperatures and declining rainfall significantly increased fire activity, particularly in central, southern and eastern Ukraine.
At the same time, Russia’s attacks create additional risks. Shelling and missiles can ignite farmland and grassland, while mines and unexploded ordnance make it more dangerous for firefighters to reach affected areas.
Damaged roads and disrupted institutions can further delay emergency responses.
Southern Ukraine faces a water crisis
Water shortages could pose an even greater long-term challenge.
Before the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023, its reservoir supplied 31 irrigation systems across the Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
In 2021, those irrigation systems helped produce around 4 million tons of grain and oilseeds.
After the dam was destroyed, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry warned that at least 500,000 hectares deprived of irrigation could effectively become desert.
The dam was destroyed while the area was under Russian occupation. Ukraine accused Russia of destroying it, while Russia blamed Ukraine.
The Kakhovka Reservoir had also been the main source of cooling water for the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Europe’s largest nuclear facility.
After the reservoir emptied, wells were used to provide replacement water, but they were insufficient. An International Atomic Energy Agency official told Reuters that water consumption would increase dramatically if all the reactors restarted.
Russia faces climate risks too
Russia is also vulnerable to extreme weather.
In 2025, roughly 1 million hectares of crops in the Rostov region were lost or damaged by drought or frost. The damage was severe enough for Moscow to elevate the agricultural emergency to the federal level.
Newsweek noted that this context makes a recent Russian analysis particularly revealing.
On Aug. 10, Anatoly Tikhonov, head of the Center for International Agribusiness and Food Security at the Russian Presidential Academy, published an essay through Russia’s state-run TASS news agency arguing that Europe’s agricultural difficulties could create an economic opportunity for Russia.
Tikhonov argued that Europe could become more dependent on Ukrainian grain and food imports from South America, the United States and Russia as its own harvests suffer.
He described the situation as an opportunity for Moscow to take advantage of the moment.
Russia cannot control Europe’s climate, but the combination of extreme weather and attacks on Ukraine’s infrastructure could still work in Moscow’s favor.
Ukraine has spent years building alternative routes and backup systems to reduce the impact of Russian attacks. But those alternatives now face two pressures simultaneously: Russia’s campaign against critical infrastructure and a hotter, drier and more volatile European climate.

Gallery: Artist Natalia Mirzoyan captures Estonia through a newcomer's eyes
Animator and artist Natalia Mirzoyan, director of the acclaimed short film "Winter in March," has opened a solo exhibition sharing her experience with settling in Estonia.
"Observations from Estonia" opened Thursday at the Nõmme House in Nõmme, the Tallinn district where Mirzoyan lives and works.
Born in Yerevan, Mirzoyan has studied sociology, painting and animation, earning a master's degree from the Estonian Academy of Arts (EKA). She left Russia after it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine and moved to Estonia, where she has continued her creative work.
Her new solo exhibition features paintings and drawings inspired by her new surroundings, from Nõmme streets and Tallinn's urban landscape to Estonia's changing seasons and little everyday moments.
Mirzoyan's work combines the storytelling of animation with the immediacy of painting, offering a newcomer's perspective on familiar scenes.
Her animated short "Winter in March," made using fabric manipulation and stop-motion techniques, was selected for the La Cinef competition at the Cannes Film Festival last year. It has since screened at major animation festivals, won several awards and made the shortlist for the European Film Awards.
"Observations from Estonia" will remain on view at the Nõmme House through the end of September.

Israeli settlers cut Palestinian water supply, set up swimming pool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:50:19 UTC
17:50:19 KST

On a scorching summer afternoon in the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers gathered to swim in a pool fed by water diverted from Palestinian farmland, turning a vital local water source into a recreational attraction.
The pool sits near Fasayil, a Palestinian village in the fertile Jordan Valley where residents have relied on the spring for generations. Its water has supported crops, provided jobs and helped families cope with irregular supplies through Israeli-controlled networks.
For farmer Saad Nemer, the loss of access has come at a steep cost.
“Our water supply remains cut off to this day, depriving us of the water we depend on for our homes, our livelihoods and our agricultural land,” Nemer said.
In June, settlers seized Nemer’s irrigation pipeline and redirected the water to an ancient pool at a nearby archaeological site.
The pool was soon promoted as an Israeli tourist attraction, with Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich pledging 3 million shekels ($1 million) toward its restoration and development.
“They are now in the process of developing a recreational park around the pool,” Nemer said.
The development has left Nemer unable to plant his fields and greenhouses, which would normally produce eggplant, zucchini and watermelons during the summer.
“The settlers cutting off our water has caused us losses and has meant that many families will lose their work and their livelihoods,” he said.
Nemer said one of his employees was beaten by settlers and that he had faced threats himself when trying to approach the spring, including incidents dating back two years.
The seizure of the water source in Fasayil is part of a broader pattern that Palestinians and rights groups say is aimed at making life increasingly difficult for Palestinian communities in the West Bank.
United Nations data shows Israeli settlers have attacked at least 160 water and sanitation facilities across the Palestinian territory this year.
At Fasayil, Israeli settlers now freely use the pool while Palestinian villagers say they are afraid to approach it.
Yishai Shreiber, a 21-year-old Israeli settler who visited the pool on a recent August afternoon, said the growing number of Israeli visitors had effectively kept Palestinians away.
“Now that they see this entire mass of people, all these large groups of Jews coming here to bathe, they are afraid to come here,” Shreiber said.
He said he believed the West Bank belonged to the Jewish people and argued that Palestinians who did not accept Jewish authority should leave.
Nemer showed Reuters a 2025 land ownership document issued by COGAT, the Israeli military agency responsible for implementing civilian policy in the occupied territories. He also produced a map from a 1957 land registration showing that his property included both the spring and the pool.
COGAT and Smotrich did not respond to requests for comment.
The dispute over Fasayil’s spring comes amid a sharp increase in Israeli settlement activity and settler violence across the West Bank.
Israel's far-right coalition government has backed extensive settlement construction. Smotrich has said the policy is intended to prevent the establishment of a Palestinian state.
More than 150 of the 193 U.N. member states recognize a Palestinian state comprising the Gaza Strip and West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
The United Nations and most governments consider Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank illegal under international law. Israel disputes that characterization and says the territory is contested.
Palestinian communities have increasingly reported losing access to natural springs, which are particularly important in the Jordan Valley.
Palestinian field researcher Fares Foqahaa estimated that settlers have seized control of 95% of springs in the northern Jordan Valley, contributing to the displacement of Palestinian communities.
In the West Bank village of Qusra, settlers were still besieging three Palestinian homes on Thursday, residents said. The homes had also been cut off from water and electricity.
Adel Yassin, an official with the Palestinian Authority's water authority, described the campaign as an attempt to make Palestinian communities economically and physically unsustainable.
“I see this as a water war. It is the silent bullet that kills Palestinians without a sound,” he said.
The pool at Fasayil has also become a point of contention over archaeology and competing claims to the land.
In early June, Eliav Libi, a settler leader who has been targeted by sanctions from Canada and other countries, posted a video showing the pool beginning to fill with water.
Libi and other settlers have said the pool belonged to the biblical-era Jewish King Herod.
But Alon Arad, an archaeologist with the Israeli rights group Emek Shaveh, said the origins of the pool remain uncertain.
Arad accused settlers of using archaeology to reinforce claims that the West Bank is exclusively Jewish and said filling the archaeological site with water could damage it.
“We see in many cases the use of archaeology ... to create this feeling that the West Bank is exclusively Jewish,” Arad said.
A billboard outside the pool advertised Smotrich's 3 million shekel investment in the site, describing the project as the restoration and development of “Herod's Pools.”
The pool and nearby spring were crowded with Israeli families swimming and wading in the water. No Palestinians were seen there.
Fasayil is not the only Palestinian community where access to natural springs has become increasingly contested.
Near Nablus, the springs at Wadi al-Badhan have long been a popular destination for Palestinians seeking relief from the summer heat. Families would gather around plastic tables set in shallow streams, eating meals and cooling their feet in the running water.
The springs had rarely faced incursions by Israeli settlers before this year.
But hundreds of settlers descended on the area earlier this summer, according to five Palestinians who witnessed the visits. They sat at the tables and walked through the pools, changing the atmosphere of a place that had traditionally been a local gathering spot.
Nizam Fares, who owns a natural spring park in al-Badhan, said Palestinians now feel uneasy about returning.
“People have become scared and jumpy. They come and ask if the settlers are coming or not?” he said.

Engine fragments smashed a cabin window on a Ryanair flight from Thessaloniki to Munich last month, leaving a passenger partially sucked out of the aircraft before fellow passengers pulled the passenger back inside, an investigation has found.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a report Thursday that the Malta Air flight, operating as Ryanair, suffered a failure of a fan blade in its right engine while climbing after takeoff from Thessaloniki International Airport in Greece.
Investigators found that the fan blade separation sent engine fragments into the fuselage and right horizontal stabilizer.
"The pressurized section of the fuselage was penetrated 1) through the passenger cabin window located at row 11, as well as 2) lower lobe fuselage skin behind the right wing-to-body fairing," the report said.
Investigators found that the passenger seated in 11F "was partially lodged in a damaged cabin window, and that the entire window was missing."
Other passengers helped pull the injured passenger back into the cabin, according to the report.
Investigators also found bird remains, including feathers, in several parts of the engine.
The July incident left the passenger injured, while the aircraft returned safely to Thessaloniki.

“We will choose the best possible candidate who will continue what we have started,” he said.

Guidance: Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14

Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
Guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme for veterans who served under, and were impacted by, the Ban on LGBT personnel in HM Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
Documents
Details
LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Please find below the data detailing scheme progress which will be shared on a monthly basis.
Data as of 27/07/26:
Total individual applicants*: 1,635
*Applicants may have more than one case due to there being two payment types.
Total decisions made on cases: 2,008
Value of total payments made: £56,402,000
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme was recommended by the LGBT Veterans Independent Review which was published in July 2023.
The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme is a payment scheme open to those who served under and were directly impacted by the Ban on LGBT personnel serving in the Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
This page provides information and guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, including eligibility and how to apply.
Types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments
There are two types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments:
1. LGBT Dismissed or Discharged Payment. This payment is for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged because of the Ban, including officers who were ordered or instructed to resign or retire by their respective Service Board.
2. LGBT Impact Payment. A payment to recognise other experiences of those who served under the Ban, as outlined in the Financial Recognition Payment Types and Tariff Table. (LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme Rules, Annex B).
Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above before starting an application.
How to Apply
Online applications
The Ministry of Defence encourages all eligible applicants to submit their applications online.
An app for the scheme can be accessed on Defence Gateway from 13 December 2024.
This platform will ensure that your data and any uploaded documents are secure. The app dashboard will keep you updated about the status of your application.
The online application process has two steps:
Step 1: Register for a Defence Gateway Account so you can access the online Financial Recognition Scheme application form.
Step 2: Sign in to your Defence Gateway account and submit your Financial Recognition Scheme application form via the Financial Recognition Scheme app.
Hard copy applications
If you would prefer to submit a hard copy (paper) application form, read scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above.
Hard copy application forms can also be obtained from Veterans UK.
Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Help with applying to the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme
Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion have partnered with the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme to provide support to veterans who are applying to the scheme.
These charities can assist with completing the application form, provide guidance on writing the necessary evidence and answer any questions applicants may have.
Royal British Legion
- Email: info@britishlegion.org.uk
- Phone: 0808 802 8080
For more information on the support the Royal British Legion can offer, visit Royal British Legion - Applying for restorative measures for LGBTQIA+ Veterans.
Fighting with Pride
For more information on the support Fighting with Pride can offer, visit Fighting with Pride LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme.
Veterans Welfare Service
Additional support is also available from the Veterans Welfare Service (VWS) who provide information, guidance and support to veterans and their families, as well as supporting veterans through a network of case managers across the UK and Republic of Ireland.
To find out more, visit Veterans Welfare Service or contact the Veterans’ Helpline using the details below.
- Email: veterans-uk@mod.gov.uk
- Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
- Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)
Other restorative measures
For information on non-financial restorative measures visit LGBT veterans: support and next steps.

Ukraine may face storage shortfall for 8-11 mln tonnes of grain – Vysotsky
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
11:47:00 EEST
17:47:00 KST

Due to blocked port operations and limited export volumes, Ukraine could face a domestic grain storage shortfall of 8-11 million tonnes in November, Agrarian Policy and Food Minister Taras Vysotsky told reporters on Friday.
"As of today, the storage situation is as follows: at the current limited pace of exports, we could reach a point in November where there is a shortfall in domestic storage capacity. This shortfall could range from 8 to 11 million tonnes," Vysotsky said.
He said the range reflects the difficulty of forecasting the corn harvest, though the ministry is already planning for a maximum yield.
Vysotsky said Ukraine has asked international partners for help with temporary storage equipment, namely grain storage bags placed in fields that can each hold up to 250 tonnes of grain.
"As of today, we have confirmation of about $10 million in assistance. Plus, we’re finalizing $25 million with the World Bank for these purposes. That’s 6 million tonnes or more," Vysotsky said.
He said that, taking this funding into account, Ukraine expects to cover the critical situation and secure sufficient grain storage capacity.

Poland's Defence Ministry dismisses concerns over transfer of several Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Polish Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk has dismissed criticism from former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak regarding the possible transfer of several Patriot system missiles to Ukraine, stating that this would not weaken Poland's defence capabilities.
Source: European Pravda, citing Tomczyk on Polsat News
Details: The minister stated that only a madman could think that transferring two or three missiles would weaken Poland's capabilities.
"If we truly believe that Poland would somehow lose its capabilities by transferring two or three missiles to a Ukrainian system, where everything that reaches Poland – and we know this happens from time to time – is first on Ukrainian territory and can be shot down there, then it means only a madman would come up with these arguments," Tomczyk said.
Politicians from the Law and Justice party, including Błaszczak, have claimed that the government would be giving away missiles that are meant to protect Polish skies, Polish cities and Polish families.
"I want to emphasise once again that no decision has been taken and that countries such as, for example, the frequently mentioned Germany, are currently transferring far more equipment to Ukraine than Poland is," Tomczyk stressed.
Background:
- On 13 August, Polish Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka stated that a decision on transferring Patriot system missiles to Ukraine could be taken in the coming days.
- In July, Poland's Defence Ministry officially confirmed that Poland had transferred PAC-3 missiles, designed for Patriot systems, to Ukraine several months earlier. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that the package contained five missiles.
- Following the latest incident in which a missile fell on Polish territory, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced that Warsaw will shortly consider transferring additional missiles for Patriot air defence systems to Ukraine.

— NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum – JFCBS (@NATOJFCBS) August 12, 2026
According to the Latvian ministry, their Armed Forces worked with the JEF to escort the vessels safely, oversee their entry into port and handle the unloading of equipment and its onward movement to deployment locations.
NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said rapid movement is a key part of credible deterrence, and that Baltic Express demonstrates how JEF nations can coordinate and move forces across Northern Europe, strengthening military mobility, interoperability and readiness.
Moving heavy equipment into the Baltic states is the problem the exercise exists to solve. The region is connected to the rest of NATO by sea and by the Suwalki gap, the stretch of Polish and Lithuanian border running between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, and reinforcement in a crisis would depend heavily on ports and the roads and railways leading inland from them.
Baltic subsea cables and pipelines have been damaged repeatedly since 2023, including the Balticconnector gas pipeline and several telecommunications cables, and NATO stood up Baltic Sentry in January 2025 to increase patrolling in response. Suspected shadow fleet tankers have been detained by regional navies, and GPS interference across the region has been attributed by several governments to Russian sources.
The Joint Expeditionary Force is a British-led grouping of ten Northern European nations: the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It operates outside the NATO command structure but is designed to complement it, allowing a smaller group of countries with common interests in the High North and the Baltic to act faster than an alliance of thirty-two members can.
Lion Protector 26 covers the maritime, air and land domains from the Arctic to the Baltic. Latvia describes it as complementing NATO’s vigilance and deterrence measures while strengthening the ability of participating nations to deploy forces rapidly.

NATO fighter, one drone, one district: a jammed intercept lands over Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:43:24 UTC
17:43:24 KST

A NATO fighter patrolling Baltic airspace shot down a drone over Latvia early Friday, the Latvian Armed Forces said, in the second Baltic-region drone incursion this week.
The interception happened over Balvi Municipality, near Latvia's borders with Belarus and Russia. Latvian officials said the drone entered the country's airspace after being knocked off course by Russian electronic warfare systems — not as a deliberate strike on Latvian territory. Russia has regularly bombarded Ukraine's Baltic-facing neighbors with stray drones since intensifying its own long-range strike campaign, and on 12 August, Romania detonated two Russian drones that washed up near its Black Sea gas field.
Latvian forces reported an "airspace threat" in four districts bordering Belarus and Russia shortly after 04:00, and announced the drone's destruction roughly 30 minutes later. Ieva Bērziņa, a representative of Latvia's Joint Armed Forces Staff, said the crash site had been located but its exact position was not being disclosed, and that debris may be scattered over a wide area because the drone was shot down at high altitude.
The incident coincided with a large-scale drone attack on Russian targets in Leningrad Oblast overnight.
This is not the first time drones have crossed into the Baltic states during Russian strikes on its own territory. In May, a drone that entered from Russia damaged fuel tanks at an oil depot in Rēzekne, about 40 kilometers from the border. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in March that Russia was deliberately steering Ukrainian drones toward Baltic airspace using electronic warfare, adding that Moscow later uses the resulting incidents in information operations targeting the region.
Latvia is weighing the purchase of Brazilian-made A-29 Super Tucano light attack aircraft for counter-drone missions, funded through more than €1 billion the government has earmarked for stronger air defense.

Kyiv uncovers large-scale real estate fraud scheme in Pechersk – prosecutor general
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
11:42:32 EEST
17:42:32 KST

A large-scale real estate fraud scheme has been uncovered in a new residential building in Kyiv’s Pechersk district, in which apartments that already had owners were sold, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has said.
The prosecutor general said on Telegram on Friday that, according to the investigation, the fraud scheme was organized by a former Dnipro City Council deputy.
"He acquired corporate rights to a group of companies that owned several unfinished properties in the center of the capital, including a residential complex in Pechersk," Kravchenko said.
He said the same apartments were sold twice. "They changed the technical specifications of the premises, used forged documents and re-registered property rights to new buyers," he said.
According to the prosecutor general, most apartments in the building had already been sold to investors, and property rights to another 50 apartments belonged, by court decision, to one of Ukraine’s state banks, leaving only a portion of the premises actually free.
"However, the scheme’s participants disposed of the entire building as if the previous owners didn’t exist. To sell the apartments whose rights belonged to the state bank, they changed the technical specifications of the properties and used forged documents. In this way, 50 apartments were alienated in favor of third parties," he said.
As a result, the prosecutor general said, the state bank’s losses exceeded UAH 164 million.
"Eight more apartments, whose property rights already belonged to individuals, were resold using the same scheme. People paid for housing, but those same square meters were later registered to other buyers," Kravchenko added.
The prosecutor general noted that, to make it harder for defrauded investors to establish their rights, the scheme’s participants changed the residential complex’s legal address, and the building, originally designed as 27 stories, became 32 stories after completion.
"The total established losses exceed UAH 175 million," the prosecutor general said.
According to the investigation, the illegally obtained funds were cashed out, run through controlled companies, and invested in property acquisitions and other construction projects.
Kravchenko added that nine people have so far been notified of suspicion: the organizer and eight accomplices. Depending on each person’s role, their actions have been classified as fraud, legalization of criminally obtained property, and use of forged documents. A decision on preventive measures is pending.
"And this may not be the full scale of the scheme. We are checking information about other possible double sales, and establishing the full number of victims and the movement of illegally obtained funds," he said.

18 of the 26 vessels used by Russia to transport oil, petroleum products, liquefied natural gas, and stolen Ukrainian grain are not sanctioned by any of Ukraine’s partner countries.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine reported this.
Information on these vessels is available in the Maritime Vessels section of the War&Sanctions portal.
Oil tankers transport Russian crude oil and petroleum products from ports in the Black Sea and Baltic regions on behalf of Lukoil, Rosneft, Surgutneftegas, Novatek, Tatneft, and Gazprom.
Bulk carriers transport agricultural products from Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories through the ports of Berdiansk, Sevastopol, Kerch, and Feodosia.
The list also includes LNG carriers transporting liquefied natural gas from the sanctioned floating storage unit SAAM FSU (IMO 9915090). The vessel stores LNG from the sanctioned Russian Arctic LNG 2 project.
Among the vessels not under sanctions is the bulk carrier LAMAR S (IMO 9154505). In 2026, it repeatedly loaded wheat at the Avlita terminal (Aval LLC) in temporarily occupied Sevastopol for onward delivery, including to Syria.
The general cargo vessel NAYA FALCON (IMO 8033120) transported baking soda and wheat bran from Sevastopol to Egypt and Cyprus in 2026.
The list also includes the tanker GREGAL (IMO 9378876), which is part of the fleet of UAE-based Cymare Navigation FZC, affiliated with Russia’s Sovcomflot.
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine reports that energy exports remain one of the main sources of funding for Russia’s war against Ukraine. Russia uses the theft and export of Ukrainian agricultural products as a tool to exert influence over other countries, including to secure political and economic concessions.
The agency emphasizes the need to coordinate sanctions efforts and detain vessels involved in violations in order to restrict Russia’s maritime logistics and deprive it of resources to continue the war.
Last week, Sweden’s Supreme Court ruled that the confiscated CAFFA vessel, which was part of Russia’s shadow fleet, should be transferred to Ukraine.

The law enforcement agency further alleged that Pirogov made cryptocurrency transfers to the Ukrainian military and purchased and delivered ammunition from Poland to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy cannot find a candidate for the position of Ukraine's ambassador to the United States - Politico
Kyiv • UNN
President Zelenskyy has still not found a candidate for the position of Ukraine's ambassador to the United States due to the difficulty of working with the Trump administration. Potential candidates, including Deputy Prime Minister Svyrydenko, are declining the position.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy still cannot find a candidate for the position of Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States who would have sufficient political weight and influence to work with Donald Trump’s administration. Potential candidates are in no hurry to agree to the position because of the difficulty of working in Washington amid the war. Politico reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to two former high-ranking Ukrainian officials and four lawmakers, the president of Ukraine is making significant efforts to find a person with enough influence to represent Kyiv in the administration of President Donald Trump.
According to a former high-ranking Ukrainian official and a Republican foreign policy expert, Zelenskyy previously accelerated plans for personnel changes in order to offer the ambassadorial post to Deputy Prime Minister Yuliia Svyrydenko, but she declined, derailing his plans, the publication уточнює.
It is no secret that I was counting on Yuliia Svyrydenko and offered her the position of ambassador to the United States
He also said at the time that he was looking for a candidate with the highest possible qualifications: "a person at the level of deputy prime minister, minister, or prime minister."
However, since then, other potential candidates have likewise declined the difficult task of managing Trump’s "unpredictable administration," Politico notes.
Former Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration of Ukraine Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze said that candidates with sufficient authority and qualifications fear that they will not like the conditions necessary to perform the job properly.
She noted that this sharply narrows the range of options for Zelenskyy. According to Klympush-Tsintsadze, such a person would most likely have to come from his inner circle, but there is no one among them who would seriously fit the role.
According to a former Ukrainian lawmaker who wished to remain anonymous, there are people on Zelenskyy’s team who want to take the position, but "none of them is actually suitable."
It would be an oversimplification to portray the situation as though no one wants to take the position. Of course, there are people who aspire to this job, but none of them is actually suitable. It is difficult for Zelenskyy to find a replacement
Journalists also note that there are signs that the White House may soon try to resume peace talks.
In this case, it is extremely important to have an ambassador in Washington who has the political weight to reach agreements, the authority to speak on Zelenskyy’s behalf, and the ability to navigate an administration where policy can change rapidly. As well as lobby for interests in Congress
Politico also emphasizes that Ukraine may be left without an influential politician in Washington precisely when decisions are being made on weapons, air defense, logistics, and intelligence sharing, as well as on the conditions for resuming peace talks.
It is quite possible that Zelenskyy will not appoint anyone before the U.S. midterm elections. It will be difficult to judge who would fit best into the political situation until these elections take place
We remind you
On August 3, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Olha Stefanishyna from the position of ambassador to the United States. The relevant decree No. 696/2026 was published.

Nearly three years since Israel's war in Gaza began, and despite a lengthy case brought before the High Court of Israel, journalists remain unable to enter the Strip to report independently on the widespread destruction, the ongoing humanitarian crisis and the IDF's occupation of more than half of the Strip.
Histadrut national union official Peter Lerner, who served as the IDF's Spokesperson to International Media until 2024, says the IDF's reluctance to allow journalists in is a symptom of the war being drawn out and Israel's increasing isolation from the global community.
"The time passed two years ago," to let journalists enter Gaza, Lerner said. "I recommended it to my superiors, that holding out this long is not beneficial to Israel; it just superimposes the fact that people will say that you're hiding something. …The fact is that there will be negative stories about the negative consequences of war."
Lerner and host Amir Tibon also discussed the reasons why Israeli soldiers passively watch – or even partake – in settler-led attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank, and the ways in which the government fuels the total lack of accountability. "When I watch the attacks of these families in their homes, and they're so helpless – as someone who experienced October 7 very, very close, it's traumatic to watch," shared Tibon, a longtime resident of Kibbutz Nahal Oz.
State-backed settler violence has also accelerated against journalists in the West Bank, where Haaretz correspondent Matan Golan and photographer Itai Ron were attacked this week by settlers that have besieged Palestinian homes in Qusra, near Nablus, as IDF soldiers looked on.
Abby Seitz, a features editor at Haaretz, joins the podcast to recount the threats, illegal orders from soldiers and right-out lies that she and reporter Nagham Zbeedat encountered in a single day in the southern West Bank last month. Zbeedat and Seitz reported from Umm al-Khair as the community marked one year since Awdah Hathaleen recorded his own death at the hands of internationally sanctioned settler leader Yinon Levi.
When asked for comment on why Border Police, with the army, dispersed the village's memorial ceremony, a police spokesperson told Haaretz that it was an "unlawful gathering, which was intended to serve as a demonstration of support for a terrorist who was neutralized" – a statement that contradicts the state's own stance, as prosecutors filed reckless manslaughter charges against Levi last week.
"This is not uncommon, and it's increasingly happening against international and Israeli journalists, but it's also been happening against Palestinian journalists for a long time. There are Palestinian journalists right now in administrative detention, held for months without charges, simply for filming what's been going on" in the West Bank, Seitz said.

Türkiye's Justice and Development (AK) Party marks 25th anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:40:36 UTC
17:40:36 KST

Türkiye's ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party, led by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, is marking 25 years on the country's political scene.
Its record has been unmatched since the beginning of the country's multiparty era in 1946.
On Aug. 14, 2001, the AK Party was founded as Türkiye's 39th political party, under the “Virtuous People Movement” led by Erdogan, who was then mayor of Istanbul.
“From today onward, nothing will be the same in Türkiye,” Erdogan said at the launch event.
Years later, historians would describe the moment as the beginning of a new era in Turkish politics.
Erdogan was unanimously elected chairman at the AK Party's Founders' Board meeting on Aug. 16. The party's political journey began, eventually producing four prime ministers and two presidents through a series of electoral victories.
Just 15 months after its establishment, the AK Party contested the Nov. 3, 2002, general elections under the slogan “Alone in power, ready to work.”
With Erdogan unable to run due to a political ban, the party won 34.28% of the vote and emerged as the largest party, leading to the formation of the 58th government, headed by Abdullah Gul.
After an amendment to Article 312 of the Turkish Penal Code lifted his political ban, then-party chairman Erdogan was elected as a lawmaker in the March 9, 2003 by-election in Siirt, entering the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye.
Following the resignation of the government led by Gul, Erdogan was tasked by then-President Ahmet Necdet Sezer with forming a government. He established the 59th government on March 15, 2003, becoming prime minister.
The AK Party faced its first electoral test under Erdogan's premiership in the 2004 local elections.
Winning 41.7% of the vote, the party emerged as the largest party and took control of 1,750 municipalities, including 12 metropolitan municipalities.
The AK Party increased its vote share to 46.58% in the 2007 general elections, retaining its single-party government, and also received the highest share of the vote in the 2009 local elections.
An indictment by then-Chief Public Prosecutor of the Court of Cassation Abdurrahman Yalcinkaya, seeking the closure of the AK Party and a five-year political ban on 71 people, including Gul and Erdogan, was submitted to the Constitutional Court on March 14, 2008.
The court's acceptance of the indictment on March 31, 2008, marked the beginning of a new process for the AK Party.
The case, based on an indictment that came to be known in political history as the "Google indictment," was concluded on July 30, 2008.
Six members of the court voted in favor of closing the party, while five voted against. However, the required qualified majority was not reached as required by the Constitution, and the closure case was rejected.
One of AK Party's major political tests came with the 2010 referendum on constitutional amendments, held on the 30th anniversary of the Sept. 12, 1980 military coup.
The amendments were approved with 57.88% of the vote.
The AK Party secured 49.83% in the 2011 general elections and 45.54% in the 2014 local elections, winning 818 mayoralties, including 18 metropolitan municipalities.
Following the end of Gul's term, Erdogan was elected on Aug. 10, 2014, with 51.79% of the vote, becoming Türkiye's first president elected directly by popular vote and the country's 12th president.
Following Erdogan's election as president, Ahmet Davutoglu, a lawmaker from the central Konya province, assumed the AK Party chairmanship.
Under Davutoglu's leadership, the AK Party faced its first electoral test in the June 7, 2015 general elections and subsequently in the Nov. 1 snap elections, when it regained a single-party majority.
At the AK Party's second Extraordinary Congress on May 22, 2016, Binali Yildirim, one of the party's founders, was elected chairman. Yildirim subsequently formed the 65th government and became prime minister.
The July 15, 2016 coup attempt by the Fetullah Terrorist Organization (FETO), one of the bloodiest coup attempts in Türkiye's history, was thwarted after citizens responded to Erdogan's call to gather in city squares and airports and stood against tanks to defend democracy.
The solidarity between the AK Party and the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) following the coup attempt laid the foundations for the People's Alliance.
The AK Party took another major political step with the April 16, 2017 constitutional referendum.
The groundwork for the referendum was laid on Dec. 10, 2016, when a constitutional amendment proposal signed by 316 AK Party lawmakers, including then-Prime Minister Yildirim, was submitted to the Grand National Assembly.
Following parliamentary votes on the articles, Erdogan approved the constitutional amendment law on Feb. 10, 2017, and sent it to the prime minister's office for publication and submission to a referendum.
The referendum passed with 51.41% voting "yes" and 48.59% voting "no." The provision stating that "the president-elect shall sever ties with his party" was removed from the Constitution, paving the way for Erdogan to retain party membership. Voters also approved the transition to the Presidential Government System.
Following the referendum, Erdogan returned to the AK Party after 979 days, signing a membership declaration and rejoining the party.
At the party's third Extraordinary Grand Congress on May 21, 2017, held following a decision to convene an extraordinary congress, Erdogan was unanimously re-elected as AK Party chairman, receiving all 1,414 valid votes, 998 days after leaving the post.
A law allowing political parties to form electoral alliances opened the way for parties in Türkiye to contest elections in alliances for the first time.
The AK Party and MHP's "People's Alliance" faced its first electoral test in the June 24, 2018 elections.
Following an early election proposal by MHP Chairman Devlet Bahceli, Erdogan and the party's authorized bodies evaluated the proposal, and June 24, 2018, was set as the election date.
Voters went to the polls on June 24 to elect both the president and lawmakers on the same day for the first time.
Erdogan won the presidential election with 52.59% of the vote, becoming the first president under the Presidential Government System, while the AK Party secured 42.56% in the parliamentary elections and remained the largest party for the 13th consecutive general election.
Erdogan took the oath of office in parliament on July 9 and announced the first Cabinet of the new system on the same day.
At the AK Party's sixth Ordinary Grand Congress on Aug. 18, 2018, Erdogan was re-elected chairman with all 1,380 valid votes.
The party's bylaws were amended to incorporate political party electoral alliances following the June 24 elections. A provision was also added stating that membership of the Central Executive Board could not be held concurrently with the position of vice president or minister.
The AK Party and MHP also maintained the People's Alliance in the March 31, 2019 local elections.
The alliance was formed in 51 provinces, including 30 metropolitan municipalities. The AK Party fielded candidates in 27 metropolitan municipalities, while the MHP fielded candidates in Adana, Mersin and Manisa.
The AK Party remained the largest party in the elections, securing 44.33% of the vote.
The AK Party's seventh Ordinary Grand Congress process began in the fall of 2019 at Erdogan's instruction but was suspended after the COVID-19 pandemic began affecting Türkiye in March 2020.
The congress process resumed after pandemic conditions eased, and the congress was held on March 24, 2021, under the theme "Walk the path you believe in." Erdogan was unanimously re-elected chairman with all 1,428 valid votes.
Speaking at the Presidential Complex on March 10, 2023, Erdogan signed a decision under Article 116 of the Constitution to bring forward the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally scheduled for June 18, to May 14.
In the May 14 presidential and parliamentary elections, Erdogan, the People's Alliance candidate, received 49.52% of the vote but failed to secure the more than 50% needed to win in the first round. The AK Party received 35.62% of the vote and won 268 seats in parliament.
In the May 28 runoff, Erdogan won the presidency with 52.18% of the vote.
The AK Party, which has emerged as the largest party in every general election since its establishment, maintained its record as the party with the longest uninterrupted period in power since the beginning of Türkiye's multi-party political era in 1946.
Following the elections, the AK Party held its fourth Extraordinary Grand Congress on Oct. 7, 2023.
Erdogan was unanimously re-elected chairman, receiving all 1,399 valid votes.
The newly elected Central Decision and Administrative Board included 49 new members, while 14 of the 18 members of the Central Executive Board retained their positions.
The AK Party received 35.49% of the vote in the March 31, 2024 local elections, winning 24 provincial and 357 district municipalities.
Following the election results, Erdogan said the party would "surely take the necessary steps by weighing the messages given by the nation at the ballot box in the most accurate and objective manner on the scales of reason and conscience."
Following the election, a renewal process began within the party's organization, with provincial chairmen replaced in Adiyaman, Afyonkarahisar, Erzincan, Gaziantep, Kastamonu, Osmaniye, Zonguldak, Rize, Sanliurfa, Mardin, Kahramanmaras and Batman, as well as several district organizations.
The AK Party held its eighth Ordinary Grand Congress on Feb. 23, 2025, determining the members of its Central Decision and Administrative Board, Central Disciplinary Board, Political Virtue and Ethics Board, and Central Headquarters Party Internal Democracy Arbitration Board.
In the new Central Decision and Administrative Board, 36 members retained their positions while 39 were not included in the new party leadership. With 39 new members joining, 52% of the board was renewed.
The congress also amended Article 81 of the party's bylaws, based on a proposal prepared by the Bylaw Amendment Commission. Three new departments were established for relations with Turkic states, health policies, and culture and arts policies.
Meanwhile, Sevilay Tuncer, the AK Party's head of environmental and urbanization policies, handed over her position to Nilhan Ayan, an AK Party Central Decision and Administrative Board member and Istanbul lawmaker, on April 9, 2026.
Following the eighth Ordinary Grand Congress, a renewal process began within the AK Party's provincial organizations. Provincial chairmen were replaced in 15 provinces: Adana, Adiyaman, Afyonkarahisar, Ardahan, Bitlis, Canakkale, Diyarbakir, Elazig, Giresun, Karaman, Mugla, Nigde, Ordu, Siirt and Tunceli.
Significant progress has been made toward the "Terror-Free Türkiye" goal launched with MHP leader Devlet Bahceli's call on Oct. 22, 2024, and embraced by President Erdogan.
As part of the process, a National Solidarity, Brotherhood and Democracy Commission was established in parliament to work on removing terrorism from Türkiye's agenda, strengthening social cohesion, reinforcing national unity and solidarity, and advancing freedoms, democracy and the rule of law.
The commission was established following a letter sent by Parliamentary Speaker Numan Kurtulmus to political parties represented in parliament and began its work on Aug. 5, 2025.
The commission's report on the National Solidarity, Brotherhood and Democracy was submitted to a vote and adopted by a qualified majority at its 21st meeting on Feb. 18, 2026.
As part of the "Terror-Free Türkiye" process, the Law Proposal on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration was submitted to the Grand National Assembly on Aug. 5, 2026.
The proposal sets out procedures for suspending ongoing investigations, prosecutions and sentences, as well as other measures, once security authorities determine that the PKK/KCK and affiliated groups have ended their physical presence and surrendered their weapons and ammunition, and the National Security Council confirms the development in a decision published in the Official Gazette.
The bill was approved by the Parliamentary Justice Commission on Aug. 8 and passed into law by the General Assembly on Aug. 10, with 467 votes in favor, 87 against, seven abstentions and two duplicate votes.

Octavio: I would love to face Iran with Morocco
TEHRAN - The newly appointed head coach of Morocco’s national beach soccer team, Marco Octavio, has expressed his desire to face Iran in a friendly international match, saying such a game would be a valuable experience for his players.
Octavio has recently taken charge of Morocco’s national beach soccer team. The Brazilian coach has fond memories of his time with Iranian beach soccer and played a major role in some of the national team’s greatest achievements.
A few months ago, there had also been reports of a possible return to Iran in a consultancy role, but the move ultimately did not materialize.
Octavio is now set to lead Morocco’s national team and is hoping to achieve major milestones with the “Atlas Lions.”
Speaking exclusively to Tehran Times, Octavio discussed the challenges of coaching Morocco.
“The biggest challenge for me in coaching Morocco is that I have never coached a team in African beach soccer before. Another major challenge is trying to qualify Morocco for the FIFA Beach Soccer World Cup for the first time. As you know, Morocco have never previously managed to qualify for a World Cup,” he said.
Octavio can rightly be described as one of the architects of Iranian beach soccer. During his time in charge of Iran, he guided the national team to numerous achievements, including winning the Intercontinental Beach Soccer Cup after defeating major powers such as Brazil and Russia.
Asked whether he would like to face Iran in a friendly match, the Brazilian coach said: “Absolutely. I would really, really love to return to Iran and arrange a friendly match against the national team because it would help our team grow tremendously. The Moroccan players can learn a lot from the Iranian players.
“I hope the political situation in the region calms down and peace and stability return. For me, as someone who coached in Iran for many years, it would be a wonderful opportunity to meet my friends again in a very special setting. They have always had a special place in my heart.”
Octavio concluded by expressing his gratitude to Iran for the years he spent in the country.
“Fortunately, thanks to the internet, I am still in contact with my friends in Iran. The internet has allowed me to follow my friends and former players there. Every day, I pray that the people of Iran and my friends there are safe, live in peace and remain protected from danger.
“I want to thank Iran for all the years it gave me the opportunity to live and work there. I have many friends in Iran, and I will always carry them in my heart.”

745 km² recaptured in Ukraine’s eight-month Oleksandrivka counteroffensive, Kyiv says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:40:13 UTC
17:40:13 KST

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the results on 12 August after a briefing from Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, Chief of the General Staff Ihor Skybiuk, and Airborne Assault Forces Commander Oleh Apostol.
Kyiv says the operation recaptured 745 km² and 26 villages across Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The Airborne Assault Forces and attached units carried it out. The goal was to stop Russian forces from advancing further and push them beyond the administrative border of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast. The President's Office put Russian losses at at least 9,550 killed and over 6,600 wounded. Ukrainian forces are continuing to build on the gains. The operation also added to Ukraine's prisoner exchange pool.
Since its 2023 counteroffensive stalled, Ukraine has mostly defended while Russia grinds forward, making any sustained Ukrainian advance rare. With Western aid uncertain and its own troops stretched, Ukraine rarely gets to trade defense for offense on its own land.
A reversal Russia paid for across the front
Ukraine has spent most of the past year on the defensive. The Oleksandrivka counteroffensive broke that pattern. For over six months, Ukrainian forces pushed forward rather than holding ground, and they did it in Ukraine's own Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, not on Russian territory.
The operation also hurt Russia elsewhere. Every unit Moscow sent to defend in the Oleksandrivka direction was a unit it could not use to attack other parts of the front, the US-based think tank ISW assessed. Russian recruitment is declining, which makes that tradeoff harder to absorb.
The numbers across the whole frontline tell the same story. Between late January and 12 August, Russian forces seized roughly 383 km² but lost about 234 km², according to ISW. The net Russian gain was far smaller than in previous seasons.
How Ukraine clawed the ground back
The counteroffensive began on 29 January, according to ISW. Texty reported it ran in two stages: January to May and May to August. It was one of two mutually reinforcing Ukrainian drives in the Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole directions. Both aimed to push Russia from Dnipropetrovsk Oblast and disrupt preparations for Russia's 2026 offensive.
Kyiv says the following 26 villages were liberated: Tolstoi, Novokhatske, Hrushivske, Zirka, Zelenyi Hai, Piddubne, Myrne, Tsehelne, Pryvillia, Zlahoda, Krasnohirske, Pryvilne, Novohryhorivka, Stepove, Kalynivske, Berezove, Novomykolaivka, Voskresenka, Oleksandrohrad, Yalta, Rybne, Maliivka, Sichneve, Ternove, Novoheorhiivka, and Zaporizke. The settlements span all three oblasts.
Where Kyiv's map and ISW's diverge
ISW described the results as evidence that Ukrainian forces can still carry out significant tactical advances and bring back limited mechanized maneuver on parts of the frontline.
It assessed that the success was likely the result of several factors working together: better Ukrainian operational planning, a campaign to suppress and destroy Russian air defenses, deeper strikes against Russian supply lines, Ukraine's advantage in tactical drones, and the 01 February Starlink cutoff that hit Russian forces in Ukraine.
Geolocated footage from 11 August showed Ukrainian forces holding positions southeast of Ternuvate and Vozdvyzhivka. Russian sources had claimed advances in those areas. ISW assessed those claims were likely largely exaggerated.
ISW's own mapping recorded roughly 627 km² of Ukrainian gains across the Oleksandrivka and northern Huliaipole directions combined. Even that two-direction total falls below Kyiv's 745 km² for the Oleksandrivka direction alone. ISW noted its conservative methodology likely underestimates Ukrainian advances.
The Airborne Assault Forces Command added that some flag-raisings over liberated villages were done at a "safe distance" from actual positions for operational security. This suggests forces had moved beyond the settlements they publicly named.

The history and characteristics of Finnish cuisine: what people eat in the land of a thousand lakes

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14

The history and characteristics of Finnish cuisine: what people eat in the land of a thousand lakes
Kyiv • UNN
Finnish cuisine was shaped by the climate and nature, combining simple and hearty dishes made with fish, game meat, berries, and dairy products. Traditional dishes such as kalakukko and kalakeitto reflect a unique combination of ingredients.
Finnish cuisine developed over centuries under the influence of the climate, natural conditions, and the way of life of local residents, combining simple and hearty dishes. UNN will tell you more about Finland’s culinary traditions, their history, which dishes are considered national, and what is special about Finnish cuisine.
The History of Finnish Cuisine
Finnish cuisine developed in conditions where the choice of products largely depended on nature. In the country, lakes, the sea, forests, and agriculture were important sources of food. Therefore, fish, wild game, grains, potatoes, mushrooms, and berries became staples of the traditional menu.
The origins of this cuisine date back to ancient times. In particular, as early as the Stone Age, local residents combined products that may seem unusual today. They prepared dishes made from meat and fish, among other things.
The need to preserve food for long periods played an important role in the formation of culinary traditions, so before winter, Finns smoked or dried fish, dried mushrooms, and stocked up on other products. For example, herbs such as kalakukko were convenient for storage and travel.
Neighboring countries also influenced the development of the cuisine, so Finnish gastronomy was shaped by Swedish and Western European influences, while preserving its own traditions. One of these was the use of local products provided by lakes, forests, and fields. Traditionally, Finnish cuisine was quite simple, and for a long time it used few spices, mainly salt and black pepper.
Features of Finnish Cuisine
One of the main characteristics of Finnish cuisine is the large number of fish dishes. This is natural for a country with many lakes and access to the sea. Traditional recipes use salmon, herring, trout, whitefish, and other fish.
The meat of wild animals is no less important. Finnish cuisine includes dishes made from reindeer, elk, hare, and game. The meat is often combined with forest berries, primarily lingonberries and cranberries, which are served as sauces, side dishes, jams, or jellies.
Another characteristic feature is the highly specific combination of products. Traditional recipes may combine several types of meat, meat with fish, or fish with dairy products. The latter combination is quite unusual for many other national cuisines.
Plant-based products are also important. Because of the northern climate, the range of fresh vegetables was traditionally limited. The main products included carrots, beets, and rutabagas, while potatoes appeared in the 18th century. At the same time, the forests were abundant in berries.
Rye bread also remains an important product in Finland. One of its traditional varieties is round reikäleipä with a hole in the middle, while rye dough is also used to make Karelian pasties and kalakukko. Finnish cuisine is also known for its wide range of dairy products, which are used not only as beverages but also in the preparation of soups and other dishes.
Coffee holds a special place in Finnish food culture. It is consumed throughout the day, and pastries are often served with the drink. Traditional sweet products include pulla (pulla), a yeast bun flavored with cardamom.
Traditional Dishes of Finnish Cuisine
Kalakukko is a fish pie that was stored for the winter. It consists of fish and pork fat baked inside rye dough. The finished product resembles a large round loaf on the outside, while the dish itself originated as a nutritious food that could be prepared in advance and stored for a long time. Before eating, kalakukko was reheated. Thus, fish, pork fat, and rye dough were combined in one hearty dish.
Kalakeitto is a traditional Finnish fish soup made with fish and milk. One version of the dish is soup with salmon, potatoes, and milk. The combination of fish and dairy products is one of the notable features of Finnish cuisine. Traditional soups also include klimpisoppa, a fish soup with dumplings.
Kalalaatikko is a traditional main course based on potatoes and herring. The ingredients are stewed together and seasoned with sauce. This dish clearly demonstrates the character of Finnish cuisine: simple, accessible products are combined into hearty home cooking.
Karelian pasties are made from rye dough with a filling. The traditional version contains rice cooked in milk or mashed potatoes. The pasties are eaten freshly baked. They are also served with munavoi — a mixture of butter and chopped boiled eggs with salt.
Among traditional Finnish desserts, mämmi stands out — a dish made from rye flour and malt. It also contains salt and sugar. Mämmi is cooked in the oven for a long time and served with cream, sugar, or vanilla cream.
Another popular accompaniment to coffee is pulla. It is a sweet yeast bun flavored with cardamom.
Top 7 Interesting Facts About Finnish Cuisine
-  The water in Finland is exceptionally pure. It can be safely drunk straight from the tap without heat treatment, thanks to a multistage filtration system and utilities that are always kept in working order. 
-  Finns consume more coffee than anyone else in the world — about 12 kg per Finn on average. In Finland, drinking 8 cups of coffee throughout the day is a normal pattern of consumption. 
-  Finns eat reindeer, bear, and moose meat. 
-  In Finland, people eat the delicacy "surströmming" — fermented fish with one of the strongest odors. 
-  Finns do not eat sweets for breakfast — at most, they have only berries with porridge. 
-  Tipping is not customary in Finnish establishments. 
-  In Finland, they make coffee with cheese, called kaffeost.

Quick hits: Tempers flare as Aussies wilt, Starc's heart-in-mouth moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:39:26 UTC
17:39:26 KST

Test cricket quick hits: Mitchell Starc's tangle with the Darwin turf, Tanzid Hasan's breakthrough century and Steve Smith's catching redemption
Mitchell Starc vents his frustration at a Bangladeshi batter, while a star is born on treacherous Darwin turf.
Here are the quick hits from another torrid day for Australia against Bangladesh.
1. Smith grounds one
There is toiling, and then there is whatever the Australian bowlers were doing during the first session of day two.
The much-vaunted Aussie quartet, with Cam Green and Beau Webster in support, combined for just a single wicket during the opening two hours of play.
The ball found its way past Bangladeshi willow on a few occasions, but for the most part, chances were at a premium.
So, it was far from an ideal time for the usually so-reliable hands of slipper-supreme Steve Smith to let him down.
But with rookie opener Tanzid Hasan already past 50 and Australia having just taken their first wicket of the day, Smith floored one.
Tanzid edged a Nathan Lyon delivery into the elbow of Alex Carey, the ball ricocheted towards slip, and a diving Smith was unable to gather cleanly.
It was far from a sitter, but one Smith will be disappointed to have missed.
Tanzid given a life on 62.
2. Tanzid Hasan's maiden Test ton
Coming into this series, there were serious questions surrounding Bangladesh's opening pair, with the Tigers having struggled to nail down a reliable top two in recent years.
Up steps Tanzid Hasan, the 25-year-old opener playing just his second Test match.
Tanzid was considered and composed against the much-vaunted Australian attack, providing the foundation for a brilliant Bangladeshi team effort.
He already had an ODI century to his name, having scored 107 against Pakistan in Mirpur in March, and he also has scored five first class tons for an average of 39.60.
Talk about nervous 90s, though.
First, Pat Cummins whacked the 25-year-old on the arm with a vicious, 140km/h bouncer.
Then, Tanzid almost holed out to the substitute fielder at long off when on 96, skying a Lyon slower ball with a lofted drive that plugged in the outfield after falling just short of the fielder.
He moved to 99 with a neat clip, and then celebrated his century with a push down the ground off Lyon, a superb hundred celebrated accordingly.
3. The Darwin turf bites at the Australians
However, Tanzid was unable to turn his maiden Test ton into a truly big one, holing out to Lyon only a matter of balls later.
But Australian hearts were in Australian mouths as Mitchell Starc slid to make the catch and then flipped over ungainfully.
Starc, wincing as he got up, looked to be in some discomfort, and the replays showed that the Darwin turf may have been to blame.
The fast-bowler's knee had been caught in the grass, with a cloud of dust and thatch of grass disengaging from the ground.
Thankfully, Starc appeared to recover well, but it wasn't the first time the Marrara Stadium outfield had appeared a little loose, with the ever-energetic Marnus Labuscagne ripping out his fair share of greenery.
With the surface only likely to disintegrate more dramatically over the coming three days, both teams should be wary of not getting twisted up in the outfield.
4. Steve Smith's hat-trick of slip catches
Australia desperately needed something to happen to interrupt the Bangladesh momentum — and it arrived with the new ball.
Josh Hazlewood, Mitch Starc and then Pat Cummins all extracted edges with the new pill, claiming the wickets of Hossain Shanto (84), Litton Das (0) and Mushfiqur Rahim (36) as Bangladesh crumbled from 3-297 to 6-308.
And all three of them were caught by Steve Smith at second slip, making dramatic amends for his earlier fumble.
That trio of catches put Smith level with Joe Root with 218 catches, the most ever by a non-wicketkeeper in Test cricket.
Australia's pacemen are worth their weight in gold, but Smith certainly pays his way in the field to help them out.
5. 'Get off the wicket!'
With that new-ball blitz an increasingly distant memory, and with the Australian bowlers beginning to wilt in the late Darwin sun, the hosts' frustration was on full display late in the evening session.
Into the 103rd over of the innings, Starc was bowling to all-rounder Mehidy, who was well set and intent on seeing the day through.
Mehidy set off for a single and came very close to colliding with the Australian spearhead.
Starc wasn't impressed.
"It's my follow through, not your follow through. Get off the wicket," Starc could be heard saying through the stump mic.
"I didn't see!" Mehidy could be heard saying during the next over, still perhaps apologetic about the near-collision.
But of course, the all-rounder shouldn't be taking the altercation personally.
The Australians' frustration was all of their own making.
6. You call that a knife?
There's nothing worse as an athlete than getting mud or grass caught between your cleats or spikes.
Nathan Lyon clearly had this issue during the second session, when going through his usual array of warm ups and stretches on the boundary at Marrara Oval.
But what can you do about it when in the middle of a Test match as you're about to prepare for a bowling spell?
Turns out, you ask someone in the kitchen if they have a spare a butter knife they don't mind soiling with some outfield dirt.
Much like the Northern Territory's best known international export, Crocodile Dundee, one can almost imagine one of the locals querying Lyon's choice of implement with quips like "you call that a knife …"

Wildfires grip Europe as heat dries forests, strains firefighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:39:01 UTC
17:39:01 KST

Wildfires tore through parts of Europe on Friday as another wave of record-breaking heat left forests tinder-dry, forcing evacuations in France, Germany, Croatia and Greece and putting firefighters under growing pressure.
France was among the hardest hit, with a new blaze racing through the pine forests of the southwestern Landes region and forcing 525 people to leave their homes in the village of Luglon. About 500 firefighters, backed by six aircraft, were battling the flames, regional officials said.
The fire had burned about 1,100 hectares (2,700 acres) by Friday and advanced to within 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) of Luglon's center, regional official Gilles Clavreul said. Roads north and south of the village were closed as authorities moved residents to safety.
"The situation is unfavorable," Clavreul told reporters.
The Landes region has been repeatedly battered by wildfires this summer. Nearby areas around Arcachon Bay were devastated by two major fires in late July that burned more than 50,000 hectares (124,000 acres) and prompted the evacuation of as many as 220,000 people.
The latest blaze came as France endured what officials described as an unprecedented wildfire season. The area burned so far has surpassed the previous national record set in 2022.
France's exceptionally dry conditions have made its extensive pine forests especially vulnerable to fire. Temperatures approached 41 degrees Celsius (106 degrees Fahrenheit) Thursday in several parts of the country, including Aquitaine in the southwest and the Rhone River valley in the east. Similar temperatures were expected Friday before cooler conditions arrived over the weekend.
The fires have not been confined to southern Europe or traditionally fire-prone areas. Flames have also spread through northern France and Brittany, regions that normally experience cooler and wetter conditions.
In Germany, a wildfire in the Hürtgen forest in North Rhine-Westphalia state forced all 1,800 residents of the nearby village of Gey to evacuate as flames threatened homes.
Nearly 300 hectares (740 acres) of forest were burning Friday morning. Firefighting efforts were complicated by unexploded World War II ammunition scattered through the forest, authorities said.
Explosions could be heard as the ammunition detonated in the heat and flames, forcing firefighters to keep their distance from some areas. The fire moved to within about 300 meters (1,000 feet) of Gey, while a change in wind direction overnight increased the threat to the village.
Hundreds of emergency personnel were deployed, with the German army sending tanks and firefighting helicopters providing aerial support. Authorities said the cause of the fire remained unknown and further evacuations had not been ruled out.
In Croatia, a wildfire near the coastal town of Omis forced more than 1,000 people to flee overnight as strong winds pushed flames into a residential area.
Fourteen people were hospitalized, seven of them in life-threatening condition early Friday, according to authorities. The fire approached the town center, damaged homes and other property, burned cars and caused power outages in parts of Omis.
Local media showed residents packed into a sports hall after being evacuated. Witnesses told public broadcaster HRT that some people jumped into the sea as boats caught fire.
Firefighters had brought the blaze under control by Friday morning, but crews and aircraft were sent farther south to battle another wildfire that broke out overnight on the Peljesac peninsula.
Albania was also fighting multiple fires, with 11 active blazes reported Friday. Authorities said the largest, in the Gure-Lure area, had been contained near residential areas, reducing the immediate threat to homes.
Three people have been prosecuted in connection with a fire that engulfed part of Lura National Park. Authorities said they were suspected of failing to take adequate measures to protect the area under their responsibility from fire.
In northern Greece, more than 300 residents and vacationers were evacuated by sea Thursday after a wildfire swept through a pine forest and threatened homes along the coast.
The latest fires came as Britain recorded its hottest day of the year Thursday, with temperatures reaching 38.1 degrees Celsius (100.6 degrees Fahrenheit) in west London.
Wildfires raced through parts of the West Midlands, destroying several homes and prompting a major emergency response. Simon Tuhill, chief fire officer for the region, described the blazes as among the most significant incidents the service has ever handled.
A total of 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.
The extreme heat and fires are being intensified by human-caused climate change, which is increasing the frequency and severity of heat waves and leaving landscapes dangerously dry.
Many European countries are particularly vulnerable because buildings and infrastructure have historically been designed for colder climates, while air conditioning remains less widespread than in hotter parts of the world.
