Other health emergencies must not be neglected in eastern DRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:38:48 UTC
17:38:48 KST

While the response to the Ebola disease outbreak is mobilising significant resources in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns of the need to maintain care and funding for other health crises in the east of the country to prevent a worsening of the humanitarian situation. Cholera, measles, malaria and violence linked to the ongoing conflict continue to threaten thousands of people in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. 
Since the Ebola disease outbreak was declared in May, media attention and resources have focused largely on the response to this emergency. While this mobilisation is essential to contain the outbreak, it must not come at the expense of other health and humanitarian needs that persist in North Kivu and South Kivu. 
This outbreak is occurring in a context already marked by multiple health and humanitarian crises. Communities are already living under the pressure of armed conflict. Repeated clashes cause displacement, interrupt vaccination campaigns, limit access to safe drinking water, and make healthcare harder to access. 
Added to this already fragile situation is the fear now associated with Ebola disease. In general, fear of exposure to the Ebola disease outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus can deter some patients from attending health facilities in provinces already affected by the outbreak. This fear could lead to delays in care or deaths, including from common diseases, thereby worsening situations that are otherwise preventable, and further weakening access to general healthcare. 
“The Ebola disease outbreak is a major emergency, but it is not the only one,” explains Joshua Eckley, MSF head of programmes in South Kivu. “Every day, we receive patients suffering from various diseases, people injured in fighting, and [victims and] survivors of sexual violence.”  
“For these communities, all these emergencies coexist and require a simultaneous response,” says Eckley. “When basic healthcare is interrupted, more people risk dying from preventable diseases. It is essential to preserve continuity of care and access to general healthcare in order to treat all other conditions.”  
The Ebola disease outbreak is a major emergency, but it is not the only one.
In the shadow of Ebola disease, measles and cholera are spreading in the east of the country
While the Ebola disease outbreak is the focus of attention, other outbreaks are spreading in eastern DRC. According to official data, more than 108,643 suspected measles cases, with 1,394 deaths, were reported across the country from January to 19 July 2026. Nearly half of these cases — more than 50,827 — are concentrated in North Kivu and South Kivu.1 At the same time, the country has already recorded more than 35,464 suspected cholera cases and more than 1,051 deaths. Of these notifications, 14,819 are concentrated in the two provinces. 
MSF has mobilised in the fight against measles in North Kivu and South Kivu. Teams have carried out six responses to measles outbreaks. The most recent are still ongoing, taking place in Shabunda, South Kivu province, and Walikale, North Kivu province. Together, these responses have already made it possible to treat more than 12,050 patients and vaccinate more than 283,150 children. 
At the same time, teams are facing a worrying resurgence of cholera. In Bukavu and Shabunda, South Kivu, MSF continues to care for patients following a surge in cases recorded last year in the province. In Goma, teams were also mobilised to tackle a cholera outbreak between May and early August 2026. In total, more than 2,410 people with cholera have been treated in MSF-supported facilities. 
“For the families we care for, there is no hierarchy between crises,” says Dr Yvan Mbangi, MSF Deputy Medical Coordinator in Goma. “Whether a child dies of measles or malaria, whether a person succumbs to cholera or Ebola disease, every life matters.” 
Beyond our response to Ebola disease, and measles and cholera outbreaks, MSF continues to provide essential healthcare in Masisi, Mweso, Walikale, Bambo, Kibirizi, Kirotshe, Goma, and Rutshuru in North Kivu province, and in Minova, Bunyakiri, and Uvira, in South Kivu province. But given the scale of the needs, this mobilisation remains largely inadequate. These crises require much greater commitment from health authorities and humanitarian organisations to guarantee access to care for communities.
Do not push other crises into the background
While humanitarian needs continue to increase, available funding is decreasing. North Kivu could notably be excluded from the next three-year Global Fund funding cycle dedicated to the fight against malaria. 
Yet malaria remains the leading cause of morbidity in DRC, including in North Kivu. Displacement caused by fighting forces many families to seek refuge in forests or isolated areas, where exposure to mosquitoes is greater and access to healthcare is particularly limited. 
“We risk seeing a reduction in the resources dedicated to the disease that nevertheless kills the most people in this region,” says Dr Mbangi. “It would be a tragic paradox: mobilising considerable resources against one outbreak while weakening the response to a disease that continues to cause a far higher number of deaths every day.”  
Years of conflict, massive displacement, and chronic insecurity, as well as a drastic reduction in humanitarian aid funding, have weakened the health system in North Kivu and South Kivu. Many health centres and hospitals operate with reduced capacity due to a lack of staff, medicines, and equipment, while others have had to suspend their activities because of violence. In several areas, hundreds of thousands of people remain without regular access to healthcare. 
“While medical-humanitarian needs continue to grow in eastern DRC, we call on the authorities, donors and all humanitarian organisations to maintain and strengthen their investments in all responses to the many and diverse needs of people,” says Eckley. “It is vital that all emergencies be addressed simultaneously.”

"Increased caution": Why is the US warning against travel to Germany?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:38:08 UTC
17:38:08 KST

Unlike for Switzerland, Austria, Norway and Poland, the US is maintaining its travel warning for Germany; France and Italy remain at level 2.
Where should the journey go? In 2026, many tourists now think very carefully about that. And among US tourists, Germany may now lose out as a destination.
The reason: in the US State Department's travel advisories, the Federal Republic remains at security level 2. Travellers are therefore advised to exercise "increased caution".
Switzerland, Austria, Portugal and Poland are classified by the US authorities at security level 1 as countries without a particular warning level.
Norway also benefits from this positive rating, which was updated at the beginning of July 2026.
While security level 2 applies to the whole of Spain, Washington issued a level 3 warning on 1 August for the exclave Ceuta.
Trips to this area should be reconsidered, a travdl advisory warned saying: "The massive and uncontrolled influx of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta could lead to unpredictable and dangerous security situations. In view of this serious situation, Spain has deployed the Spanish military, the Spanish National Police and the Guardia Civil. Given the risks to their safety, US citizens should reconsider travel to this area."
US cites terrorism risk in Germany
Alongside Germany, Sweden, France and Italy are also listed by the US government at security level 2. In these countries, travellers from the US are urged to be particularly vigilant in busy places because of an increased terrorist threat.
"Terrorist groups and lone actors remain a constant threat in Germany and Europe, attacking people in public places with knives, small arms, improvised explosive devices and vehicles. Such attacks can occur with little or no warning and target: tourist sites, transport hubs (airports, railway stations or bus terminals), markets and shopping centres, municipal facilities, hotels, clubs and restaurants, places of worship and educational institutions, parks, major sporting and cultural events, schools."
Pickpockets in France
On France, the US State Department website primarily warns about pickpockets and mobile-phone theft, which allegedly "occur frequently, especially in crowded areas."
It then adds: "Terrorist groups continue to plot possible attacks in France and may strike with little or no notice. In addition, peaceful demonstrations and strikes regularly take place in Paris and other cities across France."
Are El Salvador, Zambia and Senegal safer than Germany?
US security level 2 also applies – as it does to Germany – to Egypt, Morocco and India.
By contrast, El Salvador, Zambia and Senegal are considered safe and placed at level 1 for US travellers.
In red on the US list and subject to a full level 4 travel warning,- meaning US tourists are advised to avoid these countries, - are, among others, Russia, Ukraine, Iran, Iraq and Syria.
The US State Department's map showing the individual countries can be found here.
Germany is far removed from that, and many US visitors are therefore likely to keep coming to Berlin, Heidelberg or to Munich for the Oktoberfest in future.

US accuses dozens of countries of helping China avoid Trump’s tariffs
White House report claims tens of billions of dollars in annual revenue lost to transshipments.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has accused dozens of countries of helping China to illegally dodge United States tariffs, depriving government coffers of tens of billions of dollars in annual revenues.
In a report published on Thursday, the White House said more than 40 countries have participated in a shadow logistics network facilitating the flow of Chinese goods into the US under false labelling.

China’s biggest enablers in the “Great Transshipment Scam” include the European Union, Mexico, Canada, India, Japan and South Korea, the Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy said in the report.
Southeast Asian countries, including Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Cambodia, also play “an important role” in the network, the trade policy office said.
US manufacturing sectors hit hardest by the transshipments include electrical equipment, integrated circuits, aluminium products and motor components, according to the report.
“Every dollar lost to this Great Transshipment Scam is a dollar stolen from American workers, manufacturers, and taxpayers,” the office headed by Trump appointee Peter Navarro said in the report.
China’s embassy in Washington, DC, did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside of regular office hours.
The dozens of countries named in the report have yet to publicly respond to its claims.
Warning that countries facilitating transshipments are being “put on notice”, the White House said border authorities have employed artificial intelligence to integrate shipment data and other information as part of strengthened enforcement efforts.
“The message to the world is simple. The age of untraceable illegal transshipment is over,” the trade office said.
“What once seemed like quiet paperwork manoeuvres – relabelling, repackaging, re-invoicing – has become a matter of economic sovereignty and national will.”
Trump has shaken up global trade with a slew of protectionist trade policies since returning to the White House in January last year.
In its latest trade salvo, the Trump administration announced levies of 10-12.5 percent on imports from dozens of countries accused of turning a blind eye to forced labour.
A group of 25 Democratic-led US states, including New York, California and Colorado, has challenged the tariffs in court, calling the measures a pretext to reimpose Trump’s sweeping “Liberation Day” duties, which the US Supreme Court struck down in February.
Amitendu Palit, a trade expert and professor at the National University of Singapore, called the White House report the latest effort by the Trump administration to coerce countries into accepting greater market access for US goods.
“The delegitimisation of liberation day tariffs have meant huge loss for the Trump administration: both in terms of the refunds that it has had to pay, as well as in credibility,” Palit told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore it is seeking out more and more ‘innovative’ forms of weaponising market access. This follows the earlier Section 301 tariffs imposed on various countries for not being able to limit use of forced labour.”

US threatens Iran with 'economic isolation, like never seen'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:37:18 UTC
17:37:18 KST

Breadcrumb
US threatens Iran with 'economic isolation, like the world has never seen'
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened Thursday to subject Iran to economic isolation "like the world has never seen before," adding that new measures are expected next week.
"It will be a combination of economic isolation, like the world has never seen before," Bessent told conservative television network Newsmax, adding that "the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz... will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports."
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week," he said.
Bessent described a two-pronged approach featuring financial pressure and a physical blockade of the ports.
The tougher stance contrasts with remarks by Bessent on 4 August, when he told CNBC that an agreement with Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could be reached within days.
Those comments sent Wall Street higher and oil prices lower.
Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance said earlier that the top US priority in the US-Israeli war on Iran presently was bringing oil and gasoline prices down for Americans, with preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon ranking second.
Vance's comments underscored the stark reality that the war now centers on control of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical fuel supply conduit that was open before US President Donald Trump started the war along with Israel in late February.
Iran has all but shut it down in retaliation and thus found a crucial bargaining chip against Trump as he struggles to find a way out of the war and shies away from resuming large-scale attacks.
The 80-year-old president's approval rating is plummeting, the war is unpopular among Americans and midterm elections are approaching in November.
Republicans fear Trump and the war, which has caused gasoline prices to soar, will cost them their control of Congress.
"I know that oil is down today and it's way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict," Vance said on Fox News. "That's goal number one -- keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country."
"And then obviously goal number two is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon," he added.
'Low-keying it'
The vice president has been among the members of the administration most skeptical of the offensive launched against Iran in late February.
These remarks, however, appear to confirm the more cautious approach now favored by the US president, which involves maintaining strong economic pressure on Iran by blockading its ports and preventing it from selling oil.
Heralding more economic punishment, Bessent threatened to subject Iran to economic isolation "like the world has never seen before." He said new measures are expected next week.
Only days ago Trump had said an agreement to reopen the strait was imminent. Now his administration seems to be digging in, with diplomacy on hold as he hopes economic suffering will cause Iran to yield.
"We are low-keying it," Trump said Sunday. "We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump told the news outlet Axios.
The US military reportedly burned through stockpiles of costly high-tech missiles and other weapons in the months since the war started at a cost of billions and is now reportedly running low, limiting Trump's options for resuming attacks on Iran.
"Sometimes we're focused on the energy piece of it because we want Americans to be able to afford the price of oil and gas. Sometimes we're obviously focused on the military... on the nuclear program," Vance also said.
Trump had said recently he would hold off on attacking Iran again only if an agreement were reached quickly to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Now Iran has set a list of conditions for reopening the passageway that the Trump administration is unlikely to accept: an end to the war on all fronts, the lifting of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen assets and compensation for wartime damage.
Those conditions echo the terms of a so-called memorandum of understanding which was reached in June and collapsed as fighting resumed. It included a provision to create a $300 billion reconstruction fund for Iran.

Troops and fighter jets in live fire exercise on Falklands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:36:50 BST
17:36:50 KST

Typhoon fighters flew simulated close air support for infantry assaulting enemy positions during Exercise Cape Upholder in the Falkland Islands, an exercise that closed out the latest roulement infantry company rotation, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The exercise ran from 29 June to 3 July and brought together the 5th Battalion, The Rifles, the Falkland Islands Defence Force and 1435 Flight, the Typhoon detachment within 905 Expeditionary Air Wing.
According to the department, the multi-phase exercise involved live firing from mortars, snipers and machine guns, along with a section attack to take key enemy positions supported by the Typhoons overhead.
Four Typhoon FGR4 aircraft from 1435 Flight hold round-the-clock quick reaction alert covering the airspace over the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. The flight is the smallest fast jet unit in the RAF and is stationed at RAF Mount Pleasant on East Falkland.
Its aircraft carry individual names rather than squadron markings, a practice dating to the unit’s origins defending Malta during the Second World War, where its aircraft were named Faith, Hope, Charity and Desperation. These were, of course, not Spitfires, apologies to our readers for my earlier suggestion they were.
The roulement infantry company is the standing British Army presence on the islands, drawn from a different unit on each rotation and typically deployed for around six months. Its role covers ground defence of Mount Pleasant and the wider infrastructure, along with training across the islands’ terrain, and exercises of this kind are usually run as the outgoing company hands over.
The Falkland Islands Defence Force is the islands’ own volunteer unit, recruited locally and funded by the Falkland Islands Government rather than the Ministry of Defence. It trains alongside British forces and would form part of the ground defence in a crisis.
British Forces South Atlantic Islands is the joint command covering the region, operating Typhoons, A400M and Voyager aircraft, the infantry company and air defence at Mount Pleasant, alongside HMS Medway on the South Atlantic Patrol Task.
The garrison has been maintained continuously since 1982, when the islands were retaken following the Argentine invasion. Argentina continues to claim the territory and raises the question annually at the United Nations, while the British position rests on the 2013 referendum in which islanders voted by 1,513 votes to three to remain a British Overseas Territory.
Photography from the exercise was taken by Corporal James Braithwaite.

Feature: Bloody legacy of "Death Railway" carries hard-learned peace lesson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
16:36:27 CST
17:36:27 KST

by Xinhua writers Chen Qianci and Chang Tiantong
KANCHANABURI, Thailand, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Located approximately 120 kilometers northwest of Bangkok, capital of Thailand, Kanchanaburi Province is home to a dark steel bridge lying at the throat of a 415-km railway steeped in blood and tears.
Sitting at the bridgehead, local musician Somprasong, cradling a guitar and with a harmonica hanging around his neck, emotionally sang a song composed for the bridge that goes, "How many lives were buried here; those who survive must grit their teeth and move on..."
The lyrics echo the historical truth that during World War II, the Japanese forced more than 60,000 Allied prisoners of war (POWs) and hundreds of thousands of Asian laborers to build a railway simultaneously from Thailand to Myanmar.
Under the coercion of the Japanese army, the project, which should have taken six to seven years, was completed in just over a year, leaving more than 100,000 people to perish due to heavy labor, shortages of necessities, rampant epidemics, and other causes, and giving the railway its name -- the "Death Railway."
According to Somporn Ajirasak, a resident of Kanchanaburi, the Japanese military decided to build this railway because maritime transport was vulnerable to attacks by Allied aircraft and submarines. At that time, the area around Kanchanaburi was densely forested, making the railway a relatively concealed overland military supply route.
"They used this railway to transport weapons, ammunition, and other supplies to the front lines to continue their offensives against other cities and countries," Somporn noted, adding that the laborers and POWs involved in the railway construction came from many countries and regions and totaled about 300,000, with Asian laborers making up the largest group.
"For those POWs, death was easy; the hard part was how to stay alive," Somporn said. After Asian laborers died, some bodies were even thrown directly into the River Kwai, giving rise to the saying "one railway sleeper equals one life," which reflects the human cost of this railway.
Boarding a train from the bridge over the River Kwai and traveling northwest for about an hour brings passengers to Tham Krasae, the most perilous section of the "Death Railway," where the tracks run on a wooden trestle structure built between cliffs and the river below.
When a train passes through, it slows to a near crawl for safety, yet even as a passenger, the experience is breathtakingly perilous. To build this railway section, laborers at that time had to scale the cliffs to lay the tracks with their flesh and blood.
Chulanee, a teacher who led a study tour group from a secondary school in Nonthaburi Province to visit the section, said they had specially chosen landmarks along the "Death Railway" in Kanchanaburi for the trip, aiming to help students learn about history and remember it through real-life experiences.
Continuing dozens of kilometers northwest from the cliff section leads passengers to the "Hellfire Pass." The name "Hellfire" comes from the fact that POWs and laborers were forced to work day and night; the flickering firelight cast shadows of figures, resembling the inferno described by Dante. Locals, however, more directly call it the "Broken Pass," citing its topographic features -- a testament to the immense hardship of manually cutting through the mountain to build the road at that time.
Now, a memorial museum has been established here at Hellfire Pass, with the clinking and clanging sounds of stone chiseling echoing through the indoor exhibition hall from time to time.
At the exit leading to the Hellfire Pass Railbed, a quote by Australian POW Max McGee is inscribed on the wall: "Every man who worked on the railway, in whichever section, would have an automatic passport to Heaven. They have all done the requisite stretch in Hell."
A guestbook at the information desk collected reflections of visitors from countries such as Australia, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Thailand: "Never forget, never repeat the same mistakes!" "I have come here to pay my respects many times." "A very immersive and sobering experience." "I have learned a great deal and will definitely come back again."
However, in stark contrast to the world's commemoration and remembrance, the Japanese government has covered up and downplayed the atrocities. "Most of the Japanese I met said they knew nothing about it; if they hadn't come to Kanchanaburi, they would have had no idea that their country had committed such brutal crimes in Thailand," Somporn said.
Even more worrying is that Japan's defense budget requests have repeatedly broken records, and it plans to introduce offensive weapons and adopt "new ways of warfare".
Sondhi Limthongkul, a Thai media figure who has been following this issue, bluntly noted, "Japan is very frightening now... its rearmament is a fait accompli. The core question is whether the Asia-Pacific community has a sufficiently robust diplomatic framework to manage and coordinate the risks of this new giant war machine?"
"It is a history lesson that came at an extraordinarily high cost. It should never have happened, and it must never happen again in the future," Sahaphan Rungrojpanich, a Thai senator born in Kanchanaburi, told Xinhua that he had submitted relevant proposals to parliament and the government, in a bid to promote the nomination of the "Death Railway" and the Bridge over the River Kwai for UNESCO World Heritage status.
Sahaphan said that he hopes to tell the story of suffering to peace along the "Death Railway," so that every visitor can feel the preciousness of peace while looking back at history.
"What we should do is tell this part of history to young people and the next generation, and let them know that today's peace comes from the sacrifices of those in the past," Sahaphan said. ■

Malaysia's economy grows 6 pct in Q2 as exports, demand strengthen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
16:36:12 CST
17:36:12 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's economy expanded 6 percent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, accelerating from 5.4 percent in the first quarter, supported by resilient domestic demand and stronger exports, the country's central bank said on Friday.
Household spending was supported by steady income growth and ongoing policy measures, while investment continued to benefit from spending on structures and machinery and equipment, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) said in a statement.
Exports also accelerated, led by sustained strength in electrical and electronics (E&E) products and services, alongside a rebound in liquefied natural gas (LNG) and non-E&E manufacturing exports.
On the supply side, growth was driven by the services and manufacturing sectors.
On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the economy grew 2.5 percent, compared with a marginal contraction of 0.03 percent in the first quarter.
For the first half, the economy expanded by 5.7 percent, higher than the 4.5 percent growth in the corresponding period of 2025.
BNM governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said the economy remained on a firm footing, with 2026 growth projected at 4 percent to 5 percent, although recent developments suggest it could be around 5 percent.
"While the outlook continues to be shaped by external developments, Malaysia is well-positioned to navigate these challenges from a position of strength and policy readiness," he noted. ■

SYDNEY, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Australia's Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong warned in a speech on Friday that calls for Australia to exist as a monocultural society make the country weaker and more vulnerable.
Wong said in a keynote lecture at the Lowy Institute in Sydney that Australia has only ever existed as a multicultural society, warning that pursuing the "melancholic fantasy of monoculture" would make the nation a more hostile place.
Her comments were a response to populist Senator Pauline Hanson, who in June said that Australia must exist as a monocultural society.
"The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and to cut off our connections. To look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, and no opportunities to grow from," Wong said on Friday.
Hanson's right-wing One Nation party, support for which has risen across Australia in 2026 according to opinion polls, has vowed to cut immigration, reduce foreign aid and withdraw Australia from multilateral institutions if it wins power at the next general election due to be held in 2028.
Polling conducted by YouGov Australia in July found that 26 percent of Australians said they intend to vote for One Nation at the next election, up from the 6.4 percent of votes the party received at the 2025 election.
The same poll found that support for the governing Labor Party has fallen from 34.5 percent at the 2025 election to 28 percent, while voter support for the conservative Coalition has fallen from 31.8 percent to 20 percent.
The annual Lowy Institute poll for 2026, released by the think tank in June, revealed that 55 percent of Australians think the total number of migrants coming into the country is too high, up from 53 percent in 2025 and 48 percent in 2024. ■

Israel shocked by pace of Iran’s military recovery – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:34:50 UTC
17:34:50 KST

Israel shocked by pace of Iran’s military recovery – media
Israeli defense officials have been shocked by the rapid recovery of Iran’s military capabilities since the heavy bombardment by the US and Israel in the opening stages of the conflict, the Jerusalem Post has reported.
Earlier this week, a senior adviser to the chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) said that Iran’s output of ballistic missiles and drones exceeds the rate at which they are being deployed. “Even if the war lasts for several years, our ballistic missiles will continue to rain down on the enemy,” Brigadier General Mohammad-Reza Naqdi told Press TV.
In an article on Thursday, the Jerusalem Post said it has independently confirmed that statements by senior Iranian officials of accelerated arms production in the country are accurate.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has claimed for months that Iran’s defense industry was set back years after US and Israeli forces attacked the country around 30,000 times, striking over 2,600 missile and industrial military targets, during the hottest phase of the conflict in late February and early April, the article read.
But now both the IDF and Mossad intelligence agency acknowledge that they did not expect Tehran to restore its stockpiles of ballistic missiles and other key weapons so quickly, it said.
According to Israeli officials, the Iranians were not only able to swiftly access underground missile sites affected by the US-Israeli airstrikes, but also figured out other creative ways to rebuild their arsenals.
If Tehran keeps manufacturing between 100 to 300 missiles per month, it could become a prohibitive threat for Israel already in 2028, the paper suggested.
This possibility will likely influence broader Israeli strategy about when and if another attack on Iran might be needed, it added.
When approached for comment by the Jerusalem Post, an Israeli military spokesperson said that “from the nature of the issues at hand, it is not in our ability to specify concrete evaluations regarding the pace of the [Iranian] rehabilitation because giving such specifics could expose IDF sources and methods.”
“The IDF will continue to analyze developments and to be prepared accordingly,” the spokesman stressed.
While Israel has refrained from military action against Iran since June, the standoff between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz continues.
The traffic in the key waterway, which accounts for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas trade, has reduced to eight ships per day amid reports of more strikes on vessels, according to Reuters. It stood at between 130 and 140 ships daily before the conflict.
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the Americans had “total control” over the strait. Tehran denied the claim the next day, saying that the waterway remains “under Iran’s control and management” and will stay closed until the US changes its behavior.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday closed criminal proceedings against comedian Samay Raina and four other social media personalities over remarks concerning people with disabilities, while recognising their subsequent efforts to promote awareness and dignity for the community.Along with Raina, the court quashed the FIRs and related proceedings against comedians Vipul Goyal, Balraj Paramjeet Singh Ghai, Sonali Thakkar and Nishant Jagdish Tanwar.The proceedings stemmed from jokes made by the five, which were flagged by the M/s SMA Cure Foundation, an organisation working with people affected by Spinal Muscular Atrophy and other rare diseases.The case took a different turn after the Supreme Court asked the influencers to take constructive steps towards supporting people with disabilities. The court noted that they had since organised a chess tournament for specially-abled people in March and helped raise awareness about organisations working with people with disabilities.The bench, comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said their efforts appeared to be producing positive results."Once there are genuine efforts, positive results are bound to be there," the bench said as per news agency PTI.
"They are very bright youngsters. If they have started working in the positive direction, they will bring positive results," it added.Senior advocate Aparajita Singh, appearing for the SMA Cure Foundation, told the court that the influencers had made "genuine efforts" and had attempted to engage with the foundation following the court's earlier intervention."This matter was going nowhere till this court took a very strong stand last time," Singh said.The court subsequently quashed the FIRs and other criminal proceedings against the five and said their case was now closed.However, the Supreme Court said it would separately examine the larger question of how the dignity of people with disabilities can be better protected and whether comprehensive directions are required.The court's observations came a day after the CJI and other judges met a delegation of people with disabilities from different fields."It was quite a learning and an eye-opener for us also," the CJI said, adding, "We have requested them to send their suggestions also.""It was quite a satisfying experience what we saw yesterday and what we interacted," he said.The delegation included 20 people, among them Paralympians and athletes such as Nidhi Mishra, Ankur Dhama and Major D P Singh, as well as Chhonzin Angmo.
During Friday's hearing, the bench also noted that the influencers had engaged in meaningful discussions with the SMA Cure Foundation and were willing to invite people living with SMA to their shows.More programmes are also planned to raise funds for people affected by the condition.The influencers had earlier volunteered before the Supreme Court in November to organise at least two events every month, either online or in person, to raise money for a proposed corpus that could provide financial assistance to people living with SMA.The court's decision therefore brings the criminal proceedings against the five to an end, while leaving the broader question of protecting the dignity of people with disabilities open for further consideration.

Russia and Ukraine traded accusations Friday over overnight drone attacks targeting logistics, port and other infrastructure, with Ukrainian authorities reporting at least three deaths and 27 injuries.

"The resulting smoke was quickly extinguished. No employees were injured. Emergency services are on site to ensure the continued safety of the facility," Korolev said.
Wildberries confirmed the attack on Telegram, saying its logistics facility sustained minor damage but was evacuated in accordance with safety regulations. No goods were damaged.
Ukraine has intensified drone strikes on Wildberries logistics facilities in a campaign that began in mid-July and has spread across several Russian regions.
Since July 18, Ukrainian drones have targeted Wildberries logistics centers in the Moscow, Tambov, Leningrad, Krasnodar, Volgograd and Stavropol regions, as well as in Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014.
Kyiv has accused the e-commerce retailer of playing a role in Moscow's military supply chain, while Moscow and Wildberries maintain that the facilities are purely civilian.
Separately, Leningrad Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko reported damage and a fire at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a Ukrainian drone attack.
"All consequences of the attack in the port of Ust-Luga have been cleared. There are no casualties," Drozdenko later said, claiming 54 Ukrainian drones were downed during the attack.
In a later statement, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed targeting Ust-Luga, claiming that, according to preliminary information, it struck two processing units at a gas condensate processing complex operated by Novatek, Russia's second-largest natural gas producer.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down a total of 553 Ukrainian drones over 18 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea.

"Damage and fire occurred in a nine-story residential building," it said, adding that firefighters extinguished the blaze caused by the strike.
The Izmail District State Administration in the southern Odesa region said Russian strikes hit local infrastructure and sparked several fires, which were quickly extinguished by emergency crews.
In the northeastern Sumy region, Gov. Oleh Hryhorov said two people were killed and four others injured when Russian drones struck a residential building.
In the eastern Donetsk region, Gov. Vadym Filashkin said one person was killed and 18 others injured in an airstrike on the city of Kramatorsk that damaged an apartment building.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said strikes were also reported in several other regions.
"Every day, Russia uses about 220 guided aerial bombs against our frontline communities, which the aggressor's defense industry continues to produce and modify despite sanctions," Zelenskyy said on US social media platform X.
"Pressure is needed on every supply chain for foreign components and every enterprise working to enable strikes against lives," he added.
Ukraine's Air Force claimed its air defenses downed 90 of 112 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Russia's Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed its forces struck two seagoing tugboats in the Black Sea southwest of Mykolaiv late Thursday, alleging they were "used to escort dry cargo ships carrying Western weapons" for the Ukrainian military.
It also said Russian drones struck the railway station at the port of Izmail overnight, claiming the facility was “used for loading, storing, and transporting military cargo and fuel.”
Independent verification of claims by Russia and Ukraine is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers as well as port and energy infrastructure during the ongoing war.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Just like with the yen, America cannot save the AI bubble
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Just like with the yen, America cannot save the AI bubble
The Japanese currency and US tech stocks share the same fatal problem: momentum can’t survive broken fundamentals
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Dr Andy Xie is a Shanghai-based independent economist specialising in China and Asia, and writes, speaks and consults on global economics and financial markets. 
In a rare intervention, the US has propped up the Japanese yen. The move is seen as a bid to hold off a further rise in yields for US government bonds – amid Japan’s sell-off of US Treasuries to fund its shoring up of the yen – a rise that threatens the US artificial intelligence bubble.
That the United States bought yen for the first time in decades – coordinating with Japan – had a bigger psychological impact on the market than Tokyo’s interventions alone. But give it three or four weeks and the yen-to-dollar rate is likely to snap back above 160.
The yen has been fundamentally weakened by a double shock: the rise in Chinese electric vehicles has hit Japan’s car exports and the energy price spike following the Iran war has hit the wider economy. Technical interventions will not stop its slide.
The car industry is Japan’s last economic stronghold but neither the government nor businesses are doing enough to pivot towards electric vehicles, and Chinese competition will only grow. Unless another export industry rises in replacement, the yen can only depreciate. Energy import costs are also rising rapidly in Japan, which depends on the Middle East for 90-95 per cent of its oil. The unexpectedly large trade deficit in June is an indicator of things to come.
Tokyo is obviously running down its reserves to keep the economy afloat. As the Iran war drags on, the odds are rising that oil infrastructure in the Middle East will be destroyed – which would leave Japan’s economy in mortal peril. Starting January, China has also banned “dual-use” exports to Japan in opposition to its remilitarisation, and has put dozens of Japanese companies on the export-control list. The Japanese economy faces a huge downside in the coming months.
Japan has essentially no room to raise its interest rates to defend its currency. National debt, at about 13.5 trillion yen (US$84.8 billion), is already more than twice the gross domestic product. To properly defend the yen, Japan’s rates will need to match US ones, which are 2-3 percentage points higher, but the resulting rise in interest payments on national debt will trigger a fiscal crisis.

EU decision could halve Ukrainian steelmaker Zaporizhstal's capacity and force shift to pig iron

Unknown Publisher

EU decision could halve Ukrainian steelmaker Zaporizhstal's capacity and force shift to pig iron
Ukrainian steelmaker Zaporizhstal may shift from steel production to pig iron production, leaving around 50% of its capacity idle due to new European Union import restrictions.
Source: Oleksandr Myronenko, Chief Operating Officer of the Metinvest Group (Zaporizhstal's parent company), in a comment to Reuters
Details: Myronenko told Reuters about the possibility before the latest Russian strike on the plant.
From 1 July, the EU almost halved its annual quotas for duty-free steel imports and imposed a 50% tariff on imports exceeding the quotas. Ukraine's quota will be around 1 million tonnes – 60% below its 2025 trade volumes, according to calculations by Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.
The restrictions could prompt Zaporizhstal to increase its production of pig iron, which is not subject to the quotas. Reducing the output of higher-value-added steel products would mean shutting down some production lines and the company would have to reassign employees to other work.
The Federation of Employers of Ukraine estimates that the new restrictions could result in a US$1.2 billion loss in foreign-currency export revenues and reduce GDP by 0.6%.
The situation is further complicated by Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping routes and industrial facilities. As Metinvest has redirected imports of coking coal through European ports, Zaporizhstal's costs have risen by US$30-40 per tonne. Since August, producers have also been paying 30% more for rail freight.
From 1 January, exports to the EU are also subject to additional carbon charges. Before the full-scale war, Metinvest planned to spend US$8 billion over 15 years to transition to "green steel" production, but Myronenko said this is unrealistic under wartime conditions.
Background:
- In January-April 2024, Ukraine increased its revenue from ferrous metal exports by 16.6% to US$959 million. Steel production rose by 33% over the same period, while rolled steel output increased by 30.5%.
- The Zaporizhstal steelworks completely halted operations following a Russian ballistic missile strike. Seven employees were killed and another 21 people were injured.

437 killed, over 2,600 injured: Ukraine’s deadliest month for civilians since 2022, UN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:27:03 UTC
17:27:03 KST

At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured across Ukraine in July, the highest monthly death toll since May 2022, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU), which published the figures on 12 August. The toll was 30% higher than June and 70% higher than July 2025.
The deadliest single attack came on 2 July, when Russia launched 74 missiles and nearly 500 long-range drones at Ukraine, mainly targeting Kyiv. Ukrainian air defenses downed 524 of 570 aerial targets, but the 46 that got through — including 25 ballistic missiles — killed 30 people and destroyed a nine-story apartment block in the capital's Darnytskyi district. Russia fired at least 429 missiles at Ukraine over the course of the month, more than double June's total.
A trend that keeps getting worse
"Every month this year the number of killed and injured civilians has increased," HRMMU head Danielle Bell said. "That trend accelerated sharply in July. The number of civilian casualties in July was the highest we documented in a single month since March 2022."
Child casualties also hit a new high: 17 killed and 166 injured, the worst toll since April 2022. Over the first seven months of 2026, HRMMU verified 12,477 civilian casualties — 1,839 killed and 10,638 injured — a 44% increase over the same period in 2025 and more than double the 2024 figure.
Long-range weapons still the top killer, but glide bombs surged
Long-range missiles and drones caused 38% of all July casualties (183 killed, 967 injured), most of them far from the front line in cities. Casualties from aerial glide-bomb strikes jumped 143% compared with June — from 45 killed and 308 injured to 105 killed and 753 injured — making glide bombs the second-leading cause of civilian harm. Short-range drones near the front line killed 111 people and injured 710, the highest monthly toll from that weapon since 24 February 2022.
Kyiv, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, and Sumy took the heaviest losses among the 14 regions where casualties were recorded. HRMMU also verified 25 killed and 50 injured in Russian-occupied territory, cautioning that shrinking access to information there means the real toll is likely far higher.
Attacks on Black Sea shipping and port infrastructure in Odesa and Mykolaiv oblasts also intensified, with at least 39 strikes — 20 of them on vessels — killing 19 port and crew personnel and wounding 25.
Since the full-scale invasion began on 24 February 2022, the UN has verified at least 16,874 civilians killed and 51,173 injured.

UAE Orders New THAAD Launchers From U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:26:01 UTC
17:26:01 KST

The United States has awarded a contract to produce additional launchers for the THAAD missile defense system for the United Arab Emirates, Pentagon announces.
Under the contract, Lockheed Martin Space received an additional order worth more than $211.4 million as part of a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) agreement.
With this new order, the total value of the contract to manufacture THAAD systems for the Emirates has exceeded $1 billion.
Under the additional order, the contractor will produce and deliver new THAAD launchers in Configuration 3 (C3). Work under the contract will be carried out from August 2026 through January 2031.
Back in December 2011, the United Arab Emirates signed an agreement to purchase the THAAD system.
In 2015 and 2016, the UAE trained the first two cohorts of military personnel for the THAAD units at Fort Bliss.
On January 17, 2022, the UAE’s THAAD system was used in combat for the first time, intercepting a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis.
Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) is a missile defense system capable of intercepting ballistic targets outside the atmosphere.
The THAAD system uses a hit-to-kill interception concept, meaning it destroys the target using only the kinetic energy of the missile, without an explosive warhead.
The THAAD interceptor is a single-stage, solid-fuel missile, with its rocket motor developed by Pratt & Whitney.
The missile is equipped with an infrared seeker that operates in the mid- and long-wave infrared bands.
The system uses command-inertial guidance. The interceptor can engage targets traveling at speeds of 3.5–4.8 km/s.
The system’s radar can detect targets at distances of up to 1,000 kilometers.

Nigel Farage wins UK by-election as satirical candidate claims 'moral victory'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:52 UTC
17:25:52 KST

Hard-right British politician Nigel Farage reclaimed his seat in a by-election, according to the final tally on Friday, though his main rival and joke candidate Count Binface took a larger than expected share of the ballot.
Farage, who triggered the vote by resigning the parliamentary seat he had held since 2024 over an investigation into his finances, swept 63 percent of the ballots in the English constituency of Clacton.
While votes were still being counted, Farage had declared victory.
"The verdict is in and it is a convincing and overwhelming win," he said as supporters chanted his name at an event in Essex that was broadcast on X.
But his main rival, Count Binface, the alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, exceeded expectations by earning 9,455 votes, 27 percent of the total.
Analysts had anticipated a win for Farage but underestimated the appeal of the self-styled "intergalactic space warrior", who campaigns wearing a rubbish bin on his head, forecasting a large share of the vote approaching but not exceeding 20 percent.
The vote had been shunned by Britain's main political parties, including the governing Labour Party, as a stunt by the Reform UK leader, once touted as a potential prime minister, to dodge scrutiny of his dealings.
That gave dozens of fringe candidates including Binface to seize the spotlight.
"The moral victory is already mine," he told AFP at the counting centre early on Friday ahead of the final tally.
Farage did not attend the count, where candidates traditionally gather for the declaration of results, saying Essex Police had warned him that an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" was planned.
Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said election officials had worked with police to ensure the process was "completed safely and securely", adding there was "no reason not to proceed with the count process at this time".
Binface said it had been his "humble duty" to be Farage's opposition, adding he would respect the results.
"If a majority of the voters of Clacton say they would like him to be returned as their MP, that is to be respected," he said.
Turnout reached about 44 percent, down from 59 percent in the 2024 general election but not an unusual rate for a by-election.
A record 33 fringe candidates, including Binface, stood in the vote, with some of the longest ballot papers in the country's history seen being unfolded at the Clacton Leisure Centre, where the count was held.
Farage, whose party had topped national opinion polls for 18 months before falling behind recently, surprised voters with his July 7 resignation amid a probe into his finances.
The investigation by the parliamentary sleaze watchdog is examining allegations he and Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, failed to declare financial gifts. They deny any wrongdoing.
Farage has framed Thursday's vote as "the people of Clacton versus the Establishment", aimed at thwarting the "stitch-up" over his finances.
"The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," he said in a video released before casting his vote.
One Clacton voter, Phil, predicted the vote was "not going to change anything", saying that the parliamentary probe would restart with Farage's re-election.
Political pundits have downplayed the vote's wider significance in a constituency that overwhelmingly backed Brexit a decade ago.
"It will be astonishing if Farage were not to win," political scientist John Curtice told AFP.
But some assessed Farage's election gambit had backfired as his Reform party slips down national polls.
"Farage's plan to turn this by-election into a serious political battle failed," Queen Mary University of London politics professor Stijn van Kessel told AFP, noting the resulting spectacle "makes Farage look rather silly".
Farage netted 46 percent of the vote in the 2024 general election to become an MP on his eighth attempt.
Police probe
The probe into Farage, which paused when he resigned, relates to a five million pound ($6.7 million) donation from the cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne.
Meanwhile, London police have confirmed starting a investigation last year into donations to Reform before the 2024 election.
UK media have reported that probe concerns undeclared financial support from longtime Farage ally and convicted fraudster George Cottrell and his mother.
The controversies have coincided with the drop in Reform polling support and in popularity for Farage, long a divisive figure loved and loathed in largely equal measure.

AK Party and 25 years of remaking Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:39 UTC
17:25:39 KST

We are witnessing the AK Party’s 25th anniversary this week. The party competed in the national elections just about a year after its formation and won its first election.
And now, it has governed Türkiye under single-party governments for almost 24 years, including the eight years since the country transitioned to the presidential system in 2018.
This is a phenomenal track record given Türkiye’s modern political history. But putting it in perspective makes its scale even clearer.
Türkiye spent the decade prior to the AK Party’s rise under a succession of coalition governments from 1991 to 2002.
The longest continuously governing party in Türkiye’s democratic history was the Democratic Party, which held power for a full decade from May 1950 to May 1960.
Nevertheless, despite winning three consecutive elections, the party was overthrown with a military coup in 1960; its leader and Prime Minister Adnan Menderes was executed along with the ministers of foreign affairs and finance.
The party was banned, and its members were persecuted. This was when the military tutelage system took hold in Turkish politics.
This was a system in which the military bureaucracy drew red lines over a very rigid formulation of secularism and over matters related to Türkiye’s foreign-policy alignment.
Elected governments were expected, even dictated, not to cross those lines.
When governments failed to comply, they were toppled by the military, sometimes through direct intervention (the 1960 and 1980 coups) or through harsh ultimatums (the 1971 and 1996 coups).
The fragmented, shaky, and short-lived coalition governments and the military tutelage system reinforced each other. This pattern continued into the AK Party era.
The AK Party also made considerable efforts to erase those lines and avoid being dictated to by the military.
The picture in 2002 was rather bleak in this regard.
The military elites challenged the AK Party’s right to govern and sought to impose their terms, as demonstrated by the 2007 e-memorandum.
Throughout its almost 24-year rule, the AK Party has distinguished itself from its predecessors by not trying to reconcile with the military bureaucracy.
Recep Tayyip Erdogan, during his tenure as party leader, prime minister, and president, has been quite vocal about the idea that whoever wins an election has the right to govern the country without seeking permission from bureaucrats.
From the 2007 ultimatum to the 2016 FETO coup attempt, he never yielded and consistently resisted such pressure.
In the most recent coup attempt in 2016, an assassination squad targeted Erdogan’s residence, many public buildings, including Parliament, were hit by fighter jets, and 253 citizens were killed by fire from FETO terrorists.
Nevertheless, for the first time since 1960, Türkiye has normalised its civil-military relations. From legal reforms to military education, a wide range of institutional reforms has brought the military under democratic oversight.
Rights were restored
As democratic decision-making and implementation became the norm following the military’s withdrawal from domestic politics, two processes of normalisation proceeded hand in hand.
Two of the country’s largest excluded communities—the Kurds and pious Turks—also underwent major changes.
As for the Kurds, the AK Party years lifted restrictions on the Kurdish language and culture through a series of major reforms.
The first private Kurdish-language institutes opened in 2004 across many places, from Batman to Istanbul.
The public broadcasting agency TRT started its own Kurdish TV channel in 2009, which still operates as TRT Kurdi.
The same year, Kurdish-language institutes began operating at Turkish universities.
Looking back today, all of this may seem like a distant past, but it was very recent and met with strong reactions not only from the established bureaucratic class but also from the main opposition parties.
Another normalisation concerned Türkiye’s population.
Women who wear headscarves, and comprise more than half of Türkiye’s women, were barred from accessing education.
Such a ridiculous policy was considered normal at the time, with the backing of the bureaucratic class from the military to the high judiciary.
AK Party’s removal of such bans again faced backlash not only from this bureaucratic class but also from the main opposition parties and many so-called civil society and business circles.
These rights were restored not through broad social consensus but through President Erdogan’s bitter struggle with entrenched power centres in bureaucracy, politics, and business.
His voters wanted him to fight for these rights—and he did.
It was not just the large segments of society, such as Kurds or women wearing headscarves, whose long-denied rights were granted.
The changes extended beyond these larger communities. Smaller communities also found new space, including the opening of the first church to be built in 100 years for Istanbul’s Syriac Christians.
Refugees, too, were welcomed by Erdogan.
While almost every other party was playing the immigration card against him over the presence of some four million Syrian refugees in the country at the time, right before the 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections, Erdogan was clear in his vision.
“We will continue to keep our doors open to those in need. Yesterday, they came from Iraq, Syria and Afghanistan. Today, they are coming from Ukraine. Tomorrow, we do not know where they will come from. But this country will always be a refuge for the oppressed. You can have no doubt about that,” he had said at that time.
By staying committed to his belief, Erdogan managed to turn the tables on so-called liberal, leftist, and even Islamist parties that were using the issue against him.
Economic gains
What also distinguished the AK Party’s years in power was the socio-economic realm.
The party came to power after the devastating 2001 economic crisis.
While Greece’s GDP was 60 percent of Türkiye’s in 2002, Türkiye now has a greater GDP than all eight of its neighbours combined.
However, what made the AK Party years an era of economic transformation was not the cumulative figures themselves.
The years after 2002 are now remembered for numerous large-scale infrastructure projects, from intercontinental bridges and undersea tunnels to dams, airports, hospitals, and social housing.
Istanbul Airport, inaugurated in 2018, is the world's largest airport terminal building under a single roof and Europe’s busiest airport.
The 1915 Canakkale Bridge, inaugurated in 2022, is the world's longest suspension bridge, with a main span of 2023 meters between its towers.
Yusufeli Dam, inaugurated in 2022, is Europe’s tallest concrete arch dam.
The Avrasya Tunnel, inaugurated in 2016, holds the global record as the world's first two-story highway tunnel constructed underneath the seafloor.
The list goes on: the largest, the longest, the tallest. President Erdogan gained a reputation for building dozens of such monuments. But it is not just about making it into the record books for size.
President Erdogan also pushed the limits in terms of reaching the people in the street.
The Housing Development Administration of Türkiye (TOKI) has built and delivered approximately 1.76 million housing units nationwide since 2002.
TOKI has delivered over 455 thousand housing units in the earthquake-affected region alone since the tragic 2023 earthquake.
This is why the AK Party increased its vote share even in the earthquake-affected areas, despite the widespread pain and suffering in the region.
These are the major points that Western pundits overlook when trying to explain the AK Party’s electoral victories, one after another.
Of course, such a long tenure in office creates a substantial incumbent advantage for AK Party candidates, but you need more than that to sustain such an enduring legacy.
Defence industry outputs
Since the defence industry has become another hallmark of the AK Party years, it would be unfair to end this piece without touching on it.
AK Party dramatically changed the country’s self-conception with the skyrocketing defence industry outputs.
While Türkiye was once almost exclusively dependent on defence-product imports, its home-grown products now range from MPT infantry rifles and a broad family of unmanned aerial vehicles to warships and a wide variety of armoured combat and transport vehicles, including the Hurjet advanced jet trainer and light combat aircraft, as well as the T129 Atak attack helicopter.
The industry is now making progress with its indigenously developed Altay tank and fifth-generation Kaan fighter jet.
This defence ecosystem has now placed five Turkish defence companies on the top 100 lists of global defence companies.
While export revenues increase year after year, Türkiye sees this defence industry boom as more than just economic gains and uses it to circumvent relevant sanctions and prohibitions on its own operations.
Further, Türkiye also uses this boom as diplomatic leverage to build new alliances and partnerships.
Overall, what the AK Party has delivered over the past two decades has transformed Türkiye across a number of domains, from energy drilling and refining infrastructure to healthcare services, from the transport network to the defence industry.
Erdogan’s rule has built a much higher state capacity in the country while delivering long-denied rights to the excluded and silenced majority.
The AK Party has faced one test after another and still seems to be by far the favourite in the 2028 elections.
All of this may sound straightforward, but the AK Party has already cemented its reputation as the longest-serving party in Turkish multiparty politics, despite a number of serious contenders.
The party's future will depend on its perseverance in delivering rights and services to younger generations, who have not faced the challenges and hardships of the early years of the AK Party.

Futile Clacton byelection has done Farage no favours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:33 UTC
17:25:33 KST

Dawn had long broken in the Essex town of Clacton-on-Sea when the results for the byelection came in. After a gruelling count, an atmosphere of deep exhaustion had settled over the room. Even the man with a dustbin on his head looked weary.
As it was declared that Nigel Farage had won, as expected, there was no cheering in the room, which had been boycotted by the Reform UK leader and his supporters; instead there was only an overwhelming sense of futility.
Farage forced the byelection at the start of July in an attempt take control of a narrative tide that had turned against him. After the Guardian revealed he had received a £5m personal gift from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, in April 2024, he had been dogged by questions about his financial backing. Other revelations followed and questions mounted.
The parliamentary standards watchdog announced it was opening a formal investigation into gifts received by Farage, and his regular long press conferences abruptly stopped. When he did a very limited number of interviews, Farage, normally performatively affable, was testy and defensive.
He resigned as the MP for the Clacton constituency at the start of July, saying the “people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions”, and billing the fight as a “people versus the establishment” byelection. The establishment, however, chose not to play. All of the major parties declined to field candidates and take part in what they called a “media circus” and “vanity project”.
Instead, Count Binface, the self-declared “entirely independent space warrior” created by the comedian Jon Harvey, stepped into the void. It felt, at times, less like an election campaign and more of a showcase for British humour, the ultimate distillation of the concept of a summer “silly season” of news.
And while the people of Clacton did back Farage again, it was no overwhelming victory. He won 22,239 votes, 63.34% of the vote. Convincing, yes, but significantly short of the 72% won by David Davis in 2008 when he resigned his seat and stood again as a protest over the issue of civil liberties.
With no other mainstream options, the parody candidate Count Binface, was Farage’s nearest competitor, winning 9,455 votes, or one in four of the votes cast. In his “victory speech” posted on X, he noted that this was a 10,000% increase on the 95 votes he managed against Andy Burnham in the Makerfield byelection. “A new dawn has broken, has it not?” he wrote, echoing Tony Blair’s 1997 victory speech. “Literally, because it’s past 6.30 in the morning here in Clacton-on-Sea.”
In the end, Farage was not there for the count. Overnight, Reform UK said police had told him not to attend because of a “credible threat” against him, although Essex police contradicted this claim. A victory press conference was also cancelled.
Labour said the result was “no victory” for Farage, with the party’s chair, Bridget Phillipson, saying the “mountain of sleaze and scandal he and Reform are now engulfed in has grown while he’s been trying to distract the public by fighting a byelection against a bin”. The Liberal Democrats said Farage had come away from the byelection “looking daft”. Farage himself was atypically restrained, writing on X: “The result in Clacton speaks for itself.”
This election reportedly cost Reform UK about £10,000. It cost the taxpayer about £250,000, after the government said it would be illegal for Reform to cover the costs, as the party had offered. It also cost Farage time and energy.
Last summer he dominated the news agenda with a series of press conferences and public appearances. This year he held his first press briefing since May on 3 August, and another a week later. Meanwhile, the Labour leader and prime minister, Andy Burnham, has – unlike his predecessor – refused to cede the battlefield, taking off on a summer tour of his own with a flurry of announcements about “everyday fixes”.
Farage has instead used his social media channels to post videos of his most loyal supporters. He may soon have to call on them again. The parliamentary standards inquiry, which will also look into allegations that Farage was financially supported by the crypto gambler and convicted fraudster George Cottrell, was paused when Farage forced the byelection, but it resumed on Friday morning.
If parliament imposes sanctions for failing to declare the gifts, Farage may be suspended from the House of Commons and potentially face a second byelection. The result and high turnout here may make the main parties wary of that. But they will take heart from polling: after Farage forced the election, support for Reform fell nationally, from just under 27% to about 24%, where it remains. The MP for Clacton’s seat looks safe, but his route to Downing Street is less certain.

Vietnam seizes nearly 1.2 tons of illegal ivory, animal bones shipped from Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:29 UTC
17:25:29 KST

Saadet Gokce
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Vietnamese authorities have seized nearly 1.2 metric tons (2,630 pounds) of illegal elephant ivory and about 80 kilograms (176 pounds) of animal bones hidden inside timber crates shipped from Africa, VietNamNet reported Friday.
The shipment, which arrived from the Republic of Congo in three containers, was intercepted at Quy Nhon Port in central Vietnam, according to Gia Lai Provincial Police.
Authorities began inspecting the cargo, which was declared as nearly 65 cubic meters (2,295 cubic feet) of sawn timber, on Aug. 6 after scanners detected suspicious empty spaces inside 12 reinforced wooden boxes.
Investigators found 221 pieces of elephant ivory weighing 1,193 kg (2,630 lb), along with 79.3 kg (175 lb) of animal bones.
The ivory and bones had been sealed in wax and concealed beneath timber to avoid detection.
Tests showed that the tusks came from elephants, while the bones were from big cats.
Both are protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which regulates international trade in endangered species.
Police launched a criminal investigation and temporarily detained several suspects linked to the importing company.
Officials said the case was one of the largest illegal wildlife trafficking cases uncovered in central Vietnam and the biggest seizure ever recorded at Quy Nhon Port.
The investigation into the suspected smuggling ring is ongoing.

DRC’s Ebola outbreak hits 6th province as death toll tops 2,100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:19 UTC
17:25:19 KST

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has spread to a sixth province after a man died in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province, the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said Thursday.
The man died in Buta, the provincial capital, after traveling there from Isiro in neighboring Haut-Uele province, said Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa CDC.
Jean-Jacques Muyembe, head of Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research, said the man was a motorcycle-taxi driver who sought treatment at several hospitals before his death. Afterward, some of his colleagues attempted to take his body by force, prompting police to intervene and raising concerns that others may have been exposed to the virus, Muyembe said.
The outbreak in eastern Congo is considered the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record and is on pace to surpass the deadliest outbreak in history, which struck West Africa between 2014 and 2016 and killed more than 11,000 people, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments.
More than 2,100 people have died among more than 4,500 reported cases, according to the latest government figures. The death toll has been reached nearly three times faster than during the 2014-16 West Africa outbreak, the deadliest Ebola epidemic on record.
The outbreak is unfolding in some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, with strikes by some unpaid health workers, threats from rebel groups, anger among long-traumatized communities and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.
Bas-Uele is a vast province in northeastern Congo that borders the Central African Republic, where recurring armed violence has forced thousands to flee and seek refuge in the province. Access can be difficult because of poor and poorly connected roads, as well as limited communications networks. There are also frequent population movements related to gold mining and displacement caused by conflict.
As of Thursday, six of Congo’s 26 provinces had been affected. About 90% of all cases and 80% of deaths are concentrated in Ituri province, the WHO said Wednesday.
Mercy Corps, an aid group, warned Thursday that Ebola cases have been reported along a major travel route about 35 kilometers (22 miles) from Congo’s border with South Sudan, expressing concern over the outbreak’s “widening footprint.” No cases have been confirmed in South Sudan so far.
Meanwhile, health workers at the Nizi Treatment Center in Ituri province, one of the areas most affected by the outbreak, went on strike Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the center after they said they had not been paid for three months.
Kaseya on Thursday called on the Congolese government to pay the outstanding salaries.
“We need to pay health workers,” he told reporters. “This is the responsibility of the government, not partners. And they told us that money is available.”
The real scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared May 15, but the WHO now says sequencing showed it began months earlier, in February.
Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are being recorded outside the group of contacts being monitored and that the disease is spreading at an “alarming” rate. Contact tracing helps break chains of transmission by identifying exposed people early and responding quickly if they develop symptoms.
“We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us,” the WHO regional director for Africa, Dr. Mohamed Yakub Janabi, said this week.
On Thursday, Kaseya of Africa CDC said, “The concept of contact tracing in DRC has become useless.”
Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted through bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, as well as through contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.
Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri, the most affected of the five provinces in Congo where cases have been reported.
Two vaccines developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus are now being tested in people for the first time, the WHO said Wednesday.
The WHO also plans to test whether an existing Ebola vaccine could protect people against the virus after studies in animals showed promising results.
Kaseya said Thursday that Africa CDC supports the use of Ervebo, a vaccine authorized against the Zaire Ebola strain, in provinces affected by the Bundibugyo virus. He said some studies show that the available vaccines may provide some cross-protection.
“We are in a gray area,” he said. “And when you are in a gray area, you have to make strong decisions to stop seeing people dying.”

US accuses India of operating ‘shadow network’ to aid China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:25:15 UTC
17:25:15 KST

US accuses India of operating ‘shadow network’ to aid China
A new US report that includes India among the countries allegedly helping China to evade steep American tariffs has added another wrinkle to India-US relations.
The White House report, titled ‘The Great Transshipment Scam’, flagged over 40 US trading partners, including India, for aiding Chinese tariff evasion by operating a “shadow trans-shipment network.”
The concern raised in the report is about the practice of a country facing steep US tariffs sending its goods through a third country that faces lower tariffs – which Washington calls “illegal transshipment.”
The report by Peter Navarro, the top trade adviser to US President Donald Trump and a known India-baiter, said “India’s Pune-Gujarat-Chennai production belt absorbs pumps and compressors… affecting industrial supply chains in Cincinnati, Dayton, and Columbus.”
“A Chinese pump that leaves Pune as Indian is a pump not machined in Cincinnati, Dayton or Columbus,” Navarro told reporters on Thursday.
He categorized the countries in the so-called shadow network into three groups: those where the transshipment risk was “embedded within broad legitimate trade flows,” those that were integrated with China-linked supply chains, and ones with preferential US access that made them “attractive opportunistic targets” for rerouting.
India is included in the first group, along with Canada, the EU, Israel, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, and Taiwan.
New Delhi has not yet responded to the report.
The US has used sweeping sanctions and tariffs as it tries to bend the world to comply with its geopolitical, technological, and economic goals. China exports face an average of 23.2% US tariffs, while India faces 10% tariffs on about 70% of its exports to the US.
India – which faced up to 50% tariffs from the second Trump administration before they were thrown out by a US court earlier this year – has held back on finalizing a trade deal with the US, even as Washington piles on the pressure with additional trade investigations and a new sanctions bill targeting Russia’s top oil buyers that has cleared the US Senate.
Navarro’s report adds another pressure point to the tense dynamic between Washington and New Delhi. “Countries that relabel or reroute tariffed goods to evade U.S. law should face immediate interdiction, penalty tariffs, sanctions, and potential loss of market access,” it warned.
The report gave a wide range for the annual value of the transshipped goods, from $40 billion to $303 billion, based on the methodology and definition used. The Customs and Border Protection agency, it said, is using an AI architecture that fuses “anomaly detection, link analysis, capacity validation, and mirrored-flow verification” to detect such practices.
In 2023, Washington issued a so-called ‘Compliance Note’ to detail how Russia allegedly uses third-party intermediaries and transshipment points to circumvent restrictions and obscure the true identities of Russian end users.

At least a dozen people have reportedly been hospitalised in Croatia after blazes tore into the tourist town of Omis.
Thousands of people have been forced to evacuate across Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Croatia and Greece due to intense wildfires that have torn through villages and woodlands.
The blazes follow successive heatwaves this year that have scorched approximately 500,000 hectares (1.24 million acres) of land across the European Union.

In Croatia, strong winds drove a wildfire into parts of the tourist town of Omis on Friday, enveloping settlements and forest areas while damaging buildings and cars. Authorities said on Friday that they found the remains of one charred body in the burned-out area of the town.
Another 40 people were treated at a nearby hospital in Split, with at least seven in serious condition. In total, some 2,000 people were evacuated from villages near Croatia’s coast.
Croatia’s fire chief, Slavko Tucakovic, described the blaze as “one of the worst in Croatia’s history”.
“It was frightening even to watch. Many houses, cafes, restaurants, cars, and boats that were on dry land were damaged,” he told national radio.
During a visit to the area, Croatia’s Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic stressed the dangers of the fire and praised the efforts of the firefighters.
