Temples to Minoan palaces: Greece is opening 126 ancient sites for free under the August full moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:03:01 UTC
17:03:01 KST

Sites will be open until around midnight, and several will have live concerts, choirs or guided tours built into the programme.
If you’re heading to Greece at the end of August, there’s a nationwide event that should be on your radar.
Each year, the country’s Ministry of Culture unlocks over a hundred archaeological sites, monuments and museums after dark to coincide with the full moon and lets visitors in for free.
This year, it will fall on Friday 28 August. From around 7:30 pm until midnight, visitors can enjoy historical treasures from temples to Minoan palaces under the moonlight, several with live concerts, choirs or guided tours built into the programme.
See Greece’s most famous archaeological sites by moonlight
Of the 126 sites, several are some of the top visited attractions in Greece, so seeing them in a different light is extra special.
One not to miss is Delphi, a sanctuary and town on Mount Parnassus where the ancient world travelled to for the Oracle's word on wars, colonies and marriages. On 28 August, there is free entry to the site up to the Temple of Apollo terrace from 7:30/8 pm to midnight.
In the western Peloponnese of Greece, Ancient Olympia, the birthplace of the Olympic Games, will have free entry to both the site and museum, with guided tours by archaeologists, between 8 pm and midnight.
If you’re headed to Sparta, you can visit the medieval ghost town of Mystras, which will be open from 8 pm to midnight with a musical event.
In Athens, the Acropolis Museum remain open continuously from 9.00 am until midnight. Regular admission fees will apply to the permanent collections; ticket desks and shops will remain open until 11.30 pm.
Visitors will also be able to enjoy free admission to the temporary exhibition Inspiration: Ancient Greek Art in Italy, which runs until 30 August.
The exhibition brings together 38 significant works in ceramic, bronze and marble from museums across Italy, many of which have left their home collections for the first time.
A guided tour of the temporary exhibition, led by a museum archaeologist, will also take place at 6.00 pm on 28 August. Advance online booking through the museum’s reservation platform is required.
Lesser-known ancient treasures to have on your radar
There are also dozens of sites often overlooked in favour of the big hitters, which are well worth your time if you’re in the area, according to Yahya Dawood, founder of Bnbstay, a villa rental company across Greece and Cyprus.
He recommends the Nekromanteion of Acheron, in Epirus, an ancient sanctuary above the Acheron valley, believed by ancient visitors to be an entrance to the underworld where pilgrims consulted the spirits of the dead (free entry, 7.30/8 pm to midnight).
"Everything about this site was built around darkness and ritual, so visiting it after dark under a full moon isn't a gimmicky experience - it's actually one much closer to how it was meant to be experienced than a midday visit ever could be," he says.
Dodona in northwestern Epirus is considered to be Greece's oldest oracle site – older than Delphi – and was built around a sacred oak believed to speak for Zeus. You can visit for free between 8 pm and midnight.
On the island of Crete, Malia, a Minoan palace complex on the north coast, will open between 7.30/8 pm with a musical event featuring Greek singer Manolis Mitsias and a full choir.
Gortyna, also on Crete, will have free entry and a musical evening. The site is home to the Gortyn Code, the longest surviving ancient Greek inscription – 600 lines of 5th-century BCE civil law carved directly into stone.
Nafpaktos Castle is a Venetian castle overlooking the Gulf of Corinth from above the harbour town of Nafpaktos in Western Greece. "It's the water that will really make this one special, because you'll get the moon reflecting off the gulf as well as lighting the castle itself,” Dawood says.
For opera lovers, Dawood highlights the Sanctuary of Ammon Zeus in the village of Chalkidiki. The coastal sanctuary on the Kassandra peninsula is hosting a full staged opera performance of Orpheus and Eurydice this year.
The full list of sites can be found on the Ministry of Culture’s website.

NASA shows Crimea as Russian on a map during its eclipse broadcast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:01:47 UTC
17:01:47 KST

On the evening of 12 August 2026, NASA displayed a map on which Crimea was marked as Russian. It happened during the live broadcast of a total solar eclipse: on the graphic, the peninsula was separated from mainland Ukraine by a border line and presented as part of Russia.
Crimea is a Ukrainian region that Russia occupied after its illegal annexation in 2014. Ukraine and the overwhelming majority of the world's states do not recognize that annexation, and no cartographic error changes the peninsula's status under international law. Each uncorrected map treats as ordinary what international law still calls an illegal occupation.
What happened during the broadcast
The US agency streamed the total eclipse, whose path crossed Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, live to a global audience. The error appeared on one of the visibility maps NASA showed during the broadcast: on it, Russia's border was drawn along the land boundary between mainland Ukraine and the peninsula, creating the impression that Crimea belongs to Russia.
Not the only case
In December 2024, FIFA eventually apologized for a map it displayed during the qualifying draw for the 2026 World Cup that left occupied Crimea outside Ukraine's borders. The graphic was meant to show pairs of teams that cannot be drawn against each other for geopolitical reasons, among them Spain and Gibraltar, Kosovo and Serbia, and Ukraine and Belarus. It marked out Ukraine but drew the country without the peninsula. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi objected, Kyiv called the omission an unacceptable error, and football's world governing body pulled the image.
On 24 September 2024, the British broadcaster Sky News published an investigation into a scheme for supplying sanctioned goods to Russia through third countries, Georgia among them. The report was accompanied by three maps of vehicle-transport routes into Russia, on each of which Crimea was marked as Russian territory, Detector Media reports. The maps have since been edited, and Crimea is now marked as part of Ukraine.
The Polish broadcaster TVN showed a map of Ukraine on which occupied Crimea was marked in a separate color during the entertainment show The Floor. The episode aired on Polish television, and the broadcaster published its video on its website in 2025.
Behind Putin's sacred Crimea stood Sevastopol's airfields
Explaining the annexation, Putin spoke not of the military but of sacred things. In his December 2014 address to the Federal Assembly, he called Crimea a place of "enormous civilizational and sacral significance," comparing the peninsula to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Europe rejected that mythology: just ten days after the sham referendum, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 68/262 by a vote of 100 to 11 and declared the annexation illegal.
But behind Moscow's "spiritual" rhetoric lay a different purpose for Crimea. Sevastopol, its airfields, and its logistics turned the peninsula into a springboard for the 2022 invasion, and it is largely for this reason that Ukraine's forces are now focused on striking Crimea. Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces on 10 August said that the strikes are the first phase of a campaign meant to render the peninsula unusable for Russian troops.
"Crimea is one of the key conceptual pillars on the path to ending the war," Madyar told the Associated Press.

‘They do look majestic’: tears and pride as first white storks set free in Cornwall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:00:21 UTC
17:00:21 KST

They took a little coaxing at first – after all, they had got used to a safe, comfortable aviary tucked away in woodland on the edge of Bodmin Moor. But after a few minutes, the birds stepped out into freedom and the bolder ones were soon soaring into the blue, the first white storks to be released into the wilds of Cornwall.
Yan Swiderski, the founder of the Cornwall Stork Project, had tears in his eyes. “I do feel a bit emotional,” he said. He sounded a little like a proud father wanting to play down the achievements of his offspring – and failing. “They’re a little bit clumsy at the moment. They aren’t used to flying free … but they do look majestic, don’t they?”
Twenty-one white storks, most of whom hatched on the moor this year, were released on Thursday. They will probably spend a couple of months in Cornwall getting used to freedom before heading south for the winter, perhaps to southern Spain or Morocco.
If all goes well, they will return in a few years’ time to the area where they hatched and produce their own young. “That will be so exciting,” Swiderski said.
The project is based at Hamatethy farm, which produces organic beef and pork but also runs rewilding schemes. Its stork project began in 2021 and it now has five pairs of adults that were either rescued or bred in captivity.
Swiderski, a fund manager turned farmer, said it was not possible simply to release any old white stork into a landscape as it would try to return to the place where it was born.
“The way to do it is to set up breeding aviaries. You can then release the chicks that are born in those aviaries. They’re like swallows, they have a very strong homing instinct, so they will migrate in the autumn, then hopefully come back and nest pretty much where they came from.”
The project follows the model established at the Knepp estate in West Sussex, which has been operating since 2016 and has successfully reintroduced storks. It is possible the Bodmin storks will team up with the Knepp ones to fly away for winter.
Natural England, the government’s adviser for the natural environment in England, does not sound very enthusiastic about white stork releases, though it says they are not banned. It argues that neither white nor black storks were ever native breeding birds in England.
It said there was one breeding record of the white stork in Scotland in 1416 and records of imports of storks from Calais in the 16th century.
While recognising the value of white storks as a visible and charismatic species in engaging people, Natural England said releases of white storks “are not a priority for us”.
Swiderski said: “To head off any controversy about native versus non-native, I think the important point here is that with climate change, the European natural range of birds is moving northward. We can point to the European bee-eater, the glossy ibis, the pallid harrier.”
Swiderski was distracted as one of the storks came in low over the trees. “I don’t think I’ll get tired of the sight of them – they’re so brilliant,” he said.
There was a tense moment when a crow appeared to be alarmed at the sight of a stork in its airspace and swooped in close, but nothing came of the confrontation.
Swiderski said upland Cornwall was a decent habitat for white storks. “Bodmin Moor is good in the sense that you’re not in the middle of a chemical landscape. They just need healthy soils, earthworms and insects and a bit of wetland here and there,” he said.
“People sometimes ask me what the ecological function of a white stork is and my answer is always that they engage humans with nature. If you can interest people in birds like storks – what they eat, where they come from, where they go – you can have all those conversations about healthy soils, the importance of organic farming for insects, the importance of not overgrazing for small mammal populations, thriving wetlands. And that is worth a lot.”

‘We will miss glacier meltwater,’ warns Swiss scientist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

‘We will miss glacier meltwater,’ warns Swiss scientist
Today's droughts are being intensified by a warmer climate. Rising temperatures draw more moisture from the soil, making dry spells more severe than in the past, says Swiss climatologist Erich Fischer. The disappearance of glacier meltwater will only deepen future droughts.
Erich Fischer is a climatologist at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich. He researches extreme weather events and develops worst-case climate scenarios to help society, policymakers and businesses prepare for the future. He is also a lead author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) reports.
SRF News: Climate scientists and the IPCC have been criticised for not warning strongly enough about the risks of climate change.
Erich Fischer: We hear that quite often now. A journalist recently asked a French colleague who has worked in climate communication for 20 years: ‘Why didn’t you tell us how serious the situation would become?’ Yet ten years ago, we were often accused of being alarmist. When you look at the images we’re seeing today, reality itself is alarming.
SRF News: Why hasn’t the message got through?
E.F.: The challenge is translating scientific figures into something people can feel. If we say there are now three times as many tropical nights, many people struggle to grasp what that means in practice – it can still be over 30°C at ten o’clock at night.
More
Drought causes Swiss water levels to fall to record lows
SRF News: The current drought is being compared to the drought of 1540 [an unprecedented 11-month megadrought]. Is that a fair comparison?
E.F.: Although this dry spell has not lasted nearly as long, the context is different. We are living in a warmer climate, and warmer atmosphere is effectively thirstier. Air that is 3°C warmer can draw up to 20% more moisture from the soil. So even with the same rainfall deficit, the situation is worse today.
SRF News: Will conditions get worse?
E.F.: Yes. In the future, we will also miss the meltwater supplied by glaciers. For now, it still helps sustain Alpine rivers. Once the glaciers are gone, this compensating factor will be lost.
More
Why melting glaciers affect us all
SRF News: For the next IPCC report, you are studying climate tipping points, including changes to the Gulf Stream. Tell us more about this.
E.F.: We know from Earth’s history that tipping points exist. The key question is whether they could be triggered in the near future. The Gulf Stream is partly driven by a circulation system in the North Atlantic that relies on dense, salty water sinking. Large amounts of meltwater could reduce salinity and weaken that mechanism. We are investigating such possibilities through “what-if” scenarios.
More
Scientists sound alarm over climate ‘tipping points’ ahead of COP30
SRF News: What could happen?
E.F.: One worst-case scenario is a much drier Europe in summer, combined with significantly colder winters, especially in Northern Europe. Climate models indicate winter temperatures could be between 1°C and 10°C lower. Such changes would dramatically increase seasonal contrasts and create major challenges for society.
SRF News: Would the effects be limited to Europe?
E.F.: No, the consequences would be global. One of our biggest concerns is that monsoon systems would also be severely affected. Two to three billion people depend on these systems. The heat that no longer reaches us would have an impact elsewhere.
Erich Fischer is Professor of Climate Science at the federal technology institute ETH Zurich. He completed his doctorate in 2007 at ETH’s Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science. He subsequently worked as a postdoctoral researcher at the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado, and as a visiting researcher at the University of Reading in the UK before returning to ETH Zurich.

Ukrainian drones struck Russia's Ust-Luga port overnight on 14 August, sparking a fire at the Baltic Sea terminal — the sixth attack on the facility since March, according to Russian and Ukrainian reporting.
Leningrad Oblast Governor Alexander Drozdenko said air defenses shot down 51 drones over the region and that "damage was recorded" at the port, with a fire breaking out and firefighters responding. By morning he raised the regional tally to 54 drones destroyed. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin separately claimed 10 drones downed approaching the Russian capital overnight, with no casualties reported in either city. Drozdenko did not specify which facility inside the sprawling port complex was hit or the scale of the damage.
Ust-Luga is Russia's largest Baltic Sea port and, as of January 2026, handled nearly half — 47.4% — of the Baltic basin's total cargo turnover, according to industry data cited by Censor.NET. Its oil terminals ship crude and refined products, including naphtha, fuel oil, and jet fuel, and serve as the endpoint of the Baltic Pipeline System-II.
Sixth strike since March
Ukrainian forces have hit Ust-Luga repeatedly through 2026. The first major strike came overnight on 24–25 March, when long-range drones hit the NOVATEK gas condensate complex; Euromaidan Press reported the SBU and Special Operations Forces both claimed the operation. Follow-up strikes hit the port again on 27 and 29 March, and a fourth wave on 31 March damaged a mazut storage tank and two NOVATEK fuel tanks, according to Euromaidan Press's own coverage. A fifth strike reached the wider St. Petersburg port area on 3–4 July.
Drone strikes on Ust-Luga forced the terminal to cut oil-export operations by roughly half in September, Reuters reported at the time, dropping throughput to about 350,000 barrels per day after Ukraine also struck the Unecha pumping station that feeds the port.
Wednesday's strike came two days after Ukrainian drones hit Russia's Sheskharis terminal at Novorossiysk on the Black Sea — the country's largest oil-export hub after Primorsk and Ust-Luga — and follows a late-July strike on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal, also on the Black Sea. Combined, Ust-Luga and Primorsk normally move about 40% of Russia's seaborne oil exports, according to Reuters figures cited by The Moscow Times.

Ukraine debuts new drone interceptor for city defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:55:31 UTC
16:55:31 KST

- Ukrainska Bavovna's Last Shadow T200 interceptor extended its tested range to 122 km during recent combat trials, up from a stated 70 km.
- The drone reaches 300 km/h and a 5 km ceiling, and is built to intercept Shahed, Geran, Gerbera and Molniya threats.
Ukrainian company Ukrainska Bavovna has pushed the tested range of its new interceptor drone, the Last Shadow T200, to 122 km (76 miles) during recent combat trials, well beyond the 70 km (43 miles) it originally claimed, Militarnyi reported after the company presented the aircraft at an event hosted by the Technological Forces of Ukraine association.
The Last Shadow T200 is built to defend cities and operate along the front line, intercepting threats including Shahed and Geran attack drones, along with Gerbera decoys and Molniya drones, company representatives told Militarnyi.
The aircraft has a stated top speed of 300 km/h (186 mph) and a practical ceiling of 5 km (16,400 ft). Endurance runs about one hour at cruising speed and roughly 40 minutes at higher speeds. During the recent trial, the drone covered the extended 122 km distance while maintaining a stable video link, according to the company.
The airframe and its warhead are both codified with Ukraine’s defense ministry, and work on the aircraft began last year. The warhead’s initiation board is configurable to operator needs and fires on a pulse-width modulation signal when engaging aerial targets.
“It has a very good power margin. About 7 kg of thrust. In practice, much less is used. So the motor and propeller could actually pull two such aircraft. It reaches 35 m/s (115 ft/s), that’s a very good indicator,” a representative of Ukrainska Bavovna told Militarnyi.
The design includes a camera that lowers and raises to improve target search, along with a system that switches video channels and frequency bands to counter Shtora, a Russian video-spoofing system built to disrupt drone video feeds.
The airframe is currently produced by 3D printing, but the manufacturer plans to shift to casting within a few months to increase durability and allow the aircraft to be reused after multiple landings. Developers are also integrating an automatic terminal-guidance module that would let a pilot lock onto a target with a toggle switch, handing off the final engagement to the aircraft.
Ukrainska Bavovna says it maximizes localization of its component base inside Ukraine and, as an integrator, offers joint research and development, testing, and maintenance, repair and overhaul services to foreign partners.
To train operators, the company has partnered with the Dovzhyk pilot school, where more than 70 veteran instructors train crews to fly various drone types, including interceptors.

The hidden politics of time: How clocks, calendars and time zones came to be
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:53:02 UTC
16:53:02 KST

The hidden politics of time: How clocks, calendars and time zones came to be
NEW YORK (AP) — It flies. It heals all wounds. It can be of the essence, and it can be money. We thrill in the best of it, lament the worst. We’re warned not to waste it, since we can’t turn it back — even as we try to make up for when it’s lost.
And probably more than anything when it comes to time, most of us try to manage it — in our everyday lives and on a global scale, from the biology of our circadian rhythms to what constitutes a work day. Clocks. Calendars. Pendulums. Hourglasses. Sundials. Time zones.
For something that’s been a pretty universal impulse to mark the shift of light and dark, the movement of the stars and the rhythms of the tides, the cycles of summer heat and winter cold, one might assume there’s been a universal way of measuring time. That assumption would be wrong.
Take the shifting of the clock twice a year in most of the United States, once forward and then back again, a system that “moves” the time to let people enjoy daylight hours later into the evening.
While people love the light, a lot of them loathe having to make the change. So much so that the House of Representatives last month overwhelmingly passed legislation calling for the shift to become permanent year-round. Its prospects for passage in the Senate aren’t high, and when the country tried it in the 1970s it was wildly unpopular and short-lived. But it continues to be brought up, an indication that the way we keep the clock counts.
The methods different peoples and communities have used to track their lives haven’t existed in a vacuum. They’ve been impacted by culture, by religion, by economics and technology, by the governing principles both within nations and among them.
Turns out, like pretty much anything where people are involved, there’s a politics to time.
Measurements of time are made up, but they matter
“Every measurement of time is arbitrary,” says Elizabeth Cohen, a political science professor at Boston University who has written about how we chronicle time and how it impacts the way people relate to each other. “Every deadline could have been a fraction of a second or a large increment of time different than it was,” she says. “None of it is natural.”
Take calendars. We use them to give a structure to our lives, but the spectrum of what that has looked like is vast through human existence. Some followed the sun, others the moon, and others still a combination of both. Maybe all the months were the same length, maybe they weren’t. What we call a seven-day week might have had four, or six, or some other number of days in other timekeeping systems.
Even today, when the main calendar in use globally is what we know as the Gregorian calendar, with its 12 months and leap years, other calendars are still consulted for religious or cultural purposes in places from Israel to Thailand. And daylight saving time? With its connection to our perceptions of what hours of light become available to us, it reflects “a desire for natural time,” says Michael O’Malley, professor of history at George Mason University.
People “are outside longer, so they feel it as a connection to nature,” he says. “But it only makes sense in a society that’s completely hypnotized by clocks so you think the clock is time.”
The culture of the clock is evolving
It’s not just about the how. When we think about how culture evolved around time, there’s also the why.
For most of human history, there were ties to the rhythms of the natural world: the phases of the moon, the rising and setting of the sun, the ebb and flow of the tides. And in agricultural societies, the importance of when to plant and when to harvest.
Tracking the sun’s journey across the sky was a local endeavor. While the idea of a day broken down into 24 equal segments was important to groups like astronomers or seafarers, daily life was broken into “systems that tended to expand and contract based on the time of year and the location,” says Kevin Birth, a professor of anthropology at Queens College.
“But since people weren’t really traveling back and forth with any great rapidity back,” he says, “then it really didn’t matter.”
Industrialization — in the form of the Industrial Revolution that started in 18th-century England and spread — pushed people to shift notions of time. No longer was it about the sun’s cycle or the turn of the seasons. Industrial production meant schedules — people paying attention to the clock because they were due for specific shifts.
“It was one of the goals of industrialization to instill in people this regular, unvarying sense of time,” O’Malley says.
Contrast that to a preindustrial farmer, he says. “You could have an ethic of hard work, but that work is not going to be governed by a clock. It’s typically going to be governed by natural cues. The clock establishes this external authority that’s not you.”
In the United States, by the mid-1800s, another issue arose: time zones. There were more than 40 based around cities, which O’Malley says forced railroad companies to switch dynamically as trains traveled.
Worried that other entities would standardize the zones and disrupt their businesses, the companies acted. “The American Railway Association got all the American railroads to agree that on Nov. 18, 1883, they would declare a four-zone system in effect in America,” O’Malley says. “And they just announced it.”
Time can be a cudgel
It’s hardly the only occasion where the perception of time has involved national or global concerns.
Take the Prime Meridian, the entirely made-up longitude line running from the North Pole to the South Pole, that divides Earth into eastern and western hemispheres and is used as the basis for global timekeeping as well as navigation.
It runs through Greenwich, England, and was selected at an international conference in 1884. Was that because Greenwich was the ideal place? No, Birth says — it simply was established during “a period when the British Empire was one of the dominant empires in the world.”
Time zones themselves “are about politics,” he says, pointing out that they are not divided in a standard format. Countries decide their own, and in the U.S., the individual states can decide if they observe Daylight Saving or not.
A prime example is China, which stretches more than 3,000 miles (5,000 kilometers) across Asia. It has one official time zone for the country, instituted when the Communist Party took power in 1949 as a form of national unity.
The entire country runs officially on Beijing time, but the reality on the ground when the sun rises in eastern China hours before it rises in western China is people adjust with their own local times for daily life, Birth says.
Time can also be a tool used in a society to manage dissent and protest, Cohen says. She pointed to examples like governments instituting curfews or protesters engaging in slowdowns or strikes.
“Time has a lot of power,” she says, “and people are battling over it to try and impose themselves on others or remove the yoke that has been imposed on them.”

A second Taliban official is killed in attack in Afghanistan, as the takeover anniversary nears

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14

16:53:02 KST

A second Taliban official is killed in attack in Afghanistan, as the takeover anniversary nears
KABUL, Afghanistan (AP) — The mayor for Afghanistan’s northeastern Badakhshan province has been killed in an explosion, officials said, the second high-ranking official of the Taliban administration to be the target of deadly attacks in the region in the past two weeks.
Habib Ur Rahman Mansoor was killed in the blast in the provincial capital of Faizabad late on Thursday while he was in his vehicle, the Interior Ministry said, without providing further details on the attack.
A senior official on Friday also confirmed the killing, which comes as the Taliban prepare to mark the fifth anniversary of their sweeping back to power on Aug. 15, 2021, following the withdrawal of U.S. and other NATO forces. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly on the incident.
Two weeks ago, a pair of gunmen shot and killed Zabihullah Amiri, Badakhshan’s director of information and culture, as he headed from a local district to Faizabad. His security guards immediately opened fire on the attackers, killing one and capturing the other, officials said.
There was no information on the motive for the attacks.
Targeted killings of high-ranking Taliban officials have been rare but not unknown since the Taliban seized power.
In December 2024, the country’s refugee minister, Khalil Haqqani, was killed in a suicide bombing in the capital Kabul. Haqqani was the uncle of Interior Minister Sirajuddin Haqqani, who leads a powerful network within the Taliban.
In June 2023, a car bomb in Faizabad killed Badakhshan’s deputy governor, Nisar Ahmad Ahmadi, as well as his driver. A regional affiliate of the Islamic State group, known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province, claimed responsibility for the attack, as well as a suicide bombing that struck a memorial service for the deputy governor days later, killing at least 13 people.
In March 2023, the governor of the northern province of Balkh was killed in a bomb attack on the governor’s office.

France and England battle multiple wildfires as record heat grips Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:53:02 UTC
16:53:02 KST

European countries battle multiple wildfires as record heat grips the continent
PARIS (AP) — Firefighters across Europe struggled against multiple fires Friday as a new wave of record-breaking heat baked a swath of the continent, their task further complicated by exceptionally parched landscapes.
The historic temperatures are linked to human-caused climate change, and are hitting countries more used to long cold seasons and ill-equipped for this sort of heat, with limited air conditioning.
More evacuations in France as fire affects more regions
With France experiencing its driest year ever, a new fire raced through woodlands overnight in the Landes region on the southwest coast. The blaze forced more than 500 people to evacuate their homes in the town of Luglon as hundreds of firefighters deployed to the area, the regional administration said Friday.
It’s one of several fires scorching forests around France this week, including in normally cooler and wetter regions in the north and Brittany. A historic fire devoured forests near Bordeaux last month and pushed a quarter of a million people from their homes.
France also has shut down six nuclear reactors in recent days because of extreme heat and drought — and because a mass of jellyfish washed up outside one power plant on the English Channel coast, utility company EDF said. Large numbers of jellyfish are appearing on many French beaches in connection with unusually warm sea temperatures.
In a statement, the company said the shutdowns had minimal impact on France’s electricity production. It said extreme weather poses no safety risks to the reactors themselves.
UK wildfires come as London records its hottest day of the year
In the central English town of Stourbridge, where a huge blaze started Thursday, TV footage showed the fires consuming houses, with many left without roofs as flames burned inside the charred walls. About 20 to 30 homes were completely destroyed, Stourbridge lawmaker Cat Eccles told the BBC.
A woman who was evacuated from her Stourbridge home said police knocked on her door and urged her to leave immediately.
“They thought the fire was changing directions, and they didn’t know which direction it was going in,” Jane Baxter told BBC Radio. “So, it was literally ‘grab what you need and get out.’”
Simon Tuhill, chief fire officer of West Midlands Fire Service, said an investigation will be launched but the fire was believed to have started in the grassland before spreading to homes nearby.
Nineteen people and six firefighters were hospitalized for smoke inhalation and other injuries from multiple wildfires in the West Midlands region. In nearby Stoke-on-Trent, a 23-year-old man and a 24-year-old woman were arrested Friday on suspicion of arson over a large grass fire that spread quickly.
The Met Office, the official weather agency, said 38.1C (100.6 F) was recorded in west London on Thursday, marking the hottest day of the year. While temperatures cooled slightly on Friday, many parts of the country have seen little to no rain for weeks. This July has been the driest in England and Wales since records began in 1836.
Spain moves kings’ remains to avoid fire
Spanish authorities on Thursday night transferred the remains of three 11th Century kings from a monastery in the northeastern Aragón region near an active wildfire.
The remains were taken to a museum about 80 kilometers (50 miles) south of the 10th-century San Juan de la Peña monastery, which remained unharmed Friday, according to regional authorities.
Paintings, liturgical objects and the clothes of a notable 18th-century Spanish count were among the other items removed from the monastery.
The wildfire was not yet contained midday Friday with some 800 residents evacuated. Temperatures were expected to cool slightly Saturday.
A separate, much larger wildfire in southern Spain has burned more than 300 square kilometers (120 square miles) in the province of Huelva, also forcing evacuations.
Firefighters battle forest fire in Germany
All 1,800 residents of the village of Gey in western Germany were evacuated after a wildfire with shifting winds in the nearby Hürtgen forest threatened to reach their homes. Nearly 300 hectares (1.16 square miles) of forest were ablaze on Friday morning, local authorities said.
Unexploded ordnance from World War II in the forest hampered firefighting efforts, German news agency dpa reported.
The fire advanced to within 300 meters (1,000 feet) of Gey, which sits on the edge of the forest near the Belgian border. The cause of the blaze remains unknown.
Germany has set a new record for heat-related deaths so far this year, surpassing the 2018 level for the entire year, the Robert Koch Institute said Thursday. An estimated 12,500 people died from heat-related causes between Jan. 1 and Aug. 2.
Fire in Croatia leaves 1 dead, 14 hospitalized
In Croatia, one person was killed and 14 people were hospitalized, of whom seven remained in life-threatening condition early Friday, from a fire that raged overnight by the coastal town of Omis and forced more than 1,000 people to evacuate their homes. The person’s body was found as police combed through the burned-out area.
The fire erupted late Thursday in an Omis suburb and quickly spread because of strong wind. The regional maritime authorities said 194 people, including children, were plucked from the sea and from various boats as they tried to flee the fire.
Firefighters put out the blaze by Friday morning as other crews in planes headed further south toward the Peljesac peninsula, where another wildfire broke out overnight.
Firefighters keep Albania’s largest wildfire from spreading to homes
Albania has been battling dozens of wildfires in recent weeks, with 11 active fires reported across the country Friday.
The largest fire is in the Gure-Lure area, where the perimeter near residential homes has been brought under control.
Three people have been prosecuted over that fire, which engulfed Lura National Park. They are suspected of failing to take measures to protect the territory from fire, authorities said.
Meanwhile, in northern Greece, more than 300 vacationers and residents were evacuated by sea Thursday after a wildfire swept through a pine forest and threatened seaside homes, authorities said.
Belgium expected to set another heat record
Belgium was expecting to hit its highest temperature of the summer on Friday, climbing to 37 C (98.6 F) in the capital, Brussels.
The mercury was also set to hit 37 C (98.6 F) in the neighboring Netherlands. The country is suffering from severe drought, with water shortages in some areas, but Dutch authorities have held off declaring a water crisis as rain is expected in the coming days.

Hui reported from London. Stefanie Dazio in Berlin; Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland; Zana Cimili in Pristina, Kosovo; Jovana Gec in Belgrade, Serbia; Lorne Cook in Brussels; and Suman Naishadham in Madrid contributed to this report.

France wildfire forces 525 people to flee as Landes forest burns

The fire broke out shortly before 2.30 p.m. on Thursday, 13 August, and was driven by strong, shifting winds, reaching within a few hundred metres of homes in Luglon. By Friday morning, the Landes prefecture said more than 1,100 hectares had burned. No homes had been destroyed, but residents and a nearby campsite were evacuated as a precaution and taken to a reception centre in Sabres. Around 500 firefighters were deployed alongside 40 forest‑fire vehicles, with aircraft including Canadairs, Dash water‑bombers and Air Tractors supporting the operation. Rising humidity overnight slowed the flames, but authorities warned that stronger winds could quickly worsen conditions.
The fire came during a severe heatwave, with temperatures above 40 °C recorded in parts of the Landes. It followed several major fires in south‑western France this summer, including a blaze near Biscarrosse that burned about 3,700 hectares and destroyed around 200 homes and buildings.

From witnesses to property regime: new details on Cristiano and Georgina's wedding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:51:00 UTC
16:51:00 KST

Documents seen by "Jornal de Notícias" show that one of the world’s most high-profile couples chose separation of property, with their five children and four witnesses attending the ceremony.
New information has emerged about the most eagerly awaited wedding of the year. The "Jornal de Notícias" (source in Portuguese) obtained the marriage certificate of Cristiano Ronaldo and Georgina Rodríguez, reporting that the civil ceremony took place at the couple's home in Cascais on Tuesday 11 August, at 1.30 pm.
On site, in addition to their five children,as had initially been revealed by the agency representing the player, there were also four witnesses. They were Miguel Paixão, a friend of the footballer since his youth days at Sporting, Ivana Rodríguez, Georgina's sister, and Jose Rodríguez Sangil and Monica Gonzalez Martinez, a Spanish jeweller and his wife.
The marriage was formalised by Maria Manuel Folhadela de Oliveira, a registrar who travelled from the city of Porto to perform the ceremony.
The document also reveals that the Portuguese footballer and his wife opted for the separation of property regime (source in Portuguese). Under this arrangement, each spouse generally retains as their own the assets they already held before the wedding, as well as those they acquire afterwards.
However, the separation of property regime is not the default model for marriages in Portugal and, to choose it, couples must sign a prenuptial agreement. In Cristiano and Georgina's case, the document shows that this agreement was signed the day before the ceremony, at a notary's office in Lisbon.
Moreover, according to the document seen by "Jornal de Notícias", neither of them adopted the other's surname following the ceremony, and they continue to list the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as their usual place of residence.
The couple, who have been together since 2016 and announced their engagement in August 2025, thus formalised a relationship that had been the subject of speculation for months.
And, contrary to what many had expected, Ronaldo and Georgina chose an intimate ceremony to take this step. In fact, on the previous Saturday, hundreds of people had gathered near Funchal Cathedral in Madeira, where the footballer was born, convinced they would witness the wedding of one of the world's most high-profile couples – which did not happen.
The document now made public by "Jornal de Notícias" does not list Dolores Aveiro, Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, nor the footballer's sisters, Elma and Katia Aveiro, among those present at the celebration.

Moreover, according to the document seen by "Jornal de Notícias", neither of them adopted the other's surname following the ceremony, and they continue to list the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as their usual place of residence.
The couple, who have been together since 2016 and announced their engagement in August 2025, thus formalised a relationship that had been the subject of speculation for months.
And, contrary to what many had expected, Ronaldo and Georgina chose an intimate ceremony to take this step. In fact, on the previous Saturday, hundreds of people had gathered near Funchal Cathedral in Madeira, where the footballer was born, convinced they would witness the wedding of one of the world's most high-profile couples – which did not happen.
The document now made public by "Jornal de Notícias" does not list Dolores Aveiro, Cristiano Ronaldo's mother, nor the footballer's sisters, Elma and Katia Aveiro, among those present at the celebration.

Ukraine’s drones crushed a US armored brigade in a war game in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:50:25 UTC
16:50:25 KST

Ukrainian drone operators overwhelmed US Army troops at a training exercise in Germany this year, the Wall Street Journal reported. The drill showed how far American forces still trail on the cheap front-line drones that dominate Russia's war on Ukraine, despite billions in Pentagon spending.
Drones now decide who moves and who dies along Ukraine's front, and Western armies are scrambling to master a way of fighting Kyiv rewrote under fire—some even copying its tools and procurement wholesale.
The dust gave them away
The exercise, Combined Resolve, ran in April and May. Around 3,500 US personnel, mostly from the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team, tried to seize a position defended by an opposing force reinforced with Ukrainian drone troops of the 412th Regiment of Unmanned Systems Forces, or Nemesis. The Ukrainian operators "eliminated" the attacking armored brigade, US officials briefed on the drill told the Journal.
Heavy vehicles kicked up dust that reconnaissance drones caught at once. Explosive-dropping and first-person-view drones, flown straight into their targets, did the rest. Kills came so fast that US vehicles had to be "re-spawned" as fresh units to keep the drill running, a US official told the Journal.
For first time, NATO ally built its entire military exercises around Ukrainian Azov Brigade lessons
Years of fighting Russia made the difference
Ukrainian crews have fought Russia for nearly four and a half years, repairing and adapting drones on the move, while US operators have never had to fix and arm them under fire, one person present told the Journal. Midway through, the Ukrainians switched sides and coached the Americans on attacking with drones. Eliot Cohen of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said mastering drones is now vital for the US military, and that so far it has not.
Not everyone agrees on why. Some US officers say drones dominate only because the front barely moves, and that maneuver warfare would revive the tank, the Journal noted. Ukraine's former commander-in-chief, Valerii Zaluzhnyi, argues drones have frozen maneuver for now, the reason the eastern front barely shifts.
Not the first Western army to lose
It keeps happening. Ukrainian drone teams beat British, Estonian, and other NATO troops, including Americans, at a Baltic exercise in May 2025, and outdid Swedish-led NATO forces this spring, the Journal reported. Back in 2023, a US officer training Ukrainians realized the lesson ran the other way.
What Washington is doing about it
The Trump administration, despite friction with Kyiv, has been reaching out to Ukraine, the Journal reported. It is testing Ukrainian drones it may buy, and used counter-drone tools proven in this war to defend its troops against Iran's drones. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in May that he was sending more Americans to study drone warfare in Ukraine. By Washington's own reckoning, no US maker can match Ukraine's combat-forged drones.

Ukraine converts Chinese drone into MICH 2000 deep striker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:50:23 UTC
16:50:23 KST

- Ukraine's MICH 2000 deep-strike drone, used exclusively by the SBU's Alfa unit, began as a Chinese civilian airframe purchased in 2023.
- The drone flies up to 2,000 km, carries up to 60 kg of explosives, and has hit targets across occupied Ukraine and Russia.
In early August, Ukrainian forces struck the cargo ship Nadezhda near Novorossiysk with a drone that resembled Iran’s Shahed rather than Ukraine’s familiar Lyutyi or FP-1 long-range attack drone, according to Ukrainian defense outlet Oboronka, whose journalists visited the weapon’s production facility. The drone is called MICH 2000. It began as a Chinese civilian airframe before Ukrainian engineers turned it into a deep-strike weapon used exclusively by the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alfa special operations center.
MICH 2000 can fly up to 2,000 km and carry as much as 60 kg of explosives, and the list of targets it has hit grows weekly, Oboronka reported.
Ukraine had relied on Chinese-sourced drones for deep strikes since 2022, before its own long-range platforms were ready. Military teams converted civilian Mugin-5 PRO aircraft, fitted them with explosives and launched them at Russian rear-area targets. Each cost about $15,000, carried 25 kg of explosives and flew up to 500 km.
The attacks drew media attention, and in summer 2023 China restricted direct export of civilian drones. That December, a team of Ukrainian developers traveled to China to buy ready-made airframes directly from manufacturers and found a factory building dozens of ZTK-150 drones closely resembling the Shahed, distinguished mainly by front canards.
“We were at a very large production facility and saw all the processes. Then we negotiated for several days with Chinese intermediaries until they came up with the idea to sell us the technology so we could make everything ourselves. That’s when they planted the idea that we could really build drones in Ukraine instead of buying and shipping them,” a member of the team told Oboronka.
Ukrainian military leadership welcomed the proposal, but when the team returned ready to buy the technology, the factory’s management refused. The intermediaries who had brokered the talks offered a workaround instead: assembling drones at a site outside China’s export restrictions, plus training Ukrainian pilots on the aircraft.
“We went there to train pilots to fly the Chinese drones. And while training, we photographed everything there was, from the production process to the layout of the shelves and cabinets,” the team told Oboronka.
The team returned with trained pilots and eight Chinese-built drones. Testing began in summer 2024. The first launch covered about 1 km before crashing on a weight-balance error. The second flew for roughly an hour before vibration sheared off its propeller. A third failed after the drone lost signal under electronic warfare, showing the airframe could not fly in contested electromagnetic environments.
“When we started making our own fuselages, we made a lot of mistakes, aerodynamic, structural, that caused us constant problems. For about a month and a half to two months we were crashing planes at the range until our customer told us: ‘You’ve worn out your welcome, it’s time for combat.’ We said we hadn’t started flying properly yet. But Alfa wasn’t interested in that. They needed results,” the company’s owner told Oboronka.
The first combat sortie flew in October 2024. Of three MICH drones launched, one was shot down and two missed their targets by about 10 meters. Alfa judged the result sufficient and approved the drone for production.
The airframe is a flying wing, so the fuselage itself serves as the wing. Finished bodies are weighed as a final check, one of dozens of inspection steps the company uses to verify manufacturing precision.
“Repeatability of the technology matters to me. The lighter the airframe, the more fuel it can carry, and the fewer problems can occur in flight. Any millimeter, or a misplaced comma in the code, can cause an error,” the owner said.
The catalog now includes eight versions for “deep strike” or “middle strike” missions, with a range up to 2,000 km and a warhead between 25 kg and 60 kg. Operators can choose analog, digital or Starlink communications, plus different warheads and guidance options. The Chinese original cost about $50,000; the Ukrainian version starts at $48,000, with final pricing depending on add-ons such as terminal guidance and CRPA antenna channels for jam-resistant navigation.
Over two years the company built a network of dozens of subcontractors producing engines, warheads, fuselages, ignition boards and rocket boosters with their own fuel. CRPA antennas, made by only a handful of manufacturers, remain imported at $20,000 to $25,000 depending on module count. A MICH 2000 without one reaches about 85 percent localization by cost; with the antenna installed, that drops to 55 percent.
“We had an unpleasant incident where third-party boosters burned about a million dollars’ worth of our equipment. After that we were banned from launching on those boosters … We went to the range, launched the first aircraft, and the booster misfired, producing more impulse than it should have. Chemists and engineers worked all night reworking the rockets right there at the range. The next day three drones flew. After that we started scaling up and switching to our own boosters,” the owner told Oboronka.
The company produces about 6,000 drones a year, a fraction of the 100,000 annual drones that Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point has said it aims to build. Unlike Fire Point’s FP-1, fielded across multiple units, MICH 2000 has a single customer.
“We know our drones won’t just fly off somewhere into the swamps. They’ll fly to a specific target, because Alfa is about analytics and results,” the company told Oboronka.
Oboronka identified at least eight videos showing MICH 2000 in flight or striking targets. The company’s head said Alfa has launched thousands of the drones and hit hundreds of targets in occupied Ukrainian territory and inside Russia, including strikes on Moscow, the destruction of a Tu-95MS strategic bomber at the Engels airfield, a Wildberries logistics hub in Ryazan region, an electronic warfare system near Vladimir Putin’s residence in Gelendzhik, and an attack on a Russian Baltic Fleet naval base. Satellite imagery has separately confirmed the Tu-95MS’s rear section was destroyed beyond repair, and Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported an earlier MICH 2000 strike on an optical-mechanical plant in Azov, Russia, on July 4. The largest single strike hit the port of Ust-Luga, where more than 20 MICH drones reached their targets.
“During one attack with guided MICH drones, so many reached the target area that there weren’t enough targets left for them. They ended up chasing a Pantsir air defense system down the road after it had fired off all its ammunition,” the company’s head said, laughing.
The company is developing MICH+, a “middle strike” variant without front canards, carrying a 70 kg warhead with terminal guidance and a range up to 600 km, priced at roughly $40,000. It plans to raise annual output to 10,000 drones and is hiring workers, adding production sites and reinvesting about $1 million a month in research and development.
With Alfa as its only customer, the company says financing further expansion is difficult, and it is exploring joint production with Baltic states under the Build with Ukraine program to draw on European funding.
“Honestly, I don’t want to guess anymore what happens after 10,000. I just want the war to end. But if we need to keep working, we’ll keep working,” the company’s head said.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung favors a four-year, two-term presidential system that would strengthen the National Assembly’s powers, viewing it as the constitutional reform option most likely to win public support, a presidential official said Friday.

“The president's position is that a constitutional reform should be pursued through (bipartisan) consent,” the official said.
The official described that as Lee’s long-standing position on constitutional reform, emphasizing that the president believes parliament, rather than the presidential office, should lead the process.

China on Friday rejected a New Zealand intelligence report that identified Beijing as the only country conducting espionage against New Zealand "at scale," calling the allegations "groundless."
"Its false allegations against China either smear normal exchanges and cooperation as so-called espionage or interference, or are entirely groundless and fabricated out of thin air. We firmly oppose this and will never accept it," the Chinese Embassy in New Zealand said in a statement posted on US social media platform Facebook.
An embassy spokesperson highlighted improvements in bilateral relations in recent years, pointing to increased trade and growing numbers of Chinese tourists and students visiting New Zealand, and said the report's release "at this particular juncture is no coincidence."
"It forms part of a new wave of attacks, slander and vilification against China orchestrated by certain international forces, and may well itself be a product of foreign interference," the spokesperson said.
The New Zealand Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS) report said the country's public and private sectors were being targeted by foreign states and their proxies seeking access to critical assets, including intellectual property, innovative technology and other non-public information.
"There are several states that conduct espionage against New Zealand, but the People's Republic of China (PRC) is the only country we have detected doing it at scale," the report said.
It also alleged that Chinese intelligence officers had targeted current and former New Zealand government officials with access to classified or sensitive information.
Responding to the allegations, the Chinese Embassy spokesperson accused "certain forces, both within and outside New Zealand," of spreading "disinformation" to create tensions between the two countries, undermine public trust and damage bilateral relations.
"Manufacturing distractions in foreign relations will not solve New Zealand's own problems -- it will only prove counterproductive," the spokesperson said, urging "these forces" not to "quench their thirst with poison, and not to lift a rock only to drop it on their own feet."
The spokesperson expressed hope that Wellington would "work in the same direction as China, rather than the opposite."
"Should it fail to do so, the responsibility for any consequences that may arise will not rest with the Chinese side," the spokesperson added.

In Germany, more than 1,800 people were evacuated because of a forest fire; the flames approached a village near the border with Belgium
Kyiv • UNN
German authorities evacuated around 1,800 people from the village of Geich because of a forest fire that approached the border with Belgium. The fire engulfed 25 hectares, and the B399 road was closed.
German authorities ordered the evacuation of around 1,800 people from their homes on the morning of Friday, August 14, after a wildfire in the western region spread toward a village near the border with Belgium. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
Residents of the village of Gei were told to leave their homes immediately and go to an assistance center set up at the primary school in the neighboring village of Strass, municipal officials said in a statement at 4:00 a.m. (02:00 GMT).
They were advised to take only essential belongings, identity documents, and necessary medication.
On Thursday, authorities said that a large-scale emergency response operation had been deployed because of a wildfire that had affected around 25 hectares (62 acres) of nearby woodland.
Firefighters and emergency services battled the blaze, trying to contain its spread, while the B399 road through the area was closed.
According to meteorological services, much of Germany is suffering from dry weather and a high risk of wildfires.
Across the European continent, the fastest-warming region in the world, an exceptionally active wildfire season is continuing. It has been fueled by a wetter winter, which stimulated vegetation growth, followed by heatwaves that dried it out.

UK Reform party leader Nigel Farage defeats main opponent Count Binface to return to parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:46:38 UTC
16:46:38 KST

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage regained his parliamentary seat on Friday in an election he triggered to bolster his position against allegations of financial impropriety, a strategy that was undermined when his main challenger, a comedian dressed as a trash can, won more than a quarter of the vote.
Farage, one of Britain's leading Brexit campaigners, in a highly unusual move, did not turn up at the vote count in the southern English seaside resort of Clacton because he said the police had advised him there was a campaign to disrupt the result. He also canceled a victory speech planned for later on Friday.
"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," Farage told supporters at a party before the result was announced.
The election was triggered after Farage resigned from parliament last month to seek a fresh mandate from voters in what he described as a war against an establishment bent on discrediting him over taking undeclared gifts from donors.
The result, while a victory, underscored the political risks of Farage's gamble. With a parliamentary investigation into his finances set to resume, the vote may have done little to remove a threat he wanted to sideline.
Comedian character wins over one-quarter of votes in UK parliament election
After Britain's main parties pulled out of the race, calling it a self-serving stunt, Farage's main challenger ended up being Count Binface, a figure created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has become a fixture of fun at British elections.
While Farage took 62.8% of the vote, Count Binface, whose policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using a speakerphone on public transport, secured 26.7%.
After enjoying a lengthy lead in the opinion polls, Reform has seen its popularity wane, driven partly by the funding accusations made against Farage, who is under investigation in parliament over whether he should have declared a £5 million gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire investor.
After declaring his decision to trigger the election in Clacton little more than a ploy to distract from those allegations, other British parties pulled out of the race, leaving even some of Farage's strongest supporters questioning whether the veteran politician had been wrong-footed.
Laura Richards-Gray, a politics lecturer at Birkbeck University in London, said the absence of major-party opponents undermined his attempt to turn it into what he called a "people versus the establishment" contest.
"This has backfired, particularly nationally, as Farage lost control of the narrative," she said, adding some voters saw the election as "a waste of time and money."
Farage's position has not been helped by a rise in support for the governing Labour Party.
Since Andy Burnham became prime minister last month, Labour has been enjoying a bounce in ratings, with the party leading Reform 28% to 25%.
Burnham has dominated the airwaves and social media in his first few weeks in office, and while the next national election is expected in three years' time, he appears to be consolidating a left-leaning bloc around Labour.
Reform, on the other hand, is competing for a divided right-wing vote with the Conservative Party and the anti-immigration party Restore Britain gaining in support.
Farage still under investigation for undeclared billionaire gift
Despite winning this vote, the parliamentary watchdog is expected to continue its investigation into his financial declarations once he returns to parliament.
At the heart of the investigation is whether he should have declared the gift from a Thailand-based billionaire before the 2024 national election. Under parliamentary rules, members of parliament must declare any donations received in the year preceding an election within one month of taking office.
Farage has admitted receiving the money, but not declaring it, saying he has done nothing wrong because it was a personal gift.
If the parliamentary authorities, who are investigating, conclude that Farage breached declaration rules, he could face a suspension from parliament, and another vote to retain his seat, where the main parties would probably field candidates.

Israel Katz and the Likud are ‘boom-boom-booming’ politics away – opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:46:32 UTC
16:46:32 KST

If you have not yet seen Defense Minister Israel Katz’s “boom, boom, boom” primaries video, you should.
You are in for a treat – and also a revealing glimpse into just how pitiable Israeli party politics can become, and what even the most senior officials, including those who are supposed to spend their days making decisions of life and death, feel compelled to do.
The video is embarrassing, but the story behind it is even more telling.
Until this week, Katz was preparing to run in the Likud primaries, scheduled for next week. The video included the message that Katz is the first real right-wing defense minister in the country’s history.
Then Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked the party’s governing body to approve a special exemption that would guarantee the defense minister a place on the Likud list without having to compete in the primary.
The justification was that Katz is too busy dealing with Israel’s security challenges to spend his time campaigning.
On its face, the idea sounded reasonable. Israel is still fighting threats on multiple fronts, the IDF is stretched, and the defense establishment is grappling with manpower shortages, procurement needs, and the lessons of nearly three years of war.
A defense minister should probably have better things to do than shake hands with Likud activists.
The problem is that Katz has somehow found plenty of time for exactly that.
PM’s request that Katz be exempt from competing in Likud primaries is ironic
He has developed a reputation over the last two years of attending countless bar mitzvahs, weddings, and assorted celebrations of Likud activists and political power brokers, even when they come at the expense of important national security meetings.
One striking example was last week when Rabbi Yoshiyahu Pinto held an engagement party for his son. Katz reportedly skipped a security cabinet meeting to attend.
Other political and security figures – two additional ministers and the former Mossad chief David Barnea – were there as well.
There are two problems with this.
The first is the obvious one: Why would the defense minister, the man responsible for overseeing the IDF, miss a security cabinet meeting for an engagement party?
The second is a question of ethics. Pinto is not merely a prominent rabbi with political connections; he is a convicted criminal who served time in prison after pleading guilty to attempting to bribe a senior police officer.
Why do senior Israeli ministers feel the need to attend his family celebrations?
The answer says something uncomfortable about the state of Israeli politics. If you want to get ahead, it means that doing your job is not enough.
You need to shake the right hands, attend the right celebrations, and rub shoulders with the right political operators – even when some of them have criminal records. The objective is to remain, as Ariel Sharon once put it, on the political wheel.
We can also be fairly confident that Netanyahu is not rescuing Katz from the primaries simply out of concern that his defense minister is overworked. Katz also does not really have any electoral value. Very few people are going to vote for Likud because of him.
Within parts of the defense establishment, many of his decisions are viewed as deeply political, sometimes seemingly designed as much for the Likud base as for Israel’s security needs.
So why give him a guaranteed slot?
One possible explanation is simple political expediency.
Netanyahu needs Katz happy. The last thing a prime minister heading into an election wants is a disgruntled defense minister turning against him, particularly one who has spent the last two years inside the rooms where some of Israel’s most consequential military decisions were made.
A safe place on the Likud list gives Katz every incentive to remain loyal.
Defense minister is kept happy to keep Netanyahu happy
But this phenomenon is not limited to Likud.
On the other side of the political map, Naftali Bennett is confronting a very different problem. He is experiencing something that usually happens to him much later in an election campaign: his support is falling.
Bennett has a history of beginning campaigns with impressive polling numbers only to finish considerably lower. A few months ago, he appeared to be Netanyahu’s most formidable challenger, polling above 20 seats and at times approaching 25.
Today, he is hovering closer to the low teens.
That is a dangerous place for him to be, particularly since many of those voters are also being courted by other opposition parties.
As his numbers have declined, Bennett has returned to the campaign style that has characterized him in the past: moving aggressively from issue to issue, searching for the subject that might reconnect him with voters.
One day it is the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft; another it is Qatar, which Bennett has said he will declare an enemy state. Then there was a video he made pointing at the holes in the security fence along the Jordanian border.
There is also the cost of living and the monopolies, which he says he will break up.
More recently, he has begun holding what might best be described as political living-room conversations in Likud strongholds, sitting with longtime Netanyahu supporters and trying to explain why they should consider voting for him.
One video from this week was particularly revealing.
Bennett is sitting near the beach in Ashdod speaking with a man who describes himself as a longtime Netanyahu supporter.
The man explains that he cannot support Bennett because he broke his promise before the 2021 election not to form a government with Yair Lapid or with an Arab party, and then did exactly that when he created the so-called change government.
Bennett does not really dispute the accusation. Instead, he adds a part of the story the man apparently does not know.
Before Bennett formed his government, he said, Netanyahu had repeatedly courted Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, in an effort to build a coalition of his own. Netanyahu met Abbas multiple times and even asked Bennett to meet with him.
When it seemed that Netanyahu might succeed in getting Abbas to sit with him, some of Netanyahu’s most loyal media supporters suddenly began speaking about the Arab politician in positive terms.
People who today portray cooperation with an Arab party as almost an act of treason were, at the time, enthusiastic about the possibility.
Only after Netanyahu failed to form a government did Bennett move forward with Lapid, Abbas, and the coalition that eventually replaced him.
What makes the video interesting is not that Bennett is trying to persuade the man sitting across from him. He probably will not. The real target for Bennett is center-right voters who dislike Netanyahu but remain suspicious of Bennett.
The story behind Abbas-Netanyahu fall through
They need to hear that the story they have been told about 2021 is incomplete. Netanyahu did not reject Abbas on principle. He tried to work with him and failed because of a veto by Bezalel Smotrich, who refused to sit with Abbas. 
Bennett tried afterward and succeeded.
This is not just political history. It could become one of the most important questions Israel faces after the October 27 election.
Based on current polling, there is a real possibility that neither political camp will be able to form a government on its own. Netanyahu may not have enough seats with his current right-wing and ultra-Orthodox partners.
The opposition parties – led by figures such as Eisenkot and Bennett – may also fall short with their natural partners.
If that happens, Israel will once again confront the question it has spent years trying not to answer honestly: Is cooperation with an Arab party legitimate?
There are arguments on both sides, and much will depend on which Arab parties are elected, what they stand for, and what kind of coalition they are prepared to support.
But voters deserve to have that debate based on facts.
And that is what connects Bennett’s video to Katz’s “boom, boom, boom” video.
They are very different politicians facing different political challenges, but both stories expose the same problem: Israeli politics has become an arena in which almost everything is filtered through personal survival, partisan loyalty, and carefully constructed narratives.
Even facts.
Netanyahu’s supporters can condemn Bennett for relying on Abbas while ignoring Netanyahu’s own attempt to do so. Bennett can reinvent himself around a different issue every week, hoping that one of them will stop his slide in the polls.
Katz can be too busy with national security to compete in a primary while apparently still finding time for political celebrations.
And everyone carries on as if these contradictions do not exist. This is what Israelis should be thinking about as they prepare to vote.
The election should not just be about who can produce the best video, who can frighten voters most effectively, or who can mobilize the most loyal political base.
It should be about what these politicians actually intend to do with power.
Those questions matter far more than “boom, boom.”
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD Forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His latest book (with Amir Bohbot), While Israel Slept, is a bestseller in the United States.

Delhi high court receives bomb threat via email
NEW DELHI: A day before Independence Day, the Delhi High Court, Terminal 3 of Delhi airport and several government offices in the national capital received bomb threats via email on Friday.Police declared all the threats hoaxes after carrying out searches and security checks at the locations.A police source said the Delhi Cantonment SDM Office received an email at 11.18 am, followed by Terminal 3 of Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGI) at 11:32 am, Jamnagar House at 11.40 am, Saket SDM Office at 11:42 am and Jhandewalan at 11:57 am. The threats were reported to the Fire Control Room.
The threatening email reportedly referred to August 15 and carried the warning, “Lal Qila ta nishana hove ga” (the Red Fort will be targeted). It also claimed that those carrying out the bombing would be dressed in khaki, apparently suggesting the involvement of uniformed personnel in the alleged operation.Teams from the Delhi Police, bomb squad and fire brigade were sent to all five locations, and the threats were declared hoaxes after checks.
"The bomb threat appears to be fake... Everything is under control. Bomb squad and sniffer dogs are scanning the entire premises.
There is no threat as of now," said joint secretary of the Delhi High Court, Advocate Kunal.Security has been heightened across the national capital ahead of Independence Day, with police personnel deployed at strategic points and additional checks being conducted at entry and exit routes.Security teams are also keeping a close watch on public places and areas expected to see increased movement ahead of August 15.

Flight delays not due to strike, IAA confirms

The authority said the congestion was being addressed and that efforts were underway to reduce the delays and restore normal operations as soon as possible.

"We urge these forces and individuals not to quench their thirst with poison, and not to lift a rock only to drop it on their own feet," it said.
The spy agency also warned this week that Beijing's spies were seeking to recruit citizens with access to state secrets on professional networking sites.
It said it had disrupted an attempt by the Chinese military-linked Purple Mountain Observatory to set up Ground Based Space Infrastructure (GBSI) covertly in New Zealand.
The local company involved — which it did not name — was likely not aware that the equipment would be able to collect intelligence of "military value".
"It was not the first time this organisation has attempted to install its own GBSI in New Zealand and is unlikely to be the last," the report warned.

Colombia vows to find all missing quake victims as rescue hopes fade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:45:00 UTC

Colombia vows to find all missing quake victims as rescue hopes fade
- A 7.4-magnitude earthquake devastated Colombia’s western cities, killing 281 people, injuring nearly 4,000, and leaving 379 missing amid massive home destruction.
- Rescue hopes are fading but authorities vow to continue searching, while survivors face displacement and long-term recovery challenges.
- National and international aid efforts are mobilising, despite some political tensions over foreign rescue teams entering Colombia.
AI generated
Cali – Colombia’s disaster relief chief vowed to find the hundreds of people still missing after a massive earthquake, as rescuers dug through rubble early on Aug 14 following the end of a critical life-saving period.
The strongest quake to hit Colombia this century devastated the western cities of Cali and Pereira and destroyed nearly 13,000 homes across the coffee-growing region and along the coast.
The 7.4-magnitude tremor struck on Aug 10, killing 281 people and injuring almost 4,000, President Abelardo de la Espriella told reporters, while 379 others remained missing.
Rescuers had little hope of finding more survivors, who are typically saved in the first 72 hours after an earthquake.
David Tamayo, head of Colombia’s disaster relief agency, acknowledged that the “likelihood of finding survivors is going to diminish”.
“But our commitment is to never stop searching... The order is to not rest until we find all the missing persons,” he said in a video posted by his agency late on Aug 13.
In Cali, many families that lost their homes sought refuge in makeshift camps set up in streets and parks.
Maria del Carmen Rodriguez, 72, lost the apartment she had saved for her entire life.
Cradling a cup of coffee, she gazed at her decimated home from the football pitch where she has bedded down with her husband, 76.
“We wonder what aid we’re entitled to, whether they’re going to relocate us somewhere else, because this is going to last a long time,” she told AFP.
Homes lost
De la Espriella has declared the disaster an “economic emergency” and announced three days of national mourning.
“We will do what is necessary,” the newly appointed leader said, vowing to “emerge again as a country and as a society”.
Javier Alzate, a 79-year-old psychologist, was trying to remove tiles and chunks of debris that were obstructing access to his damaged home in Pereira.
“It’s very distressing. Very sad. You work 40 or 50 years to buy a little house, struggling all that time to get it. I finally got it, and a few days later it’s gone,” Alzate said. “I lost my home and my car.”
The impoverished Choco region on the Pacific coast also suffered immensely, with some of its remote communities yet to be surveyed.
In the neighbouring Valle del Cauca region, Governor Dilian Francisca Toro said officials were conducting a census of damaged and destroyed homes to determine which buildings could still be occupied.
“We have to begin working because people simply cannot bear staying out on the streets any longer,” she said.
“People are telling us: ‘If you give us the materials, we’ll do the work ourselves,’” Toro said, describing plans for community-led reconstruction efforts.
Community support
Many Colombians have mobilised to help, bringing water, food and supplies to affected neighbourhoods, while long lines have formed outside blood donation centres.
Quake victims “are not alone – that is a message we want to convey”, said Laura Mendoza, a 47-year-old volunteer organising donations in the capital Bogota.
“We are here giving what we can so that they at least have the most basic things,” she said.
A musician in Cali took to offering hugs to anyone who needed emotional support.
“We are going through a collective trauma, and I think the best way I could help was by giving away the energy I have and the vitality I have left,” said Andres Solomon, 46.
Colombia was preparing to receive international urban search-and-rescue teams from the United States, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel, the disaster authorities said.
Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Aug 13 that Colombia had refused entry to Mexican rescuers over a claim that they lacked correct certification.
De la Espriella’s administration is facing criticism over allegedly blocking rescue teams from countries with leftist leadership, but it has denied the accusation. AFP
