Diamond buyer jailed for stealing HK$11 million in gems to fund gambling habit
Judge says thefts by ex-Tse Sui Luen Jewellery employee Mui Ka-fai between April 2023 and February 2024 ‘carefully executed and covered up’
A Hong Kong court has sentenced a former jewellery procurement manager to six years and eight months behind bars for stealing HK$11 million (US$1.4 million) worth of diamonds from suppliers to fund his gambling habit.
Mui Ka-fai, 63, pleaded guilty on Monday to three counts of theft for reselling the small diamonds he misappropriated for personal gain while working for Tse Sui Luen Jewellery between April 2023 and February 2024.
Sentencing the defendant on Friday, High Court Judge Andrew Chan Hing-wai said Mui had abused his position and betrayed the trust placed in him by his employer and clients.
“The thefts were carefully executed and covered up,” he said. “But for the imminent termination of his employment, those thefts would not have been discovered instantly.”
The court heard that the defendant, an industry employee with 35 years of experience, stole 2,557 carats worth of diamonds while in a position that left him solely responsible for procuring small diamonds on behalf of the listed company.
Under the jeweller’s agreement with suppliers, diamonds supplied for inspection and examination had to be returned upon the suppliers’ request.
Each exchange was recorded on consignment forms, which Mui was responsible for entering into the company’s computer system. He was also required to keep them in a safe to which he had sole access.

US vows to maintain Iran blockade indefinitely as cease-fire talks stall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

The United States said Thursday it could sustain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely while stepping up economic pressure on Tehran as ceasefire talks stall, global oil supplies tighten and tensions across the region escalate.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. military has the capacity to sustain a naval presence in the region to enforce the blockade, which has already inflicted severe economic damage on Iran.
“The United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that indefinitely because we’ll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we’ll continue to,” Hegseth told reporters during a trip to Panama.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent separately said Thursday that Washington planned to further increase financial pressure on Iran as part of its broader effort to weaken Tehran’s economy.
“Watch this space for more announcements coming next week because we are going to apply measures like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” he said in an interview on Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” program.
With a tentative June deal to end the war in tatters, Iran has sought to exert leverage on Washington by controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
It has attacked some vessels attempting to transit the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas traveled before the war began in February.
Two vessels operated by state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. were attacked while transiting the strait Thursday evening, the UAE state news agency WAM reported. The United Arab Emirates government condemned the incident as an Iranian attack.
U.S. President Donald Trump is under pressure at home to end a war that is deeply unpopular, with high fuel prices weighing on his approval ratings and potentially eroding his party’s control of Congress in November’s midterm elections.
Trump has repeatedly asserted that the U.S. has “total control” over the strait, prompting Iranian denials. Tehran has said it will not allow the waterway to reopen until its conditions are met, including the removal of economic sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to eight vessels Tuesday, compared with a 10-day average of about 12 vessels and 130 to 140 ships before the war.
The U.S. lifted its blockade of Iran’s shipping and ports for a month in mid-June but has since reimposed it, cutting off Tehran’s primary source of hard currency and compounding earlier losses from wartime strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Washington previously said it would lift the blockade once Iran and Oman, which sit on either side of the strait, reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping.
Trump has also repeatedly threatened to escalate military strikes and “hit Iran hard,” although he has so far resisted deploying ground troops, seizing strategic islands or bombing desalination plants. Earlier this week, Trump suggested he would rely on economic means rather than military action.
The U.S. has tightened economic sanctions against Iran and other individuals and entities that it says are helping Tehran procure weapons, but the pressure campaign has failed to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Stress is mounting on the global economy. The International Energy Agency on Wednesday forecast that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day, or about 4%, this year.
Just a month ago, the agency had forecast a decline of 3.7 million barrels per day.
Oil prices settled more than 2% lower Thursday after a week of gains as investors focused on signs of weaker global demand and a sharp increase in U.S. crude inventories.
But reports that Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis had targeted a Saudi Aramco refinery with drones unsettled the market, renewing concerns about a widening regional war.
Global economists have forecast a sharp drop in global growth as a result of the war and potentially a swing into recession in some areas, warning that the impact will grow if the war is not ended soon.
Hegseth declined to comment when asked whether, in retrospect, it was a mistake to declare a ceasefire in April, a move that ended high-tempo bombing of Iran in exchange for peace negotiations that have failed to resolve the conflict.
“I’m never going to comment on that. We’re doing exactly what we need to, to ensure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon,” Hegseth said.

Russia plans to abolish border zones with occupied territories of Ukraine

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:41:00 EEST
16:41:00 KST

Russia plans to abolish border zones with occupied territories of Ukraine
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) is planning to abolish the border zones that operate on the boundaries between Russia's Rostov and Voronezh oblasts and the occupied territories of Ukraine and between annexed Crimea and the occupied part of Kherson Oblast.
Source: Russian news outlet Agentstvo, with reference to draft FSB orders
Details: The FSB has proposed invalidating its previous orders establishing border zones on the territory of Russia's Rostov and Voronezh oblasts and in occupied Crimea.
These orders effectively turned entry to and exit from the occupied territories of Ukraine into a procedure almost identical to crossing a state border.
In its drafts, the FSB explains the changes by the so-called "admission into the Russian Federation" of the occupied territories of Donetsk, Luhansk and Kherson oblasts.
In occupied Crimea, a border zone will remain "within the boundaries of the Black Sea islands belonging to the Russian Federation". The FSB's regional directorate is to determine the locations and times for entry into the zone and to install warning signs.
Background:
- In March 2014, Vladimir Putin annexed Ukrainian Crimea, exploiting the change of power in Kyiv and using a sham referendum conducted on the peninsula in the presence of Russian military personnel as a cover.
- Immediately afterwards, Russia began staging provocations in Luhansk and Donetsk, fuelled the armed conflict in eastern Ukraine and supported it by all means for eight years before launching its open full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
- After 24 February 2022, Russian forces occupied further parts of eastern and southern Ukraine, while they were forced to withdraw from the north.
- On 30 September 2022, Putin signed "treaties on accession to Russia" of the seized Ukrainian territories of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and declared that their residents were henceforth citizens of the Russian Federation.
- According to the "treaties" submitted to Russia's State Duma (lower house of the Russian parliament), the boundaries of the so-called "Donetsk People's Republic" and "Luhansk People's Republic" terror organisations, as well as Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts, which Russia purportedly "incorporated", were to be determined by the borders that existed "on the day of their formation and admission into Russia".

New Zealand central bank maintains loan-to-value ratio settings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
15:40:41 CST
16:40:41 KST

WELLINGTON, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's central bank said Friday that it will maintain current loan-to-value ratio (LVR) restrictions following its annual review of macroprudential policy.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Financial Policy Committee considered house price developments, the risk profile of recent mortgage lending, financial strain among existing borrowers and the resilience of the banking system, the bank said in a statement.
"Housing risks are currently contained," Assistant Governor for Financial Stability Angus McGregor said, noting that national house prices have remained broadly flat in recent years, while mortgage lending growth has been modest and higher-risk lending remains manageable.
Under the current settings, which have been in place since December last year, banks can have up to 25 percent of new lending to owner-occupiers with an LVR above 80 percent. For investors, up to 10 percent of new lending can have an LVR above 70 percent.
Debt-to-income restrictions will also remain in place, complementing the LVR restrictions and acting as a safeguard against the buildup of high-risk lending, particularly during periods of low interest rates and strong housing demand, McGregor was quoted as saying.
The central bank said that it will continue to monitor house prices, mortgage lending and broader financial stability risks. The next review is expected in about 12 months, but could be brought forward if conditions warrant. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Torch Festival flames light up more benefits in SW China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
15:40:41 CST
16:40:41 KST

CHENGDU, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- No one needs an invitation to join the dance around the bonfire, as those watching from the sidelines are drawn into growing circles and hold hands with people beside them.
The participants keep moving to the quickening rhythm of the Dati dance, an iconic traditional communal circle dance of the Yi, an ethnic group in China. Silver ornaments flash in the firelight and pleated skirts swirl as the circles expand.
Such scenes have unfolded across the Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in southwest China's Sichuan Province this summer during the Torch Festival, one of the most important traditional celebrations of the Yi communities.
Many rituals remain much as they were in generations past. Around the 24th day of the sixth lunar month, torches are lit with wishes for good fortune, a good harvest and family well-being. Yet the villages illuminated by the flames have taken on a different life.
Liangshan, home to China's largest Yi community, held 98 Torch Festival events across its 17 counties and county-level cities from July to August this year. During festival periods, hotels in several counties reached full occupancy, while bookings in Xichang, the prefectural capital, reached 92 percent.
For many visitors, however, the bonfires are only the beginning. Increasingly, they are venturing beyond festival venues into villages that were once difficult for outsiders to reach.
Sanhe Village in Zhaojue County is one of them.
In 2019, villager Jihao Yeqiu and his family moved into a new 100-square-meter home. Before targeted poverty alleviation efforts, the family's annual per capita income was around 3,000 yuan (about 442 U.S. dollars). By 2025, it had risen to 26,294 yuan.
The family's changing livelihood reflects broader shifts in the village. Sanhe still grows potatoes and buckwheat and raises Wujin pigs, but villagers are also experimenting with winter peaches and red pears.
New ways of selling and processing farm produce are adding value. Last year, a livestreaming sales team purchased about 30 tonnes of locally grown potatoes at four yuan per kilogram, doubling the price previously offered at the field. Free-range Wujin pigs are also being processed into cured pork for markets further afield.
Tourism has become another part of village life. Sanhe received more than 35,000 visits in 2025, while tourism created 25 local jobs.
Nearby Huopu Village has taken a different route. With the help of agricultural researchers, it began trial planting 10 mu, or about 0.67 hectares, of cold-resistant blueberries in 2019. The plantation has since expanded to 1,000 mu.
At the village's higher elevation, the berries ripen mainly from August to October, avoiding the peak marketing period of many other producing areas. Their harvest season now overlaps with the Torch Festival, creating new possibilities for combining farming with rural tourism.
In May, Sanhe and Huopu were among six villages in Sichuan selected as model villages under the Villages Recognition Initiative of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, which highlights rural heritage, innovation and sustainable livelihoods.
Farther in the prefectural capital of Xichang, tourism has brought more visible changes to the Dashiban Community, where many young residents once left to work elsewhere and houses stood vacant.
Since around 2020, historic buildings have been restored and converted into homestays, restaurants and businesses offering traditional-costume photography and other tourism experiences.
The community benefited from around two million visits in 2025. More than 420 young people have returned home to work or start businesses, while tourism-related income now accounts for more than 70 percent of local household earnings.
Beyond the bonfires, local culture is visible in the clothes woven and worn.
Among the crowds, Yi costume inheritor Wmu Ximei is able to identify where in Liangshan an outfit comes from simply by looking at its headdress, colors and patterns.
The former makeup artist from Meigu County began designing traditional clothing in 2012. Over the following decade, she traveled across Liangshan collecting old garments and studying regional variations in Yi attire.
"Many people simply think the patterns look beautiful at first sight," she said.
For those unfamiliar with Yi culture, she explained, the motifs can easily appear to be little more than geometric decoration. But each carries inherited meanings: the fire-striker pattern symbolizes prosperity, the spiral pattern is associated with mountains, flowing water and the continuation of life, while the meander pattern evokes home and protection.
Wmu Ximei has brought Yi attire and style to a wider audience through collaborations with the Chinese edition of Harper's Bazaar and Britain's Glass magazine. To make traditional clothing more suitable for modern life, she has experimented with fabrics, colors and cuts, while insisting that culturally significant motifs retain their original meaning.
"Tradition can be reinterpreted, but its cultural roots should not be erased," she said.
More than 500 young people have learned traditional styling, embroidery and related skills through her training programs, some of which are held directly in villages. Wmu Ximei hopes young women from the mountains can earn an income from the craft while helping to keep it alive.
The market for Yi embroidery is widening as well. A design competition themed on Liangshan Yi embroidery received more than 730 entries in 2025, including submissions from designers in France, Britain and Brazil.
In Yuexi County, the Yi embroidery industry generated 41.8 million yuan in output value in 2025 and directly created jobs for more than 540 people. A local Yi embroidery brand also made its debut at the China Fashion Week this March.
As the craft travels farther, the festival itself is drawing people from farther away.
In neighboring Yunnan Province, Pakistani student Ali Shahid traveled from Kunming to Shilin Yi Autonomous County because he had long been curious about how the Yi people celebrate the Torch Festival.
By day, he explored Shilin's towering karst formations. At night, he joined crowds gathered around blazing bonfires, where local residents and visitors danced together to traditional Yi music.
"The most unforgettable moment was seeing everyone dancing around the fire," Shahid said. "People of different ethnic groups and even different nationalities were all together. Even as a foreigner, I was warmly welcomed to join."
His experience echoed a scene unfolding hundreds of kilometers away in Liangshan: a circle around a fire, widening as more people step in.
The torches are lit much as they were generations ago. What they illuminate today are villages with more ways to make a living, young people taking traditional crafts into new markets, and old traditions finding new places in everyday life.
Around the fire, there is always room for another hand in the circles. ■

SEOUL, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- The South Korean economy strengthened its recovery amid lingering uncertainties such as geopolitical risks in the Middle East and inflationary pressure, a finance ministry report said Friday.
The Ministry of Finance and Economy said in its monthly report, called Green Book, that the Asian economy recently showed signs of a strengthening recovery, powered by a sharp increase in exports and an improving domestic demand.
The ministry, however, cautioned that burdens on people's livelihood persisted due to inflationary pressure, affected by high oil prices, alongside difficult employment conditions for vulnerable groups amid ongoing uncertainties from the Middle East conflict.
While the global economy maintained moderate growth, uncertainties remained over the Middle East conflict and the U.S. tariff measures, the ministry explained.
Exports jumped 62.8 percent in July from a year earlier on strong demand for semiconductors, computers and ships.
The composite consumer sentiment index added 0.2 points from a month earlier to 106.8 in July, while the composite business sentiment index in all industries gained 0.8 points to 98.5 last month.
Retail sales, which reflect private consumption, grew 2.7 percent in June compared to the previous month.
Consumer prices rose 2.8 percent in July on a yearly basis after going up 3.2 percent in the previous month.
The number of jobs climbed 108,000 in July from a year earlier, faster than the prior month's increase of 63,000. ■

U.S. Army seeks commercial controllers for drones, ground robots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:40:01 UTC
16:40:01 KST

- The U.S. Army is seeking commercial controllers and HMIs for small drones, launched effects and ground robots to integrate with its new C2 architecture.
- Initial white papers are due Aug. 26, 2026, though the call remains open on a continuous, rolling basis.
The U.S. Army has opened a call for commercial vendors of controllers and human-machine interfaces for small drones, launched effects and ground robots, seeking systems that can plug directly into a new Army command-and-control network, according to a solicitation posted Aug. 13, 2026.
The notice was issued by U.S. Army Contracting Command-Redstone Arsenal on behalf of the Capability Program Executive for Aviation. It falls under the Army’s broader Uncrewed Aircraft System Marketplace Commercial Solutions Opening, W58RGZ-26-S-C001, using contracting authority granted under 10 U.S.C. § 3458. The listing carries Product Service Code 1550 for unmanned aircraft and NAICS code 336411 for aircraft manufacturing.
The call does not seek to buy drones, launched effects or ground vehicles themselves. It seeks controllers and human-machine interfaces for Group 1-3 UAS, Launched Effects and Unmanned Ground Vehicles, for a Command and Control Software Development Kit Integration event run by the Army’s Program Manager for Uncrewed Aircraft Systems. Vendors whose systems pass the evaluation will be invited to test their equipment against the Army’s network and receive feedback from soldiers.
The Army’s problem statement says its current portfolio of disparate, stove-piped control systems prevents soldiers from operating multiple robotic and autonomous systems as an integrated team, creating operational gaps an adversary could exploit. The attached Statement of Objectives lists six control capabilities the Army wants from a unified C2 architecture: asymmetric, distributed, intelligent, intermodal, policy-based and resilient control.
Vendors must build to a Modular Open Systems Approach and, where applicable, align to the Future Airborne Capability Environment technical standard, according to the solicitation. The Army is also seeking Government Purpose Rights, at minimum, for data and software tied to external interfaces such as controllers, platforms and the C2 architecture itself, along with commercial license rights broad enough to let government personnel maintain, repair and train on the equipment.
Eligibility requirements are extensive. Offerors must certify that no critical flight components come from covered foreign countries, including China, under Section 848 of the fiscal 2020 defense authorization act, and must be ready to produce a bill of materials to prove it. Companies also need an active System for Award Management registration, a Commercial and Government Entity code, certification through the Defense Logistics Agency’s Joint Certification Program, a current NIST SP 800-171 cybersecurity assessment posted to the Supplier Performance Risk System, and registration in the government’s invoicing system.
Offerors first submit a five-page white paper covering their product, technical maturity and integration plan, formatted to specific Army page-count and font rules. Papers rated Fully Compliant or Partially Compliant can move to a live C2 SDK Integration Event, where the Army will run flight or test-card demonstrations, coordinate spectrum access, and require vendors to sign a software use, distribution and non-disclosure agreement before receiving its C2 software development kit, an example of which the solicitation names as WARHEX. Systems rated Successful are eligible for onboarding to the UAS Marketplace and the government’s C2 software development environment. Systems rated Unsuccessful may continue testing if time remains, or wait for a future event.
Initial submissions are due Aug. 26, 2026, 21 days after the notice posted, to be prioritized for the first evaluation cycle. The call is otherwise open on a continuous, rolling basis, and SAM.gov lists the opportunity as inactive starting Aug. 27, 2031. This call covers only controllers and HMIs. The Army intends to hold C2 SDK Integration events quarterly and plans future calls covering Group 1-3 UAS, launched effects and UGV systems on their own.
The integration effort supports Next Generation Command and Control, the Army’s initiative to replace fragmented, function-specific command systems with a single data architecture across echelons. The Army declared NGC2 ready to scale in July 2026 following trials with the 4th Infantry Division and 25th Infantry Division at Project Convergence-Capstone 6, and it has since selected Anduril Industries to lead the program’s common data layer baseline, working alongside Palantir and Raft on the underlying data-sharing tools.
The UAS Marketplace itself launched March 24, 2026, at Redstone Arsenal as a digital storefront built with Amazon Web Services and the Army Enterprise Cloud Management Agency, intended to let Army units, government partners and allied nations order vetted commercial drone systems.

DM Katz prepares plan to transfer civilian enforcement in the West Bank from the IDF to the Israeli police
The transfer would not give police independent authority to operate in Areas A and B, where they currently require IDF accompaniment.
Defense Minister Israel Katz has instructed the IDF to prepare a plan to transfer responsibility for civilian law enforcement in Israeli communities and among Israeli civilians in the West Bank to the Israel Police.
The move follows a meeting with IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the head of Military Intelligence and other senior commanders.
Under the plan, the police would establish a dedicated force to handle civilian enforcement involving Israeli residents in the West Bank and would receive the necessary authority and funding.
The transfer would not give police independent authority to operate in Areas A and B, where they currently require IDF accompaniment.
Katz said the change would allow the military to focus on its core security missions, particularly combating Palestinian terrorism and protecting Israeli communities and borders. “The IDF’s role is to fight Palestinian terrorism, focus on defending the borders and the communities against threats, and not to chase after youths on the hills,” Katz said.
The directive comes after recent clashes around the Palestinian village of Qusra, where Israeli civilians established illegal outposts on privately owned Palestinian land. The IDF later evacuated the outposts amid protests by Israeli activists.
Katz said the transfer would strengthen law enforcement and governance while allowing the IDF to concentrate on growing security challenges. "This is also a significant step in strengthening governance and the rule of law and order in the territories of Judea and Samaria and the evacuation of the IDF to carry out its main missions."
He also pointed to the expected increase in the Israeli population in the West Bank following government decisions to establish new communities and legalize agricultural farms.

Germany news: Wildfire forces evacuations in western woods

Germany: Vast wildfire forces evacuation in Eifel forest
Published August 14, 2026last updated August 14, 2026
What you need to know
- A wildfire near the Belgian border has forced around 1,800 people to leave their homes
- Authorities say residents will not be able to return to their homes overnight
- Flames burned within 400 meters of one village
- Police have launched an appeal for information on the cause of the blaze
- It is the biggest forest fire in the history of Germany's most-populous state, NRW
Don't let the algorithm hide the news. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google so you'll always see our verified news first.
Pausing our coverage
We're putting this blog on hold for now, but it will reopen over the weekend with the latest developments.
RECAP — Massive wildfire hits Hürtgenwald area, nearby village to stay empty overnight
In case you're just joining us, here's the lowdown on developments in Germany's far west near the Belgian border this Friday.
A large forest fire in the Hürtgenwald forest, not far east of Aachen, forced authorities to clear a nearby village early in the morning.
Various emergency services and the military have rushed to the area to try to contain almost certainly the largest such blaze in the history of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, thought to cover an area of at least 200 hectares.
Authorities said on Friday that around 400 personnel were in service simultaneously across various agencies.
The village of Gey, home to around 2,000 people, will remain evacuated overnight. Five people, four of them rescue workers, have suffered injuries amid the response to the fire.
The state premier has cut short his vacation and expects to arrive on site on Saturday afternoon.
Emergency services anticipate that efforts to contain the fire will last all weekend, and perhaps longer. Hot summer weather and a dry forest floor are not helping the response.
Weather forecasts do point to falling temperatures over the weekend, and even a roughly 50% chance of light rain in the area on Saturday.
Police are investigating the cause and have appealed to the public for information, particularly photos or videos from the area taken around the time the fire began.
Interior Minister Dobrindt calls fire 'shocking,' praises rescuers
Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called the images of Friday's forest fire "shocking" and voiced thanks to local and federal first responders alike for their contributions.
"All emergency services are performing exceptionally in the toughest conditions, to fight the flames, protect people, and limit damages. As well as firefighters, state police and the military, the federal police is in operation with its airborne units and the THW [Germany's federal civil protection agency, made up largely of volunteers, that assists in emergency situations] is helping with logistics and operational coordination," Dobrindt said.
Dobrindt's ministry had similarly listed the efforts by various services in a social media post earlier on Friday.
It also noted that there were "several localized vegetation fires" dotted around the country in various states — North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland and Saxony — on Friday, but said that, with the exception of Hürtgenwald, they were "for the most part under control and have been almost completely extinguished by regional responders."
5 injured amid fire: 4 rescue workers and 1 elderly resident
Local politician Christian Nolten has told the dpa news agency that five people have suffered injuries amid Friday's evacuation and firefighting efforts.
One elderly man suffered a heart complaint during the operations to clear the village of Gey, Nolten said.
And four rescue workers sustained light injuries, such as cuts and circulatory problems, amid their work.
The public gathering point for those affected has been moved further away from the site of the fire, to a special needs school in Düren, for people's safety.
Two initial gathering points closer to the fire have since been closed because of a buildup of smoke and ash in the area.
The next village of Grosshau, to the south of Gey and the heart of the fire, has not yet been evacuated. Düren's Mayor Stephan Cranen said that authorities currently hoped this step would not be necessary, but noted that the situation was still considered fluid and subject to change.
Rescue official tells reporters village of Gey will remain cleared overnight
One of the leading rescue officials in the area, Wilfried Thielen, has told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger (KSTA) newspaper that the village of Gey will remain evacuated overnight.
"The Gey settlement has been evacuated. And for safety reasons, we will not allow residents to return tonight," Thielen told the KSTA.
He said that the situation remained fluid, to such an extent that rescue teams were having to reposition their own facilities.
"We've just had to dismantle our staging area because it, too, is at risk because of the changing weather conditions," he said. "This means we're reorganizing, redeploying our personnel and planning our next steps."
Thielen said that authorities had already planned for personnel deployments on a rough basis through to Monday morning, "and then we may need to reassess the situation and potentially request additional personnel."
What was the Battle of Hürtgen Forest, the reason WWII ordnances are strewn about the area?
Friday's fire is taking place on the site of one of the longest and most costly single battles in the US military's history.
That's why the area is strewn with unexploded munitions from World War II that are at risk of exploding, both aiding the fire's spread and potentially endangering emergency services.
The Battle of Hürtgen Forest, or Schlacht im Hürtgenwald in German, was a three-month push by US forces. They were trying at first to pin down German forces and stop them providing reinforcements in the nearby Battle of Aachen, and then later to push through the forest and advance to the Rur River.
The September-December 1944 battle tried to get through heavy fortifications as part of what the Allies knew as the Siegfried Line, a series of defensive structures that served as one of Nazi Germany's last effective lines of defense as Allied forces tried to move east toward Berlin after the D-Day landings.
Germany's military was already planning its Winter Offensive, which would be known as the Battle of the Bulge, in the same area by this point, and so its troops were given all possible resources for their defensive efforts.
The battle was seen as a comparatively rare Nazi victory in their attempts to stop the Allied advance, with at least 33,000 US casualties, and some estimates ranging considerably higher than that. Germany, with more strains on personnel and supply but also with the defenders' advantage and favorable terrain, suffered an estimated 28,000 casualties.
It's less well remembered than the much larger and more widespread Battle of the Bulge, whose main thrust was located slightly further south but in the same Eifel region. Nevertheless, it was the longest continuous battle on German ground during World War II and the second-longest single battle the US Army has ever fought.
Cologne police launch appeal for information on fire's outbreak
Police in the city of Cologne are investigating the cause of the Hürtgenwald fire and are appealing for help from members of the public who might be able to shed light on how it started.
Police said in a press statement and public appeal that they had set up an online web portal where people could upload information in an "uncomplicated and direct" manner, straight to law enforcement.
"The Cologne Police asks the public for support in the ongoing investigations. Of particular interest are clues and particularly picture or video recordings from the rough time of the start of the fire," police wrote. "Such recordings could deliver important findings and help the investigative work meaningfully."
The appeal provided a link to the site where uploads are possible, and police wrote that "any clue could be meaningful" as they seek to establish the cause of the fire.
Almost all forest fires are ultimately man-made — whether they're caused by accident or oversight or as a more deliberate act of arson.
Even in the driest and hottest summer temperatures, the heat required to trigger a fire among trees is almost never achieved by natural means — with the only plausible all-natural scenario being a lightning strike. The high summer temperatures and dry forest floor, rather than starting the fires, provide conditions suitable to enable and accelerate the spread after it's begun.
State premier Hendrik Wüst breaking off holiday to return
The head of North Rhine-Westphalia's state government is breaking off his vacation to return amid the fire.
Christian Democrat politician Hendrik Wüst wanted to gather first-hand information on the situation, and told German media on Friday that he expected to reach the Düren municipality area by Saturday afternoon.
Earlier on Friday, Wüst had thanked emergency services for their work on site since Thursday afternoon, "many of them without a break," saying "out state stands together!"
Hürtgenwald smoke can be seen, and scented, from Bonn area
The plume of smoke from the Hürtgenwald, some 60 kilometers (around 35 miles) to the west, can be seen from the Rhine River here in Bonn, and particularly the hills on its right bank.
Hikers on the Petersberg summit just to the south of the city had a clear view of the smoke on Friday.
Some residents even confused the smell of smoke for a fire much closer to home.
One woman in the western district of Endenich told local public broadcaster WDR how she had called the fire service, to tell them she had reason to believe a fire had broken out in the nearby woods in Kreuzberg.
"Then the fire department told me, 'no, that really is from the Hürtgenwald. The cloud is passing over Bonn,'" she told the broadcaster. "And a minute later, a warning arrived on the NINA warning app."
NINA (the Notfall-Information und Nachrichten App) is the federal government's emergency information and news app.
State government says fire is likely the biggest in NRW's history
North Rhine-Westphalia's Agriculture Minister Silke Gorissen is visiting the area.
She said the government in Germany's most populous state is now working on the assumption that this was the largest forest fire in the state, at least in decades if not on record.
"We at least are not aware of a forest fire that reached this size," Gorissen said. "It could well be that it really is the biggest since our state was founded, and that shows what we're dealing with here."
She said she was working on the assumption that at least 200 hectares were affected but acknowledged that higher estimates were in play, saying "perhaps we're even knocking on the door of 300."
Gorissen told the dpa news agency that she could already see the smoke as she was approaching the scene.
"It really is a bit apocalyptic," she said. "It's a very imposing sight, a sad sight, seeing the forests in flame," she said.
She praised the emergency responders and the speed with which such a large multi-force response was put together.
Gorissen also appealed to people to avoid the forests in a bid to prevent any more such fires from breaking out, saying "almost all forest fires are man-made."
IN PICTURES — Emergency services respond to Hürtgenwald wildfire
Fire service: 'Under no circumstances' are residents likely to return this evening
A firefighters' spokesman, Peter Berndgen, has told the dpa news agency that he does not expect locals in Gey to be able to return to their homes on Friday. By his estimation, Berndgen said, "under no circumstances" was this likely.
Local politician Ralf Nolten similarly suggested the evacuation could continue, saying "we need to be able to work freely," with clear roads to allow vehicles easy access to the area.
Berndgen said the efforts to extinguish the blaze could take days.
"We have very unfortunate conditions for fighting a forest fire today," he said, calling it a "red flag day" — with high temperatures, high humidity and high winds all fanning the flames.
Berndgen said specialist teams were using machine saws, tanks and other equipment to try to rapidly cut trees and form a 15-meter (49-foot) containment line around the fire, seeking to deny it the fuel it needs to spread.
Where is the Hürtgenwald region of Germany?
Merz thanks emergency services fighting Eifel wildfires
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has voiced thanks to emergency services fighting the wildfires near the Dutch and Belgian borders.
"Wildfires are burning in many parts of the country. I am being continuously updated on developments," Merz wrote in a post on social media. "Where ever it's possible, federal police and the military are providing assistance. I thank all the emergency services for their tireless endeavors, often to the point of exhaustion."
WWII munitions complicate Eifel firefighting
Bundeswehr forces joined in the fight against a forest fire raging in the Eifel on Friday, adding two water transport helicopter to the operation aimed at extinguishing the Hürtgenwald blaze.
Complicating matters are the numerous munitions scattered across the area since the end of the second world war.
In an effort to safely expedite access to the area, the Bundeswehr also deployed two rescue tanks to clear munitions and cut fire roads.
"The terrain is very difficult, and because of the high concentration of ammunition," as local councilman Ralf Nolten (CDU) told Germany's dpa news agency, "we can't send individual firefighters in with firefighting backpacks," said Nolten adding, "We also heard the explosions" that went off overnight.
In the fall and winter of 1944 and 1945, the Hürtgenwald was the scene of heavy fighting between US and Nazi-German troops as US tanks sought to finish their push east into Germany to end the war.
The ferocity and scale of the fighting led US soldiers stuck there waiting for reinforcements and facing entrenched German defenses to dub it "the death factory."

- Secretary of War Pete Hegseth visited U.S. troops training at a jungle warfare course in Panama this week, addressing the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met with U.S. service members training in the jungles of Panama this week, telling them that U.S. Southern Command’s mission has shifted toward defending American and partner-nation sovereignty across the Western Hemisphere, Pentagon News reported.
Hegseth visited the Combined Jungle Training Center-South in Cristobal Colon, on the northern side of the Panama Canal, where instructors run the Jungle Operations Training Course-Panama. Marines assigned to Littoral Combat Force-24 were also at the site as part of Panamax 2026, a multinational exercise hosted by Panama and sponsored by Southcom.
The visit coincided with Hegseth’s address to the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, a security alliance the Trump administration launched in March 2026 to combat transnational drug cartels, curb illegal migration and limit foreign interference in the hemisphere. The coalition is also known as the Shield of the Americas.
“I think this is what … the warrior ethos looks like; it’s what reestablishing it looks like,” Hegseth said. “It happens in training centers like this, with Americans like this, who do really difficult things in really tough places.”
Hegseth said Southcom’s mission has changed substantially in recent months.
“This is a different Southcom; this is a different mission,” he said. “We are focused on military capabilities against real threats who need to be deterred and defeated, and we’re going to give them everything they need to do it, on behalf of the American people.”
Marine Corps Gen. Francis L. Donovan has led Southcom since Feb. 5, 2026, when he assumed command from acting commander Air Force Lt. Gen. Evan Pettus. Donovan succeeded Adm. Alvin Holsey, who retired after less than a year leading the command.
Hegseth described the administration’s approach as an extension of the Monroe Doctrine, the 1823 policy that barred European colonization and interference in the Western Hemisphere. President Theodore Roosevelt expanded the doctrine in 1904 to allow U.S. intervention to protect American interests in Latin America.
“It is a recognition that [designated terrorist organizations] … will not control our hemisphere … and we will not allow foreign malign influence to take over … key terrain like the Panama Canal,” he said.
Colombia joined the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition as its 19th member this week.
“The A3C had formed, but in some ways, it missed part of its core,” Hegseth said. “Colombia is going to be [an] incredible partner. They offered to be a headquarters or a hub for the A3C as the brand-new 19th member. They’ve got … hundreds of thousands of capable members of their military and decades of training with the United States … that mil-to-mil relationship has been long-standing, and that’s why they’re coming to this jungle course soon.”
Hegseth also announced a new motto for the coalition during his remarks: “We do bad things to bad people.”

UK: Nigel Farage beats a trash can in Clacton by-election
August 14, 2026
UK right-wing populist leader Nigel Farage won Friday's by-election in Clacton, regaining the parliamentary seat he resigned a month earlier to trigger the vote.
He took about 63% of the vote, while his main challenger, comedian Jon Harvey running as trash-can-costumed "Count Binface," secured roughly 27% — his best result yet in eight election attempts. The turnout was 44%.
What triggered the Clacton by-election?
Reform UK's Farage called the special election to prove his voter support amid a parliamentary investigation into an undeclared £5 million ($6.75 million, €5.85 million) gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Britain's major parties boycotted the race, calling it a self-serving stunt. This left Farage facing 33 mostly independent and novelty candidates.
Farage skipped the official vote count, saying police warned him of an "organized campaign to disrupt" the result. Essex police disputed reports of a credible threat but said a "proportionate and robust" security operation was in place. He also canceled a planned victory speech.
"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," he told supporters.
What happens next?
The win doesn't resolve Farage's political troubles. The parliamentary standards investigation, paused when he resigned, is expected to resume and could still force him from his seat. Farage says the money was a personal gift he wasn't required to declare.
Last month, a Survation poll put Farage's share of the vote at 73%, a figure he fell short of. It comes as Reform UK's national polling is also slipping behind a resurgent Labour Party under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Who is Count Binface?
Count Binface is the alter ego of Harvey, a British comedian, writer and producer who uses the character to satirize UK politics.
He is a self-styled "intergalactic space warrior" who campaigns wearing a trash bin on his head. While he was expected to receive a large share of the vote, the figure was not expected to exceed 20 percent.
Binface has become somewhat of a serial candidate, challenging prime ministers past and present in line with a long tradition of novelty candidates in UK politics.
With the other parties boycotting the election, he became Farage's default rival with a comical platform vowing to "cut your taxes, and raise everyone else's," build one affordable home and nationalize singer Adele.
"The moral victory is already mine," Harvey, aka Binface, told the AFP news agency at the counting center ahead of the final count.

25 years of glory: How AK Party helped shape modern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:31:27 UTC
16:31:27 KST

As the Justice and Development Party – better known as the AK Party – marks its 25th anniversary on August 14, the spotlight is firmly on its political ideology and social vision, which have influenced and shaped the country over the past quarter century.
Under the leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the party has won every general election it has contested over 25 years.
The AK Party has delivered broad-based economic growth and ensured that its benefits trickle down to the marginal and deprived segments of society – a fact amply reflected by improving human development benchmarks.
Baris Ertem, an analyst and associate professor at Istanbul Technical University, defines the AK Party not as a conventional right-wing, nationalist or purely neo-Ottomanist organisation, as frequently mistaken by the West.
“If we were to define the AK Party in the most concise and precise terms possible, we could describe it as a ‘conservative democratic’ party,” he tells TRT World.
“(Its) politics are fundamentally rooted in conservative values,” he says, adding that no party remaining in power for 25 years can stay unchanged in a dynamic country like Türkiye.
“What undoubtedly distinguishes the AK Party… is its leader,” he says.
Erdogan’s roughly 52 percent support in the last three presidential elections speaks to the “exceptionally strong and genuine bond” between him and his supporters.
“In Türkiye’s history of multiparty politics, no leader has ever been embraced by his electorate to the same extent as Erdogan,” he says.
The AK Party came into being in 2001 under the leadership of Erdogan, who became prime minister of Türkiye in 2003 – a position he held for the next 11 years.
Since 2014, he has led the country as president.
The two and a half decades of party rule haven’t been without challenges – foremost among them was the July 2016 defeated coup attempt by the FETO terrorist group.
The government led by the AK Party survived the putschists’ bid to take over power, thanks to the fearless resistance put up by the Turkish people on the streets of Istanbul and Ankara.
As many as 253 people paid the ultimate sacrifice that day to preserve democracy and protect the Turkish republic.
According to Muhammed Ali Ucar, chairman of the Vienna-based think tank PLUS Institute, Western labels such as nationalist, right-wing, or populist fall short of describing what the AK Party truly stands for.
The AK Party emerged from Türkiye’s own distinctive historical, social and political circumstances, drawing on the country’s history, geography, culture and diversity, he tells TRT World.
With more than 11.5 million members spanning all social classes and ethnic backgrounds, the party is not confined to any single constituency, he says.
“The AK Party is not a party based solely on one particular ideological or sociological constituency, but one that has succeeded in reaching a remarkably broad section of society,” he says.
Ucar sees “substantial continuity” with the fundamental political vision of justice, development, equality, freedom, and democracy set at its founding.
Its defining trait is “belief in democracy and in the will of the people,” with the ballot box as the source of legitimacy.
The birth of a movement
Analysts say that the circumstances that gave birth to the AK Party were those of exclusion and crisis.
Ertem recalls that the party aimed to restore rights to large segments of society denied public office and, in some cases, university education until the 2000s.
“The February 28, 1997, process further intensified the perceived need for such a political party and political leadership,” he says, while referring to the so-called postmodern coup in which the military exerted pressure on the elected government to resign in order to pave the way for a host of anti-democratic measures, particularly a ban on headscarves in public universities.
“Looking at the situation today, many of the party’s major objectives – particularly bringing large segments of society that had been excluded from the political centre for nearly a century back into the mainstream, as well as restoring their rights to education and public service – have been achieved to a very significant extent,” Ertem says.
Party voters continue to trust Erdogan to resolve current challenges, just as he did after 2001, a tumultuous time in Turkish history that gave birth to the AK Party, he says.
Ucar also places the party’s founding amid the debates raging across Türkiye in the 1990s and the early 2000s over democracy and freedom.
Women wearing the headscarf faced barriers to education and public life, while religious sections of society experienced exclusion, he says.
The party emerged from a “long-standing search for democracy, freedom, equality and broader social representation,” alongside economic crises, healthcare shortcomings and infrastructure gaps.
Erdogan’s founding-era statement that “from now on, nothing in Türkiye will be the same as before” captured the ambition.
Twenty-five years later, Ucar says that important changes have taken place in many areas of fundamental rights and freedoms, particularly with regard to the headscarf and freedom of religion, alongside far-reaching advances in healthcare, transport, infrastructure, defence and technology.
“I believe the AK Party has fulfilled a significant part of the objectives it set out at the time of its establishment, and continues to uphold the fundamental political commitments upon which it was founded,” he says.
What sets the AK Party apart from other political groups in the country is its direct bond with society and its leader’s consistency, analysts say.
Ucar highlights the party’s non-elitist character as one of its many distinct qualities: it emerged from within the people and carries society’s demands into politics, he says.
Its nationwide organisation and ability to respond to diverse expectations explain its longevity at the centre of politics.
Envisaging a hypothetical scenario where the AK Party is absent, Ucar says Türkiye would still be locked in unresolved debates over basic rights, and the transformations in healthcare, transport, defence and technology would not have occurred.
How the West views AK Party
Matthew Bryza, former US ambassador to Azerbaijan and an Istanbul-based expert on Eurasian affairs, observes that the current US administration under President Trump views the AK Party as the ruling party of a democratic NATO ally with the alliance’s second-largest army and critical geography.
President Trump views President Erdogan as a “friend whom he admires” and views Türkiye as a critical NATO ally, he tells TRT World.
“Observers have come to regard Türkiye less in ideological terms and more as an important partner and ally,” he adds.
Veysel Kurt, professor of political science at Istanbul Medeniyet University, says Western views about Türkiye under the AK Party have never been uniform, though pragmatism cuts across differences.
In the early 2010s, Western actors increasingly adopted a much more ideological approach towards the AK Party and Erdogan, Kurt tells TRT World.
This divergence became more pronounced during the refugee crisis and in the military operations against terrorist organisations in Syria, he adds.
This situation persisted for approximately 10 years. But with the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, Western actors “needed Türkiye”.
“(They) were forced to adopt a more moderate approach and abandoned many of the accusatory stances they had previously taken, particularly towards President Erdogan,” he says.
Türkiye’s global standing has risen markedly over the last many years.
Kurt recalls that before the 2000s, the country struggled with internal economic, security and political problems, limiting Ankara’s regional and global roles.
After 2000, however, institutional capacity and policy choices enabled competition with global actors in terrorism, defence industry, intelligence and foreign policy, he says.
Türkiye holds a dominant position in its immediate neighbourhood – the Middle East, Balkans, Eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea and even Eastern Europe – while remaining active in Africa and Central Asia, he notes.
It also possesses the capability to strike a balance between major powers when necessary, he adds.
“Its ranking among the top five or 10 countries in numerous indices – based on indicators such as the growth and utilisation of military capabilities, intelligence effectiveness, defence industry exports, and soft power elements – serves as concrete evidence of this,” Kurt says.
Feathers in AK Party’s cap
Bryza points to several concrete results produced by good governance: massive infrastructure investment, visible daily in Istanbul’s tunnels and bridges, improving the standard of life for everyday people.
GDP per capita is now more than $18,000, up from barely above $3,000 in 2001.
Similar improvements have taken place in export growth, human development benchmarks, and poverty reduction over the same period.
Ertem lists three lasting achievements of the AK Party that have shaped the Turkish national character over the last quarter century.
First is the defence industry’s “extraordinary transformation” under the AK Party rule. Türkiye has become a leading developer, manufacturer and exporter of unmanned aerial systems, selling to approximately 40 countries, including NATO and EU members.
Second are foreign-policy gains: successful defence of Eastern Mediterranean rights and interests, the most significant contribution to ending Syria’s civil war and establishing stability, mediation in the Russia-Ukraine war, a strong response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the NATO Summit in Ankara on July 7-8.
Third is democratic consolidation: ending the “era of coups” that repeatedly interrupted politics between 1960 and 2000.
“The fact that the state, together with the people, resisted the coup attempt of July 15, 2016, represented a major victory and a lasting achievement for Turkish democracy,” Ertem says.
Ucar considers the strengthening of democracy, expansion of freedoms, and reinforcement of fundamental human rights as the greatest achievements of the AK Party.
Placing the will of the people and the ballot box at the centre of legitimacy has deepened democratic foundations. Resolution of issues such as the headscarf has ended long sources of conflict, ensuring people are not excluded from education or public life because of beliefs or identities, he says.
“One of the defining features of Erdogan’s political leadership has been his confidence in popular support and his view that political legitimacy derives directly from the will of the nation,” he says.

Japan weighs sanctions after Putin’s first visit to disputed Kuril Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:30:48 UTC
16:30:48 KST

Japan is considering new sanctions on Russia after President Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the disputed Kuril Islands on 13 August, a senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official told reporters, according to Kyodo News.
Putin traveled to Iturup — Etorofu in Japanese — the largest of the four Russian-held islands Japan claims as its own, days after overseeing Russian Pacific Fleet exercises in the Far East. It is the first time a Russian president or prime minister has set foot on the islands. Tokyo summoned Russia's ambassador and lodged a formal protest, calling the visit "totally unacceptable." Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the islands are "an inherent part of Japanese territory both historically and under international law."
The Institute for the Study of War assesses that the Kremlin is likely using the visit to deter Japan from adopting a more assertive defense posture, and to discourage EU seizures of Russian shadow-fleet vessels — tying a Pacific island dispute directly to the pressure campaign around Russia's war on Ukraine.
An 80-year-old dispute, reopened on Tokyo's clock
Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty ending World War II, entirely because of the Kurils. The Soviet Union seized the four southernmost islands — Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai islets — in the war's final weeks, expelling the Japanese residents. Japan calls them the Northern Territories and has never dropped the claim.
Putin's visit lands as Tokyo's posture toward Moscow hardens. Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper, published earlier this month, named Russia as one of the country's principal threats — a paper Putin criticized directly on Wednesday, saying the islands became Russian territory "as a result of World War II" and accusing Japan of imposing "unprovoked sanctions" over what he called the "Ukraine conflict."
The timing cuts against the diplomatic track Tokyo pursued for years. Under former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, Takaichi's political mentor, Japan met Putin 27 times seeking a peace treaty, and in 2018 the two sides agreed to accelerate talks on a 1956 declaration that would have returned Shikotan and the Habomai islets after a treaty was signed. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine froze those talks in 2022, and Putin's visit closes even the pretense that they might resume soon.
Ukraine has already staked out a position in the dispute: Kyiv's parliament in 2022 recognized the islands as Japanese territory, and President Zelenskyy signed a decree affirming Japan's sovereignty over its "Northern territories" — a reciprocal gesture in the broader alignment between Kyiv and Tokyo against Moscow.
What Japan is weighing
A Foreign Ministry official said only that Tokyo is "considering what step to take going forward," with an additional sanctions package under consideration. No specifics on scope or target have been announced.
The precedent for a symbolic response exists: in 2010, then-President Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian head of state to visit the islands, traveling to Kunashir — a visit that also drew formal protest without derailing bilateral contact entirely. Putin's visit as president is a harder marker, arriving alongside Russia's sustained war footing rather than a peacetime dispute.

How can we transport ourselves to natural environments when we find ourselves in entirely urban contexts? The materiality of spaces is one of the factors that determines the atmosphere we inhabit. In this regard, the incorporation of natural materials in interior architecture can help introduce textures, colors, and qualities inherent to nature into our daily spaces. In this article, we explore the specific use of cork as a resource in interior design and the different ways it can transform the experience of a space. Cork is the bark of the cork oak, a tree species that, when harvested without harming the tree, can be transformed into a material suitable for multiple applications in architecture and design.
Three Little Pigs House / EME157
Continuity between exterior and interior finds material expression in this Madrid home, where the cork used on the facade extends into the interior spaces. The material also appears on a sliding door that allows the kitchen to be closed off or integrated into the rest of the home, becoming an element capable of transforming the spatial configuration. Its natural texture and tone maintain a visual link between the envelope and the interior, while its mobile presence allows the same material to participate in both the architecture and the daily dynamics of living in it.

Swiss farmers fear worse drought losses than 2003
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:28:14 UTC
16:28:14 KST

Swiss farmers fear worse drought losses than 2003
Swiss Farmers’ Union president Markus Ritter estimates that losses caused by the heatwave will be higher than the CHF500 million of 2003.
Losses are certain to be higher this year as the heat and drought has affected all regions of the country, said Ritter in an interview with the CH Media group.
The situation is exceptional because the soil was already suffering from a water deficit at the start of the summer. “I have personally never experienced a drought like this before,” said Ritter. The outlook is poor for potatoes and sugar beet. Maize yields are also set to be lower.
+ Swiss farmers hold greater sway than ever
The consequences are also likely to be felt in food prices. Price rises are particularly likely for potatoes and sugar beet. The situation looks better for wheat and barley, as a large proportion had already grown before the drought and could be harvested successfully.
Retailers have indicated that they are prepared to shoulder certain additional costs resulting from the drought. “There will be negotiations,” said Ritter. Nevertheless, the agricultural sector will bear the brunt of the financial damage.
For example, a vegetable farmer’s yield could down by a third while producer prices rise by only 10%.
The situation is also particularly strained for livestock farmers. Due to a shortage of feed, many have already had to dip into their winter reserves. Hay prices have risen by up to 50%.
In June and July, 7,000 more cows had already been slaughtered compared with the previous year. With animals returning early from the Alps, slaughter figures are likely to rise further.
Nevertheless, Ritter rejects the idea of declaring a state of emergency. “The most important thing is not to panic.” The Farmers’ Association is in close contact with the government. Among other measures, water is being flown in to certain alpine pastures and customs duties on feed imports have been waived.

As blazes strain fire services from the Mediterranean to the Midlands in the UK, questions are being asked about Europe's ability to deal with continued heatwaves.
A three-kilometre wall of flames up to 30 metres high forced hundreds of tourists into the sea off northern Greece, as wildfires also tore across, France and the UK amid a punishing summer heatwave.
More than 200 firefighters, water-bombing planes and helicopters battled for hours to stop a blaze spreading across the Halkidiki peninsula, south of Thessaloniki, as it bore down on the resorts of Siviri and Fourka, packed with summer tourists.
Judging evacuation by road too dangerous, officials sent around 500 tourists into small boats, coast guard vessels and fire brigade craft, including roughly 200 taken to a ship waiting offshore, while cars trying to flee by road became gridlocked.
"We are on the beach and looking for a way to get away," one local homeowner, Sophia, told AFP, saying flames had already reached the town's houses.
Two firefighters were hospitalised, and authorities banned public access to the region's pine forests as forecasters warned of winds up to 100 km/h.
The fire was later brought under control, though crews stayed on alert for flare-ups.
Greece remains under its highest wildfire alert nationwide, still reeling from a blaze near Athens this month that killed two helicopter crew and burned 110 square kilometres of forest.
On high alert
Météo France placed four departments under its highest wildfire alert on Friday, warning that weather conditions make the risk of fires starting and spreading "very high compared with summer norms".
Overnight, firefighters brought the Aude blaze near Carcassonne under control after saving 73 homes, while the Pas-de-Calais fire near Mont-Frieux remained active into Friday morning.
With the heatwave persisting, authorities across France are urging continued vigilance heading into the weekend.
Teenager detained over fatal blaze
A 15-year-old has been placed under formal investigation and held in juvenile detention over a forest fire near Bordeaux airport that killed two firefighters trapped in their truck on 21 July.
The deaths, along with that of a volunteer firefighter in southeast France, have angered fire unions, whose representatives met Interior Minister Laurent Nunez this week but said his commitments fell short, threatening strike action in September over inadequate resources.
A wildfire with multiple points of origin tore through homes near Stourbridge in the UK on the region's hottest day of the year, damaging at least six properties and forcing evacuations.
Three firefighters and a child were hospitalised, while six others were treated for smoke inhalation.
West Midlands' Chief Fire Officer Simon Tuhill called it "one of the most significant incidents" the service had ever attended, blaming rapid spread on "tinder-dry" conditions.
Nearly three-quarters of England is in drought, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged retailers to limit sales of disposable barbecues.

Farage wins UK by-election as Count Binface claims 'moral victory'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:23:59 UTC
16:23:59 KST

Hard-right British politician Nigel Farage reclaimed his seat in a by-election, according to the final tally on Aug. 14, though his main rival and joke candidate Count Binface took an larger than expected share of the ballot.
Farage, who triggered the vote by resigning the parliamentary seat he had held since 2024 over an investigation into his finances, swept 63 percent of the ballots in the English constituency of Clacton.
While votes were still being counted, Farage had declared victory.
"The verdict is in and it is a convincing and overwhelming win," he said as supporters chanted his name at an event in Essex that was broadcast on X.
His main rival, Count Binface, however, exceeded expectations by earning 9,455 votes, 27 percent of the total.
Analysts had anticipated a win for Farage but underestimated the appeal of the self-styled "intergalactic space warrior", who campaigns wearing a rubbish bin on his head, forecasting a large share of the vote approaching but not exceeding 20 percent.
The vote had been shunned by Britain's main political parties, including the governing Labour Party, as a stunt by the Reform U.K. leader — once touted as a potential prime minister — to dodge scrutiny of his dealings.
That gave dozens of fringe candidates including Binface — the alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey — to seize the spotlight.
"The moral victory is already mine," he told AFP at the counting centre early Friday ahead of the final tally.
Farage did not attend the count, where candidates traditionally gather for the declaration of results, saying Essex Police had warned him that an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" was planned.
Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said election officials had worked with police to ensure the process was "completed safely and securely", adding there was "no reason not to proceed with the count process at this time".
Binface said it had been his "humble duty" to be Farage's opposition, adding he would respect the results.
"If a majority of the voters of Clacton say they would like him to be returned as their MP, that is to be respected," he said.
Turnout reached about 44 percent, down from 59 percent in the 2024 general election but not an unusual rate for a by-election.
In the coastal community, many voters appeared unenthusiastic about the vote, with even some Reform party volunteers describing the contest as a joke.
"It's a bit ridiculous," party campaigner Jane Embelton told AFP.
"It's all to make Nigel Farage look like an idiot, basically. But he doesn't look like an idiot to me or his supporters."
A record 33 fringe candidates, including Binface, stood in the vote, with some of the longest ballot papers in the country's history seen being unfolded at the Clacton Leisure Centre, where the count was held.
Farage, whose party had topped national opinion polls for 18 months before falling behind recently, surprised voters with his July 7 resignation amid the probe into his finances.
The investigation by the parliamentary sleaze watchdog is examining allegations he and Reform's deputy leader, Richard Tice, failed to declare financial gifts. They deny any wrongdoing.
Farage has framed Thursday's vote as "the people of Clacton versus the Establishment", aimed at thwarting the "stitch-up" over his finances.
"The people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," he said in a video released before casting his vote.
One Clacton voter, Phil, predicted the vote was "not going to change anything", saying that the parliamentary probe would restart with Farage's re-election.
Political pundits have downplayed the vote's wider significance in a constituency that overwhelmingly backed Brexit a decade ago.
"It will be astonishing if Farage were not to win," political scientist John Curtice told AFP.
But some assessed Farage's election gambit had backfired as his Reform party slips down national polls.
"Farage's plan to turn this by-election into a serious political battle failed," Queen Mary University of London politics professor Stijn van Kessel told AFP, noting the resulting spectacle "makes Farage look rather silly".
Farage netted 46 percent of the vote in the 2024 general election to become an MP on his eighth attempt.

Conti Federal Services LLC of Orlando, Florida, has been awarded a $78 million contract to build a set of ordnance storage magazines at Naval Air Station Sigonella, Italy, the U.S. Navy announced this week.
The contract, listed under project number P-111, covers construction of four earth-covered magazines with seismic upgrades, two modular storage magazines, and a maintenance facility for an ammunition rework and overhaul shop. Work will be performed at Sigonella and is scheduled for completion by August 2030.
Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command Atlantic, based in Norfolk, Virginia, is the contracting activity for the award, listed under contract number N62470-26-C-0005. The Navy competed the contract through SAM.gov, and four offers were received.
NAS Sigonella sits in eastern Sicily, near Catania, and operates as a joint U.S. and Italian Air Force installation. The U.S. Navy has maintained a permanent presence there since 1959. The base serves as a logistics and support hub for U.S. 6th Fleet operations in the Mediterranean and hosts NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Sigonella, part of a network of Navy supply commands across Europe and Africa.
The magazine project has been in planning for several years. Earlier Navy programming documents for P-111 described construction of six magazines: four standard Box Type-D earth-covered magazines and two 7-bar reinforced concrete box earth-covered magazines, along with a high-bay facility for ammunition rework and overhaul. The scope in this week’s contract announcement, four earth-covered magazines and two modular storage magazines plus a maintenance facility, tracks closely with that earlier plan.
Conti Federal Services, founded in 1906 and headquartered in Orlando, is a construction and design-build firm that works almost exclusively on U.S. government projects, including military construction for the Department of War. The company has prior experience in the same region: it holds a $30 million NAVFAC EURAFCENT contract to modernize buildings at Naval Support Activity Naples, Italy. Conti Federal also holds larger construction vehicles elsewhere, including a $990 million Indo-Pacific Multiple Award Construction Contract and a $15 billion Navy design-build contract covering projects in Guam and the broader Pacific.
Funding obligated at the time of award totals $67.7 million, drawn from fiscal 2024 military construction funds. Those funds will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year, unlike operations and maintenance money, which typically must be spent within the fiscal year it is appropriated.
The contract announcement did not specify design details for the magazines beyond their general categories, including capacity figures or the types of ordnance to be stored. Work is set to run for roughly four years, through August 2030.

Former Akhmat Fighter Defects to Ukraine, Reveals Other Such Cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:21:01 UTC
16:21:01 KST

A former fighter with the Chechen Akhmat unit defected to Ukraine and joined the International Legion of the Main Intelligence Directorate (DIU) of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine.
The Chechen man told this in a video by Dmitry Karpenko.
The volunteer’s name is Magomed. Before defecting to the Ukrainian side, he had been held captive by Ukraine for nearly a year—since August 29, 2025.
At first, he fought near Svitlodarsk, and later near Bakhmut, where, among other things, he helped evacuate the bodies of the fallen. After that, he and his unit were transferred to Horlivka.
Magomed recalls that two Chechens had already defected to the Ukrainian forces before him, after which the command tightened its supervision of the soldiers, including by checking their phones.
Magomed surrendered to a Ukrainian drone. According to him, it was a risky move, as if the drone had turned out to be Russian, it could have dropped munitions on them, given previous instances of Chechens defecting to the Ukrainian side.
As they made their way toward the Ukrainian positions, the soldiers dropped everything the Chechens needed—medicines, painkillers, water, and a radio.
However, during the transfer, a Russian FPV drone attacked the Chechens, killing one of them.
After the defection, Magomed was met by Ukrainian military personnel and handed over to the Assault Brigade Liut of the National Police of Ukraine after which he was taken prisoner.
The Chechen man also said that the Russians had killed his brother, attributing the death to an ‘epileptic seizure.’ After that, Magomed decided to fight against the Russians alongside other Chechens.
Earlier, on July 14, it was reported that in Kadyrovites Akhmat special forces unit, there are approximately six recruits from other regions of Russia for every Chechen.

Semiconductor price hikes spread upstream to Taiwan materials suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:18:59 UTC
16:18:59 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Semiconductor materials suppliers are benefiting as price increases spread across the supply chain, CTEE reported Thursday.
Price increases now cover much of the semiconductor manufacturing process, including silicon wafers, sputtering targets, electronic-grade hydrofluoric acid, and underfill materials. Analysts said the trend differs from the short-term inventory restocking typically seen during traditional semiconductor cycles, reflecting not only stronger AI chip production but also efforts to localize supply chains.
Kinik Co. reported first-half revenue of NT$4.8 billion (US$149.7 million), up 23% from the same period a year earlier. In addition to higher prices, the semiconductor process consumables supplier said it benefited from increased shipments of diamond discs.
Diamond discs are used in chemical mechanical polishing, a process that smooths and flattens semiconductor wafers by removing excess material. Kinik’s largest diamond-disc customer accounted for 63% of its diamond-disc sales, while products used in advanced processes at 5 nanometers and below accounted for 61.2% of diamond-disc sales, according to Kinik.
Revenue from products for 2 nm and 1.6 nm processes featuring backside power delivery also increased significantly in the second quarter. The technology is considered an important development in extending Moore’s Law, which describes the trend of fitting more transistors onto increasingly smaller chips. It can improve heat dissipation, reduce voltage drops, and increase chip density, according to CTEE.
Kinik expects 2 nm products to become a major source of shipments in the second half of the year. Products for the 1.4 nm process have also begun contributing to revenue, as the company expands its business to support customers in the early production stages of newer chip technologies.
PentaPro Materials Inc. reported revenue of NT$102 million in the first six months of the year, an 89.8% increase from the same period a year earlier. The company makes high-purity chemicals used to form thin layers on semiconductor wafers for advanced logic chips, memory chips, and compound semiconductors.
Its 8N-grade metal-organic precursors are used in advanced processes such as atomic layer deposition (ALD). As chipmakers move to 2 nm and smaller processes, they are adopting new transistor designs that require more thin layers to build each chip, increasing the use of ALD and boosting consumption of the chemicals needed to form those layers.
Institutional investors expect PentaPro’s growth to continue in the second half of the year as 2 nm production capacity ramps up. To meet growing demand, the company plans to begin construction of its second plant at Southern Taiwan Science Park in the fourth quarter, with investment expected to reach NT$3 billion.
The new facility is planned to increase production capacity to six to 10 times its current level. It is expected to become a key manufacturing base for customers moving to processes below 2 nm from 2028 onward.
