Bath Iron Works launches future USS William Charette destroyer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:18:01 UTC
16:18:01 KST

- Bath Iron Works christened the future USS William Charette (DDG 130) Aug. 1 and launched it into the Kennebec River days later.
- DDG 130 is the fifth Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer and the second built at Bath Iron Works, named for Medal of Honor recipient William Charette.
General Dynamics Bath Iron Works said this week that the future USS William Charette (DDG 130) has cleared two construction milestones, moving the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer a step closer to joining the U.S. Navy fleet.
The shipyard christened the vessel Aug. 1 in its dry dock in Bath, Maine. Days later, the ship launched into the Kennebec River, where it will remain pierside while crews continue outfitting work toward the next milestone, known as Aegis Light Off. That milestone marks the first time the ship’s Aegis combat system is powered up and tested aboard the vessel.
“We extend our appreciation to our dedicated shipbuilders whose efforts have brought the ship one step closer to joining the Navy fleet,” Bath Iron Works said in a social media post Thursday.
DDG 130 is the fifth Flight III variant of the Arleigh Burke class and the second Flight III destroyer built at Bath Iron Works. It is also the 43rd Arleigh Burke-class destroyer the shipyard has produced since the program began construction there in 1988. The Navy awarded the contract for the ship in September 2018, and Bath Iron Works started fabrication in November 2020. The keel was laid Aug. 29, 2024.
The ship is named for Master Chief Hospital Corpsman William R. Charette, a Navy corpsman who received the Medal of Honor for his actions during a Marine Corps engagement at Outpost Vegas in Korea on March 27, 1953. It carries the motto “Valor in Service.”
Flight III destroyers keep the external profile of earlier Arleigh Burke-class ships but carry a different combat system. The central change is the AN/SPY-6(V)1 radar, an active electronically scanned array that replaces the AN/SPY-1D(V) radar used on earlier variants. It pairs with the Aegis Baseline 10 combat system and 96 Mk 41 vertical launch cells. DDG 130 displaces about 9,850 metric tons (9,700 long tons) and carries three 4-megawatt generators that give the class roughly a third more electrical power than earlier Flight IIA ships, power needed to run the new radar and its cooling systems.
USS Jack H. Lucas (DDG 125), the first Flight III destroyer, is already in service. USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128) is expected to join the fleet later this year. As of July 2026, the Navy counted 75 Arleigh Burke-class destroyers delivered, with 24 more planned, under contract or in various stages of construction.
Bath Iron Works currently has several other Flight III destroyers under construction, including Louis H. Wilson Jr. (DDG 126), Quentin Walsh (DDG 132), John E. Kilmer (DDG 134), Richard G. Lugar (DDG 136), J. William Middendorf (DDG 138) and Thomas G. Kelley (DDG 140). The shipyard is a business unit of General Dynamics and one of Maine’s largest employers, with about 6,700 workers as of the fourth quarter of 2025.

Isabel Serra: Europe's 'war project' faces growing resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:17:57 UTC
16:17:57 KST

Breadcrumb
MEP Isabel Serra to The New Arab: Europe is becoming a 'war project'
Isabel Serra has been a member of the European Parliament since 2024 as part of the Left group and is currently vice-chair of its subcommittee on human rights.
Before joining the European Parliament, she was a member of the Spanish parliament, where she was re-elected twice.
Serra also served as spokesperson for Spain's left-wing Podemos party and worked as an adviser to Spanish Equality Minister Irene Montero between 2021 and 2023.
Serra belongs to the left-wing movement and is considered by some to be part of the most radical wing of the Spanish political scene.
She has made human rights, migration, Palestine, anti-racism and anti-colonialism central to her political work in the European Parliament. In an interview with The New Arab, Serra strongly criticises the European project, which is undergoing major transformations, most notably, she says, its transformation "into a war project".
She places Palestine at the heart of these transformations, arguing that Brussels' position on the genocidal war in Gaza reveals its deep complicity with Israel and the European Union's subordination to US President Donald Trump and the United States.
 
The Ceuta incident has brought migration to the forefront of European debate. As a member of the European Parliament, how do you explain what happened, and what responsibilities does the European Union bear?
The crisis has so far left 141 people dead, while dozens remain missing. At this moment, thousands of people are sleeping in the streets in inhumane conditions, without adequate care, and many of them are minors. This is the most important issue, and all institutions must address it.
Nevertheless, we see how the far right in general, as well as institutions such as European institutions, which are directly or indirectly run by the far right, have not issued any message to the victims' families. If they had been white, European people from Ukraine, for example, we would have had months of condolences and mourning. But because they are dark-skinned and come from the Global South, this situation suits the far right and the European Commission perfectly, allowing them to justify greater Frontex involvement and more anti-migrant rhetoric.
Of course, 70,000 people cannot cross the border without incitement or even facilitation by the Moroccan regime, a regime that has condemned its people to poverty and unemployment, illegally occupies Western Sahara and systematically uses violence against the Sahrawi people.
This is the same regime that has important agreements with the United States and Israel, which will become stronger over time. But at the same time, there is something I think it is important to point out in light of the public debate over the past few days: I do not favour this pro-Spanish government discourse, framed in nationalist terms, which portrays an operation by Trump, Morocco and Israel to destabilise Sanchez and Spain, targeting our sovereignty and territorial integrity, ultimately adopting the terms "invasion" and "hybrid war", and claiming that the most important thing is to defend our sovereignty.
According to this discourse, Spain is a victim of Morocco. Migrants are merely tools, and the most important thing is protecting the border and sovereignty.
These narratives ignore the fact that Spain, whether the right-wing People's Party or the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, has always maintained the best possible relationship with Morocco and its regime, which has committed injustices against the Moroccan people.
These narratives ignore the fact that people from the Global South have died. They also ignore that Morocco influences because it is a stronghold for the United States and Israel but, at the same time, is simply another country in the Global South.
The problem is that the politicisation of borders not only empowers countries such as Morocco but also constitutes violence against peoples so that Europe can continue claiming to protect human rights while pushing others to violate them.
In short, I do not support this nationalist narrative that equates the Moroccan regime with those suffering under its rule. These people are the working class with whom we should stand in solidarity, build alliances and confront this colonial, imperialist, capitalist world that is becoming increasingly inhumane.
Has the European model of border control failed?
The model of politicising borders generates systematic violence and death. It is a model in which countries in the Global South are blackmailed into militarising their borders and building detention centres for people fleeing terrible circumstances in exchange for aid and development funding.
It is a catastrophic and failed model, not because it threatens our territorial integrity, but because it involves the use of violence against people. The European Union is increasingly promoting this model.
The current project of this European government, in which social democracies and the far right share power, is a war project. War with Russia is one side of it, while the other is war against migrants.
It is a project based on the idea that Europe – this Western civilisation – is threatened by Russia and by those who want to come here, to the countries of the continent, to live and work.
In the face of this situation, everything must be militarised. For this purpose, companies are making enormous fortunes manufacturing weapons for Ukraine, in addition to drones to monitor people and security systems as well. They are useful for everything.
So, this is the current project: more border surveillance. But there is pressure on other countries to do this work, to the point that countries aspiring to join the European Union must first pass a review of agreements with Frontex, the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, and, in general, migration monitoring.
If they behave properly–that is, if they do not violate human rights on a large scale–they can join.
But there is something very important: Why does the far right adopt this agenda, this project, which is being implemented by both Trump and Ursula von der Leyen?
Well, first of all, I do not want them to prevent people from coming, but they want them to arrive in the most submissive, disciplined and dehumanising ways possible.
If you have to endure everything to get here, and you are among the few who were lucky enough to make it, you will accept anything here. Notice, I am not saying migrants will accept anything, but the entire institutional system is designed to achieve that.
Then the migrant will work from sunrise to sunset for low wages, while Spanish employers will exploit them to exhaustion to take all the profits, the surplus value.
It is a mechanism of class oppression through racism. Migration laws, such as Spain's shameful law, which deprives people of their rights and condemns them to precarious and unpaid work for years until they obtain residency, serve this purpose.
This is why I am deeply angered by the pro-Spanish government discourse that ignores Spain's colonial position towards the Global South and its racist position towards those who want to cross and those who arrive there.
So, this is the main function: exploitation and overexploitation.
It is globalised capitalism that exports companies to poor countries in the global South to extract greater profits by stealing natural resources and exploiting workers, and also by importing undocumented workers, thereby producing more undocumented workers.
Moreover, if these narratives generate intense hatred towards a scapegoat, you make people stop looking upwards and recognise that the person exploiting them is their boss and that the one plundering them is the greedy investment fund.
This is how they come to hate those at the bottom of the social ladder, and society becomes more authoritarian in the absence of a working class driven by the shared interests that unite us all, whether we are white or Black, men or women
How do you assess the Spanish government's reaction to Ceuta crisis and the reactions of some EU countries, such as Italy and Finland, which proposed excluding Spain from the Schengen area?
I never imagined that I would one day agree with Margarita Robles, the Spanish defence minister, more than anyone else in the Spanish government.
It seems to me that if we want to confront Trump, we must take a firm position: support the right to self-determination for Western Sahara; defend the need for legal and safe corridors; question Europe's role in the Global South throughout history; and clearly affirm that the migration of people to the Global North is the result of the North plundering the resources of the South and that it continues to do so.
We must also defend freedom of movement and the right to migrate as a universal right. We must cut ties with Israel, which supports Morocco, and stop selling weapons to and buying weapons from a state committing genocide.
We cannot afford to be afraid in ideological debates. The far right is attacking with all its might, and the world is changing. We have reached a point of no return. Nothing will return to how it was. Therefore, it is absurd to defend what prevailed in past decades.
That world and the international order that prevailed after the Second World War, a world shaped by fascism and the Holocaust, no longer exists. It was built on those events, while naturally ignoring other events, such as the genocides and Holocausts suffered by other peoples.
From this construction and from those narratives, such as the claim that the Jewish people were the only people to suffer, or the people who suffered the most, we live as we do today.
But in conclusion, I believe there is no room for half-measures. I believe we must be consistent.
I also believe that what Spain and its government urgently need is to guarantee the rights of people living in appalling conditions in Ceuta and, of course, not deport anyone against their right to seek asylum and not return any unaccompanied child.
They have the right to be treated and cared for by Spanish institutions exactly like any child born in Spain. Clearly, human rights violations are being committed, as many non-governmental organisations have reported
As vice-chair of the Subcommittee on Human Rights, do you believe that the European Union adheres to the values it claims to defend?
It is becoming more difficult day by day. Even European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen no longer hesitates to express this.
For example, after Trump's and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's illegal attack on Iran, von der Leyen said that "the old order is no longer valid" and asked, "Why defend international law?"
There is no doubt that von der Leyen stands alongside a system whose perpetrators are committing genocide. Naturally, she does not defend international law, because in the case of Iran, for example, this essentially means defending Iran's right to defend itself against an illegal attack by another state.
By the way, this is a right Israel does not have because it is a state occupying the territory of another state.
The same applies to the European Union's cooperation and development policy. Commissioners are no longer ashamed to acknowledge that development aid, or official development assistance, is not intended to lift any country out of poverty but rather to provide an institutional bridge for European private companies to plunder the resources of the Global South, in Africa, for example.
And now they say it openly: we want to compete with China, and we will do everything we can to achieve that. We will demand that African countries militarise their borders if they want funding (part of the budget will be allocated for this purpose), and in return, our companies will plunder their resources. This is exactly what they are doing.
They have always done this, but at least they used to hide their actions. Now they are doing it openly and in broad daylight, without shame and with growing enthusiasm.
As for migration policies, note that they have recently succeeded in passing the return law. It is not fundamentally different from what Trump is doing in the United States through mass deportations. We are facing a policy of mass deportation.
Just as Trump puts migrants in Guantanamo, in Europe they will soon put them in other countries known for human rights violations. This means torture, human trafficking and forced labour.
These are not the actions of the mafias or networks they refer to in their rhetoric. They are the actions of the states they pay to do this: Egypt, Libya, Turkey and Mauritania, for example.
With the new laws, it will become easier: families, children, people imprisoned for more than two years, and people fleeing wars started by the West and its allies, such as Israel, will be imprisoned for years.
Nothing remains of what Europe once claimed to be. Nevertheless, if you look a little deeper, you will see that even that was a great lie. The Western civilisation they fiercely defend was built on the extermination of indigenous peoples, on the colonisation of other peoples, and on describing these peoples as "barbarians".
The far right did not have to invent much. It only had to read the history books on European colonialism: the few books that tell the truth about how things happened.
Palestine occupies a central place in your political work. In your view, why does the European Union always fail to take effective action against Israel?
It fails because it does not want to get it right on this particular issue. The European Union wants to be a partner of Israel because it is an extension of the West, or rather its outpost in what they incorrectly call the "Middle East".
Palestine does not matter to them, and they do not care about it. It matters to them only insofar as it serves their interests in waging wars.
For example, in the US-Israeli war against Iran, in strengthening American imperialism, to which Europe is subordinate, and in suppressing the rights of European peoples and restricting their freedom.
Look at what Germany, France and Britain have done against protesters supporting the Palestinian people. They have implemented policies criminalising them. It is as though civil and fundamental rights no longer exist.
And now what? Will they imprison us simply for saying: long live a free Palestine?
We cannot allow them to move towards this form of authoritarianism, mass surveillance and control over people through social media networks and artificial intelligence.
At the heart of all this, there is also the sanctions policy imposed by the European Union, which does not receive enough public discussion. The EU imposes these sanctions on organisations it describes as terrorist because of their positions in defence of Palestine.
We must talk about all of this. There is a mistaken belief that the European Union is a neutral democratic entity and a standard-bearer for human rights.
The European Union is run almost entirely by technocrats. They are ultimately politicians, and many of them are from the right and far right, and they are embracing the extremist ideological project day by day.
Their only project is war, colonialism and imperialism. They are obsessed with competing with China. They are not very different from Trump, at least Ursula von der Leyen and EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas.
Their war project needs Israel, its war machine, its weapons and security systems, and its position in West Asia.
What steps have you and the Left blocs in the European Parliament taken for Palestine, and what obstacles have you faced in imposing sanctions on Israel?
Waging the political battle. This is the most important thing. And contributing to raising public awareness of what is happening and of what its "democratic institutions" are doing.
We have strengthened and expanded the solidarity movement with Palestine and launched a campaign for the European Union to cancel its association agreement with Israel.
We cannot stop talking about Palestine. Nor can we settle for a social democracy that says one thing and does the opposite: not only continuing trade with Israel but also expanding contracts under the pretext of rearmament and provoking wars.
Palestine is a cause of humanity. It is the centre of the struggle and resistance for broader struggles against racism, colonialism and imperialism.
These struggles will become more violent in the next phase because we are living in a time when elites and capital owners have decided to reorganise themselves and reshape the world into a more unequal form.
Therefore, the struggle for Palestine is a space and an arena for raising awareness among new generations and politicising them. The young generations fighting for Palestine today are likely to be decisive in determining the next phase and the shape of the world to come.
Do you believe that the European Union can formulate an independent policy towards the Middle East from US influence?
No. The European Union has made its decision. It has decided to be obedient and subordinate to Trump and the United States and to its imperialist project.
Now, could there be another Europe? With a different European Commission and different governments? Perhaps. But unfortunately, at present, the project of the far right and European capitalist elites dominates the European project.
The real problem is that the European Union is not what we want it to be. Since its establishment under the Maastricht Treaty, the Dutch treaty, in 1992, it has remained a structure designed to serve certain elites and specific countries.
For example, Germany, thanks to the European Union, has greater influence than the rest of the EU countries, as the EU mechanism has contributed to pushing some countries towards deindustrialisation and the loss of a more advanced productive model.
Other countries were assigned an economic model based on construction and tourism: speculation in the housing market, the consequences of which we are experiencing today with the housing crisis and the sun-and-beach economy.
Here I am specifically talking about Spain. I could give other examples.
The European Union is not a union serving its European peoples. It is quite the opposite. Today, this European project is becoming a war project.
And we are now in urgent need of a peace project. An anti-imperialist project that builds alliances with other forces and peoples, such as Palestine, and pushes Europe in the opposite direction to the path it is taking today.
Hundreds of thousands of citizens across Europe have mobilised for Palestine, while EU institutions have maintained a more cautious position. Is there a gap today between European states and their peoples?
Absolutely. We have witnessed enormous crowds. Yes, a majority of Europeans are with Palestine, regardless of what their governments do, whether they oppose them or not.
I think the Vuelta a España cycling race was a powerful moment (in 2025, against the backdrop of the participation of an Israeli team). We stopped it; we boycotted it. We, the people, did that while our government continues to trade with Israel.
People are facing legal action for mobilising for Palestine. But we must continue. In fact, I think it is impossible to understand Trump's colonial peace plan without recognising the Zionist goal of dismantling the international solidarity movement.
Huge crowds have mobilised for Palestine in many countries.
I think we must understand that through mobilisation and participation in politics in their true sense and in an organised way like this, we can change everything and that we have no other option.
I also think the issue of Iran showed that the United States is not an absolute power but is weak and vulnerable to defeat and does not have everything in its favour, even if it resorts to undemocratic methods to remove elected governments and install its proxies, whether in the Middle East or Latin America.
We are witnessing the rise of the far right in many European countries, which has clearly affected European policies, whether on security or migration. Do you believe the identity of the European Union is changing?
There is no doubt that the European project is now under threat, and this is not solely because of the far right. It is enough to look at Germany, which is adopting a clear strategy based on militarism, to see this.
It is enough to read its recently published national strategy (rearmament and building the strongest army in Europe). Germany is not only now forcing its citizens to return to military service but is also implementing austerity policies because rearmament will inevitably lead to cuts in spending.
In addition, they are talking about a major war against Russia in 2029. Russia and its invasion of Ukraine have strengthened the EU's war system as a pretext, particularly for Germany, which is seeking economic and political gains.
The problem is that this path will lead to greater divisions between EU countries, and we will reach a point where the project becomes unable to protect the interests of those who wanted to establish it.
We must add to this the contradictions of the far right itself: it says it defends the nations of Europe, their interests and sovereignty, but in reality it defends the interests of the United States and Israel.
Therefore, I believe the European project will face major tensions in the coming years.
As for the philosophical foundations on which the Union was built, they are also collapsing. And this goes beyond human rights and this hypocritical narrative. I am referring to the idea of progress itself, which was central to modernity and the European Enlightenment.
This idea is based on the notion that what we are and what we can become are not the same thing and that there is a gap between them based on aspirations. This gap has widened, partly because of technological progress, but also because of political and cultural changes.
For example, comprehensive education, which could have made us better at managing our relations with others through diplomacy and democracy, is now threatened by the narrative that war is inevitable.
Climate change has also led many people today to feel that they may die before reaching old age. This is a major transformation in European societies.
There are also many, many other changes. This change may not be as pronounced in countries that have experienced wars for which the West was responsible. Perhaps other countries, such as China and others, do not experience the same degree of a sense of decline, collapse and fear.
But this feeling is growing in our European societies at a time when the elites are not offering a better alternative. Therefore, we, the peoples of Europe, must work with the peoples of the Global South to build a better alternative.
What is the biggest threat to democracy in Europe today?
Ursula von der Leyen and the tendency towards racial and ethnic supremacy, whether it is Israel's racial and ethnic supremacist tendency or that of the racist far right as a whole, which portrays black people and migrants as enemies, a source of problems and the cause of every disturbance.
Likewise, the social democracies, which, in the face of the seriousness of the situation the world is experiencing today, have decided to remain silent, turn a blind eye to what is happening, or follow those who are leading us towards the abyss.

In Kyiv, a man shot at a BMW during a conflict and was served with a notice of suspicion

In Kyiv, a man shot at a BMW during a conflict and was served with a notice of suspicion

U.S Navy awards $119 million contract for USS San Antonio repairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:12:52 UTC
16:12:52 KST

- Marine Hydraulics International received a $119.4 million contract to maintain, modernize and repair USS San Antonio (LPD 17) during a fiscal 2027 availability.
- The contract could grow to $143.7 million with options exercised, and work in Norfolk is scheduled for completion by July 2028.
Marine Hydraulics International LLC of Norfolk, Virginia, has been awarded a $119.4 million contract to maintain, modernize and repair the amphibious transport dock USS San Antonio (LPD 17), the U.S. Department of War announced Aug. 13, 2026.
The work falls under a fiscal 2027 selected restricted availability. That is a scheduled maintenance period set by the Chief of Naval Operations for work that keeps a ship in overhaul status while docked. If the Navy exercises contract options, the cumulative value of the award could reach $143.7 million.
The contract covers labor, supervision, equipment, production, testing, facilities and quality assurance needed to prepare for and complete the availability. Work will be performed in Norfolk and is scheduled for completion by July 2028.
USS San Antonio (LPD 17) is the first ship of the San Antonio-class amphibious transport docks. The U.S. Navy commissioned the vessel on Jan. 14, 2006, and it is homeported at Naval Station Norfolk. The class displaces roughly 25,000 tons full load, runs about 208 meters (684 feet) overall, and is built to carry Marines, landing craft, and MV-22 or helicopter aircraft for amphibious operations.
San Antonio returned to Norfolk on April 28, 2026, after an eight-and-a-half-month deployment with the Iwo Jima Amphibious Ready Group and the 22nd Marine Expeditionary Unit. In the U.S. 4th Fleet area of operations, the ship supported Operation Southern Spear, conducted counter-narcotics and embassy reinforcement missions, and provided humanitarian assistance to Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa.
Marine Hydraulics International, which does business as MHI Ship Repair & Services, is a Norfolk-based contractor that performs repair and conversion work for the U.S. Navy, Military Sealift Command and the Maritime Administration. The company has handled comparable maintenance periods on other San Antonio-class ships in recent years. In 2024 it received a contract worth up to $147.2 million for the fiscal 2024 availability of USS Mesa Verde (LPD 19). In 2025 it won a contract worth up to $111.4 million for the fiscal 2025 availability of USS New York (LPD 21), a competition that drew three offers.
The Navy competed the San Antonio contract through full and open competition posted on the System for Award Management website. Four offers were received.
Funding obligated at the time of award totals $119.4 million and draws from three sources. Fiscal 2026 other procurement (Navy) funds account for $104.6 million, or 88% of the total. Fiscal 2026 operations and maintenance (Navy) funds account for $14.7 million, or 12%. Fiscal 2025 other procurement (Navy) funds make up the remainder, about $38,000, less than 1%. The $14.7 million in operations and maintenance funding will expire at the end of the current fiscal year.
Naval Sea Systems Command in Washington, D.C., is the contracting activity for the award, listed under contract number N0002426C4417.

Engine parts shattered Ryanair window that passenger was partly sucked out of, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:12:48 UTC
16:12:48 KST

Broken engine parts were responsible for shattering a window on a Ryanair plane, causing a passenger to be partly sucked out mid-flight in July, US investigators have said.
A preliminary report by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) found an engine fan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on the 10 July flight from Greece to Germany shattering the window and damaging the fuselage.
The Serbian entrepreneur Ljubisa Karović, sitting by the window in seat 11F, had his head and right arm sucked out of the broken window in the incident.
Karović was saved from being completely sucked out of the window by other passengers, who grabbed hold of him.
The 61-year-old told the Guardian he was lucky to be alive after the incident on Ryanair flight FR1879 and said his wife, Svetlana, told him he had fainted several times, including after he had been pulled back inside the cabin.
The NTSB said the flight, which was scheduled to fly from Thessaloniki in Greece to Memmingen near Munich, “experienced a No 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out from the Thessaloniki international airport (SKG)”. The flight was operated by the budget airline’s subsidiary Malta Air.
Investigators found the cabin depressurised and the two pilots decided to return to Thessaloniki airport, where they “made an uneventful landing”.
A few days after the incident, the NTSB was “delegated the investigation in full” by the Greek authorities. The flight crew’s timeline of the event was set out by the NTSB, detailing how they experienced a “high vibration” engine alert during the flight climb. They reduced the engine power in response and carried out a series of checks.
The engine vibration reduced and the crew continued the climb on autopilot. However, the vibrations then increased significantly and the crew heard a loud bang. The flight crew put on their oxygen masks, declared an emergency and began an immediate descent.
The flight attendants reported “hearing and feeling a loud continuous vibration and seeing a small amount of fog/smoke before the oxygen masks dropped”, the report found.
Four bird strikes to the plane’s right engine were reported by flight crews in the 12 months preceding the incident, the report found, adding that bird remains were reportedly found in two of the cases. The fan blades had undergone ultrasonic inspections in recent months with “no findings”.
Karović told the Guardian less than a fortnight after the incident that he did not remember much but had a painful head and neck. “It could have been the seatbelt, the fact that I was still strapped in. But maybe it is fate. I believe in God and I thank him every day,” he said.
The Boeing 737-800 plane had 149 passengers and four flight attendants on board.
Ryanair said it would not comment on the preliminary report, or on whether Karović would receive compensation, until after the final report was published.
The airline’s finance chief said last month it was “way too early” to discuss whether Ryanair would have to compensate the couple while the airline awaited the outcome of an investigation into the incident.
Boeing and CFM, the engine maker, are assisting with the investigation.
Jeff Guzzetti, a former NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) investigator who reviewed the preliminary report, told the Associated Press that the required maintenance appears to have been performed on schedule.
However, investigators are expected to examine how the previous inspections were conducted and whether the previous suspected bird strikes contributed to pre-existing damage. “We know what happened and even to some extent why it happened, but there’s still unanswered questions that the NTSB will get at,” Guzzetti said.
In 2025 the FAA issued three directives requiring airlines to strengthen parts of the engine coverings on Boeing 737 planes, following two previous fan blade failures that sent pieces of the engine covering flying. In one accident, a passenger was killed on a Southwest Airlines plane in 2018, after debris knocked out a window.
The FAA gave airlines until July 2028 to complete the modifications, and the NTSB report found the required changes had not yet been made to the Ryanair plane.
Guzzetti said the latest accident could prompt the FAA and NTSB to examine whether that deadline should be moved up.

New Trump tariffs set to hit Ukraine’s drone export ambitions
US President Donald Trump has imposed steep tariffs on imported drones and their components, potentially complicating Ukraine’s plans to expand UAV sales to Washington. 
Under a proclamation signed on Thursday, drones weighing more than 25 kg and those equipped with thermal imagers will face tariffs of 100%, along with certain docking stations and critical components. Smaller unmanned aircraft will be subject to a 25% levy.
Lower rates will apply to selected US partners, including 15% tariffs for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan, and 10% for the UK. The measures are set to begin taking effect in 21 days, with some delayed for 180 days.
Trump said a Commerce Department review found that the US was “too reliant” on foreign drones and components. The White House said the measures are intended to reduce supply-chain and security risks while rapidly expanding domestic production. 
The move, however, could complicate Kiev’s recently revived push to sell drones to the US. 
Trump said last month that Washington would buy Ukrainian UAVs, while Reuters later reported that Kiev had agreed to export drones for the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program. During discussions last year, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky suggested a broader drone deal with the US could eventually be worth between $10 billion and $30 billion.
Ukraine was not listed among the countries receiving reduced tariff rates in Trump’s proclamation. Neither Washington nor Kiev has explained whether the planned purchases will receive an exemption or how the new duties could affect the proposed agreements.
Trump’s new tariffs come as the Pentagon has been racing to expand its own unmanned capabilities, with US officials acknowledging that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the rapidly evolving use of cheap reconnaissance and attack drones in the Ukraine conflict.
Kiev, meanwhile, has been aiming to turn its domestic weapons production into a major source of export revenue despite continuing to heavily rely on Western military and financial support. 
Ukrainian officials have spoken of earning billions from weapons sales and opening export hubs across Europe. At the same time, the country’s defense sector has been hit by major corruption scandals, including investigations into alleged embezzlement and inflated procurement contracts. European officials have also raised concerns over weapons supplied to Kiev disappearing and potentially reaching criminal networks.

'No substitute': Kuwait's future tied to Hormuz Strait fate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:09:32 UTC
16:09:32 KST

Kuwait's once prosperous oil sector has stood largely paralysed for months, with petroleum exports plummeting as fighting raged across the Gulf — triggering the country's largest crisis in decades.
Half a year into the war, Kuwait remains a hostage to its uncompromising need to access the Strait of Hormuz — where the war between the U.S. and Iran has choked off the once plentiful energy exports that moved across its waters.
Oil has long been the bedrock for the tiny Gulf state's economy — where more than 90 percent of government revenue and nearly all export earnings rely on reliable crude sales. The country is also home to roughly six percent of total oil reserves globally.
Unlike Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait has no pipelines bypassing the strait — forcing its crude exports to sail through the contested waterway to the international market.
"Without a doubt, this is the toughest and biggest crisis that we have faced in the oil sector in Kuwait since the 1990 invasion by Iraq," said Kuwait Petroleum Corporation (KPC) chief executive Shaikh Nawaf Saud Al-Sabah.
Then, as Saddam Hussein's forces retreated from a U.S.-led onslaught to liberate Kuwait, the Iraqi army torched hundreds of wells, destroyed massive storage tanks and targeted refineries — causing catastrophic damage to much of the country's oil sector.
Kuwait has been spared the same levels of destruction during this war but has not emerged unscathed.
Just days into the war, the state-owned KPC declared force majeure — a legal maneuver that protects an enterprise when they cannot meet their contractual obligations due to unforeseeable events, like wars and natural disasters. The notice was lifted in June.
The country has also weathered repeated waves of Iranian strikes targeting water desalination plants and energy installations, including petroleum infrastructure along with salvos aimed at U.S. military bases.
"This crisis has presented us with a new challenge," Al-Sabah told AFP during an exclusive interview.
Before the war, Kuwait was producing slightly more than 2.6 million barrels of oil per day, with an ambitious plan to reach 4 million barrels daily by 2040.
"Once the strait is open, it reverts to free movement, then we can easily go back to our pre-war production levels and even higher," said Al-Sabah.
But when asked how much Kuwait was now able to deliver on a given day, the executive refused to provide a figure.
"It's something that — during this crisis — we prefer to keep to ourselves," he told AFP.
According to preliminary official data, Kuwait's economy contracted 4.6 percent year-on-year during the first quarter of 2026, with its oil-sector GDP collapsing by 12.5 percent.
The true toll is likely more damning, with available economic data only accounting for the first month of the conflict.
"Kuwait's dependence on Hormuz has become a strategic vulnerability," said Amena Bakr, head of Middle East insights at Kpler.
According to Bakr, estimates predict that Kuwait's oil production could likely be restored to pre-war levels in two to three months.
"The country does have financial resources to withstand a serious temporary shock," said Bakr.
"But the longer the war drags on, the more the economy is exposed to the risks of not having a safe export route for this oil."
But Al-Sabah warned there was "no substitute" for unfettered access to the strait.
"If you do not have free flow of hydrocarbons through the Strait of Hormuz and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, you will end up with another energy crisis very quickly," he said.

Artifacts from the 6th millennium BC that were attempted to be exported to the United States have been handed over to a museum in Zhytomyr Oblast
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv customs officials handed over three flint cores dating to the 6th millennium BC to the Ovruch Region History Museum. The artifacts were discovered in an international postal shipment from Kryvyi Rih to the United States.
Kyiv customs officers transferred three flint cores — ancient blanks for making stone tools, dating back to the 6th millennium BC — to the Ovruch Region History Museum. The artifacts were discovered during customs inspection of an international postal shipment traveling from Kryvyi Rih to the United States. The State Customs Service of Ukraine reported this, UNN writes.
Details
Kyiv customs officers transferred three cores — flint blanks from which prehistoric people made tools — to the Ovruch Region History Museum in Zhytomyr region. The artifacts have cultural and historical value.
These polished stones with distinct edges were discovered during customs inspection of an international postal shipment traveling from Kryvyi Rih to the United States
It is noted that in ancient times, sharp blades were chipped off them and then used as stone tools, including knives.
These artifacts belong to materials of the archaeological cultures of late prehistory — the period of the "Neolithic–Bronze Age," approximately the 6th–2nd millennia BC.
The cores are authentic and originated in the northwestern and western parts of Ukraine. The largest of them is 15 cm long.
The transfer of cultural valuables to the state section of the Museum Fund of Ukraine is carried out by decision of the Expert and Museum Fund Council under the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine.

Nigel Farage defeats Count Binface to reclaim UK parliamentary seat

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has regained his parliamentary seat, besting his main challenger Count Binface in a by-election he triggered by resigning his post last month.
Farage received 22,239 votes in the Clacton by-election compared with 9,455 for serial joke candidate Binface, who wears a rubbish can on his head and calls himself an “intergalactic space warrior”. The United Kingdom’s main political parties boycotted the election, creating the embarrassing face-off for Farage who had sought to use the election to boost his standing after allegations of financial impropriety.

Around 7,000 people were forced to spend the night at Narita Airport after train and bus services were disrupted.
Chiba's Chuo Ward recorded 115 millimetres of rain in one hour on Thursday night, roughly equivalent to its average rainfall for the entire month of August.

Palestinians divided over Hamas participation in elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:03:10 UTC
16:03:10 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinians divided over Hamas participation in long-delayed upcoming elections
Hamas's plans to contest upcoming Palestinian elections as part of a broad national coalition have exposed sharp divisions among Palestinians regarding the movement's political future and the direction of the Palestinian political system.
Palestinians are grappling with the devastation caused by the Israeli genocidal war on Gaza, the longstanding split between Palestinian factions, and growing international pressure for political reform.
During an interview with Hamas-affiliated Al-Aqsa channel, Husam Badran, a senior Hamas official, announced that the movement "will participate in the elections within the broadest possible national coalition."
Badran said Hamas had begun contacting Palestinian factions about a month ago to form an electoral bloc representing the widest possible political spectrum.
He described the elections as an opportunity to "bring about change in the Palestinian situation and end the monopoly on Palestinian national decision-making," arguing that Hamas, which he described as deeply rooted in Palestinian society, should have a role in the political process.
Among the Palestinian public, the announcement has been met with sharply different views.
Some see Hamas's participation as a political right that should not be denied, while others fear its return to political institutions could bring renewed confrontation with Israel, international isolation and further suffering for Palestinians.
Between blame and fear
In Gaza, where nearly three years of the Israeli genocidal war have caused widespread destruction, displacement and death, attitudes towards Hamas's participation are closely tied to personal experiences and fears over what comes next.
"I am categorically opposed to Hamas taking part in the elections or returning to a position of political power," Ibrahim Jalal from al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza told The New Arab.
Ibrahim, who lost over 15 family members, his home, and his grocery store—his main income source—during the war, said Gaza's destruction is linked to Hamas's political and military choices, while also blaming Israel for what he called "great crimes" against Palestinians.
"Israel bears responsibility for its crimes and its war against us, but Hamas gave it the pretext it wanted without considering the fate of the people," Jalal said.
He argued that Hamas should not return to a position from which it could make major decisions affecting Palestinians, warning that continued political dominance by the movement could recreate conditions that contributed to the war.
Jalal argues that Gaza's priorities are now to end wars, rebuild homes and infrastructure, lift restrictions, and restore a normal life.
"People today do not need a struggle over political positions. They need security, reconstruction and a chance to live," he said.
Ahed Hamada, from Gaza City's al-Daraj neighbourhood, supports Hamas's right to participate in political life but does not want the movement to control the next government.
"A Hamas victory under current conditions could mean more wars, destruction, death and siege," he remarked to TNA, arguing that the international community still does not appear ready to accept Hamas as a governing party.
"I believe Hamas should reconsider this step, not because its popularity has declined, but because it needs to reassess its priorities and allow the people to rest after years of war," he said.
He suggested Hamas could remain a major political force without taking sole responsibility for government, allowing it to participate in political institutions while reducing the risks of another confrontation with Israel and the international community.
The next phase, he said, requires a "new Palestinian formula" that includes all factions while avoiding a repetition of the political isolation, blockade and wars of previous years.
West Bank fears and political calculations
In the occupied West Bank, opinions over Hamas's participation are also shaped by the potential response from Israel and the international community.
Sari Nubani, a resident of Nablus, opposed Hamas's participation, saying its entry into Palestinian political institutions could give Israel and other international actors further justification to increase pressure on Palestinians.
Nubani told TNA that Israel would not necessarily view a Hamas electoral victory as simply the outcome of a democratic process, but could instead treat it as a security threat, potentially leading to more raids, arrests and economic and political pressure.
"We are going through one of the most difficult political phases under growing Israeli power. It would be better if neither Hamas nor Fatah participated, because neither has provided a solution," he said.
"The Palestinians need new leaders capable of dealing with the challenges imposed by Israel," he added.
However, Samir al-Natsha, from Hebron, adopts a completely different view, arguing that excluding Hamas would not resolve the Palestinian political crisis but would only deepen the existing divide.
He criticised the Palestinian Authority for decades of political failure. "It failed to protect Palestinians or make progress on their national goals," he told TNA.
"What has the Authority done for us over the past decades? Nothing. It has continued security coordination with Israel, contributed to economic deterioration and failed to protect residents of the West Bank from Israeli violations," al-Natsha said.
He argued that elections without Hamas would not represent genuine political change, saying the ballot box should be the ultimate test of each faction's popular support rather than political or international pressure determining who is allowed to participate.
Governing
Gaza-based analyst Iyad Abdel Jawad said the main question is whether Palestinians, Israel and the international community would accept the results if Hamas makes significant gains.
"Hamas wants to remain part of the political system and avoid losing its influence, but participation is different from governing," he told TNA.
He said the outcome would depend on the electoral system, factional alliances and international positions, with the key challenge being to ensure all sides accept the results and prevent a return to division.
Excluding Hamas, meanwhile, could undermine the elections by leaving out one of the Palestinian political system's major forces.
The broader question, Abdel Jawad said, is whether Palestinian factions can accommodate their differences without allowing political competition to lead again to division and war.

Trump announces tariffs of up to 100 pct on imported drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:02:32 UTC
16:02:32 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump has announced tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports of unmanned drones and their components to reduce U.S. reliance on imports in an industry dominated by China.
Trump justified the decision on national security grounds, according to a White House statement on Aug. 13.
Those with a takeoff weight of more than 25 kilograms and with so-called national security capabilities such as thermal cameras and docking stations will be tariffed at 100 percent.
Smaller drones face a 25 percent tariff.
The statement said the tariffs will "encourage increased domestic production" of drones and their components and reduce reliance on foreign supply chains.
Most of the new tariffs are to take effect Sept. 3.
The Chinese company DJI, founded in 2006, has captured more than two-thirds of the global drone market in recent years, according to several studies.
Since 2022, DJI has been on a U.S. list of Chinese companies linked to the country's military and therefore subject to restrictions on access to U.S. technology.
Last week, China announced restrictions on drone exports to the United States and blacklisted six companies in response to trade sanctions imposed by Washington over forced labor and national security concerns.

Farage’s victory over Binface won’t silence his critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:01:24 UTC
16:01:24 KST

Farage’s victory over Binface won’t silence his critics
The Reform UK leader wanted to send a “people versus the establishment” message in Clacton. But he’ll face continued scrutiny of his finances — and questions over his judgement.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who won the Clacton by-election, and Count Binface, the candidate who emerged as his closest challenger. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
LONDON — Nigel Farage’s victory in the Clacton by-election is emphatic — but it won’t let him off the hook.
Winning back his seaside House of Commons seat by an increased margin allows the Reform UK leader to claim victory in the “people vs the establishment” contest he triggered in response to intense scrutiny of his finances.
Farage won the backing of 22,239 constituents, or 63 percent of the vote. That’s 1,014 more votes in this by-election than at the U.K. general election two years ago, and a 17-point swing in his favor.
Advertisement
But second-placed this time was Count Binface, a comedian with a trash can on his head who secured — by many thousands — his highest ever vote count in a palpable protest against Farage. None of Britain’s mainstream parties took part in the contest, branding it a circus.
The Reform UK leader’s refusal to turn up at the count to hear the result Friday — a move that would have seen him pictured alongside a cast of comedy characters — underlined the struggle for him to get back on the front foot he is used to contesting politics from.
More significantly, Farage’s triumph means that parliamentary investigations into his financial affairs will now resume. That could lead to another by-election — one in which serious rivals are far less likely to stand aside to allow Farage to face-off against a long list of no-hopers.
Count Binface waits with other candidates for the declaration of the winner of the Clacton by-election at Clacton Leisure Centre, eastern England, on Aug. 14, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
Labour MPs switched out their own leader in part because of Farage’s storming success at local elections in May, but the focus on this contest has also made it harder for Farage to land blows on Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Clacton is Farage’s fiefdom. It was one of the most Brexit-voting constituencies in the country and was the place that first sent him to the Commons on his eighth time of trying.
Advertisement
But Binface, a proud proponent of the British tradition of satirical candidates contesting elections, had never won more than 308 votes in a parliamentary election before. Against Farage, he secured 9,455 votes. That means 28 percent plumped for the comedy candidate with a bin on his head.
Farage on Friday snubbed the leisure center count and the mild embarrassment of accepting victory alongside Binface that three prime ministers — Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak and Andy Burnham — have endured before him.
He told his own “Farage Fest” jamboree organized in secret away from the results venue that he’d been advised by Essex Police of an “organized campaign to disrupt and degrade the result.”
Nigel Farage engages with locals outside a polling station in Clacton-on-Sea, England, on Aug. 13, 2026. | Ben Montgomery/Getty Images
“I’m not scared of these people, far from it,” he told fans. “But I’m damned if I’m going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I’ve tried to fight for, and you’ve tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies, and I will not sadly be attending the count.”
That meant, according to reports, Farage became the first winning candidate not to turn up for a result since jailed Irish Republican Army hunger striker Bobby Sands won Fermanagh and South Tyrone in 1981.
Instead, Farage railed against the media and the “establishment” in his own event fit with branded pint cups, a ferris wheel and yurts for overnight stays. It was yet another demonstration of his attempt to bend the norms that accompany mainstream politics to his will.
Advertisement
Essex Police assured a “proportionate and robust policing operation” was in place at the count — while it was made clear that Farage was not advised to avoid the event. He cancelled a scheduled speech in Clacton, too.
Farage had gambled that a strong victory would inhibit the chances of parliamentary watchdogs imposing a severe enough sentence to set up a recall, should he be found to have breached the rules. “The bigger the vote, the bigger the message. Let’s tell the establishment where to go,” Farage said as polls opened on Thursday.
In the event, the turnout — at 44 percent — was not astonishing. That it’s less than the general election may not be surprising, but it was lower than another high-profile by-election held in this seat a decade earlier.
In 2014 Douglas Carswell resigned as the Conservative MP for the area to run for Ukip, Farage’s Eurosceptic party that helped drive Brexit.
Clacton returned Carswell in his new guise, making him the first MP elected under the Ukip banner. He won 60 percent of the vote, on a 51 percent turnout.
That day was described as a “mini-earthquake in British politics” — but Friday’s result is producing less stable ground for Reform. “Farage’s distraction by-election doesn’t clear his name – it just shows he likely has so much more to hide,” argued Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson Friday morning.
Advertisement
Probes continue
So now the uphill battle. The parliamentary standards commissioner will resume two investigations into Farage — one centering on a £5 million donation from a crypto-entrepreneur, the other into support provided by a convicted fraudster.
The MP denies wrongdoing in both instances, arguing he didn’t need to declare the donations because they were given in a personal capacity before he was elected.
But if there’s a finding of a serious rule breach then the Commons could vote to suspend Farage and trigger a recall petition.
Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose arrival drowned out some of Farage’s usual dominance, speaks to the media after chairing a COBR meeting at Downing Street in London on Aug. 12, 2026. | Kin Cheung/WPA Pool/Getty Images
The signatures of just 10 percent of registered voters in Clacton would then be needed to expel Farage from parliament — and trigger another by-election in which he could stand. Farage has expressed hopes that there isn’t such an appetite in his constituency — but the support for Binface throws that into doubt.
Clacton’s electorate is 79,785 — the 9,455 votes that Binface secured represents around 12 percent of those eligible voters, a comfortable margin for recall to be successful.
Tactical errors?
That is all potential peril for the future. Right now, the August by-election has even some supporters questioning whether this was a rare miscalculation from a veteran campaigner.
Advertisement
Farage has in recent years dominated the summer break when many MPs vacate the political playing field.
But broadcasting rules on election periods stymied this year’s effort. Media invites to the press conferences Farage did throw had to assure broadcasters he would not be mentioning Clacton. And every mention of Clacton meant presenters were obliged to read the full 34-candidate list — namedropping Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap in the process.
Reform has also been struggling to grapple with a squeeze on its right from Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain splinter party. Farage’s one-time Reform comrade touted the possibility of a pact to unite the right — but deeply held grievances on both sides mean the distraction has dragged on.
A row over one of Reform’s most senior officials, Zia Yusuf, calling a Conservative former defense secretary a “traitor to Britain” has also been generating unwanted headlines and exposing rifts inside Reform.
If that second by-election does emerge in the coming months then the Conservatives have already vowed to fight it. Farage, should he choose to stand again, would face a far tougher contest against the backdrop of parliament having ruled against him, and many voters in Clacton had been unimpressed by the “laughing stock” caused by the first election.
The Reform hardcore may be buoyed by Farage’s railing against the “establishment” — but what this saga does to his reputation with the wider electorate he needs to propel him into Downing Street remains the biggest unanswered question.

Russians dropped 8 aerial bombs on Kramatorsk: 1 killed, 17 injured
Kyiv • UNN
On August 13, Russian forces attacked Kramatorsk with 8 FAB-250 aerial bombs, hitting residential buildings. As a result of the attack, one person was killed and 17 were injured.
Russian forces dropped 8 aerial bombs on Kramatorsk in Donetsk region, killing one person and injuring 17, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office reported on Friday, UNN writes.
Details
On August 13, 2026, between 20:30 and 20:56, the Russian army launched a massive air attack on Kramatorsk using 8 "FAB-250" bombs with UMPK guidance kits. The strikes hit residential areas, including apartment buildings, the prosecutor's office said.
As of the morning, it was reported that one person had been killed and 17 injured — 7 men and 10 women aged between 47 and 85.
The injured were diagnosed with blast and traumatic brain injuries, shrapnel wounds, cuts to the head, arms, and legs, abrasions, and bruises. The injured were provided with the necessary medical assistance.
The final consequences of the strikes are being established.

Uber, Pony.ai plan over 2,000 robotaxis across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:00:39 UTC
16:00:39 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
US ride-hailing company Uber and Chinese autonomous-driving firm Pony.ai announced an expanded partnership Friday to deploy more than 2,000 robotaxis across Europe.
The partnership will expand from an existing commercial service in Zagreb, Croatia, to four additional European cities, according to a joint statement. The companies did not identify the cities or provide a detailed rollout timetable.
The expanded agreement also includes plans to deploy robotaxis in the Middle East, with further details expected to be announced in phases.
Under the partnership, Pony.ai will provide its Level 4 autonomous-driving technology, passenger-experience systems and operational expertise developed through large-scale deployments in China.
Uber will provide access to customers through its mobility platform, including booking, payment and customer services.
Daily fleet operations may be handled by established local partners selected for each market, while vehicle ownership and financing arrangements may vary by location.
“The next chapter for autonomous mobility is about moving from individual launches to repeatable commercial scale,” said Sarfraz Maredia, Uber’s global head of autonomous mobility and delivery.
Maredia said the companies would combine Pony.ai’s autonomous technology with Uber’s platform, local experience and operational capabilities to develop a model that could expand rapidly across cities.
Pony.ai founder and CEO James Peng said the expanded agreement represented “an important new phase” in the companies’ partnership.
“By combining Pony.ai’s proven autonomous driving technology and operational know-how with Uber’s global mobility platform and extensive market reach, we aim to build sustained commercial operations at scale across Europe and beyond,” Peng said.
The companies began their collaboration in May 2025 with plans to introduce Pony.ai robotaxis to Uber’s platform in international markets.
In 2026, they worked with Croatian mobility company Verne to launch a commercial robotaxi service in Zagreb, with Verne serving as the fleet owner and operator.
Pony.ai currently operates paid, fully driverless robotaxi services in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen.

‘This is hell’: British widow ‘sick’ with worry over threat of being removed from Sweden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:00:22 UTC
16:00:22 KST

The 78-year-old British widow threatened with removal from Sweden after 21 years has said she has been left feeling sick with worry after being told she had lost an appeal against deportation in a growing row over the country’s handling of Brexit.
“I am in shock. I feel sick. An individual’s life is at stake at my age. It is hell. I have done nothing wrong. I don’t take anything from this country. I am self sufficient, I put money in this country, have no criminal record,” said Joyce Thomas from her home in Sweden on Thursday.
Her plight, first revealed by the Guardian, has raised concerns in Brussels and in the UK about Sweden’s approach to the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was supposed to protect British nationals who lived in an EU member state before Brexit.
Earlier this week another family told how their father, a dementia patient in full-time care, was also threatened with removal after 25 years in Sweden.
The administrative court in Luleå upheld Sweden’s migration agency decision that Thomas was not eligible to stay because her application was made in 2023, after the cut-off date of December 2021.
Her legal representatives told the court in Luleå it was “not proportionate for her to be deported solely because she missed a deadline due to insufficient information. Furthermore, it is not acceptable that the Swedish authorities failed to inform her that she needed to file an application and of the deadline by which it was to be filed.”
Thomas now faces the prospect of a letter from the migration agency giving her four weeks to leave voluntarily , separating her from her son, her grandchildren, her network of friends, and away from her husband’s grave, which she regularly visits.
If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and “registered on a watchlist” preventing entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”.
“No circumstances have come to light that would lead to a determination that, in your situation, you are particularly vulnerable,” the court ruling said noting that she had lived most of her life in the UK, had a pension from the UK and another son in the UK.
Thomas argued that after 21 years all her support network was in Sweden, with 23 people including doctors, priests and friends and fellow churchgoers writing to testify in support of her case.
“My friends, my husband’s burial place, grandchildren, everything is here, and to have to go and start again, it’s just unbelievable that at my age I’ve got to be uprooted for my home,” she said.
“This is hell. I get up in the morning, it’s in my head, I go to bed at night, it’s in my head. It’s horrible. I mean I have done nothing wrong. I am self sufficient. I put money in the country. I don’t take money out. I can’t comprehend this,” she added.
Her husband died in 2023 from cancer just four months after his last trip back to the UK to visit family. It was on the return that he learned from border officials that they had to make a special application to stay after Brexit.
Under article 18 of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, late applications are permissible if there are “reasonable grounds” for doing so.
David Milstead, of the grassroots campaign group British in Sweden, said: “It would be difficult to find anyone who would argue that what is happening to Mrs Thomas and others in Sweden was an intended outcome of the withdrawal agreement. Problems will inevitably emerge when a new treaty is put into practice. However, the UK, EU and Sweden must act to address them. Words and expressions of concern won’t cut it.”
While the migration agency said not knowing an application was needed was not a “reasonable ground” for granting post-residency rights, Thomas is adamant neither she or her husband were notified that an application needed to be made before the end of 2021.
“The Swedish authorities have our ID cards, they have our emails, we heard nothing,” said Thomas.

‘We’re seeing lots of people who feel dizzy’: how heatwaves are taking a toll on people’s health and the NHS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:00:22 UTC
16:00:22 KST

“The big thing A&E doctors are seeing during extreme heat now is falls in the elderly,” says Dr Adrian Boyle, an A&E consultant at Addenbrooke’s hospital in Cambridge.
“During this summer’s five heatwaves I’ve seen elderly people get light-headed and dizzy and fall down a whole flight of stairs and break multiple bones, purely because of the heat. The last fall down stairs because of the heat resulted in multiple broken ribs, a wrist and her lower leg.
“These are often elderly people who are taking diuretics – water tablets, to get rid of body fluid – or drugs for high blood pressure. It’s a good thing, most of the time, to be taking them.
“But in this weather, that can make people feel very, very light-headed quickly. We’re seeing lots of people who feel very dizzy, some of whom have fallen over and hurt themselves as a consequence.
“I’m struck by how quickly such accidents happen and how long they take to get over. A wrist fracture can take a couple of months and a broken hip or lower leg more than six months.”
Boyle, who was president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine from 2022 to 2025, is reflecting on the growing impact of unusually high temperatures on the health of the population and on the NHS, which treats the illness and injuries that extreme heat causes.
He is talking on Thursday as the UK records the hottest day – 38.1C (100.6F) – of a year in which the first two heatwaves alone, in May and June, together caused 2,877 deaths, according to UK Health Security Agency estimates – almost double the 1,504 heat-related deaths it recorded during the whole of 2025.
Figures published by NHS England on Thursday pinpointed July’s two heatwaves as a key reason why a record 2.5 million people attended A&E that month. They included people whose breathing problems and other underlying health conditions were exacerbated by the heat, it said.
“Extreme heat causes other problems too,” says Boyle. “I’ve seen a lot of older people end up in kidney failure because of dehydration. Also, the heat pushes some young people to go swimming in unsuitable and unsupervised rivers where they drown.
“People taking medication for severe mental illness can also be at increased risk as their medication can leave them unable to recognise that they’re getting hot.
“And hot people stuck in the back of an ambulance outside an emergency department, who are already ill, can get either heat exhaustion or heatstroke as a result. Heatstroke is very dangerous.
“Our hospitals and ambulances are just not set up to look after people in the heat. There is minimal air conditioning in many of our hospital rooms, so ill people are being made hot and this just can’t be good for them.
“Lying on wipeable plastic mattresses in this weather is also very unpleasant, even on top of an ordinary sheet, as they get sweaty quickly.”
Dr Zuzanna Sawicka, a consultant in elderly medicine and the Royal College of Physicians’ clinical director for patient safety and clinical standards, highlights a challenge that extreme heat poses for staff rather than patients.
A doctor going in to visit a patient with an infectious disease has to wear full personal protective equipment, like they did during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“It can be quite stifling and it compromises how long you can stay with a patient because you generally start to feel sick and not so great because you’re so warm and there’s just no [air] circulation.
“I saw a case this week of reactivation of tuberculosis. We have to then put on a tight-fitting mask and a full gown until you know whether it is or isn’t. You’re in your own clothes, already sweating, and then on top of that you have to essentially put on full PPE,” she says.
The risk of infections also helps explain why so few hospitals have proper ventilation, air conditioning or fans, Sawicka explains – in case they unwittingly spread bugs.
Jean (not her real name), a nurse at a London hospital, reports: “We have some fans, but not enough for all the patients. So there have been problems and patients fighting over them. It’s high time that we got some AC for everyone so that patients aren’t fighting each other.”
Their uniforms can also make already sweaty nurses feel even hotter, Jean adds. “All our uniform is so thick [that] we’re sweating so much. We’ve been asking management for a long time for lighter uniforms for us, but they’ve not done that.
“Some of us are getting lighter uniforms from friends who have spare kit or even having to buy lighter uniforms ourselves.”

Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more   | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
07:00:21 UTC
16:00:21 KST

In this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures. The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.
Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,” said the headline above the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.
Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.
Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers – wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.
Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper, British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.
For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”, the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.
This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.
No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very careful interview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”
Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.
Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author of State of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.
Britons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist
